<CC><P>ii. Cawdor has been condemned merely upon a parenthetical line and a half from
Ross. <I>There is absolutely no other proof of his guilt in the play.</I> It is like Ross to
ignore Angus, who is also commissioned by Duncan. In Sc. iii, Angus says, &lquo;we
are sent.&rquo; The &lquo;<I>exeunt</I>&rquo; of the Folio at the end of this scene probably refers to
Ross and Angus, but not to Duncan and his attendants.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
<P>4. <B>Swine]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: So, in <I>A Detection of Damnable Driftes practized by
Three Witches</I>, etc. 1579: &lquo;&mdash; she came on a tyme to the house of one Robert
Lathburie, etc. who, dislyking her dealyng, <I>sent her home emptie;</I> but presently
after her departure, his <I>hogges fell sicke and died</I>, to the number of twentie.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>John-
son</SC>: Witches seem to have been most suspected of malice against swine. Dr.
Harsnet observes that, about that time, &lquo;a sow could not be ill of the measles, nor a
girl of the sullens, but some old woman was charged with witchcraft.&rquo;
<P>7. <B>mouncht]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: This means &lquo;to chew with closed lips,&rquo; and is used
in Scotland in the sense of &lquo;mumbling with toothless gums,&rquo; as old people do their
food. It is probably derived from the French <I>manger</I>, Lat. <I>manducare.</I>
<P>8. <B>quoth]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: From the Anglo-Saxon &lquo;cw&aelig;than,&rquo; to say, speak, of
which the first and third persons, singular, preterite are &lquo;cw&aelig;th.&rquo;
<P>9. <B>Aroynt]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: Anoint [F<SUB>3</SUB>F<SUB>4</SUB>] conveys a sense very consistent with the
common account of witches, who are related to perform many supernatural acts by
means of unguents, and particularly to fly to their hellish $estivals.&mdash;[<SC>Murray</SC> (<I>N. E.
D.</I>): Origin unknown. First used by Shakespeare in <I>Macbeth</I> and <I>King Lear</I> (1605).
The origin of aroynt, or aroint, has been the subject of numerous conjectures, none of
which can be said to have even a prima facie probability. The following passages are
usually cited as pointing to the same word: Ray, <I>North Country Words</I>, 1691: Ryntye,
by your leave stand handsomely. As &lquo;Rynt you witch,&rquo; quoth Bessie Locket to her
mother; Proverb: Cheshire. Thoresby, <I>Lett. to Ray</I>, 1703 (Yorkshire Words),
has: Ryndta used to cows to make them give way and stand in their stalls. In
parts of Cheshire and Lancashire <I>ou</I> (as in round) is pronounced &imacr; or &ymacr;; so that
<I>round</I> becomes <I>r&ymacr;nd. Ryndta!</I> is thus merely a local pronunciation of &lquo;round
thee&rquo; = move around. The local nature, the meaning, and form of the phrase, seem
all opposed to its identity with Shakespeare's Aroint.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

which they sold to the poor. The weird sister, as an insult on the poverty of the
woman who had called her <I>witch</I>, reproaches her poor abject state as not being able</CC>

<CC><P>to procure better food than offal.&mdash;<SC>Nares</SC>: This means, probably, nothing more than
<I>fed</I>, or fattened in the <I>rump.</I> It is true that fat flaps, kidneys, <I>rumps</I>, and other
scraps were among the low perquisites of the kitchen; but in such an allusion there
would have been little reason to prefer <I>rumps;</I> scrap-fed would be more natural,
and kidney-fed, or flap-fed, equal. But <I>fat-rumped</I> conveys a picture of the person
mentioned, which the others would not in any degree.&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. ii.): Long ago
a friend of mine, who was never at a loss for an explanation, queried, &lquo;Can rump-
fed mean &ldquo;nut-fed&rdquo;? The sailor's wife was eating chestnuts. In Kilian's <I>Dict.</I>
is &ldquo;<I>Rompe.</I> Nux myristica vilior, cassa, inanis.&rdquo;&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: Fed on the best
joints, pampered.
<P>9. <B>Ronyon]</B> <SC>Grey</SC>: That is, a scabby or mangy woman. French <I>rogneux, royne</I>,
scurf. Thus Chaucer, <I>Romaunt of the Rose:</I> &lquo;&mdash; her necke Withouten bleine, or
scabbe, or roine,&rquo; [l. 553]. Also in <I>Merry Wives</I>, IV, ii, 195, and as an adjective
in <I>As You Like It</I>, II, ii, 8. [Thus also, <I>Century Dictionary.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]
<P>10. <B>Aleppo]</B> <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii.): In Hakluyt's <I>Voyages</I>, 1589 and 1599, are
printed several letters and journals of a voyage to Aleppo in the ship Tiger, of
London, in 1583. For this note we are indebted to Sir W. C. Trevelyan, Bart.&mdash;
<SC>Clarendon</SC>: An account is given in Hakluyt's <I>Voyages</I>, vol. ii, pp. 247, 251, of
a voyage by Ralph Fitch and others in a ship called the Tiger, to Tripolis, whence
they went by caravan to Aleppo, in the year 1583. In the <I>Calendar of Domestic
State Papers</I> (1547-1580), vol. xxxiii, 53, under date April 13, 1564, mention is
made of the ship Tiger, apparently a Spanish vessel. Sir Kenelm Digby, in his
journal, 1628, mentions a ship called &lquo;the Tyger of London, going for Scanderone,&rquo;
p. 45 (Camden Society). Shakespeare has elsewhere given this name to a ship:
<I>Twelfth Night</I>, V, i, 65. [W. A. <SC>Wright</SC> (note V, i, 62, <I>Twelfth Night</I>, of this
ed.): A common name for a vessel in Shakespeare's day, and, if we may trust
Virgil (<I>&AElig;neid</I>, x, 166), even in the days of &AElig;neas.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]
<P>11. <B>Syue]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: Scot, <I>Discovery of Witchcraft</I>, 1584, says it was believed

<P>12. <B>tayle]</B> <SC>Capell</SC> (<I>Notes</I>, p. 4): <I>Tails</I> are the rudders of water-animals, as the
&lquo;rat&rquo; is occasionally, so that it is intimated in effect that she would find her port
without rudder as well as sail in a sieve.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: It should be remembered (as
it was the belief of the times) that though a witch could assume the form of any
animal she pleased, the tail would still be wanting. The reason given by some old
writers for such a deficiency is, that though the hands and feet, by an easy change,
might be converted into the four paws of a beast, there was still no part about a
woman which corresponded with the length of tail common to almost all our four-
footed creatures.&mdash;[<SC>Sherman</SC>: The commentators ordinarily assume that the witch
proposes, in the language here used, to take the form of a rat, though she does not
say so. It would be inartistic if the author caused this witch to go on declaring
characteristic things, such as real witches would take for granted. Shakespeare's
object is, of course, to make the audience realize what power these witches wield.
&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]
<P>13. <B>Ile doe]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: She threatens, in the shape of a rat, to gnaw through
the hull of the Tiger and make her spring a leak.&mdash;[<SC>Paton</SC>: In our opinion the
Witch, in her fiendish vindictiveness, never dreamt of acting as suggested by the
Clarendon editors. It was evidently to the destruction of the Tiger's <I>rudder</I> that
she intended to apply her energies; and this view accepted, the &lquo;Pilot's Thumb,&rquo;
that ghastly treasure, takes an appropriate and strange significance. Had the Tiger
sprung a leak, she would have gone down and &lquo;there an end on't,&rquo; but she was to
be knocked about, the sport of the elements, for more than a year and a half,
unable to sink, and probably not to be lost in the end, but to strand on some
unknown shore far from the many-mosqued City, or to drift, with her companionless
and skeleton-like skipper, into her own bay. In the eight lines in this scene, com-
mencing, &lquo;I'll drain him dry as hay,&rquo; we seem, indeed, to have the reef out of
which grew <I>The Rime of the Ancient Mariner.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

<P>35. <B>weyward]</B> <SC>Theobald</SC>: This word [wayward], in general, signifies <I>perverse,
froward, moody</I>, etc., and is everywhere so used by Shakespeare, as in <I>Two Gent.</I>
[I, ii, 57], <I>Love's Lab. L.</I> [III, i, 181], and <I>Macbeth.</I> It is improbable the <I>Witches</I>
would adopt this epithet to themselves in any of these senses. When I had the
first suspicion of our author's being corrupt in this place, it brought to mind this
passage in Chaucer's <I>Troilus and Cresseide</I>, iii, 618: &lquo;But, O Fortune, executrix
of <I>wierdes</I>,&rquo; which word the Glossaries expound to us by <I>Fates</I> or Destinies. My
suspicion was soon confirmed by happening to dip into Heylin's <I>Cosmography</I>,
where he makes a short recital of the story of <I>Macbeth</I> and <I>Banquo:</I> &lquo;These two
travelling together through a Forest were met by three Fairies, Witches, <I>Wierds</I>,
the Scots call them,&rquo; etc. I presently recollected that this story must be recorded at
more length by Holinshead, with whom I thought it was very probable that our
author had traded for the materials of his tragedy, and therefore confirmation was
to be fetch'd from this fountain. Accordingly, looking into his <I>History of Scotland</I>,
I found the writer very prolix and express, from Hector Boethius, in this remarkable
story; and in p. 170, speaking of these Witches, he uses this expression: &lquo;But
afterwards the common opinion was, that these women were either the <I>we&imacr;rd</I> Sisters,
that is, as ye would say, the Goddesses of <I>Destiny</I>,&rquo; etc. Again: &lquo;The words of the
three <I>we&imacr;rd</I> sisters also (of whom ye have heard) greatly encouraged him thereunto.&rquo;
I believe by this time it is plain, beyond a doubt, that the word <I>Wayward</I> has
obtain'd in Macbeth, where the witches are spoken of from the ignorance of the
Copyists, and that in every passage where there is any relation to these <I>Witches</I> or
<I>Wizards</I> my emendation must be embraced, and we must read <I>we&imacr;rd.</I>&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>:
From the Saxon <I>wyrd, fatum.</I> Gawin Douglas translates, &lquo;Prohibent nam cetera
<I>parc&aelig;</I> Scire&rquo; (<I>&AElig;neid</I>, iii, 379) by &lquo;The <I>weird sisteris</I> defendis that suld be wit.&rquo;&mdash;
p. 80.&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: &lquo;Be aventure Makbeth and Banquho were passand to Fores,
quhair kyng Duncane hapnit to be for ye tyme, and met be ye gait thre women
clothit in elrage and uncouth weid. They wer jugit be the pepill to be <I>weird sisters.&rquo;
&mdash;Bellenden's trans. of Hector Boethius.</I>&mdash;<SC>Nares</SC>: In &lquo;<I>The Birth of Saint George</I>&rquo;
it means a <I>witch</I> or <I>enchantress:</I> &lquo;To the we&iuml;rd lady of the woods.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Percy's Rel.</I>
iii, p. 218, ed. 1765.&mdash;<SC>Knight</SC>: We cannot agree with Tieck that the word is <I>way-
ward</I>&mdash;wilful. The word is written <I>weyward</I> in the original to mark that it consists of
two syllables.&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Remarks</I>, etc.): In <I>Ortus Vocabulorum</I>, 1514, we find: &lquo;Cloto
. . . anglice, one of the <I>thre wyrde systers.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 162): There is no just pre-
tence for supplanting &lquo;wayward&rquo; and substituting &lquo;weird.&rquo; &lquo;Weird&rquo; may be the
more proper&mdash;the more scientific term; it may come nearer the etymological root, it
may be the derivative of some ancient root of <I>word</I>, as <I>fatum</I> of <I>for</I>, and &lquo;wayward&rquo;
may suggest an erroneous origin and a wrong meaning, since we have the word
&lquo;wayward&rquo; in a well-known sense; but notwithstanding this. an editor ought not to
think himself at liberty to print <I>weird</I>, the author having written &lquo;wayward,&rquo; to the</CC>

sisters were, and why they were so designated. Shakespeare is by no means pecu-
liar in writing &lquo;wayward.&rquo; Heywood, in his <I>The Late Witches of Lancashire</I>, has,
&lquo;You look like one of the Scottish wayward sisters.&rquo;&mdash;R. G. <SC>White</SC>: This word
should be pronounced <I>wayrd</I> (<I>ei</I> as in &lquo;obeisance,&rquo; &lquo;freight,&rquo; &lquo;weight,&rquo; &lquo;either,&rquo;
&lquo;neither&rquo;), and not <I>weerd</I>, as it usually is.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: <I>Weird</I> is given in Jamie-
son's Scottish Dictionary as a verb, to determine or assign as one's fate, also to pre-
dict. He gives also &lquo;weirdly,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> happy, and &lquo;weirdless,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> unhappy.
<P>37-39. <B>Thus . . . nine]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: They here take hold of hands and dance
round in a ring nine times, three rounds for each witch. Multiples of three and nine
were specially affected by witches ancient and modern. See Ovid, <I>Metam.</I> xiv, 58:
&lquo;Ter novies carmen magico demurmurat ore,&rquo; and vii, 189-191: &lquo;Ter se convertit;
ter sumptis flumine crinem Irroravit aquis; ternis ululatibus ora Solvit.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Knight</SC>:
There really appears no foundation for Steevens's supposition that this scene was
<I>uniformly</I> metrical. It is a mixture of blank-verse with the seven-syllable rhyme,
producing from its variety a wild and solemn effect which no regularity could have
achieved. &lquo;<I>Where . . . swine</I>&rquo; [line 3 and 4] is a line of blank verse; line 5 is a
dramatic hemistitch. We have then four lines of blank verse before the lyrical move-
ment, &lquo;But in a sieve,&rquo; etc. &lquo;<I>I'll . . . another</I>&rquo; [14-16] is a ten-syllable line rhym-
ing with the following octo-syllabic line. So, in the same manner, <I>I' the . . . hay:</I>
is a ten-syllable line, rhyming with the following one of seven syllables.
<P>41. <B>Enter Macbeth and Banquo]</B> <SC>Karl Blind</SC> (<I>Academy</I>, 1 March, 1879):
It has always struck me as noteworthy that in the greater part of the scene between
the Weird Sisters, Macbeth, and Banquo, and wherever the Witches come in, Shake-
speare uses the staff-rime in a very remarkable manner. Not only does this add
powerfully to the Archaic impressiveness and awe, but it also seems to bring the
form and figure of the Sisters of Fate more closely within the circle of the Teutonic
idea. The very first scene in the first act opens strongly with the staff-rime: &lquo;<I>When</I>
shall <I>w</I>e three meet again?&mdash;<I>W</I>hen the hurly-burly's done, <I>W</I>hen the battle's lost
and <I>w</I>on.&mdash;That will be ere <I>s</I>et of <I>s</I>un.&rquo; This feature in Shakespeare appears to me
to merit closer investigation; all the more so because a less regular alliteration, but
still a marked one, is found in not a few passages of a number of his plays.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
[The Anglo-Saxon staff, or stave-rime, is the oldest form of verse, and, although allit-
eration is a marked characteristic, yet its use is governed by more stringent rules than
the recurrence of similar-sounding consonants. A complete verse consists of a
couplet, with two accents, or loud syllables, to each line, connected by alliteration.</CC>

<CC><P>Each couplet should have at least three of these alliterative or rime-letters, of which
two are placed on the accented syllables of the first line, and are called the sub-
letters, and one on the first accented syllable of the second line; the last is the chief
letter. Should the initial consonants be wanting, the vowel sounds are more com-
monly different. (See Rask, <I>Icelandic Grammar</I>, p. 205; F. A. March: <I>Compara-
tive Grammar of the Anglo-Saxon Language</I>, p. 222; Guest, <I>History of English
Rhythms</I>, p. 137 et seq.; also W. W. Skeat: <I>Essay on Alliterative Poetry</I>, in Percy's
Folio MS, ed. Hales and Furnivall, iii, xiii.) Applying these rules to the passages,
whereto Blind has called attention, it is evident that, as true Anglo-Saxon couplets,
they are deficient. For example, in the lines: &lquo;<I>W</I>hen the hurly-burly's done, <I>W</I>hen
the battle's lost and <I>w</I>on,&rquo; the rime-letters are not, in the first place, in the proper
positions in the lines; secondly, the lines themselves have more than two accents.
Alliteration is, in fact, quite as prominent throughout the speech of the Captain
(I, ii.) as in any of the Witch scenes; thus, &lquo;<I>S</I>hipwracking <I>s</I>torms and direful Thun
ders: <I>S</I>o from that <I>S</I>pring whence <I>c</I>omfort seemed to <I>c</I>ome.&rquo;&mdash;Ed. ii.]
<P>41. <B>Macbeth]</B> <SC>Dowden</SC> (p. 250): Shakespeare does not believe in any sudden
transformation of a noble and loyal soul into that of a traitor and murderer. At the
outset, Macbeth possesses no real fidelity to things that are true, honest, just, pure,
lovely. He is simply not yet in alliance with the powers of evil. He has aptitudes
for goodness and aptitudes for crime. Shakespeare felt profoundly that this care-
less attitude of suspense or indifference between virtue and vice cannot continue
long.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
<P>42. <B>foule and faire]</B> <SC>Elwin</SC>: <I>Foul</I> with regard to the <I>weather</I>, and <I>fair</I> with
reference to his <I>victory.</I>&mdash;<SC>Delius</SC>: Macbeth enters engaged in talking with Banquo
about the varying fortune of the day of battle which they had just experienced.
&lquo;Day&rquo; as equivalent to &lquo;day of battle&rquo; was frequently used.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: A day
changing so suddenly from fine to stormy, the storm being the work of witchcraft.&mdash;
[<SC>Dowden</SC> (p. 249): Observe that the last words of the witches in the opening scene
of the play are the first words which Macbeth himself utters: &lquo;Fair is foul, and foul
is fair.&rquo; Shakespeare intimates by this that, although Macbeth has not yet set eyes
upon these hags, the connection is already established between his soul and them.
Their spells have already wrought upon his blood.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]
<P>43. <B>Soris]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Forres is near the Moray Frith, about halfway between

<P>65, 66. <B>Speake then . . . your hate]</B> <SC>Hudson</SC> (ed. iii, p. 25): The contrast in
the behaviour of the two men at this point is deeply significant. Belief takes hold
of them both alike, for aught appears. Yet, while Macbeth is beside himself with
excitement, and transported with guilty thoughts and imaginations, Banquo remains
calm, unexcited, and perfectly self-poised. His intellectual forces are indeed stimu-
lated by the preternatural address, but stimulated only to moralise the occasion, and
to draw arguments in support of his better mind. He hears the speakers with
simple wonder; shows no interest in them but that of an honest and rational curi-
osity; his mind is absorbed in the matter before him; and because he sees nothing
of himself in them, and has no germ of wickedness for them to work upon, therefore
he &lquo;neither begs nor fears their favours nor their hate.&rquo;&mdash;Ed. ii.

<P>77, 78. <B>the Thane of Cawdor . . . Gentleman]</B> <SC>Libby</SC> (see note on I, ii, 53):
Macbeth means by this that Cawdor is probably where he and Banquo left him, in
the Scotch camp. It is simply incredible that these words are used of an imprisoned
rebel, who had turned traitor on the field after being in the absolute confidence of
the king. The words, &lquo;The thane of Cawdor lives, a prosperous gentleman,&rquo; are
shaded down to the simple statement of his living when Ross salutes Macbeth as
Cawdor. Will any reader believe that this is simply the result of corrupt readings?
What method there must be in the corrupting of the two scenes when they are per-
fectly coherent from speech to speech, but incongruous when compared as scenes.
But there is no incongruity whatever. Macbeth and Banquo desire every word of
the witch's predictions to come true: both know Cawdor innocent; but to carry out
the prediction Macbeth must succeed Cawdor. Ross's announcement trebles the
desire of both that Cawdor may be out of the way. If Macbeth and Banquo are not
allied in a guilty silence why do they not press Ross for an explanation of the down-
fall of so prominent a noble? <I>If Macbeth were an honest man would he not have
questioned Ross far enough to allay the expressed doubts of Angus as to how Cawdor
had been a rebel?</I> To suppose Cawdor an innocent man&mdash;traduced and ruined by
Ross, partly to curry favor with Macbeth, and partly from a natural malignity&mdash;to
suppose this most probable hypothesis is to banish every difficulty in this otherwise
hopeless scene: to reject this view is to leave Scenes ii. and iii. in a confusion much
worse than annotators have admitted, and the reasons for the presence of Angus in
both scenes, and in fact for most of Scene ii, are entirely lost.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.&mdash;<SC>Deigh-
ton</SC>: Shakespeare has here been charged with an inconsistency in making Macbeth
speak in these terms of one who in I, ii, 64-5, is said to have &lquo;assisted&rquo; the King
of Norway. Assisted does not necessarily imply assistance in person, but rather
refers to the &lquo;new supplies of men&rquo; (I, ii, 38) sent to Norway's aid by Cawdor, who
is also said to have strengthened the rebel Macdonwald &lquo;With <I>hidden</I> help and
vantage&rquo; (I, iii, 125-6). It is quite possible that Macbeth, having left the field of
battle as soon as it was over to proceed to Forres, and not having yet joined the king,
was ignorant of Cawdor's treachery and of the sentence passed upon him. If so,
there is nothing strange in his speaking of that thane as <I>a prosperous gentleman.</I>
That Cawdor's defection was the result of sudden impulse may, I think, be inferred
from Duncan's surprise when informed of it by Ross; and that the facts were not
generally known is shown by the words of Angus (I, iii, 124-7), though he, as Ross's
companion, might be presumed to have heard them so far as they had been ascer-
tained. Shakespeare nowhere states that Cawdor had taken part in the battle:</CC>

they will find that it is a question not of a new hypothesis against an old one, but
of a new hypothesis against none whatever. No one will believe that Cawdor was
a rebel prisoner through Macbeth's exertions and that Macbeth was unaware of the
fact. In an ancient battle such a thing would be absolutely impossible.&mdash;Ed. ii.
<P>79. <B>prospect]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: &lquo;The eye of honour,&rquo; <I>Mer. of Ven.</I> I, i, 137, is a
somewhat similar phrase. Compare also, &lquo;scope of nature,&rquo; <I>King John</I>, III, iv, 154.
<P>84. <B>Witches vanish]</B> <SC>Anonymous</SC> (<I>Sunday Times</I>, London, 30 Dec. 1888): We
make bold to say that Mr Irving as Macbeth in the heath scene accomplished what
high authority has pronounced impossible. His whole attitude as the bewildering
prophecy strikes upon his ear, and as the strange prophets vanish into thin air, is
that of a man who has actually held converse with the spirits of another world. He
is not only dazed, but scared; and when Ross and Angus bring him their message
from the king, it is some time before he can collect himself sufficiently to listen to
their congratulations. It is perhaps because Irving's Thane of Cawdor is essentially
a weaker man than his stage predecessors&mdash;a murderer deliberately robbed of all air
of heroism and reduced to the level of a craven criminal&mdash;that this particular effect
is rendered possible and that the witches' superhuman influence over him becomes
so marked.&mdash;Ed. ii.
<P>86. <B>of them]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: For an instance of the preposition &lquo;of&rquo; thus used
partitively see Bacon's <I>Essays</I>, &lquo;Of Atheism,&rquo; p. 65, ed. Wright: &lquo;You shall have
of them, that will suffer for Atheisme, and not recant.&rquo;
<P>87. <B>corporall]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Shakespeare always uses the form &lquo;corporal,&rquo; as in
I, vii, 94. Milton has both forms, as in <I>Paradise Lost</I>, iv, 585: &lquo;To exclude
Spiritual substance with corporeal bar.&rquo; And in <I>Samson Agonistes</I>, 616: &lquo;Though
void of corporal sense.&rquo; In <I>Paradise Lost</I>, v, 413, the original edition, 1667, has
&lquo;corporeal,&rquo; where, clearly, we should read &lquo;corporal&rquo;: &lquo;And corporeal to incor-
poreal turn.&rquo; Shakespeare has &lquo;incorporal&rquo; once, viz., in <I>Hamlet</I>, III, iv, 118. He
never uses &lquo;incorporeal.&rquo;</CC>

<CC><P>88. <B>Melted]</B> <SC>Elwin</SC>: The emphasis should be laid upon &lquo;seem'd,&rquo; and the divi-

<CC><P>97. <B>Rosse]</B> <SC>French</SC> (p. 293): This title really belonged to Macbeth, who,
long before the action of the play begins, was Thane, or more properly, Maor-

be confounded with one similar in sound, which is spelt Rosse, and is an Irish

<P>98-109. <SC>Libby</SC>: What are the facts about these inconsistent speeches, the one to
Duncan in the second scene and this one to Macbeth? Angus heard Ross deliver a
confused and ambiguous account of the battle to Duncan and heard Duncan pro-
nounce the fate of Cawdor. Angus must have enquired of Ross what Cawdor had
done that he should have been alluded to as a traitor. Ross had evidently not satis-
fied him, for Angus tells Macbeth that he does not know what wrong Cawdor had
done. It is before Angus that Ross must now give an account of that speech to
Duncan, and in such words as shall not make Macbeth and Banquo exclaim that
Cawdor is innocent. Here are some of the ambiguities of his words: (<I>a</I>) He gives
Macbeth the impression that he was not himself the messenger to Duncan, but so
carefully that Angus does not suspect it. (<I>b</I>) &lquo;Thy personal venture in the rebel's
fight&rquo; alludes to Macdonwald as Macbeth and Banquo understand it (and as the
sergeant would have also understood it), while to Angus it brings a confused notion
of Norway and Cawdor. (<I>c</I>) &lquo;Silenc'd with that&rquo; to Macbeth means that Duncan
was overcome with wonder and admiration of the awful duel with Macdonwald:
To Angus it means that Duncan was so taken up with anger at Cawdor's treachery
that he paid no attention to the news of the battle.&mdash;Ed. ii.

<SC>Elwin</SC>: His <I>wona'ers</I> and his <I>praises</I> maintain a contention whether <I>he</I> should be
more actuated <I>by</I>, or <I>you</I> more the object <I>of</I>, his <I>wonders</I> or his <I>commendations.</I>
That is, which of the two it most befits <I>him to give</I>, or <I>you to excite.</I> The two words
are used in the plural to indicate more strongly the repeated excitation of the sepa-
rate sensations of <I>astonishment</I> and <I>approbation.</I>&mdash;<SC>Halliwell</SC>: That is, the king's
wonder and commendation of your deeds are so nearly balanced, they contend
whether the latter should be prominently thine, or the wonder remain with him to
the exclusion of any other thought.&mdash;<SC>Bailey</SC>: I suggest <I>thy praises</I> for &lquo;his praises,&rquo;
and that in the next line &lquo;silenced&rquo; be placed before &lquo;thine.&rquo; That is, the king
utters exclamations of his own wonder while he reads <I>thy</I> praises in the despatches,
and these two utterances seem to contend which shall silence the other, or, in differ-
ent language, which shall have the predominance. <I>Thy praises</I> is countenanced by
line 108. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: There is a conflict in the king's mind between his aston-
ishment at the achievement and his admiration of the achiever; he knows not how
sufficiently to express his own wonder and to praise Macbeth, so that he is reduced
to silence.&mdash;[<SC>Sprague</SC>: There is no need of changing the text. The king speaks,
though vaguely, of a &lquo;greater honor,&rquo; of which the thaneship of Cawdor is but &lquo;an
earnest.&rquo; That &lquo;greater honor&rquo; can hardly be anything less than the crown itself.
Originally the claim of Macbeth to the throne was better than Duncan's, and now
Macbeth has by his valor saved Scotland, while old Duncan has done nothing.
Duncan is conscious of ingratitude in bestowing nothing but the petty Thanedom of
Cawdor as a reward for Macbeth's brilliant services; wishes &lquo;that the proportion
both of thanks and payment&rquo; might have been in his power to bestow, but feels that
more is due Macbeth than the entire kingdom can pay. The kingdom is Macbeth's
by right, Duncan's by possession. Whose shall it be? He is in doubt which thing
to give Macbeth, which thing to retain as his own. In this mood &lquo;his wonders and
his praises do contend (as to) which (<I>i. e.</I> dignity, wealth or the kingdom itself)
should (ought to) be thine (Macbeth's) or his.&rquo; Ross and Angus evidently think
the magnanimous king is on the point of abdicating in favor of his heroic cousin.
But the king, after hinting at such abdication, prudently checks himself, &lquo;silenced
with that.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

<SC>White</SC>: To say that men arrived as thick as tale, <I>i. e.</I> as fast as they could be told,
is an admissible hyperbole; to say that <I>men</I> arrived as thick as <I>hail</I>, i. e. as close

sive multitudinous rapidity.&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC>: Rowe's change was unwarrantable, and

<P>145. <B>I thanke you Gentlemen]</B> J. S. <SC>Knowles</SC> (p. 10): What business has

<P>155. <B>fantasticall]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 467): <I>I</I> in the middle of a trisyllable, if unac-

<P>155-158. <SC>Bucknill</SC> (p. 13): Let not this early and important testimony be over-
looked which Macbeth gives to the extreme excitability of his imagination. This
passage was scarcely intended to describe an actual hallucination, but rather that
excessive predominance of the imaginative faculty which enables some men to call at
will before the mind's eye the very appearance of the object of thought. It is a
faculty bordering on a morbid state, and apt to pass the limit, when judgment swal-
lowed in surmise yields her function and the imaginary becomes as real to the mind
as the true, &lquo;and nothing is but what is not.&rquo; This early indication of Macbeth's
tendency to hallucination is most important in the psychological development of his
character.

Macbeth is absorbed in thought, and struck with horror of the murder, though but in
idea; and it naturally gives him a slow undertone of voice. And though it might
appear that I stopped at every word in the line, more than usual, my intention was
but to paint the horror of Macbeth's mind, and keep the voice suspended a little.&rquo;

<CC><P>phraseology of the Poet's time. <I>Simplicity</I> and <I>singleness</I> were synonymous.&mdash;
<SC>Elwin</SC>: Macbeth calls his existence at this moment his <I>single</I> state of man, because
of the <I>two</I> faculties, <I>thought</I> and <I>action</I>, by which the life of man expresses itself,
<I>the primitive or essential quality alone</I> is recognised by him; <I>action</I>, or function,
being, as he says, extinguished by the violent agitation of the other power.&mdash;<SC>Staun-
ton</SC>: &lquo;Single&rquo; here bears the sense of <I>weak;</I> my <I>feeble government</I> (or <I>body politic</I>)
of man. Shakespeare's affluence of thought and language is so unbounded that he
rarely repeats himself, but there is a remarkable affinity both in idea and expression
between the present passage and one in <I>Jul. C&aelig;s.</I> II, i, 63-69: &lquo;Between the acting
of a dreadful thing And the first motion, all the interim is Like a phantasma, or a
hideous dream: The Genius and the mortal instruments Are then in council; <I>and
the state of man, Like to a little kingdom</I>, suffers then The nature of an insurrection.&rquo;
&mdash;R. G. <SC>White</SC>: That is, my inadequate, unsupported manhood.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>:
Man is compared to a kingdom or state, which may be described as &lquo;single&rquo; when
all faculties are at one, or act in unison, undisturbed by conflicting emotions. Or
is &lquo;single&rquo; used in a depreciatory sense, as in I, vi, 23?
<P>157. <B>Function]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: All powers of action are oppressed and crushed by
one overwhelming image in the mind, and nothing is present to me but that which
is really future. Of things now about me I have no perception, being intent wholly
on that which has yet no existence.
<P>158. <B>not]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: Compare a sentiment somewhat like this in <I>Mer. of Ven.</I>
III, ii, 184, and in <I>Rich. II:</I> II, ii, 23.&mdash;<SC>Coleridge</SC>: So surely is the guilt in its
germ anterior to the supposed cause and immediate temptation! Before he can cool,
the confirmation of the tempting half of the prophecy arrives, and the concatenating
tendency of the imagination is fostered by the coincidence. . . . Every word of his solil-
oquy shows the early birth-date of his guilt.&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC>: That is, <I>facts</I> are lost sight
of. I <I>see</I> nothing but what is unreal, nothing but the spectres of my own fancy.
So, likewise, in the preceding clause: the mind is crippled, disabled for its proper
function or office by the apprehensions and surmises that throng upon him. Mac-
beth's conscience here acts through his imagination, sets it all on fire, and he is
terror-stricken and lost to the things before him, as the elements of evil, hitherto
latent within him, gather and fashion themselves into the wicked purpose. His
mind has all along been grasping and reaching forward $or grounds to build criminal
designs upon; yet he no sooner begins to build them than he is seized and shaken
with horrors which he knows to be imaginary, yet cannot allay.
<P>159. <B>Looke how our Partner's rapt]</B> C. S. <SC>Buell</SC> (<I>Poet-Lore</I>, Vol, xi, 1889,
p. 87): Two possible explanations present themselves as to why Banquo should call

<P>167. <B>Time]</B> <SC>Mrs Montagu</SC>: That is, <I>tempus et hora</I>, time and occasion, will
carry the thing through and bring it to some determined point and end, let its nature
be what it will.&mdash;<SC>Hunter</SC>: We feel the meaning of this, and perhaps every reader
of Shakespeare feels it alike. It is a conventional expression. We need not, there-
fore, be solicitous to scan every element of the general idea, to weigh the particular
force and effect of every word. Alas for much of our finest poetry if we are to deal
with it thus! The phrase is used by good writers. As by Bishop Hacket in his
<I>Life of Archbishop Williams:</I> &lquo;Time and long day will mitigate sad accidents,&rquo;
Part ii, 20. Marlowe places at the end of his <I>Doctor Faustus</I> a line which contains
a sentiment resembling this: &lquo;Terminat hora diem; terminat auctor opus.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC>
(&lquo;<I>Few Notes</I>,&rquo; p. 119): This expression is not unfrequent in Italian: &lquo;Ma perch' e'
fugge <I>il tempo, e cosi l' ora</I>, La nostra storia ci convien seguire,&rquo; Pulci, <I>Morg. Mag.</I>
c. xv. &lquo;Ferminsi in un momento <I>il tempo e l' ore</I>,&rquo; Michelagnolo, <I>Son.</I> xix.&mdash;<SC>Elwin</SC>:
That is, to every difficulty there comes <I>its hour</I> of solution. <I>The hour</I> signifies <I>the
appropriate hour;</I> it is identi$ied in time, of which it constitutes a part, as having
the natural distinction of containing the issue of the event, the finish of the day.&mdash;
<SC>Bailey</SC> (i, 89): I propose to read, &lquo;Time's <I>sandy hour</I> runs,&rquo; etc. It will be
allowed, I think, that this alteration remedies the tautology and the incongruity of

both in cast of thought and in expression. Compare <I>1 Hen. VI:</I> IV, ii, 36, and</CC>

<CC><P><I>Mer. of Ven.</I> I, i, 25. The emendation has also in its favour the <I>ductus literarum:</I>
&lquo;Time's <I>sandy</I> hour&rquo; and &lquo;Time <I>and ye</I> hour.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Halliwell</SC>: Compare the similar
phraseology: &lquo;<I>Day and time</I> discovering these murders, the woman . . . confessed
the fact.&rquo;&mdash;Lodge's <I>Wits Miserie</I>, 1596.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: &lquo;Time and the hour,&rquo; in the
sense of time with its successive incidents, or in its measured course, forms but one
idea. The expression seems to have been proverbial. Another form of it is: &lquo;Be
the day weary, be the day long, At length it ringeth to evensong.&rquo;&mdash;R. G. <SC>White</SC>
(<I>Words and their Uses</I>, p. 237): The use of <I>tide</I> in its sense of hour, <I>the</I> hour, led
naturally to a use of <I>hour</I> for <I>tide.</I> &lquo;Time and the hour&rquo; in this passage is merely
an equivalent of time and tide&mdash;the time and tide that wait for no man. Time and
opportunity, time and tide, run through the roughest day; the day most thickly
bestead with trouble is long enough and has occasions enough for the service and
the safety of a ready, quick-witted man. But for the rhythm, Shakespeare would
probably have written, Time and tide run through the roughest day; but as the
adage in that form was not well suited to his verse, he used the equivalent phrase,
time and the hour (not time and <I>an</I> hour, or time and the <I>hours</I>).

<P>1. <B>Scena Quarta]</B> <SC>Manly</SC>: It is now pretty well agreed that this scene is to be
regarded as taking place on the day after the previous scenes. In regard to the
incidents, it is to be noted that the dramatist was under no obligations to present
a report upon the death of Cawdor. In life there would be such a report, but upon
the stage not necessarily. The presentation of it here serves as a subject for con-
versation before the entrance of Banquo and Macbeth; and, as it were, furnishes an
introduction to the important announcement in regard to Malcolm. A good deal
has been made of the &lquo;tragic irony&rquo; of many passages in this scene,&mdash;perhaps not
too much; but it is well to bear in mind that there is less scope for speeches which
palter with us in a double sense in the Romantic Drama, which undertakes to tell
the audience a new story, than in the Classic Drama, which presents a new setting
of an old theme. We who read one of Shakespeare's plays for the hundredth time
may occasionally discover a subtlety which the most responsive audience would miss,
and which&mdash;alackaday! was not intended by Shakespeare.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.

<CC><P>Cawdor, <I>or</I> whether the tidings had not yet been received by the return of those
commissioned for the purpose.&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Remarks</I>, etc.): Could any boarding-school
girl read over the speech of Duncan, and not immediately perceive from the arrange-
ment of the words that &lquo;or&rquo; is a misprint for <I>are</I>?&mdash;[<SC>Allen</SC> (<I>Rom. &amp; Jul.</I> p. 430,
of this ed.): Shakespeare, in certain cases, wrote as he pronounced. He wrote <I>pho-
netically.</I> He took no pains to indicate to the eye that of which he gave no notice
to the ear. He wrote with the hearer, and not the reader, in his mind's eye. But
the reader of that day read as he would have heard, and drew the same sense from
the page, printed without interpretive marks addressed to the eye, as he would have
drawn from the same matter addressed to the ear. We are trained to deal with the
printed page so entirely otherwise, that we see defects in the original text where none
exist, and proceed to amend them by thrusting words into the supposed gaps, when
we should fully meet all the demands even of the modern eye by merely indicating
the actual presence of what had been treated as absent. Thus: &lquo;Is execution done
on Cawdor? or (= or <I>are</I>) not those in Commission yet returned?&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]
<P>5. <B>those in Commission]</B> <SC>Sherman</SC>: The use of the plural here would seem
to confirm the stage-direction (I, ii, 53), &lquo;Enter Rosse and Angus.&rquo; Summed up,
the evidence is this: &lquo;Those in commission,&rquo; when they do come back, turn out to
be the men just named; and they have greeted Macbeth, as Duncan directed, upon
the way. Also, Angus claims (I, iii, 110) a share in Ross's responsibility here.
On the other hand, Duncan does not recognize the presence of Angus in I, ii, and
refers to the approach of Ross and his companions&mdash;if he has any&mdash;by &lquo;comes.&rquo; Also
Ross says, in the same scene, &lquo;I'll,&rquo; and later (I, iii, 115), &lquo;me.&rquo; Some critics ex-
plain the inconsistency by supposing that Ross, in spite of his promise to the King
(&lquo;I'll see it done&rquo;), executed his commission by deputies. It is easier to assume
that the editors of the Folio blundered at l. 53, in the second scene, than that Shake-
speare meant to perplex his audience, in this of all plays, with the unaccountable
disobedience or indifference of a royal servant.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
<P>7. <B>die]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: The behaviour of the <I>thane of Cawdor</I> corresponds in almost
every circumstance with that of the unfortunate Earl of Essex, as related by Stowe,
p. 793. His asking the Queen's forgiveness, his confession, repentance, and concern
about behaving with propriety on the scaffold, are minutely described. Such an
allusion could not fail of having the desired effect on an audiance, many of whom
were eye-witnesses to the severity of that justice which deprived the age of one of its
greatest ornaments, and Southampton, Shakespeare's patron, of his dearest friend.&mdash;
<SC>Singer</SC> (ed. ii.): Montaigne, with whom Shakespeare was familiar, says, &lquo;In my
time, three of the most execrable persons I ever knew, in all abominations of life,
and the most infamous, have been seen to die very orderly and quietly, and in
every circumstance composed even unto perfection,&rquo; [&mdash;, Bk. I, ch. xviii; p. 30,
ed. 1632. In the Essay entitled: <I>That we are not to judge of Man's Happiness
before his Death.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]</CC>

<P>13. <B>studied]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: Instructed in the art of dying.&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: His own
profession furnished Shakespeare with this phrase. To be &lquo;studied&rquo; in a part, or to
have <I>studied</I> it, is yet the technical term of the theatre.&mdash;<SC>Harry Rowe</SC>: An allu-
sion to the death of Socrates and Seneca, who with great propriety may be considered
as men &lquo;<I>studied in their death.</I>&rquo;&mdash;[<SC>Butler</SC> (p. 173): Johnson says that <I>studied</I> means
&lquo;instructed in the art of dying.&rquo; Here what is plain enough is rendered unintelligi-
ble by the explanation. The meaning is that he died as if he had studied to throw
away his life as a careless trifle. The comma after &lquo;death&rquo; should be omitted. The
participial form is often employed for an adjective form, as in &lquo;the <I>guiled</I> shore To a
most dangerous sea&rquo; (<I>Mer. of Ven.</I> III, ii, 97), where <I>guiled</I> = guileful. In Act
IV, sc. i, [l. 26], &lquo;the <I>ravined</I> salt-sea shark&rquo; means the ravenous salt-sea shark.&mdash;
<SC>Manly</SC>: Not a past participle, but one of those adjectives in -<I>ed</I>, of which numerous
examples may be found in Schmidt (pp. 1417, 1418), meaning &lquo;possessed of, en-
dowed with, the thing expressed by the corresponding noun&rquo;; compare <I>Lear</I> III,
vii, 43: &lquo;Be simple answered&rquo; = provided with a simple answer; also such modern
phrases as &lquo;a hard-hearted man,&rquo; &lquo;a wrong-intentioned man,&rquo; etc. No proof of its
technical use, as suggested by Malone, has been adduced.&mdash;<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I>) inter-
prets the present passage as &lquo;well versed, practised,&rquo; but does not anywhere specify
study as used in a technical sense. As meaning to learn by heart, he quotes:
&lquo;Painted cloth, whence you have studied your questions.&rquo;&mdash;<I>As You Like It</I>, III, ii,
291. &lquo;Where did you study all this goodly speech?&rquo;&mdash;<I>Tam. of Shr.</I> II, i, 264. &lquo;I
can say little more than I have studied.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Twelfth Night</I>, I, v, 190. &lquo;You could,
for a need, study a speech of some dozen or sixteen lines.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Hamlet</I>, II, ii, 565.
Under &lquo;study,&rquo; as a noun, Schmidt gives: &lquo;Have you the lion's part written? pray
you, if it be, give it me, for I am slow of study.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Mid. N. D.</I> I, ii, 68. In three
of these examples, viz. that from <I>Hamlet, Mid. N. D.</I> and the present passage,
Malone and Steevens assert that &lquo;study&rquo; or &lquo;studied&rquo; is used in a technical, theat-
rical sense, and appeal to the present usage of the stage. When, therefore, it is said
that &lquo;no proof of its technical use has been adduced,&rquo; we must weigh Schmidt's
classification against the assertions of Steevens and Malone.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

present line], &lquo;<I>in the way in which</I> (he would throw it away) were it a careless
trifle.&rquo; Often the subjunctive is not represented by any inflection, as in II, i, 38,

<P>16, 17. <B>There's no Art . . . Face]</B> <SC>Darmesteter</SC>: For the sentiment herein
expressed, compare Racine, <I>Phedre</I>, II, 4 (following Euripides, <I>Medea</I>, 516-520),
&lquo;Faut-il que sur le front d' un profane adult&egrave;re Brille de la vertu le sacr&eacute; caract&egrave;re?
Et pourquoi ne peut-on, &agrave; des signes certains, Reconnaitre le c&oelig;ur des perfides
humains.&rquo; The arrival of Macbeth at these words, which he hears on entering, and
the truth of which he is shortly to verify by his acts, forms a dramatic contrast to the
elation of Duncan. This seems condemnatory of Garrick's conception (that Mac-
beth's face was always &lquo;as a book where men might read strange matters&rquo;); Macbeth
had had ample time to recompose his face. Talma here gave him the smile of his
Nero in the interview with Agrippina.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.&mdash;<SC>Libby</SC>: This speech is Duncan's
death-warrant. It is not too much to say that in this play Shakespeare is most careful
to preserve an exalted conception of retributive justice. Even Lady Macduff is most
untrue to her noble husband before the murderers enter; Banquo forfeits his life
(not to Macbeth, but to poetic justice) by his failure to warn Duncan and to defend
Cawdor. Duncan forfeits his life by weakly condemning, on the parenthetical accu-
sation of the thane of Ross, a nobleman who had been trusted with the &lquo;bosom
interest&rquo; of the king, &lquo;a gentleman on whom I built an absolute trust;&rquo; one clearly,
who had rivalled Macbeth and Banquo in his counsels. Though the lines, &lquo;The
sin of my ingratitude,&rquo; apply to Macbeth, yet they seem an echo of his feelings for
the murdered Cawdor.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
<P>17. <B>construction]</B> <SC>Heath</SC>: That is, construe or collect the disposition of the
mind from the countenance. The metaphor is taken from grammatical construction,
not from astrological, as Warburton, nor from physical, as Johnson, interprets it.&mdash;
<SC>Malone</SC>: In the 93d <I>Sonnet</I>, however, we find a contrary sentiment: &lquo;In many's
<I>looks</I> the <I>false heart's history</I> Is writ.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: Duncan's reflections on the
conduct of Cawdor are suddenly interrupted by the entrance of one whose face gave
as little indication of the construction of his mind, upon whom he had built as abso-
lute a trust, and who was about to requite that trust by an act of still more signal
and more fatal treachery.</CC>

<CC><P>26. <B>proportion]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: That is, due proportion. See <I>Tro. &amp; Cres.</I> I,
iii, 87.
<P>27. <B>mine]</B> <SC>Collier</SC> (<I>Notes</I>, etc.): <I>More</I> says the MS Corrector. Duncan wishes
that his thanks could have been <I>more</I> in proportion to the deserts of Macbeth. This
change is doubtful.&mdash;<SC>Singer</SC> (<I>Shakespeare Vindicated</I>, etc.): I confess it seems to
me much more plausible than many that Collier considers undoubted.&mdash;<SC>Staun-
ton</SC>: For &lquo;mine,&rquo; which no one can for a moment doubt to be a corruption, we
would suggest that Shakespeare wrote <I>mean</I>, i. e. <I>equivalent, just</I>, and the like; the
sense then being, That the proportion both of thanks and payment might have been
<I>equal</I> to your deserts.
<P>29. <B>owe]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: The loyal service which I owe recompenses itself in the
very performance. The singular is used as in I, iii, 167, &lquo;service and loyalty&rquo;
representing but one idea.
<P>32. <B>Duties]</B> <SC>Hudson</SC> (ed. iii, p. 64): &lquo;Duties&rquo; is here put, apparently, for the
faculties and labours of duty; the meaning being, &lquo;All our works and forces of duty
are children and servants to your throne and state.&rquo; Hypocrisy and hyperbole are
apt to go together; and so here Macbeth overacts the part of loyalty, and tries how
high he can strain up his expression of it. We have a parallel instance in Goneril
and Regan's finely-worded professions of love. Such high-pressure rhetoric is the
right vernacular of hollowness.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.</CC>

<CC><P>34. <B>safe]</B> <SC>Blackstone</SC>: Read, &lquo;<I>Safe</I> (<I>i. e.</I> saved) toward <I>you</I> love and honour,&rquo;
and then the sense will be, &lquo;Our duties are your children, and servants or vassals to
your throne and state; who do but what they should, by doing everything with a
saving of their love and honour toward you&rquo;&mdash;an allusion to the forms of doing
homage in the feudal times. The oath of allegiance, or <I>liege homage</I>, to the king,
was absolute, and without any exception; but <I>simple homage</I>, when done to a subject
for lands holden of him, was always with a <I>saving</I> of the allegiance (the <I>love</I> and
<I>honour</I>) due to the sovereign. &lquo;<I>Sauf la foy que jeo doy a nostre seignor le roy</I>,&rquo; as
it is in <I>Littleton.</I>&mdash;<SC>As You Like It</SC> (<I>Gent. Mag.</I> lix, 713): Enclose &lquo;<I>children . . .
everything</I>&rquo; in parenthesis, and read, &lquo;<I>Safe to ward</I>,&rquo; etc.&mdash;<SC>Seymour</SC>: &lquo;Safe to-
ward.&rquo; That is, with sure tendency, with certain direction. It ought to be marked as
a compound&mdash;&lquo;safe-toward.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Singer</SC> (ed. i.): &lquo;Safe&rquo; may merely mean <I>respectful,
loyal;</I> like the old French word <I>sauf.</I>&mdash;<SC>Knight</SC>: Surely it is easier to receive the
words in their plain acceptation&mdash;our duties are called upon to do everything which
they can do <I>safely</I>, as regards the love and honour we bear you.&mdash;<SC>Coleridge</SC> (p.
245): Here, in contrast with Duncan's &lquo;plenteous joys,&rquo; Macbeth has nothing but
the commonplaces of loyalty, in which he hides himself with &lquo;our duties.&rquo; Note
the exceeding effort of Macbeth's addresses to the king, his reasoning on his alle-
giance, and then especially when a new difficulty, the designation of a successor,
suggests a new crime. This, however, seems the first distinct notion as to the plan
of realizing his wishes; and here, therefore, with great propriety, Macbeth's cow-
ardice of his own conscience discloses itself.&mdash;<SC>Elwin</SC>: Macbeth is speaking with
reference to his late defence of Duncan from the enmity that would have robbed him
of <I>the affection and reverence of his subjects;</I> and the meaning is, who do but what
they should, by doing everything that can be done, which <I>secures to you the love and
honour that is your due.</I>&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: &lquo;Safe&rquo; is used provincially for <I>sure, certain.</I>
<P>37. <B>plant]</B> <SC>Elwin</SC>: Thus in Beaumont &amp; Fletcher, <I>The Island Princess</I>, III, i,
&lquo;So is my study still to plant thy person.&rquo; And the word <I>growing</I> was formerly
used to signify <I>accruing wealth or income.</I> Thus in the <I>Letters of Cranmer</I>, &lquo;I know
he hath very little <I>growing</I> towards the supporting of his necessaries.&rquo;
<P>40. <B>No]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: We should now say, &lquo;and must be no less known.&rquo; For
instances of this double negative, which is of frequent occurrence, see <I>Mer. of Ven.</I>
III, iv, ii. [See <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 406.]</CC>

<P>50. <B>The Prince of Cumberland]</B> [&lquo;But shortlie after it chanced that king Dun-

<CC><P>53. <B>Envernes]</B> <SC>Hunter</SC>: It may seem hypercritical to remark that the Ff have
&lquo;Envernes&rquo;; and yet a nice ear will perceive that the absolute melody of Shake-
speare's verse is better preserved by the old reading than the new. In a picture by a
great master the least touch of an inferior hand is perceived.
<P>55. This line <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> iii, 252) divides at &lquo;labour,&rquo; making &lquo;which is not
used for you&rquo; a separate line.&mdash;<SC>Hunter</SC>: The word &lquo;rest&rquo; is printed with a capital
letter in F<SUB>1</SUB>, thus leaving no doubt in this somewhat ambiguous line that the Poet's
intention was to make Macbeth use a complimentary expression similar to what he
had before said. The rest which is not spent in the king's service is like severe
labour.
<P>56. <B>Herbenger]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: An officer of the royal household, whose duty it
was to ride in advance of the king and procure lodgings for him and his attendants
on their arrival at any place. It is a corruption of <I>herberger.</I> Cotgrave gives
&lquo;Mareschal du corps du Roy. The King's chiefe Harbinger.&rquo; In the sense of
&lquo;herald,&rquo; or &lquo;forerunner,&rquo; it occurs in V, vi, 16.
<P>57. <B>The hearing of my Wife]</B> <SC>Fletcher</SC> (p. 183): It is not that Macbeth
wavers either in his desire of the object or in his liking for the means; but that, the
more imminent he feels the execution to be, the more he shrinks from the worldly
responsibility that may follow, and the more he is driven to lean for support on the
moral resolution of his wife. At his parting with the king, after saying: &lquo;I'll be
myself the harbinger,&rquo; etc., immediately follows his eager exclamation which the
inveterate misapprehension on the subject compels us to repeat again and again:&mdash;
&lquo;yet let that be Which the eye fears, when it is done to see.&rquo; After this it seems
truly strange that any critic should suppose for a moment that Macbeth's very next
words, &lquo;My dearest love, Duncan comes here to-night,&rquo; may imply a relenting from
his purpose&mdash;how much soever they may indicate a fluttering in its execution. His
selfish pusillanimity is simply seeking to cast upon <I>her</I> the burden of the final
decision as to the act of murder. When to her own suggestive query, &lquo;And when
goes hence?&rquo; he answers, &lquo;To-morrow&mdash;as he purposes,&rquo; is it not most clear that,
still avoiding an explicit declaration of his immediate wish, he persists in urging the
first utterance of it from her own lips?&mdash;Ed. ii.

<CC><P>and his reason was that these in some degree justified the Thane's aspirations; but
Shakespeare was unwilling to permit them to appear to justify murder as the means
of their accomplishment. He would not lend his countenance to the unreformed
doctrine, still held by the Romanist, that &lquo;the end justifies the means.&rquo; He does,
however, provide Macbeth with an external determining cause, in the elevation of
Malcolm to the princedom of Cumberland, which made him direct heir to the throne.
We may imagine, if we please, that there had been some implied contract between
Duncan and himself, that Macbeth should be his successor, and that this condition
was violated by Duncan's present act. We see that the king, to conciliate Macbeth,
heaps up honours to him, and, it may be, regarded these as an equivalent substitute
for the privilege of which at the same time he deprived him; and further makes
amends by speaking of him in hypocritical terms of esteem, which are conceived in
that exaggerated strain of compliment adopted by people when they are not sincere.
Duncan pays deeply for this weakness, though otherwise a respectable person
enough.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
<P>60. <B>The Prince of Cumberland]</B> <SC>Irving</SC> (<I>Character of Macbeth</I>, p. 10): It
should always be borne in mind that this point is the pivotal one in the action of the
play. Macbeth has his former inchoate intention of murder crystallized into an
immediate and determined resolve to do the deed, for he realizes that the king's
unconstitutional action will day by day raise an everheightening barrier between him
and the throne. Up to this moment there was, constitutionally&mdash;in the present and
in the immediate future&mdash;but one life between him and the golden circlet. Now there
are two and possibly three, for what was done in case of Malcolm may yet be done
in case of Donalbain, and so Macbeth, who is all resolute when his mind is made up
for action, has already decided that the overleaping of the barrier must be done this
very night. When the murder is accomplished, Macbeth is spared the further exer-
cise of his craft, [owing to the escape of the two princes], and he has only to point
to their flight as an evidence of their guilt, and at once steps into his place as King
of Scotland.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
<P>62. <B>Starres]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Macbeth apparently appeals to the stars, because he
is contemplating night as the time for the perpetration of the deed. There is nothing
to indicate that this scene took place at night.&mdash;[R. M. <SC>Theobald</SC> (p. 236) sees
in this phrase an indication of Bacon's authorship, since &lquo;Bacon in several places
expresses his opinion that the stars are true fires&rquo; (<I>Works</I>, v, 538; 476 <I>Syl. Syl.</I>
31).&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]
<P>63. <B>Let]</B> <SC>Delius</SC>: &lquo;The eye&rquo; is the subject to &lquo;let.&rquo; The eye, in silent collu-
sion with the executing hand, is to let that take place which it fears to see after the
hand has executed it. &lquo;When it is done&rquo; is equivalent to <I>when it happens</I>, or <I>shall
be done</I>&mdash;not, <I>when it has happened</I>, or <I>has been done.</I>
<P>64. <B>The Eye winke]</B> <SC>Hudson</SC> (ed. iii.): &lquo;<I>Let</I> the eye wink&rquo; is the meaning.
&lquo;Wink at&rquo; is <I>encourage</I> or <I>prompt.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.</CC>

<CC><P>66. <B>True]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: We must imagine that, while Macbeth was uttering the
six preceding lines, Duncan and Banquo had been conferring apart. Macbeth's
conduct appears to have been their subject; and to some encomium bestowed on
him by Banquo, the reply of Duncan refers.&mdash;R. G. <SC>White</SC>: A touch of dramatic
art common with Shakespeare, which shows how constantly he kept the stage and
the audience in mind.&mdash;<SC>Coleridge</SC> (p. 245): I always think there is something
especially Shakespearian in Duncan's speeches throughout this scene, such pourings-
forth, such abandonments, compared with the language of vulgar dramatists, whose
characters seem to have made their speeches as the actors learn them.
<P>68. <B>Banquet]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: As Archbishop Trench has pointed out (<I>Select
Glossary</I>), &lquo;banquet used generally to be restrained to the lighter and ornamental
dessert or confection with wine which followed the more substantial repast,&rquo; whether
dinner or supper. But in this passage the sense is not so restricted. For a similar
sentiment, see <I>Wint. Tale</I>, IV, iv, 529.&mdash;[<SC>Skeat</SC> (<I>Dict.</I>): The more usual form in
old authors is <I>banket</I>&mdash;French, <I>banquet</I>, which Cotgrave explains as &lquo;a banket&rquo;;
also a feast, etc. The word has reference to the table on which the feast is spread
(or, as some say, with less likelihood, to the benches of the guests), and is a diminu-
tive of French <I>banc</I>, a bench, a table, with diminutive suffix -<I>et.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

<P>2. <B>Enter Macbeths Wife alone with a Letter]</B> <SC>Anonymous</SC> (<I>Blackwood's

whole frame was disturbed, she threw her fine eyes upwards, and exclaimed &lquo;<I>Van-
ished!</I>&rquo; with a wild force, which showed that the whole spirit of the temptation had
shrunk into her soul. The &lquo;Hail, King that shalt be!&rquo; was the winding up of the
spell. It was pronounced with the grandeur of one already by anticipation a Queen.
&mdash;Ed. ii.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: She reads the letter, not now for the first time.&mdash;[<SC>Anony-
mous</SC> (<I>Sunday Times</I>, London, 30 Dec. 1888): On her first entrance as Lady Macbeth
Miss Ellen Terry appears in a gown of peacock green and beetles wings, with a man-
tle of a kind of dull claret colour, a most picturesque figure, with rich red hair falling
over her shoulders in two very long locks. Her reading of Macbeth's letter is conse-
quently very intent and full of terrible significance, for we see the wife's mind absorbing
itself in that of her beloved husband, and interpreting the suggestion of his written
words. Miss Terry at once shows us that Lady Macbeth is, according to her reading,
a very woman whose love for her husband subordinates to it every other considera-
tion, so that the achieving of this ambition must be her first thought. She knows
his nature, and as she takes up his miniature tenderly and talks to it in loving tones
she reviews his kindliness of heart, and indicates that she must assume masculine
strength to support him in the fatal purpose that he has revealed to her, and which
she knows involves the ambition of his life. When Macbeth comes she rushes lov-
ingly to his arms, and, with her woman's instinct, at once commences to read his
thoughts, and attempts to turn them to action.&mdash;<SC>Manly</SC>: The Clarendon Editors
think she had read the letter before; perhaps so. But perhaps it is just as well
to suppose she is now reading it for the first time, but has already read several
sentences when she comes upon the stage. It is to be remembered, however, that
stage letters are not constructed on the principles followed in life. They contain
merely what furnishes to the audience a plausible excuse for the possession by the
recipient of certain information; they are, as it were, mere symbols of the transmis-
sion of information. Hence it is that in a play we often find a person in possession
of facts not contained in a letter, although that letter was the only source of informa-
tion.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

<CC><P>than the most gorgeous pageant that ever signalized the triumph of human pride, or
fulfilled the imaginings of human admiration.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.&mdash;<SC>Chambers</SC> (p. 101): Lady
Macbeth is strong just where her husband is weak, in self-conquest, singleness of

character of the two; her ambition is for him, not for herself; it is for him that she
divests herself of conscience, and, so far as may be, even of womanhood.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.

<CC><P>15. <B>Glamys thou art,</B> etc.] <SC>John Coleman</SC> (<I>Gentleman's Maga.</I> March, 1889):
Unquestionably <I>the</I> Lady Macbeth of the last two decades is Adelaide Ristori.
When she came on the stage she seemed to fill it with her majestic presence. When
she had finished reading the letter and commenced her invocation to the spirits of
evil, she crooned forth the opening words, until the voice changed almost to the
hiss of a serpent; anon it rose to the swelling diapason of an organ, her eyes
became luminous with infernal fire, the stately figure expanded, her white hands
clutched her ample bosom, as if she would there and then have unsexed herself, and
turned &lquo;her woman's milk to gall,&rquo; and it really required but little stretch of imagi-

her there and then.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.&mdash;<SC>Libby</SC>: It seems from the way of receiving these
tidings that these ambitions were common domestic topics between Macbeth and his
wife. Had they not discussed the death of Sinel and the title of Cawdor many a
time?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.

<CC><P>signification of the root, <I>natural, nature</I>, still retained in the noun <I>kind</I>, has been
lost in the adjective, which has been narrowed by modern usage to one sort of natu-
ralness, tender-heartedness; though in a derivative form the original sense is still
familiar to modern ears in the expression, &lquo;the <I>kindly</I> fruits of the earth.&rquo; In
Elizabethan English, however, the root signification still remained in all usages of
<I>kind</I> and its derivatives. In Schmidt's analysis of the adjective, two of its four
significations agree with the modern use, the other two are &lquo;keeping to nature,
natural,&rquo; and &lquo;not degenerate and corrupt, but such as a thing or person ought to be.&rquo;
Shakespeare delights to play upon the two senses of this family of words: tears of joy
are described as a &lquo;kind overflow of kindness&rquo; (<I>Much Ado</I>, I, i, 26); the Fool says
of Regan that she will use Lear &lquo;kindly,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> according to her nature (<I>Lear</I> I, v, 15);
&lquo;the worm will do his kind,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> bite (<I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.</I> V, ii, 264). How far the word
can wander from its modern sense is seen in a phrase of the present play, &lquo;At your
kind'st leisure&rquo; (II, i, 35), where it is simply equivalent to &lquo;convenient.&rquo; Still more
will the wider signification of the word obtain, when it is associated with the word
<I>human</I>; &lquo;humankind&rquo; is still an expression for human nature, and the sense of the
passage we are considering would be more obvious if the whole phrase were printed
as one word, not &lquo;human kindness,&rquo; but &lquo;humankind-ness&rquo;:&mdash;that shrinking from
what is not natural, which is a marked feature of the practical nature. The other part
of the clause, <I>milk</I> of humankind-ness, no doubt suggests absence of hardness: but
it equally connotes natural, inherited, traditional feelings, imbibed at the mother's
breast. The whole expression of Lady Macbeth, then, I take to attribute to her
husband an instinctive tendency to shrink from whatever is in any way unnatural.
That this is the true sense further appears, not only from the facts&mdash;for nothing in
the play suggests that Macbeth, &lquo;Bellona's bridegroom,&rquo; was distinguished for kind-
ness in the modern sense&mdash;but from the context. The form of Lady Macbeth's
speech makes the phrase under discussion a summing up of the rest of her analysis,
or rather a general text which she proceeds to expand into details. Not one of
these details has any connection with tender-heartedness: on the other hand, if put
together, the details do amount to the sense for which I am contending, that Mac-
beth's character is a type of commonplace morality, the shallow unthinking man's
lifelong hesitation between God and Mannon.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.&mdash;<SC>Chambers</SC> comments
upon the foregoing interpretation of Moulton, but suggests that <I>abnormal, uncon-
ditional</I>, is perhaps the more fitting word to describe Lady Macbeth's estimate of
her husband's character, rather than <I>un-natural</I>, as given by Moulton. Chambers
also calls attention to the fact that &lquo;there are several closely parallel passages, in
which milk connotes &ldquo;absence of hardness.&rdquo;&rquo; He quotes the two passages cited
by Delius [see note, line 17] and that cited by Clarendon.&mdash;Ed. ii.

<P>21. <B>would'st]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 329): &lquo;Would,&rquo; like <I>should, could, ought</I> (Latin, <I>potui,
debui</I>), is frequently used conditionally. Hence, &lquo;I <I>would</I> be great&rquo; comes to
mean, not &lquo;I wished to be great,&rquo; but &lquo;I wished (subjunctive),&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> &lquo;I should
wish.&rquo; There is, however, very little difference between &lquo;thou wouldest wish&rquo;
and &lquo;thou wishest,&rquo; as is seen in the present passage. It is a natural and com-
mon mistake to say &lquo;<I>would</I> is used for <I>should</I> by Elizabethan writers.&rquo; [See also
I, vii, 40.]

<P>25, 26. <B>And . . . vndone]</B> <SC>Moulton</SC> (p. 150): It is striking that at the very
moment Lady Macbeth is so meditating, her husband is giving a practical confirma-
tion of her description in its details as well as its general purport. He had resolved
to take no steps himself towards the fulfilment of the Witches' prophecy, but to
leave all to chance; then the proclamation of Malcolm, removing all apparent
chance of succession, led him to change his mind and entertain the scheme of
treason and murder: the words with which he surrenders himself seems like an
echo of his wife's analysis, &lquo;yet let that be Which the eye fears, when it is done, to
see&rquo; (I, iv, 64, 65).&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
<P>23. <B>Thould'st haue, great Glamys]</B> <SC>Libby</SC>: She knows his nature in reference
to such matters, not by analogy but by his words in reference to his two former
ambitions. When he was Glamis he wished to be Cawdor; when his father was
alive he wished to inherit. Had his father died or Cawdor been ruined he would
have been pleased, though he would have feared to cause the death of either. Upon
hearing of Duncan's death Banquo expressed repentance (II, iii, 108, 109), he wished
he had warned and protected Duncan; Macbeth felt only remorse, he would have
committed the crime again.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
<P>26. <B>High thee]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 212): Verbs followed by <I>thee</I> instead of <I>thou</I> have
been called reflexive. But though &lquo;haste <I>thee</I>,&rquo; and some other phrases with verbs
of motion, may be thus explained, and verbs were often thus used in Early English,
it is probable that &lquo;look <I>thee</I>,&rquo; &lquo;haste <I>thee</I>,&rquo; are to be explained by euphonic reasons.
<I>Thee</I>, thus used, follows imperatives, which, being themselves emphatic, require an
unemphatic pronoun. The Elizabethans reduced <I>thou</I> to <I>thee.</I> We have gone
further, and rejected it altogether.&mdash;[<SC>Bell</SC> (p. 302): [Mrs Siddons here] starts into
higher animation.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]</CC>

<P>30, 31. <B>seeme To haue]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: The sense evidently directs us to read <I>seek.</I>

supplied thus: <I>doth seem desirous to have.</I> An easy alteration will restore the Poet's
true reading: &lquo;doth seem To have crown'd thee withal,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> they seem already to
have crowned thee, and yet thy disposition at present hinders it from taking effect.&mdash;

to <I>appear</I>, but to <I>reveal.</I>&mdash;<SC>Bailey</SC> (ii, 21): There are many other plausible ways
of amending the defect; <I>e. g. deem, aim, mean</I>&mdash;any of them better than &lquo;seem.&rquo;

be cited <I>King John</I>, III, iv, 119. These readings, however, are none of them con-
clusive, and the same may be said of another which has occurred to me: to replace
&lquo;seem&rquo; by <I>frame</I> in the sense of <I>fabricate.</I> I have been struck by a somewhat par-
allel passage in <I>1 Hen. VI:</I> II, v, 88: &lquo;Levied an army, <I>weening</I> to redeem, And
have install'd me in the <I>diadem.</I>&rquo; This suggests <I>ween</I>, which I am inclined to regard
as the likeliest of all.</CC>

<P>34-36. <B>Thou'rt . . . preparation]</B> <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 173): Here is a stroke of nature.
Lady Macbeth had been meditating on what she considered the nearest way to the
honour which was offered to them, and, when she hears that the king was about to
put himself in her power, she speaks in reference to the ideas which had passed
through her own mind. It then occurs to her that she might have disclosed too
much; and she seeks to divert the mind of the attendant from any too strict scrutiny
of the meaning of what she had uttered, by explaining it as having no other mean-
ing than as referring to the want of sufficient notice to make preparation for the
reception of so illustrious a guest.&mdash;[<SC>Bell</SC> (p. 302): [Mrs Siddons spoke] this first

sentiments almost disclosed.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

<CC><P>174): There are probably few readers who do not understand this phrase in its plain
and I should say obvious sense, that even the raven which croaks the fatal entrance
has more than its usual hoarseness. Nothing is more common than to speak of the
raven croaking ominously.&mdash;[<SC>Manly</SC> (p. 102): Some of the editors strangely suppose
that by &lquo;the raven&rquo; is meant the messenger who is almost dead for breath. To say
nothing of the remarkable assumption that scantness of breath causes hoarseness,
this shows lack of acquaintance with the superstition of the time. Scot, <I>Discoverie
of Witchcraft</I>: &lquo;[It is most impious] to prognosticate that ghests approch to your
house, upon the chattering of pies or haggisters,&rquo; [p. 170, ed. 1584]. The approach
of an ordinary guest might be announced by a magpie, but for such a visit as Dun-
can's the hoarse croaking of a raven would alone be appropriate. This is practically
the opinion of Nicholson, the editor of Scot, who adds from W. Perkins, <I>Witchcraft</I>,
1613: &lquo;When a raven stands on a high place and looks a particular way and cries, a
corse comes thence soon.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Bell</SC> (p. 302): [Mrs Siddons uttered this] after a long
pause when the messenger has retired. Indicating her fell purpose settled and about
to be accomplished.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]
<P>44. <B>entrance]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC> (<B>&sect; 477</B>): R, and liquids in disyllables, are frequently
pronounced as though an extra vowel were introduced between them and the pre-
ceding consonant. [See also <SC>Walker</SC>, <I>Vers.</I> p. 57.]
<P>45. <B>my]</B> <SC>Hunter</SC>: The word &lquo;my&rquo; is purposely used by Shakespeare to let the
audience into the spirit of the character intended for the wife of the Thane; <I>nihil
non arrogat;</I> the castle is <I>hers</I>&mdash;not Macbeth's, not theirs jointly. It prepares for
that overbearing of the milder and gentler spirit of the Thane which follows.
<P>45. <B>Battlements]</B> <SC>Knight</SC>: If there be any one who does not feel the sublimity
of the pause after &lquo;battlements,&rquo; we can only say that he has yet to study Shake-
speare.&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC>: This passage is often sadly marred in the reading by laying
peculiar stress upon &lquo;<I>my</I>&rquo;; as the next sentence also is in the printing by repeating
&lquo;Come,&rquo; thus suppressing the pause wherein the speaker gathers and nerves herself
up to the terrible strain that follows.
<P>45. <B>Come you Spirits]</B> <SC>Malone</SC>: In <I>Pierce Pennilesse his Supplication to the
Diuell</I>, by Nashe, 1592, Shakespeare might have found a particular description of these
spirits and of their office: &lquo;The second kind of Diuels, which he most imployeth, are
those northerne <I>Marcij</I>, called the spirits of reuenge, &amp; the authors of massacres, &amp;
seedsmen of mischiefe: for they haue commission to incense men to rapines, sacri-
ledge, theft, murther wrath, furie, and all manner of cruelties, &amp; they commaund cer-

Monthly</I>, April, 1895): The impious prayer is heard; the consecration is perfected;
her perceptions are sealed to all impressions that might divert her from the object or

She is the same as before, but in a transformed condition. Every characteristic is</CC>

<P>47. <B>And . . . Toe]</B> <SC>Snider</SC> (i, 199): The somewhat prevalent notion of mak-
ing love the mainspring of Lady Macbeth's actions, and of seeing in her the tender,
devoted wife, who committed the most horrible crimes merely out of affection for her
husband, is ridiculous, and is, one may well assert, contradicted by the whole tenor
of the play. The very point here emphasized is that she abjured womanhood, with
its tenderness and love, and prayed to be filled with &lquo;direst cruelty&rquo; and her woman's
breasts to be milked for gall! To be the wife is clearly not her highest ambition&mdash;
that she is already; but it is to be the queen. There is no consistency or unity in her
character if love be its leading principle. To this passion the husband may justly
lay claim, but not the wife, who suppresses her emotional nature.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
<P>49. <B>accesse]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 490): Many words, such as <I>edict, outrage</I>, etc., are ac-
cented in a varying manner. The key to this inconsistency is, perhaps, to be found
in Ben Jonson's remark that all disyllabic nouns, <I>if they be simple</I>, are accented on
the first. Hence <I>edict</I> and <I>outrage</I> would generally be accented on the first, but,
when they were regarded as <I>derived from verbs</I>, they would be accented on the
second. And so, perhaps, when <I>exile</I> is regarded as a person, and therefore a
&lquo;simple&rquo; noun, the accent is on the first; but when as &lquo;the state of being exiled,&rquo; it
is on the last. But naturally, where the difference is so slight, much variety may be
expected. Ben Jonson adds that &lquo;all verbs coming from the Latin, either of the
supine or otherwise, hold the accent as it is found in the first person present of those
Latin verbs; as from <I>c&eacute;lebro, c&eacute;lebrate.</I>&rquo; The same fluctuation between the English
and French accent is found in Chaucer (Prof. Child, in Ellis, <I>Early English Pro-
nunciation</I>, i, 369).&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: &lquo;Access&rquo; is always accented by Shakespeare on
the second syllable, except in <I>Hamlet</I>, II, i, 110.
<P>49. <B>Remorse]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Relenting, used anciently to signify repentance not
only for a deed done, but also for a thought conceived. See <I>Mer. of Ven.</I> IV, i. 20.

and <I>compunction</I> not at all. &lquo;Compunct&rquo; is used in Wicklif's Bible, <I>Acts</I>, ii, 37,
and &lquo;compuncture&rquo; by Jeremy Taylor.</CC>

<CC><P>51, 52. <B>peace . . . hit]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: The intent of Lady Macbeth evidently is to
wish that no womanish tenderness or conscientious remorse may hinder her purpose
from proceeding to effect; but neither this, nor any other sense, is expressed by the
present reading; perhaps Shakespeare wrote &lquo;keep <I>pace</I> between,&rquo; etc., which may
signify to <I>pass between</I>, to <I>intervene.</I>&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: A similar expression is found in
<I>The Tragicall Hystorie of Romeus and Juliet</I>, 1562: &lquo;&mdash; the lady no way could
Kepe trewse betwene her greefes and her.&rquo; D'Avenant's version sometimes affords
a reasonably good comment. [See <I>Appendix.</I>]&mdash;<SC>Knight</SC>: If fear, compassion, or
any other compunctious visitings, stand between a cruel purpose and its realiza-
tion, they may be said to keep peace between them, as one who interferes between
a violent man and the object of his wrath keeps peace.&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC> (ed. ii.): One
might naturally think this should read, &lquo;nor <I>break</I> peace between the effect and
it&rquo;; that is, nor make the effect contradict, or fall at strife with, the purpose. The
sense, however, doubtless is, nor make any delay, any rest, any <I>pause for thought</I>,
between the purpose and the act.&mdash;[<SC>Hudson</SC> (ed. iii, p. 188): The attempts that
have been made to explain &lquo;nor <I>keep</I> peace&rquo; are, it seems to me, either absurdly
ingenious and over-subtle or something worse. The natural sense of it is clearly
just the reverse of what was intended. To be sure, almost any language can be
tormented into yielding almost any meaning. And we have too many instances of
what may be called a fanaticism of ingenuity, which always delights especially in a
reading that none but itself can explain, and in an explanation that none but itself
can understand. The other error, &lquo;hit,&rquo; corrects itself.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]&mdash;<SC>Bailey</SC> (ii, 24):
Let us read, &lquo;nor keep <I>space</I> between,&rquo; etc. She supplicates that no compunctious
feelings may keep space between (<I>i. e.</I> interpose between) her purpose and its
execution.
<P>53. <B>take]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: &lquo;Take <I>away</I> my milk, and put <I>gall</I> into the place.&rquo;&mdash;
<SC>Delius</SC>: It rather means Nourish yourselves with my milk, which, through my
being unsexed, has turned to gall.&mdash;<SC>Keightley</SC>: Perhaps we should read <I>with</I> for
