although they are, in their natures, separate and distinct. Her resolution thus sup-

unwilling, into the crime which brings a terrible retribution to both.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]
<P>57-59. <B>That my keene Knife . . . hold]</B> W. W. <SC>Story</SC> (p. 267): In this
apostrophe, in which Lady Macbeth goads herself on to crime, the woman's nature
is plainly seen. Macbeth never prays to have his nature altered, to have any pas-
sages to remorse closed up; never fears &lquo;compunctious visitings of nature.&rquo; But
she knows that she is a woman, and that she needs to be unsexed, and feels that she
is doing violence to her own nature; still her will is strong, and she cries down her
misgivings, and resolves to aid Macbeth in his design.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.

Not I. I said she was attached to him&mdash;and I say now that the wise men are not

a proof of her want of affection. They seem to think she ought to have rushed into
his arms&mdash;slobbered upon his shoulder&mdash;and so forth. For had he not been to the
Wars? Pshaw! The most tender-hearted Thanesses of those days&mdash;even those that
kept albums&mdash;would have been ashamed of weeping on sending their Thanes off to
battle&mdash;much more on receiving them back in a sound skin&mdash;with new honours nod-
ding on their plumes. Lady Macbeth was not one of the turtle-doves&mdash;fit mate she
for the King of the Vultures. I am too good an ornithologist to call them Eagles.

fish than he, she could not be&mdash;nor, perhaps, was she less; but she was more reso-
lute&mdash;and resolution even in evil&mdash;in such circumstances as hers&mdash;seems to argue a
superior nature to his, who, while he keeps vacillating, as if it were between good
and evil, betrays all the time the bias that is surely inclining him to evil, into which
he makes a sudden and sure wheel at last.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.

<P>65. <B>My dearest Loue]</B> <SC>Fletcher</SC> (p. 182): It is not Lady Macbeth's need of

them in every instance produced by some pressure of difficulty or perplexity upon
<I>himself</I>, which he feels his own resolution unequal to meet, and so flies for support
to her superior firmness: he does not consult her as to the <I>formation</I> of his purposes
&mdash;he is too selfish and headstrong for that; he simply uses her moral courage, as he
seeks to use all other things, as an indispensable instrument to stay his own falter-

<I>already formed.</I> [See note by D'Hugues, III, ii, 37.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

<P>68. <B>To morrow . . . purposes]</B> J. <SC>Coleman</SC> (<I>Gentleman's
Maga.</I> March, 1889):
As Salvini played this, Macbeth was not one likely to wait for his better half to
suggest the &lquo;removal&rquo; of Duncan. In reply to the enquiry, &lquo;and when goes hence?&rquo;
he paused one moment, looked furtively round as he replied: &lquo;Tomorrow, as <I>he</I>
purposes&rquo;; and when Lady Macbeth made answer: &lquo;Never shall sun that morrow
see!&rquo; his face lighted up with murder written on every line of it, His doubts and
fears in the following scenes were admirably rendered.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.&mdash;W. W. <SC>Story</SC> (p.
268): &lquo;Tomorrow,&rquo; he answers, and pauses; and adds, &lquo;as he purposes.&rquo; But in
the look and in the pause Lady Macbeth has read his whole soul and intent. There
is murder in that look; and she cries: &lquo;Your face, my thane, is as a book, where
men May read strange matters.&rquo; There is no explanation between them. He has
conveyed all his intention by a look and a gesture, as she distinctly says. . . . (p. 270):
There is no warrant of any kind that, in the simple words &lquo;And when goes hence?&rquo;
she meant more than she said. It was the most natural question that she could
possibly ask. Granting that she intended equally with him to commit the murder,
what is more natural than that she should wish to know how soon it was necessary
to carry out the plan of murder, and what time there was to make all the arrange-
ments?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.</CC>

<P>69, 70. <B>O neuer . . . see]</B> <SC>Bell</SC> (p. 303): [Mrs Siddons uttered] &lquo;O never&rquo; with

her eye steadfast. Strong, dwelling emphasis on &lquo;never shall sun that morrow see.&rquo;
Low, very slow sustained voice, her eye and her mind occupied steadfastly in the
contemplation of her horrible purpose, pronunciation almost syllabic, note unvaried.

<CC><P>In observation his faculty is microscopical; a wide and extended view of natural
scenery he will not pourtray. With unerring accuracy of eye he seizes on particular
objects, investing them with the lively hues of his exuberant imagination; he does
not see, he does not choose to describe, an entire landscape. . . . What is perhaps
the most noticeable of all is, that in his sketches, incomplete as they are, of natural
scenery, he scarcely ever mentions that form of it which is now held as the most
enchanting, sublime, and attractive to cultivated minds&mdash;the scenery, namely, of
mountainous regions. . . . Whatever else the great poet saw in nature, he apparently
could not see the grandeur of the everlasting hills; &lquo;the difficult air of the iced
mountain top&rquo; was by him unbreathed and unknown. Once only, in the whole
range of his works (unless we should except some slight references in <I>Cymbeline</I>),
does he introduce his readers to the heart of a wild and hilly region. . . . The allu-
sions to the site of Macbeth's castle happen to be perfectly correct; the wonder
is how the writer should have been conversant with such details. . . . [Whether
Shakespeare described the scene from personal observation or from an inspiration
of genius], the puzzle is how the describer should have overlooked other features
of infinitely more prominence and importance in the landscape surrounding Inver-
ness&mdash;the magnificent sweep of river and estuary, and the grand domination of the
different mountain ranges.
<P>5. <B>seat]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC> (<I>Obs.</I> 1745): I propose <I>site</I>, as the ancient word for <I>situation.</I>
[Capell also made this conjecture.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.] For the sake of the measure, I adjust
line 11, &lquo;Smells wooingly. Here is no jutting frieze.&rquo; [As Dr Johnson did not
repeat these emendations in his edition of 1765, we may presume that they were
withdrawn.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Reed</SC>: Compare Bacon's <I>Essays</I>, xlv.: &lquo;He that builds a faire
house upon an <I>ill seat</I>, committeth himself to prison. Neither doe I reckon it an
<I>ill seat</I>, only where the aire is unwholesome, but likewise where the aire is unequal;
as you shall see many fine <I>seats</I> set upon a knap of ground invironed with higher
hills round about it.&mdash;<SC>Sir J. Reynolds</SC>: This short dialogue between Duncan and
Banquo has always appeared to me a striking instance of what in painting is termed
<I>repose.</I> Their conversation very naturally turns upon the beauty of [the castle's] situ-
ation, and the pleasantness of the air; and Banquo, observing the martlets&rquo; nests in
every recess of the cornice, remarks, that where those birds most breed and haunt, the
air is delicate. The subject of this quiet and easy conversation gives that repose so nec-
essary to the mind after the tumultuous bustle of the preceding scenes, and perfectly
contrasts the scene of horror that immediately succeeds. It seems as if Shakespeare
asked himself, What is a prince likely to say to his attendants on such an occasion?
Whereas the modern writers seem, on the contrary, to be always searching for new
thoughts, such as would never occur to men in the situation which is represented.
This also is frequently the practice of Homer, who, from the midst of battles and
horrors, relieves and refreshes the mind of the reader by introducing some quiet rural
image, or picture of familiar domestic life. [See also, to the same effect, <SC>Reed</SC>,
<I>Lectures</I>, etc. p. 231.&mdash;<SC>Knowles</SC> (p. 24): I am inclined to take a different view of
the subject [from that expressed by Reynolds in the preceding note], and to con-
sider this scene as another and a higher step in the climax of the action. That
Duncan should contemplate with satisfaction the seat of Macbeth's castle, and that
Banquo should participate in the feelings of the King, are perfectly natural; but
that the audience should partake this view, is as preposterous as to suppose that we</CC>

<CC><P>could see a man about to step into a cavern which we know to be the den of a wild
beast, and participate in his admiration of the foliage which might happen to adorn
its entrance. So far, if I mistake not, from there being any relaxing of the interest
here, there is an absolute straining of it. The unconsciousness of the destined
victim to the fate that awaited it, the smiling flowers that dressed it, and its playful
motions as it walked to the altar of sacrifice must have served, not to assuage, but
to aggravate in the beholder the feeling of its predicament. There is no relief&mdash;no
repose here. How often in witnessing this scene have I felt a wish that some sus-
picion of foul play would flash across the mind of Banquo, and that he would hang
upon the robes of the king and implore him not to enter.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

which shoots forward beyond the rest. See Florio's <I>It. Dict.</I> 1598: &lquo;<I>Barbacane.</I>
An outnooke or corner standing out of a house; a jettie.&rquo; &lquo;<I>Sporto</I>, a porch, a por-
tall, a baie window, or out butting, or iettie of a house that ietties out farther than
anie other part of the house, a iettie or butte.&rquo; See also <I>Surpendu&euml;</I>, in Cotgrave:
&lquo;A <I>jettie;</I> an outjetting room.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: Shakespeare uses the verb <I>to jutty</I> in
<I>Hen. V:</I> III, i, 13.&mdash;<SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> ii, 14) conjectures that a word is here omitted.

<P>12. <B>Coigne of Vantage]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: Convenient corner.&mdash;<SC>Hunter</SC>: It is remark-

neous. In the <I>Porta Linguarum Trilinguis</I>, an <I>advantage</I> is described &lquo;a some-
thing added to a building, as a jutting.&rquo; The following, from the <I>Pacata Hibernia</I>,
contains something which approaches the nearest of anything I have found to the

French reading, perhaps, supplied him with it.&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Few Notes</I>, etc.): <I>Coigne</I>
is certainly a word of rare occurrence: &lquo;And Cape of Hope, last <I>coign</I> of Africa.&rquo;&mdash;

<CC><P>ities where the air is especially pure and delicate. The observation, however, is
borne out so far by MacGillivray, who remarks that though they are to be found
chiefly in the neighbourhood of towns, villages, and farm buildings in the more
populous parts of the country, yet small colonies of them will establish themselves
on the margin of the moors and wild glens of the pastoral regions, in the valleys of
the upper districts of the Clyde, the Tweed, the Dee, and the Tay, where they will
build on the inns and larger houses. As for their &lquo;temple-haunting&rquo; propensities,
the observation is as old at least as the Hebrew psalter.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
<P>15. <B>Enter Lady]</B> <SC>Noel</SC> (p. 16): I am inclined to believe that, could she have
seen that her own life might be wrecked in this venture, and Macbeth still secure all
that his ambition craved, her dauntless spirit would have urged her on, in spite of
everything, and her smile would have been as sweet, her tones as solicitous, and her
white hand would have neither faltered nor trembled in the grasp of her sovereign
victim.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
<P>17. <B>sometime]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: That is, <I>sometimes.</I> The two forms are used indif-
ferently by Shakespeare. In many cases editors have altered the original reading
where it contradicted the modern distinction between the words. See IV, ii, 88.
<P>17-20. <B>The Loue . . . your trouble]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: The passage is undoubtedly ob-
scure, and the following is the best explication of it I can offer: Marks of respect, impor-
tunately shown, are sometimes troublesome, though we are still bound to be grateful
for them, as indications of sincere attachment. If you pray for us on account of the
trouble we create in your house, and thank us for the molestations we bring with us,
it must be on such a principle. Herein I teach you, that the inconvenience you suffer,
is the result of our affection; and that you are therefore to pray for us, or thank us,
only as far as prayers and thanks can be deserved for kindnesses that fatigue, and
honours that oppress. You are, in short, to make your acknowledgments for in-
tended respect and love, however irksome our present mode of expressing them
may have proved. To &lquo;bid&rquo; is here used in the Saxon sense&mdash;to <I>pray.</I>&mdash;<SC>Knight</SC>:
The love which follows us is sometimes troublesome; so we give you trouble, but look
you only at the love we bear to you, and so bless us and thank us.&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC>: Dun-
can says that even love sometimes occasions him trouble, but that he thanks it as love
notwithstanding; and that thus he teaches Lady Macbeth, while she takes trouble on
his account, to &lquo;bid God yield,&rquo; or reward, him for giving that trouble.&mdash;<SC>Hunter</SC>: The
affection which urges us to desire the society of our friends is sometimes the occasion
of trouble to them; but still we feel grateful for the affection which is manifested.</CC>

lable; but the Latin word was also adapted in Old French, (<I>h</I>)<I>eremite</I>, and this was

mite&rquo; (always spelt without the unetymological <I>h</I>) is used either poetically or rhetor-

<CC><P>1. <SC>Vischer</SC> (ii, 80): This is one of the most important scenes in the whole play.
We find that conscience has gained the mastery with Macbeth. He has withdrawn
from the banquet, and stands aloof in the hall. A significant and subtile touch by the
Poet. His inward monitor gives him no rest; and, wholly lost in thought, he debates
with himself upon all that should deter him from the murder.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.&mdash;<SC>Knowles</SC>:
The closing scene of this act is a higher point of the climax still: the last debate
as to innocence and crime. It commences with the soliloquy of Macbeth, which, I con-
fess, I have seldom heard spoken with that perturbation which appears to me to suit it.
The manner in which this soliloquy is generally delivered reminds me of the seaman
who is accustomed to the gale, and sits cool and collected at the helm, though at
every yard there yawns a grave before him. I would have it an entirely different
thing. Macbeth is no such seaman. There should be infinite discomfiture and con-
fusion in it. It should be delivered by fits and starts. I would attempt to give a
reading of it did I not know that conception and execution are different things. The
one is the soul and the other the body, and the body does not always correspond to
the soul. This soliloquy is in fine keeping with the character of Macbeth, and fur-
nishes rich groundwork for the dialogue which immediately follows between him
and Lady Macbeth, and which advances the action to another stage&mdash;that where the
murder of Duncan is eventually determined upon.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
<P>3. <B>Sewer]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: In Chapman's <I>Iliad</I>, lib. xxiv: &lquo;Automedon as fit was for
the reverend <I>sewer's</I> place; and all the browne joints serv'd On wicker vessel,&rquo; etc.
Another part of the <I>sewer's</I> office was to bring water for the guests to wash their hands
with; his chief mark of distinction was a towel round his arm. In Ben Jonson's <I>Silent
Woman:</I> &lquo;&mdash; clap me a clean <I>towel</I> about you, like a <I>sewer</I>,&rquo; [III, i.].&mdash;<SC>Claren-
don</SC>: From the French <I>essayeur</I>, and meant originally one who tasted of each dish to
prove that there was no poison in it. Afterwards it was applied to the chief servant,
who directed the placing of the dishes on the table. In Palsgrave, <I>Eclaircissement de la
Langue Fran&ccedil;aise</I>, we have the verb thus: &lquo;I sewe at meate. <I>Je taste.</I>&rquo; So again in
Holinshed, ii, p. 1129, col. 2, &lquo;the Esquier that was accustomed, to sew and take
the assay before Kyng Richarde.&rquo; What is included in the word &lquo;service&rquo; may be
illustrated by the following stage-direction from Heywood's <I>A Woman Killed with
Kindness:</I> &lquo;Enter Butler and Jenkin with a table-cloth, bread, trenchers, and salt,&rquo;
[p. 265, ed. Dodsley].&mdash;<SC>Delius</SC>: After the sewer and his attendants have passed
over the stage, a long pause is to be assumed before the entrance of Macbeth, during
which the feast in honor of Duncan begins and continues.</CC>

<CC><P>5-7. <B>If it . . . Consequence]</B> &lquo;X.&rquo; (<I>Courier</I>, Boston, 25 Ap. 1857): I have
never felt perfectly satisfied with any rendering of these two lines in <I>Macbeth</I> that it has
been my fortune to hear. The words, &lquo;It were done quickly,&rquo; sound supernumerary
and out of place, as they are generally recited. They hang like an encumbrance.
They clog the movement of the verse. Above all, they drag in a new and inferior
thought, after the great argument has been sufficiently pronounced. Cut them off,
then, from their connection with the preceding line, which they do but cumber, and
see what new force you will give to the whole soliloquy: &lquo;If it were Done when 'tis
done, then 'twere well.&rquo; There is the full theme and true key-note of the piece.
It is complete in itself. It prepares the way for all that follows. It announces the
terrible problem with which Macbeth's unsteady purpose was wrestling. It reminds
us of the first line of Hamlet's bewildered self-confidence: &lquo;To be, or not to be;
that is the question.&rquo; The speaker may well pause, in both cases, when he comes
to that point of the awful debate. And there the rather, because by such a course
the sentence that follows will be as much enriched by what it gains, as the sentence
that precedes is relieved by what it surrenders. The clause, that seemed almost
impertinent where it stood, becomes a reinforcement in its new relation: &lquo;It were
done quickly, if the assassination Could trammel up the consequence,&rquo; etc. Observe
how much clearer and more compact the rest of the period becomes by beginning it
in this new way.&mdash;R. G. <SC>White</SC>: The punctuation of the Folios, in which the colon
[after &lquo;quickly&rquo;] takes the place (as it so often does) of a comma, or rather indicates
a sectional pause in the rhythm, has been preserved, with the exception of the super-
fluous comma at the end of the first line, in every edition of the play that I have exam-
ined. The consequence has been an almost universal misapprehension of the signifi-
cance of these lines, even among actors, by whom they are generally read as if they
meant, &lquo;If the murder is to be done, when I do it I had better do it quickly.&rquo; But
this thought is not only very tame, and therefore entirely unsuited to the situation,
and inexpressive of the speaker's mental state, but entirely incongruous with the
succeeding passage of the soliloquy, which is the expansion of a single thought and
a single feeling twin-born&mdash;consciousness of guilt and dread of punishment in a sen-
sitive, imaginative nature, devoid of moral firmness. Macbeth's first thought is, that
when the murder is done, the end is not yet, either here or hereafter; and this
thought possesses him entirely, until he sees the poisoned chalice commended to his
own lips. So Shakespeare, using, as his custom was, one word, &lquo;done,&rquo; in two
senses, makes the prospective murderer of his guest, his kinsman and his king say,
&mdash;and with emphasis,&mdash;&lquo;If it were <I>done</I> [ended] when 'tis done [performed], <I>then</I> it
would be well. It were done [ended] quickly if the assassination could clear itself
from all consequences,&rquo; and so on, to show that 'tis not <I>done</I> when 'tis done, and
therefore it is <I>not</I> well. Only with this punctuation, and with this signification, can
the first part of this soliloquy have a becoming dignity, and its parts a due connec-
tion. Yet, strange to say, in all that has been written about it, with a single excep-</CC>

that murder is a game which two parties can play at, that heartlessness has the
effect of drawing general attention, that ambition is apt to defeat its own object.&mdash;

<P>6-11. <B>If th' Assassination . . . to come]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: If the murder could termi-
nate in itself, and restrain the regular course of consequences, if <I>its success</I> could secure
<I>its surcease</I>, if, being once done <I>successfully</I>, without detection, it could <I>fix a period</I> to
all vengeance and inquiry, so that <I>this blow</I> might be all that I have to do, and this anx-
iety all that I have to suffer; if this could be my condition, even <I>here</I> in <I>this world</I>, in
this contracted period of temporal existence, on this narrow <I>bank</I> in the ocean of
eternity, <I>I would jump the life to come</I>, I would venture upon the deed without care
of any future state. But this is one of <I>those cases</I> in which judgement is pronounced
and vengeance inflicted upon us <I>here</I> in our present life. We teach others to do as
we have done, and are punished by our own example.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: <I>His</I> is used
instead of <I>its</I> in many places.&mdash;<SC>Jennens</SC>: &lquo;His&rquo; refers to Duncan, and the meaning
is: If the assassination of Duncan would secure me the consequence I aim at, and
procure me with his <I>surcease</I>, or death, success to my ambitious designs, etc.&mdash;
<SC>Elwin</SC>: <I>His</I> relates to <I>consequence.</I> The literal meaning of the passage is, <I>If the
assassination could net up its own consequence, and catch with his</I> (the conse-
quence's) <I>stop, success</I>, etc.&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC>: The obscurity which critics lament in this
passage is due to themselves. If, instead of taking &lquo;success&rquo; in its modern sense of
<I>prosperity</I>, they had understood it according to its usual acceptation in Shake-
speare's day as <I>sequel, what follows</I>, etc., they must have perceived at once that to
&lquo;<I>catch</I>, with his surcease, <I>success</I>,&rquo; is no more than an enforcement of &lquo;trammel up
the consequence.&rquo; The meaning obviously being: If the assassination were an abso-
lutely final act, and could shut up all consecution,&mdash;&lquo;be the be-all and end-all&rquo; even
of this life only,&mdash;we would run the hazard of a future state. [See <SC>Keightley's</SC>
just interpretation of &lquo;life to come,&rquo; line 11, <I>post.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

<P>8. <B>surcease]</B> <SC>Collier</SC>: To &lquo;surcease&rquo; is to finish or conclude, and the mean-

superseding a jurisdiction. As a substantive it is found here only in Shakespeare.
He twice uses the verb &lquo;surcease,&rquo; both times in the sense of <I>cease.</I> We are inclined
to agree with Elwin that &lquo;his&rquo; refers to &lquo;consequence&rquo;: &lquo;If the murder could pre-
vent its consequence, and by the arrest of that consequence secure success.&rquo;

<CC><P>nothing for the world to come. &lquo;Time&rquo; should be printed with a capital letter.
The &lquo;bank and shoal of Time&rquo; is a favorite image, almost trite; the isthmus be-
tween two eternities.&mdash;<SC>Elwin</SC>: Bank is used for <I>bench</I>, and <I>time</I> for <I>mortal life;</I>
which, qualified as <I>a bench and school of instruction</I>, is placed in antithesis to <I>the
life to come.</I> Here the idea of calling this life <I>the school of eternity</I>, as preparing
man for the part he is to perform there, is not only thoroughly in accordance with
the truthful genius of Shakespeare, but it is beautifully sustained in the expressions
that follow it, &lquo;that we but <I>teach</I> bloody instructions.&rquo; The feeling expressed is
this: If here only, upon this bench of instruction, in this school of eternity, I could
do this without bringing these, my pupil days, under suffering, I would hazard its
effect on the endless life to come.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: &lquo;Schoole&rquo; is the same word as
<I>shoal</I>, only differently spelt. Human life is compared to a narrow strip of land
in an ocean.

<CC><P>25. <B>Babe]</B> <SC>Vischer</SC> (vol. iii, part i, p. 127): We must be very guarded in con-
demning as offences against taste those bold flashes in passages where pathos speaks
its loftier language, and where Shakespeare for the highest poetic purpose offends
the prosaic ideas of order and measure, as <I>e. g.</I> in the frightfully grand words of
Macbeth [in the present passage]. Thus, too, the words of Goethe in the noble
Song of Mignon, &lquo;My bowels burn,&rquo; are no offence against taste, but are high above
all barren taste with its ideas of propriety.&mdash;(Vol. iii, part ii, p. 1237): In this fear-
ful vision all the consequences of Duncan's murder are grouped together; what the
drama has hitherto portrayed in chiaroscuro is here unfolded in clearer treatment: it
is not in the mouth of every character that the poet would dare to put such wild,
extravagant, phantasmagoric images; they are reserved for the hero, with his nervous
temperament, at a moment of the highest tension, when at a glance he scans a horri-
ble future. All of Shakespeare's images have something peculiarly sudden and
emotional; they remind us of flickering crimson torchlight illuminating a cavern of
stalactites, while, on the other hand, the metaphors of the Greeks and of Goethe rise
calmly like the sun, and disclose feature after feature of the landscape in sharp, clear
outline. This is epic; the Greek tragedians have undoubtedly something of Shake-
speare's impassioned, unearthly glow, but cooled in a plastic mould of feeling.&mdash;
[<SC>Paton</SC>: If not otherwise acquainted with it, Shakespeare would certainly, if
in the Macbeth country, become, in his study of local superstitions, informed of
the belief in the &lquo;little Spectres called <I>tarans</I>, or the souls of unbaptised infants,
often seen flitting among the woods and secret places, bewailing in soft voices their
hard fate.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Moberly</SC>: Either like a mortal babe, terrible in helplessness; or like
heaven's child-angels, mighty in love and compassion. This magnificent passage
seems founded on the history of Darnley's murder, &lquo;The banner (of the confederates
against Queen Mary) was spread between two spears. The figure of a dead man
was wrought on it, lying under a tree . . . and a child on its knees at its side, stretch-

(Froude, ix, p. 86).&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

<CC><P>forms were all fashioned on <I>cherubin.</I> The earliest English instances are of <I>cerubin,
cherubin</I>, taken over from ecclesiastical Latin apparently as a foreign word, and
treated implicitly as a singular, sometimes as a proper name, at other times as a col-
lective. From the Middle English period the popular forms were, as in French,
<I>cherubin</I> singular, <I>cherubins</I> plural. <I>Cherubin</I> survived in popular use to the
18th century; but in the <I>Bible</I> translations, <I>cherub</I> was introduced from the Vul-
gate by Wyclif, was kept up by the 16th century translators, and gradually drove
<I>cherubin</I> into the position of an illiterate form. In the plural, <I>cherubins</I> is found
from the 13th century; and although in MSS of the earlier Wyclifite version, <I>cheru-
byn</I> is more frequent (after the Vulgate), the later version has always <I>cherubins;</I> this
was retained in ordinary use till the 17th century. But in the 16th century acquaint-
ance with the Hebrew led <I>Bible</I> translators to substitute <I>cherubims:</I> this occurs only
once in Coverdale, but always in the Bishops' Bible and version of 1611. From the
beginning of the 17th century <I>cherubim</I> began to be preferred by scholars (<I>e. g.</I>
Milton) to <I>cherubims</I>, and has gradually taken its place; the Revised Version of
1881-5 has adopted it. A native plural, <I>cherubs</I>, arose early in the 16th century; in
Tindale, Coverdale, and later versions (but not in that of 1611) it occurs beside
<I>cherubins, -ims;</I> it is now the ordinary individual plural, the Biblical plural being
more or less collective. Briefly, then, <I>cherubin, cherubins</I> are the original English
forms, as still in French.&mdash;<SC>Vischer</SC> (p. 81): This passage suggests that some picture
of the last Judgement had recurred to the mind of Shakespeare. It is possible that
an engraving of Michael Angelo's fresco was not unknown to the Poet. Or had
he seen anywhere, perchance, a representation of some such scene; the sky full of
flying clouds, whereon spirits ride, calling down vengeance on the sins of the world?
We know not; nor does it much concern us, since what he has here said no painter
could so well express in outlines.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

scouring winds that <I>sightless</I> in the sounding air do fly.&rquo; [For adjectives with both
active and passive meaning, see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 3; compare I, iv, 15.]

<CC><C>[29-32. <B>I haue . . . th' other]</B></C>
<P>in Spenser and elsewhere, from the Latin and Italian. [This note was quoted by
Arrowsmith, <I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> vii, 522.]&mdash;<SC>Knight</SC>: We can scarcely admit the necessity
for a change of the original. A person (and &lquo;vaulting ambition&rquo; is personified)
might be said to <I>overleap</I> himself, as well as overbalance himself, or overcharge
himself, or overlabor himself, or overmeasure himself, or overreach himself. There
is a parallel use of the word <I>over</I> in Beaumont &amp; Fletcher: &lquo;&mdash; it may be your
sense was set too high, and so overwrought itself,&rquo; [<I>The Woman-Hater</I>, Act IV,
sc. ii; p. 72, ed. Dyce.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]. The word <I>over</I> in all these cases is used in
the sense of <I>too much.</I> Macbeth compares his &lquo;intent&rquo; to a courser; I have
no spur to urge him on. Unprepared, I am about to vault into my seat, but I
overleap myself and fall. It appears to us that the sentence is broken by the
entrance of the messenger; that it is not complete in itself, and would not have
been completed with <I>side.</I>&mdash;<SC>Hunter</SC>: The word <I>oft</I> seems lost before &lquo;o'erleaps,&rquo;
and the word <I>side</I> is wanting to make the sense complete.&mdash;<SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> iii,
253): Evidently, th' other <I>side;</I> and this adds one to the apparently numerous
instances of omission in this play.&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC>: <I>Side</I> may have been meant by
the Poet, but it was not said. And the sense <I>feels</I> better without it, as this
shows the speaker to be in such an eagerly-expectant state of mind as to break
off the instant he had a prospect of any news. The use of <I>self</I> for <I>aim</I> or <I>pur-
pose</I> is quite lawful and idiomatic; as we often say, such a one <I>overshot himself</I>&mdash;
that is, overshot his mark, his aim.&mdash;R. G. <SC>White</SC>: Perhaps <I>side</I> was meant to be
understood, with reference to the occurrence of the word in the preceding clause
of the sentence.&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC>: The only resolution of the enigma which presents
itself to our mind is to suppose <I>intent</I> and <I>ambition</I> are represented in Macbeth's
disordered imagination by two steeds, the one lacking all incentive to motion, the
other so impulsive that it overreaches itself and falls on its companion.&mdash;<SC>Massey</SC>
(p. 599): As the text stands, we have in shadowy imagery a most extraordinary
horse and rider. Macbeth was no more likely to wear a single spur that <I>would</I>
strike on <I>both</I> sides than the Irishman was to discover the gun that would shoot
round the corner. Moreover, his horse must have had three sides to it at the
least. Now a horse may have four sides, right and left, inside and outside, and the
street <I>gamins</I> will at times advise an awkward horseman to ride inside for safety,
but it cannot have three sides. And if the single spur had pricked <I>two sides</I>, there
could have been no <I>other</I> left for &lquo;vaulting ambition&rquo; to fall on. The truth is, that
&lquo;sides&rquo; is a misprint. The single spur of course implies a single <I>side</I>&mdash;the side of
Macbeth's intent, which leaves &lquo;<I>the other</I>&rquo; for the &lquo;vaulting ambition&rquo; to alight on
in case of a somersault&mdash;the side of Macbeth's <I>unintent.</I> Read, &lquo;To prick the <I>side</I>
of my intent,&rquo; etc.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: Macbeth says he has nothing to goad him on to
the deed&mdash;nothing to stimulate his flagging purpose, like the private wrongs which
he urges upon the murderers of Banquo&mdash;but mere ambition, which is like one who,
instead of leaping into the saddle, leaps too far and falls on the other side. The
passage supplies a good example of confusion of metaphors. If the sentence be com-
plete, &lquo;the other&rquo; must be taken to mean &lquo;the other side,&rquo; a not unnatural ellipsis,
but one for which we can adduce no example. The word &lquo;sell&rquo; occurs frequently
in Fairfax's <I>Tasso</I>, as, <I>e. g.</I> Bk. vi, st. 32: &lquo;That he ne'er shook nor stagger'd in
his sell.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Abbott</SC>: See note on I, ii, 12.&mdash;<SC>Rev. John Hunter</SC>: This seems to
me to signify <I>lights on the opposite side of what was intended;</I> that is, dishonor
and wretchedness, instead of glory and felicity.&mdash;[J. B. <SC>Bittinger</SC> (<I>Trans. Am.</I></CC>

<CC><P><I>Philological Assoc.</I> 1876): Macbeth must be a murderer before he can be a mon-
arch. If the intent to murder halts, the desire to mount the throne will be futile.
All this Macbeth knows and feels. He does not repine at any lack of ambition;
that is in full force and action; it is o'erwrought: but over his purpose he mourns&mdash;
that is infirm; over his courage&mdash;that needs &lquo;screwing to the sticking place&rquo;; and
so, like an eager rider on a sluggish steed, he o'erleaps himself and &lquo;<I>falls on the
withers</I>,&rquo; and so Shakespeare wrote. . . . This reading seems to me to meet all
the demands of the passage. <I>Withers</I> calls for no explanation, it explains itself.
Whether copied by eye or ear, it was easy to mistake in sound or appearance &lquo;other&rquo;
for <I>withers.</I> This reading charges Shakespeare with no mixed or imperfect meta-
phors. It leaves his rhetoric and imagination unsuspect, brings the whole passage
into harmony with itself and with the character of Macbeth&mdash;too ambitious to be
innocent in thought, too cowardly to be guilty in deed. His imagination sicklied
o'er with the pale cast of conscience, he is vacillating in purpose, irresolute in action,
and querulous in speech.&mdash;<SC>Sherman</SC>: That is, <I>but only ambition that leaps up from

<CC><P>54, 55. <B>I . . . none]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: The arguments by which Lady Macbeth per-
suades her husband to commit the murder afford a proof of Shakespeare's knowl-
edge of human nature. She urges the excellence and dignity of courage, a glittering
idea which has dazzled mankind from age to age, and animated sometimes the
housebreaker and sometimes the conqueror; but this sophism Macbeth has for ever
destroyed, by distinguishing true from false fortitude, in a line and a half; of which
it may almost be said, that they ought to bestow immortality on the author, though all
his other productions had been lost. [The present lines here follow.] This topic,
which has been always employed with too much success, is used in this scene, with
peculiar propriety, to a soldier by a woman. Courage is the distinguishing virtue of
a soldier; and the reproach of cowardice cannot be borne by any man from a woman
without great impatience. She then urges the oaths by which he had bound him-
self to murder Duncan, another art of sophistry by which men have sometimes
deluded their conscience, and persuaded themselves that what would be criminal in
others is virtuous in them: this argument Shakespeare, whose plan obliged him to
make Macbeth yield, has not confuted, though he might easily have shown that a
former obligation could not be vacated by a latter; that obligations, laid on us by a
higher power, could not be overruled by obligations which we lay upon ourselves.&mdash;
<SC>Steevens</SC>: A similar passage to this occurs in <I>Meas. for Meas.</I> II, iv, 134, 135:
&lquo;Be that you are, That is a woman; if you be more you're none.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Hunter</SC>: This
reading [Rowe's], which is merely conjectural, and has not the slightest show of
authority from the only copies through which we receive any information respecting
the true text as it flowed from the pen of Shakespeare, has so established itself in
public opinion, and has received such extravagant praise from Dr Johnson, that he
will be thought a rash man who shall attempt to disturb the opinion, and to show
that it is not really what the Poet wrote or intended. In the first place, the substi-
tution of <I>do</I> for &lquo;no&rquo; is most violent. In the second place, if, indeed, Shakespeare
meant to express the sentiment, which the line as <I>amended</I> implies, he has written
feebly and imperfectly, and left his sense in some, perhaps not inconsiderable,
obscurity. It will be admitted that some change in the text as delivered to us is
required; that it cannot stand as it appears in the original editions. The question is,
not whether it shall be restored, but <I>how</I> it shall be restored? and I now venture to
propose that the second of the two lines (&lquo;Who . . . none&rquo;) shall be given to Lady
Macbeth, retaining the exact text of the old copies. [See also, to the same effect,
Hunter's <I>Few Words</I>, etc. p. 20, 1853.&mdash;<SC>Vischer</SC> (ii, p. 83): Macbeth's answer is
difficult to translate into German. It is true, the German language has an advantage
over the English, in that it distinguishes between &lquo;man,&rquo; mankind [Mensch], and
&lquo;man,&rquo; the individual [Mann], but the difficulty here arises from the fact that Eng-
lish, as well as French and Italian, having but one word for the two ideas, often has
both ideas in mind. This twofold thought is here contained in the word &lquo;man.&rquo;&mdash;
<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]</CC>

<I>Advancement of Learning</I>, i, 4, &sect; 1: &lquo;&mdash; it is the manner of men to scandalize
and deprave that which retaineth the state and virtue.&rquo;

<P>67. <B>sworne]</B> <SC>Seymour</SC>: The measure of the line is complete without &lquo;so.&rquo;&mdash;
<SC>Hudson</SC>: It is said that Mrs Siddons used to utter the close of this speech in a
scream, as though she were almost frightened out of her wits by the audacity of her
own tongue. And I can easily conceive how a spasmodic action of fear might lend
to such a woman as Lady Macbeth an appearance of superhuman or inhuman bold-
ness. At all events, it should be observed that her energy and intensity of purpose
overbears the feelings of the woman; and her convulsive struggle of feeling against
that overbearing violence of will might well be expressed by a scream.&mdash;[<SC>Vischer</SC>
(ii, p. 84): This overcomes Macbeth. And here is the moral turning-point in the
drama.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]</CC>

<CC><P>69. <B>If we should faile]</B> <SC>Moulton</SC> (p. 161): Here is the critical point of the
scene. At its beginning Macbeth is for abandoning the treason, at its end he pre-
pares for his task of murder with animation: where does the change come? <I>The
practical man is nerved by having the practical details supplied to him.</I> Lady Mac-
beth sketches a feasible scheme: how that the King will be wearied, his chamber-
lains can by means of the banquet be easily drugged, their confusion on waking can
be interpreted as guilt&mdash;before she has half done her husband interrupts her with a
burst of enthusiasm, and completes her scheme for her. The man who had thought
it was manliness that made him shrink from murder henceforward never hesitates
till he has plunged his dagger in his sovereign's bosom.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
<P>70. <B>We faile?]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: Macbeth having casually employed the former part
of the common phrase, <I>If we fail, we fail</I>, his wife designedly completes it. &lquo;We
fail,&rquo; and thereby know the extent of our misfortune. Lady Macbeth is unwilling
to afford her husband time to state any reasons for his doubt. Such an interval for
reflection to act in might have proved unfavorable to her purposes. This reply, at
once cool and determined, is sufficiently characteristic of the speaker: according to
the old punctuation, she is represented as rejecting with contempt (of which she
had already manifested enough) the very idea of failure. According to the mode
of pointing now suggested, she admits a possibility of miscarriage, but at the same
instant shows herself not afraid of the result. Her answer, therefore, communicates
no discouragement to her husband. &lquo;We fail!&rquo;&mdash;is the hasty interruption of scornful
impatience. &lquo;We fail.&rquo;&mdash;is the calm deduction of a mind which, having weighed all
circumstances, is prepared, without loss of confidence in itself, for the worst that
can happen.&mdash;<SC>Mrs Jameson</SC> (ii, 319): Mrs Siddons adopted successively three
different intonations in giving the words &lquo;We fail.&rquo; At first as a quick contemptuous
interrogation. Afterwards with the note of admiration, and an accent of indignant
astonishment, laying the emphasis on &lquo;we.&rquo; Lastly, she fixed on what I am con-
vinced is the true reading&mdash;we fail, with the simple period, modulating her voice to
a deep, low, resolute tone, which settled the issue at once&mdash;as though she had said,
&lquo;If we fail, why then we fail, and all is over.&rquo; This is consistent with the dark
fatalism of the character, and the sense of the line following&mdash;and the effect was
sublime, almost awful.&mdash;<SC>Knight</SC>: We prefer the quiet self-possession of the punc-
tuation we have adopted. [See <I>Text. Notes.</I>]&mdash;<SC>Fletcher</SC> (p. 121): Her quiet reply,
&lquo;We fail,&rquo; is every way most characteristic of the speaker&mdash;expressing that moral
firmness in herself which makes her quite prepared to endure the consequence of
failure&mdash;and, at the same time, conveying the most decisive rebuke of such moral
cowardice in her husband as can make him recede from a purpose merely on account
of the possibility of defeat&mdash;a possibility which, up to the very completion of their
design, seems never absent from her own mind, though she finds it necessary to
banish it from that of her husband.&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Remarks</I>, etc.): There is in reality no
difference; whether the words be pointed &lquo;We fail!&rquo; or &lquo;We fail?&rquo; (and I much</CC>

<P>71. <B>sticking place]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: A metaphor perhaps taken from the <I>screwing

in <I>Coriol.</I> I, viii, 11. Compare also <I>Tro. &amp; Cres.</I> III, iii, 22-25 As &lquo;wrest&rquo; is an
instrument for tuning a harp, this last cited passage lends some probability to Steev-
ens's interpretation.&mdash;[<SC>Paton</SC>: The metaphor used was probably suggested by some-
thing like what may be seen in, for instance, the illustration of the Earl of Hay-
nault taking and destroying Aubenton, in Froissart's <I>Chronicles</I>, namely, two sol-
diers, lapt in proof; one with his crossbow planted at an angle against the ground,
&lquo;screwing&rquo; by means of a kind of windlass its cord to &lquo;the sticking place,&rquo; or
catch, by which it will be held at furthest stretch.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

<P>76-78. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: By the old anatomists (Vigo, fol. 6 b, ed. 1586) the brain
was divided into three ventricles, in the hindermost of which they placed the
memory. That this division was not unknown to Shakespeare we learn from <I>Love's
Lab. L.</I> IV, ii, 70. The third ventricle is the cerebellum, by which the brain is
connected with the spinal marrow and the rest of the body: the memory is posted
in the cerebellum like a warder or sentinel to warn the reason against attack.
When the memory is converted by intoxication into a mere fume (compare <I>Temp.</I>
V, i, 67), then it fills the brain itself, the receipt or receptacle of reason, which
thus becomes like an alembic or cap of a still. For &lquo;$ume,&rquo; compare <I>Cymb.</I> IV,
ii, 301. And Dryden's <I>Aurengzebe:</I> &lquo;Power like new wine does your weak brain
surprise, And its mad fumes in hot discourses rise.&rquo; See also <I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.</I> II,
i, 24.
<P>77. <B>Receit]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: See Bacon, <I>Essay</I>, xlvi.: &lquo;Fountains . . . one that
sprinckleth or spouteth water; the other a faire receipt of water.&rquo;
<P>78. <B>Lymbeck]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Derived by popular corruption from &lquo;alembic,&rquo; a
word adopted from the language of the Arabian alchemists of Spain into all the
languages of Europe. The word is formed from <I>al</I>, the Arabic definite article, and
the Greek <G><*>mbic</G>, used by Dioscorides in the sense of the cap of a still, into which
the fumes rise before they pass into the condensing vessel. The word &lquo;limbec&rquo; is
used by Milton, <I>Paradise Lost</I>, iii, 605, and by Fairfax, <I>Tasso</I>, Bk, IV, st. 75. The
Italian form is <I>limbico.</I>&mdash;[<SC>Vischer</SC> (<I>Vortr&auml;ge</I>, ii, p. 85): In the time of Shakespeare,
if poetry drew its pictures from the apothecary shop, or chemical laboratory, it was
regarded neither as prosaic nor jarring. Romeo's last words are: &lquo;O true apothe-
cary thy drugs are quick.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

<P>9-15. <B>Hold . . . repose]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: Shakespeare has here most exquisitely con-
trasted Banquo's character with that of Macbeth. Banquo is praying against being
tempted to encourage thoughts of guilt even in his sleep; while Macbeth is hurrying
into temptation, and revolving in his mind every scheme, however flagitious, that
may assist him to complete his purpose. The one is unwilling to sleep, lest the same
phantoms should assail his resolution again, while the other is depriving himself of
rest through impatience to commit the murder.&mdash;[<SC>Libby</SC>: This speech of Banquo's
is the very epitome of his character, kindly, conscientious, poetical, but weak and
vacillating: he gives up his sword and dagger that he may have no means of defend-
ing the king from the fate the witches have predicted. On hearing Macbeth his pur-
pose shifts again; he wants his sword back. &lquo;The king's abed&rquo; shows where his
thoughts are in calling for his sword&mdash;and proves his guilty silence.&mdash;<SC>Vischer</SC>
(<I>Vortr&auml;ge</I>, ii. p. 85): Sinister thoughts disturb Banquo, it is as though he felt the
coming breath of the murderous storm. He wants his sword. We see here again
how Shakespeare invests even the smallest place with life-like importance.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

<P>29. <B>I dreamt last Night]</B> W. <SC>Leighton</SC> (<I>Robinson's Epit. of Lit.</I> 15 April,
1879): I see no reason to picture Banquo as a type of all that is noble and generous,
as many commentators have done. He drank in, as greedily as his partner in arms,
the prophecies of the weird tempters, but lacked Macbeth's prompt resolution to
act; he lacked also the favouring circumstances that led Macbeth to the murder of
King Duncan; and, above all, he lacked the incitements to action, which came to the
thane of Cawdor by the fiery suggestions of his wife. No plain way to the crown
suggested itself to Banquo; in fact, he saw clearly that not only Duncan, but Mac-
beth, stood between him and regal honours. Before the king's murder he evidently
suspected Macbeth's intention, and afterwards must have been fully assured of his
guilt; yet he uttered no word of warning to his kinsman and sovereign, and after the
murder, no hint of his suspicion. Would a noble and virtuous man have kept such
doubtful silence?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.

<CC><P>43. <B>Exit Banquo]</B> <SC>Collier</SC>: Fleance no doubt stood back while his father and

<P>44. <B>Goe bid,</B> etc.] <SC>Bell</SC> (p. 306): There is much stage trick and very cold in
this scene of Kemble&mdash;walks across the stage, his eyes upon the ground, starts at
the sight of the servant, whom he forgets for the purpose, renews his walk, throws
up his face, sick, sighs, then a start theatric, and then the dagger. Why can't he learn
from his sister? Charles Bell thinks (and justly) that he should stand or sit musing,
his eye fixed on vacancy, then a more piercing look to seem to see what is still in
the mind's eye only, characterised by the bewildered look which accompanies the
want of a fixed object of vision; yet the eye should not roll or start.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.

<P>45. <B>Bell]</B> <SC>Seymour</SC>: Macbeth wanted no such mechanical signal as a bell for the

accidentally, and with much more solemnity, reminds him it is time to despatch.&mdash;
[<SC>Vischer</SC> (<I>Vortr&auml;ge</I>, ii, p. 86): By this we are not to understand, as on our stage, the
large castle-bell, but a small hand-bell. Its slight yet penetrating tinkle is much
more effective. It is the preconcerted signal that all is quiet.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

<CC><P>stained with gouts of blood&mdash;&lquo;Which was not so before.&rquo; Macbeth's interpretation of
the vision is not to be taken as the truth.&mdash;<SC>Beckhaus</SC> (p. 20): In Freitag's pictures
of German history I find underneath a portrait of a woman of the Royal palace (circa
1440) some remarks which correctly elucidate this present passage. The scene is the
night on which the holy crown of Hungary was stolen, and the emotions of Helen Kot-
taner, a woman of decided feminine character, are portrayed. She is in deadly peril; we
learn how anguish and the pangs of conscience affect her soul. But the inward strug-
gle and conscientious scruples take material form and crowd upon her as a strange
external horror. &lquo;That rousing of the senses to an activity,&rquo; says Freitag, &lquo;which
clothes with external semblance the vague horror in the soul is universal and pre-emi-
nently characteristic of the extreme youth of every people. Human freedom is not yet
sufficiently large to solve by thought and self-knowledge the inward struggles, but
this emancipation begins by a conflict with a material apparition of what tortures the
soul. The battle is fought outwardly. In such-wise, at one time, has all the
world struggled. Thus Luther fought his mighty battle. And if the incomparable
Poet, who with superior independence raised himself above the English temper of
the sixteenth century, shows us his tragic hero contending with the ghosts of his
victims and with the dagger, the instrument of his crime, such a representation,
which we now consider eminently poetic, had a significance for his audience quite
other than merely artistic. At that time they thus struggled with sin and doubt.
And if Shakespeare's phantoms seem to us too numerous, as in <I>Richard III</I>, all
who then looked on in horror knew well that such forms <I>did</I> appear to sinning man
and caused his hair to stand on end.&mdash;E. K. <SC>Chambers</SC>: I think the dagger should
not be in the air, but on a table.&mdash;W. W. <SC>Story</SC> (p. 274): In this [soliloquy] we
have Macbeth's three characteristic features brought out one after the other: the
cloudy vision of the air-drawn dagger; then the straw-fire of his poetry about
Hecate and withered murder's sentinel, the wolf, and Tarquin's ravishing strides;

<CC><P>67. <B>Whose . . . Watch]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: That is, who marks the period of his
night-watch by howling, as the sentinel by a cry.
<P>68. <B>sides]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: A &lquo;ravishing&rquo; <I>stride</I> is an action of violence, impetuosity,
and tumult, like that of a savage rushing on his prey; whereas the Poet is here
attempting to exhibit an image of secrecy and caution, of anxious circumspection and
guilty timidity, the &lquo;stealthy pace&rquo; of a <I>ravisher</I> creeping into the chamber of a
virgin, and of an assassin approaching the bed of him whom he proposes to murder,
without awaking him; these he describes as &lquo;moving like ghosts,&rquo; whose progression
is so different from <I>strides</I>, that it has been in all ages represented to be as Milton
expresses it: &lquo;Smooth sliding without step.&rquo; This hemistich will afford the true
reading of this place, which is, I think, to be corrected thus: &lquo;With Tarquin rav-
ishing, slides tow'rds,&rquo; etc.&mdash;<SC>Heath</SC> (p. 387): The objection to <I>strides</I> is founded
wholly in a mistake. Whoever hath experienced walking in the dark must have
observed that a man under this disadvantage always feels out his way by strides, by
advancing one foot, as far as he finds it safe, before the other, and that if he were
to slide or glide along, as ghosts are represented to do, the infallible consequence
would be his tumbling on his nose.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: Spenser uses the word [<I>stride</I>]
in his <I>Faerie Queene</I>, IV, c. viii, [v. 37], and with no idea of violence annexed
to it: &lquo;With easy steps so soft as foot could stride.&rquo; Again, Harington, 1591,
<I>Orlando Furioso</I>, Bk, xxviii, st. 63, &lquo;He takes a long and leisurable stride.&rquo; The
ravisher and murderer would naturally stride in order that their steps might be
fewer in number, and the sound of their feet be repeated as seldom as possible.&mdash;
<SC>Warburton</SC>: Compare <I>Lucrece</I>, 162-168.&mdash;<SC>Knight</SC>: <I>Strides</I>, in its usual acceptation,
and looking at its etymology, does not convey the notion of stealthy and silent move-
ment. We receive it as Milton uses it: &lquo;The monster . . . came as fast With horrid
strides,&rquo; etc. [<I>Paradise Lost</I>, Bk, II, l. 676.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]. Can we reconcile, then, the word
&lquo;sides&rquo; with the context? Might we not receive it as a verb, and read the passage,
&lquo;&mdash; with his stealthy pace (Which Tarquin's ravishing <I>sides</I>) towards his design,
Moves,&rquo; etc. To &lquo;side&rquo; is <I>to match, to balance, to be in a collateral position.</I> Thus
in Ben Jonson's <I>Sejanus:</I> &lquo;Whom he . . . Hath rais'd from excrement to <I>side</I> the
gods?&rquo; [IV, v; p. 108, ed. Gifford]. In the passage before us, &lquo;murther&rquo; &lquo;with his
stealthy pace,&rquo; which pace <I>sides</I>, matches, &lquo;Tarquin's ravishing&rquo; (<I>ravishing</I> a noun),
moves like a ghost towards his design. <I>Which</I> and &lquo;With&rquo; were often contracted
in writing, and might easily be mistaken by the printer.&mdash;<SC>Hunter</SC>: Tarquin seems
to have haunted the imagination of Shakespeare from his early days, when he chose
the rape of Lucretia as the subject of a poem. He appears in the plays several
times, and often unexpectedly, and certainly never less propitiously than here,
whether we read <I>strides</I> or &lquo;sides.&rquo; It would a little improve the passage if, for
&lquo;With,&rquo; we read <I>Or</I>, the two motions of the murderer, <I>stealthy</I> and <I>hasty.</I>&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC></CC>

<CC><P>1. <B>Scena Secunda]</B> <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Remarks</I>, etc.): There is no change of <I>place.</I>&mdash;R.
G. <SC>White</SC>: Not only is there no change of place, but there is no introduction of
new dramatic interest or incident. Of yet greater importance is it here that the
apparent continuance of the action is vitally essential to the dramatic impression
intended to be produced. The ringing of the bell by Lady Macbeth, the exit of
Macbeth upon that prearranged summons, the entrance of the Lady to fill the stage
and occupy the mind during her husband's brief absence upon his fearful errand,
and to confess in soliloquy her active accession to the murder, the sudden knocking
which is heard directly after she goes out to replace the daggers, and which recurs
until she warily hurries her husband and herself away lest they should be found
watchers, the entrance of the Porter, and finally, of Macduff and Lenox,&mdash;all this
action is contrived with consummate dramatic skill; and its unbroken continuity in
one spot, and that a part of the castle common to all its inhabitants, is absolutely
necessary to complete its purpose.
<P>3. <B>bold]</B> <SC>Mrs Griffiths</SC> (p. 412): Our sex is obliged to Shakespeare for this
passage. He seems to think that a woman could not be rendered completely wicked
without some degree of intoxication. It required two vices in her, one to intend
and another to perpetrate the crime.&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Remarks</I>, etc.): In not a few passages
of Shakespeare the metrical arrangement of the old editions was most wantonly
altered by Steevens and Malone. But there are some passages&mdash;and the present
speech is one of them&mdash;where a new division of the lines is absolutely necessary. The
regulation given by Knight is not &lquo;metrical,&rquo; it is barbarous. Let any one write out
the passage as prose and then read it as verse; it will naturally fall into the arrange-
ment by Rowe.&mdash;[<SC>Bell</SC> (p. 306): [Mrs Siddons spoke this line] with a ghastly

<CC><P>direction thus: Macbeth lingers yet a moment within; his unquiet mind imagines it
hears a noise in the court below, and thoughtlessly, bewildered, and crazed, he
rushes back to the balcony, and calls beneath, &ldquo;Who's there?&rdquo; In his agony,
however, he waits for no answer, but rushes back into the chambers to execute the
murder. Had Fleance or Banquo, or even any of the servants of the house, whom
he had but just sent away, been beneath, the whole secret deed would have been
betrayed. I consider this return, which appears but a mere trifle, as a striking
beauty in Shakespeare's drama. He delights (because he always sets tragedy in
activity through passion as well as through intrigue) in suspending success and
failure on a needle's point.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Friesen</SC> (p. 80): Shakespeare always takes the
greatest pains to afford, unrestricted up to the last moment, a certain freedom of
will to all his characters whose tragic paths lead to destruction. None of his
tragic heroes are so enmeshed by fate or accident or intrigue that no loop-hole
of safety is left them. This is so pre-eminently in <I>Macbeth.</I> The consummation
of the awful crime is suspended up to the last moment, when Macbeth, terrified
at some noise, once more emerges in doubt from Duncan's chamber. It were need-
less here to seek for reasons on theoretic grounds; the fearful struggle between per-
severing defiance and yearning for repentance, which so powerfully affects us in
the subsequent treatment, would be, without this antecedent, meaningless, or at
least far from tragic.&mdash;[<SC>Booth</SC>: This line is spoken by one of the drunken Cham-
berlains.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

<CC><P>23-26. <B>Did . . . descended]</B> <SC>Hunter</SC>: Any agitation of spirit, or any inco-
herence of ideas as the natural consequence, cannot demand that the lady, when she
has answered the inquiry of her guilty husband, &lquo;Didst thou not hear a noise?&rquo; by
saying, &lquo;I heard the owl scream and the crickets cry,&rquo; should then take up the hus-
band's question, and address him, &lquo;Did you not speak?&rquo; but that this is also an
inquiry of the conscience-stricken thane, whom every noise appals, and who would
have every sound translated to him. He was not satisfied with her first explanation.
The sounds had been no screaming of the owl, no crying of the cricket; articulate
sounds had fallen upon his ear, and he wished and vainly hoped that it was from
her lips, and not from those of another, that they had proceeded. The few words
which constitute that dialogue of monosyllables which follows, would then require
to be thus distributed. He asks, &lquo;Did not you speak?&rquo; To which she replies,
&lquo;When? Now?&rquo; Both words spoken with an interrogative inflection. At what
time do you mean that I spoke? Is it now? &lquo;As I descended.&rquo; Then was the
time that the articulate sounds were heard which he now wishes to have explained,
and the words should stand without a note of interrogation. The &lquo;Ay&rquo; of the lady
then possesses an effect, which as the scene stands at present it wants.&mdash;<SC>Boden-
stedt</SC>: This whispering, so laconic and yet so heart-piercing, between the two who
dare not meet each other's eyes, belongs to the most powerful that the poetry of all
ages and all times has created. But we must be on our guard against taking Mac-
beth's question in lines 42, 43 as an expression of genuine repentance. It was not
prompted by his conscience, but only by his imagination, whose irrepressible and
ever-flowing tide bore before him all the horrors of the future. . . . It is not the crime
already done that horrifies him; it is only the distressing consequences which can
spring from it. His wife misunderstands him now, just as she formerly misunder-
stood him, when she spoke of his milk of human kindness. She takes his words as
an expression of real remorse, as we see by her reply. [Hunter's foregoing distribu-
tion of speeches was adopted by Chambers and Furness.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

with which it has no etymological connection at all, though doubtless the confusion
between the words is of old standing. The spelling <I>sorry</I> with two <I>r</I>'s is etymo-
logically wrong, and due to the shortening of the <I>o</I>; the <I>o</I> was originally long; and
the true form is <I>sor-y</I>, which is nothing but the substantive <I>sore</I> with the suffix -<I>y</I>
(Anglo-Saxon -<I>ig</I>), formed exactly like <I>ston-y</I> from <I>stone, bon-y</I> from <I>bone</I>, and <I>gor-y</I>
from gore (which has not yet been turned into <I>gorry</I>). We find the spelling <I>soarye</I>
as late as in Stanyhurst, trans. of Virgil, [1582], <I>&AElig;neid</I>, ii, 651, ed. Arber, p. 64, l.
18. The original sense was wounded, afflicted, and hence miserable, sad, pitiable,
as in the expression &lquo;in a <I>sorry</I> plight.&rquo; Compare: <I>Oth.</I> III, iv, 51, &lquo;a salt and
<I>sorry</I> [painful] rheum.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
<P>30. <SC>Delius</SC>: [Pope's stage-direction] may not accord with Shakespeare's mean-
ing, if &lquo;sorry sight&rquo; refers to what Macbeth has seen in Duncan's chamber, and
which is to him so actual that he speaks of it as present before him.

<P>44, 45. <B>These deeds . . . mad]</B> <SC>Bell</SC> (p. 307): [Mrs Siddons here used the]
same action as before. Arms about neck and bosom, shuddering.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
<P>45. <B>mad]</B> <SC>Coleridge</SC> (i, 248): Now that the deed is done, or doing&mdash;now that
the first reality commences, Lady Macbeth shrinks. The most simple sound strikes
terror, the most natural consequences are horrible, whilst previously everything, how-
ever awful, appeared a mere trifle; conscience, which before had been hidden to
Macbeth in selfish and prudential fears, now rushes in upon him in her own verita-
ble person. And see the novelty given to the most familiar images by a new state
of feeling.
<P>46. <B>Sleep no more]</B> <SC>Fletcher</SC> (p. 123): These brief words involve the whole
history of Macbeth's subsequent career.
<P>46, 47. <B>Sleep . . . Sleepe]</B> <SC>Hunter</SC>: To me it appears that the airy voice said no
more than this. What follows is a comment of his own. The voice had first pre-
sented sleep in a prosopop&oelig;ia. It was a cherub, one of the &lquo;young and rosy cheru-
bim&rquo; of heaven. Macbeth invests it with its proper attributes, and would have gone
on expatiating on its gentle and valuable qualities, but Lady Macbeth interrupts him,
and asks with unaffected surprise, &lquo;What do you mean?&rquo; He proceeds in the same
distempered strain, not so much answering her question, as continuing to give
expression to the feeling of horror at the thought which had fixed itself in his mind,
that he had committed a defeat on the useful and innocent Sleep; and he repeats
what the voice appeared to him to have said, with the additional circumstance that
the voice seemed to pervade the apartments of his spacious castle, like the limbs
of the great giant which lay in the Castle of Otranto, and that it would enter other
ears than his, and lead to the discovery of his crime. And he comes at length
to the horrible conviction that a punishment which bore relation to the nature of his
offence would soon fall upon him [lines 54, 55]. In this scene we have, perhaps,
as highly wrought a tragical effect as is to be found in the whole range of the ancient
or modern drama.

<CC><P>instance of hallucination. It is rather an instance of merely excited imagination
without sensual representation, like the &lquo;suggestion&rquo; in I, iii, 150. The word &lquo;me-
thought&rquo; is sufficient to distinguish this voice of the fancy from an hallucination
of sense. The lengthened reasoning of the fancied speech is also unlike an hallu-
cination of hearing; real hallucinations of hearing being almost always restricted to
two or three words, or at furthest, to brief sentences.

<P>48. <B>Sleeue]</B> <SC>Heath</SC> (p. 387): Seward, in his notes on Fletcher's <I>Two Noble

give great trouble and embarrassment to the knitter or weaver.&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: This
appears to have signified <I>coarse, soft</I>, unwrought silk. <I>Seta grossolana</I>, Ital. See
also Florio's <I>Ital. Dict.</I> 1598: &lquo;<I>Sfilazza.</I> Any kind of ravelled stuffe, or <I>sleave

<I>soye flosche</I>, &lquo;sleave silk.&rquo;&mdash;&lquo;<I>Cadarce, pour faire capiton.</I> The tow, or coarsest part
of silke, whereof <I>sleave</I> is made.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: Florio has &lquo;Bauella, any kind of
sleaue or raw silke,&rquo; and &lquo;Bauellare: to rauell as raw silke.&rquo; Compare <I>Tro. &amp;

<P>66. <B>Infirme of purpose]</B> <SC>Fletcher</SC> (p. 127): Here is the point, above all
others in this wonderful scene, which most strikingly illustrates the two-fold contrast
subsisting between these two characters. Macbeth, having no true remorse, shrinks
not at the last moment from perpetrating the murder, though his nervous agitation
will not let him contemplate for an instant the aspect of the murdered. Lady Mac-
beth, on the contrary, having real remorse, does recoil at the last moment from the
very act to which she had been using such violent and continued efforts to work
herself up; but, being totally free from her husband's irritability of fancy, can, <I>now
that his very preservation demands it</I>, go deliberately to look upon the sanguinary
work which her own hand had shrunk from performing.
<P>68-71. <B>'tis the Eye . . . Guilt]</B> <SC>Knowles</SC> (p. 53): It is singular that even Mrs
Siddons should have missed the true import of these lines, which are quite super-
fluous and impertinent except as a taunt at Macbeth, reminding him of his own
arrangement, and the imbecility that prevents him from carrying it into execution.
&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.

object or the subject of the relative clause. The latter seems the more poetic.

had escaped Coleridge, where, excepting the Porter's scene, which he supposed to

pun or play on words in the whole drama.&rquo; The quibble, however, between &lquo;guild&rquo;
and &lquo;gilt&rquo; was often introduced with only a grave intention of enforcing thought.&mdash;
<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]
<P>72. <B>Knocke within]</B> <SC>De Quincey</SC> (p. 9): From my boyish days I had always
felt a great perplexity on one point in <I>Macbeth.</I> It was this: the knocking at the
gate, which succeeds to the murder of Duncan, produced to my feelings an effect for
which I never could account. The effect was, that it reflected back upon the murder
a peculiar awfulness and a depth of solemnity; yet, however obstinately I endeav-
ored with my understanding to comprehend this, for many years I never could see
<I>why</I> it should produce such an effect. . . . At length I solved [the problem] to my
own satisfaction; and my solution is this: Murder, in ordinary cases, where the
sympathy is wholly directed to the case of the murdered person, is an incident of
coarse and vulgar horror; and for this reason, that it flings the interest exclusively
upon the natural but ignoble instinct by which we cleave to life; an instinct, which,
as being indispensable to the primal law of self-preservation, is the same in kind
(though different in degree) amongst all living creatures; this instinct, therefore,
because it annihilates all distinctions, and degrades the greatest of men to the level
of the &lquo;poor beetle that we tread on,&rquo; exhibits human nature in its most abject and
humiliating attitude. Such an attitude would little suit the purposes of the Poet.
What then must he do? He must throw the interest on the murderer. Our sym-
pathy must be with <I>him;</I> (of course, I mean a sympathy of comprehension, a sym-
pathy by which we enter into his feelings, and are made to understand them&mdash;not a
sympathy of pity or approbation). In the murdered person, all strife of thought, all
flux and reflux of passion and of purpose, are crushed by one overwhelming panic;
the fear of instant death smites him &lquo;with its petrific mace.&rquo; But in the murderer,
such a murderer as a poet will condescend to, there must be raging some great storm
of passion,&mdash;jealousy, ambition, vengeance, hatred,&mdash;which will create a hell within
him; and into this hell we are to look. In <I>Macbeth</I>, for the sake of gratifying his
own enormous and teeming faculty of creation, Shakespeare has introduced two mur-
derers, and, as usual in his hands, they are remarkably discriminated; but, though
in Macbeth the strife of mind is greater than in his wife, the tiger spirit not so awake,
and his feelings caught chiefly by contagion from her,&mdash;yet, as both were finally
involved in the guilt of murder, the murderous mind of necessity is finally to be pre-</CC>

<CC><P>sumed in both. This was to be expressed; and on its own account, as well as to
make it a more proportionable antagonist to the unoffending nature of their victim,
&lquo;the gracious Duncan,&rquo; and adequately to expound the &lquo;deep damnation of his
taking off,&rquo; this was to be expressed with peculiar energy. We were to be made to
feel that the human nature&mdash;<I>i. e.</I> the divine nature of love and mercy, spread through
the hearts of all creatures, and seldom utterly withdrawn from man&mdash;was gone, van-
ished, extinct; and that the fiendish nature had taken its place. And, as this effect
is marvellously accomplished in the <I>dialogues</I> and <I>soliloquies</I> themselves, so it is
finally consummated by the expedient under consideration; and it is to this that I
now solicit the reader's attention. If the reader has ever witnessed a wife, daugh-
ter, or sister in a fainting fit, he may chance to have observed that the most affecting
moment in such a specacle is <I>that</I> in which a sigh or a stirring announces the recom-
mencement of suspended life. Or, if the reader has ever been present in a vast
metropolis on the day when some great national idol was carried in funeral pomp to
his grave, and chancing to walk near the course through which it passed, has felt
powerfully, in the silence and desertion of the streets, and in the stagnation of ordi-
nary business, the deep interest which at that moment was possessing the heart of
man,&mdash;if all at once he should hear the death-like stillness broken up by the sound
of wheels rattling away from the scene, and making known that the transitory vision
was dissolved, he will be aware that at no moment was his sense of the complete
suspension and pause in ordinary human concerns so full and affecting as at that
moment when the suspension ceases, and the goings-on of human life are suddenly
resumed. All action in any direction is best expounded, measured, and made
apprehensible by reaction. Now apply this to the case of Macbeth. Here, as I
have said, the retiring of the human heart, and the entrance of the fiendish heart,
was to be expressed and made sensible. Another world has stept in, and the mur-
derers are taken out of the region of human things, human purposes, human desires.
They are transfigured: Lady Macbeth is &lquo;unsexed&rquo;; Macbeth has forgot that he
was born of woman; both are conformed to the image of devils; and the world of
devils is suddenly revealed. But how shall this be conveyed and made palpable?
In order that a new world may step in, this world must for a time disappear. The
murderers, and the murder, must be insulated,&mdash;cut off by an immeasurable gulf
from the ordinary tide and succession of human affairs,&mdash;locked up and sequestered
in some deep recess; we must be made sensible that the world of ordinary life is
suddenly arrested,&mdash;laid asleep, tranced,&mdash;racked into a dread armistice; time must
be annihilated; relation to things without abolished; and all must pass self-with-
drawn into a deep syncope and suspension of earthly passion. Hence it is, that when
the deed is done, when the work of darkness is perfect, then the world of darkness
passes away like a pageantry in the clouds: the knocking at the gate is heard; and
it makes known audibly that the reaction has commenced; the human has made its
reflux upon the fiendish; the pulses of life are beginning to beat again; and the re-
establishment of the goings-on of the world in which we live, first makes us pro-
foundly sensible of the awful parenthesis that had suspended them.&mdash;[E. K. <SC>Chambers</SC>:
The knocking here seems to show that the opening of the next scene always formed
part of the play. Macbeth is not sure at first if it is real or &lquo;fantastic.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]</CC>

<P>78. <B>multitudinous]</B> <SC>Malone</SC>: Perhaps Shakespeare meant, not the seas of every

be understood to design the <I>multitude of waves.</I>

<P>89. <B>Night-Gowne]</B> R. G. <SC>White</SC>: In Macbeth's time, and for centuries later,
it was the custom for both sexes to sleep without other covering than that belonging
to the bed when a bed was occupied. But of this Shakespeare knew nothing, and
if he had known, he would, of course, have disregarded it. Macbeth's night-gown,
that worn by Julius C&aelig;ser (II. ii), and by the Ghost in the old <I>Hamlet</I> (III, iv),
answered to our <I>robes de chambre</I>, and were not, as I have found many intelligent
people to suppose, the garments worn in bed.&mdash;<SC>Keightley</SC>: This was the name
of the night-dress of both men and women. The night-gown was only used by
persons of some rank and consideration; people, in general, went to bed naked,
<I>buffing the blanket</I>, as it was termed in Ireland. [See V, i, 8; 62.]

<P>94. <B>Wake . . . knocking]</B> <SC>Malone</SC>: Macbeth is addressing the person who

address the person who was knocking. According to my conception, such a call
would be nature itself; and, I believe, would spontaneously proceed from the heart
of every man so circumstanced as Macbeth then was. In this manner I wish the
genius of Shakespeare to be tried, and not by the evidence of incorrect old quartos
and folios, ill printed, and worse revised.

results from ignorance of his art. The true dramatist will estimate it at its true
