<CC><C><B>[4-22. Here's a knocking indeede:</B> etc.]</C>
<P>natural and happy than that a Porter should say some grimly humourous words about
his own calling; and that he should wind up with that, &lquo;I pray you, remember the
Porter&rquo;&mdash;his fee! Wasn't all Scotland begging for English posts and fees from 1603
to 1607, or whenever Macbeth was written? How <I>could</I> a Scotch Porter be better
hit off? Surely he must be a dull soul who can't see the humour of this character.&mdash;
W. <SC>Leighton</SC> (<I>Robinson's Epit. of Lit.</I> 1 June, 1879): For several reasons, viz:
blundering in respect to time; something un-Shakespearian in the porter,&mdash;as style
and certain words nowhere else used by that author,&mdash;unusual coarseness in a play
otherwise correct in such respect; and similarity with Middleton's work&mdash;for these
reasons combined, there is certainly cause to suspect that the latter author patched
Shakespeare's play at this place, and did it unskilfully.&mdash;<SC>Hales</SC>: There are five points
which should be thoroughly considered before any final verdict is pronounced, as to
whether the Porter is not, after all, a genuine offspring of Shakespeare's art. (i) That a
Porter's speech is an integral part of the play. (ii) That it is necessary as a relief to the
surrounding horror. (iii) That it is necessary according to the law of contrast else-
where obeyed. (iv) That the speech we have is dramatically relevant. (v) That
its style and language are Shakespearian. (i) No one will deny that the knock-
ing scene is an integral part of the play. . . . But with the knocking the porter is
inseparably associated. If we retain it, we must retain him. And if we retain him,
he must surely make a speech of some sort; or are we to picture to ourselves a pro-
foundly dumb functionary? Are we to conceive him as crossing the stage, perhaps
brandishing his keys with a mysterious cunning, but with tongue fast tied and
bound? There is probably no student of Shakespeare who is prepared to accept
such a phenomenon. Clearly, then, the porter speaks, to whatever effect. (ii)
That some speech of a lighter kind is necessary to relieve the surrounding horror.
Now if ever in the plays of Shakespeare some relaxation is needed for the nerves
strained to the utmost; if ever some respite and repose are due to prevent the high
mysterious delight corrupting into a morbid panic, it is so in the terrible scene now
before us. A monotony of horror cannot be sustained; and any disturbance of it is
infinitely welcome. The sound of a fresh voice after we have listened so long to that
guilty conference is a very cordial. . . . (iii) Some lighter speech is necessary accord-
ing to the law of contrast elsewhere observed by Shakespeare. To the true humourist
the various colours of life are inextricably woven. It is all infinitely sad and in-
finitely comic. The beauty of summer and the blackness of winter, the gladness
of life and the dulness of death. These are omnipresent with him. And so in the
Shakespearian drama we find strange neighborhoods. Jesters and jesting in the
midst of that stupendous storm in <I>King Lear!</I> In <I>Hamlet</I> the grave-digger is one
with the clown. In <I>Othello</I>, amidst all its bitter earnest, there are foolings and rail-
leries. In fact, <I>Macbeth</I> would be unique among the tragedies of Shakespeare if the
comic element were utterly absent from it. (iv) The speech of the Porter is dramat-
ically relevant. The whole speech is, in fact, a powerful piece of irony. &lquo;If a man
were porter of hell-gate.&rquo; But is this man not so? What then is hell? and where
are its gates? . . . It may be well to notice here that the Porter of Hell was a not
unfamiliar figure in the old Mysteries. We find in Virgil, indeed, what might have
suggested some such functionary to the medi&aelig;val mind. Virgil speaks of Cer-
berus as &lquo;Janitor&rquo; (<I>&AElig;neid</I>, vi, 400) and as &lquo;Janitor Orci&rquo; (<I>Ib.</I> viii, 296). Fletcher
also, in his <I>Honest Man's Fortune</I> (III, ii.), speaks of &lquo;hell's three-headed porter.&rquo;
It was natural enough, when so much was talked of St. Peter with his keys keeping</CC>

<CC><P>the gate of Heaven, that there should be conceived an infernal counterpart of that
celestial functionary. (v) Are the style and language of the Porter's speech Shake-
spearian? Surely the fancy, which is the main part of the Porter's speech, must be
allowed to be eminently after the manner of Shakespeare. He was well acquainted
with the older stage, as his direct references to it show (see <I>Twelfth Night</I>, IV, ii;
<I>1 Hen. IV:</I> II, iv; <I>Hamlet</I>, III, iv); and this conception of an infernal janitor is
just such a piece of antique realism as he would delight in. He has it elsewhere;
see <I>Oth.</I> IV, ii, 90. The manner in which Macduff &lquo;draws out&rquo; the Porter is
exactly like that of Shakespeare in similar circumstances elsewhere. Compare the
way in which Orlando is made to elicit the wit of Rosalind, [<I>As You Like It</I>, III, ii,
323 et seq.]. If this likeness of manner has no great positive, yet it has some nega-
tive, value. We see that the manner is not un-Shakespearian, if it cannot be pro-
nounced definitely Shakespearian; and we need not go to Middleton's plays for an
illustration of it. The passage is written in the rhythmic prose that is so favourite a
form with Shakespeare (see <I>Hen. V:</I> II, iii, 9-28). And as for the language, there
is certainly nothing in it un-Shakespearian. The general conclusion justified by
what has been advanced seems to me to be this: that the Porter is undoubtedly a
part of the original play, and that the general conception of his speech is certainly
Shakespeare's: with regard to the expression, that part of it is most certainly his,
and, for the rest, no sufficient reason has yet been urged to countenance any doubt
that it too is by Shakespeare.&mdash;R. G. <SC>White</SC> (ed. ii.): This Porter I was once
misled into believing, for a little while, to be not of Shakespeare's make. I was
wrong. He is one of Shakespeare's true humourous grotesques, although not of
the best sort of them. Of the knocking that he prates about, what a woful echo in
Lady Macbeth's sleep-walking scene! and, by her pallid lips, Shakespeare claims
him for his own: this scene is surely all of one piece.&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC> (ed. iii.): Cole-
ridge thinks this part of the scene could not have been written by Shakespeare. . . .
I am sure it is like him, I think it is worthy of him, and would by no means have it
away.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

<P>16. <B>Hose]</B> <SC>Warburton</SC>: The joke consists in this, that a French hose being
very short and strait, a tailor must be master of his trade who could steal anything
from thence.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: Warburton said this at random. The French hose
(according to Stubbes in his <I>Anatomie of Abuses</I>) were in 1595 much in fashion:
&lquo;The Gallic hosen are made very large and wide, reaching down to their knees
only, with three or foure gardes apeece laid down along either hose,&rquo; [p. 56, ed. Fur-
nivall.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.].&mdash;<SC>Farmer</SC>: Steevens forgot the uncertainty of <I>French fashions.</I> In
<I>The Treasury of Ancient and Modern Times</I>, 1613, we have an account (from
Guyon, I suppose) of the old French dresses: &lquo;<I>Mens hose</I> answered in length to
their short-skirted doublets; being made <I>close to their limbes</I>, wherein they had no
means for pockets.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: Stubbes, in his <I>Anatomie of Abuses</I> (fol. 23 b,
ed. 1585), says: &lquo;The Frenche hose are of two diuers makinges, for the common
Frenche hose (as they list to call them) containeth length, breadth, and sidenesse
sufficient, and is made very rounde. The other contayneth neyther length, breadth,
nor sidenesse (being not past a quarter of a yarde side), whereof some be paned,
cut, and drawen out with costly ornamentes, with Canions annexed, reaching downe
beneath their knees.&rquo; In the <I>Mer. of Ven.</I> I, ii, 80, Shakespeare clearly speaks of
the larger kind, the &lquo;round hose&rquo; which the Englishman borrows from France, and
it is enough to suppose that the tailor merely followed the practice of his trade with-
out exhibiting any special dexterity in stealing. In <I>Hen. V:</I> III, vii, 56, the
French hose are wide by comparison.

<CC><P>etymological spelling <I>bone-fire</I>, Sc. <I>bane-fire</I>, was common down to 1760, though
&lquo;bonfire&rquo; was also in use from the sixteenth century, and became more common as
the original sense was forgotten. Johnson in 1755 decided for <I>bonfire</I>, &lquo;from <I>bon</I>,
good, and <I>fire.</I>&rquo; But the shortening of the vowel was natural, from its position;
cf. <I>knowledge, Monday, collier</I>, etc. In Scotland with the form <I>bane-fire</I>, the mem-
ory of the original sense was retained longer; for the annual midsummer &lquo;banefire&rquo;
or &lquo;<I>bonfire</I>&rquo; in the burgh of Hawick, old bones were regularly collected and stored
up, down to about 1800. <I>Cath. Angl.</I> (1483): &lquo;A banefyre, <I>ignis ossium</I> (20/1). 2.
A fire in which to consume corpses, a funeral pile, a pyre.&rquo; (<I>Obsolete.</I>) Golding,

<P>39. <B>Night]</B> <SC>Malone</SC>: It is not very easy to ascertain precisely the time when
Duncan is murdered. The conversation that passes between Banquo and Macbeth,
in II, i, might lead us to suppose that when Banquo retired to rest it was not <I>much</I>
after twelve o'clock. The king was then &lquo;abed&rquo;; and, immediately after Banquo
retires Lady Macbeth strikes upon the bell, and Macbeth commits the murder. In
a few minutes afterwards the knocking at the gate commences, and no time can be
supposed to elapse between the second and the third scene, because the Porter gets
up in consequence of the knocking: yet here Macduff talks of <I>last night</I>, and says
that he was commanded to call <I>timely</I> on the king, and that he fears he has almost
overpass'd the hour; and the Porter tells him, &lquo;We were carousing till <I>the second
cock&rquo;;</I> so that we must suppose it to be now at least six o'clock; for Macduff has
already expressed his surprise that the Porter should lie <I>so late.</I> Brom Lady Mac-
beth's words in Act V, &lquo;One&mdash;two&mdash;'tis time to do't,&rquo; it <I>should seem</I> that the murder
was committed at <I>two</I> o'clock, and that hour is certainly not inconsistent with the
conversation above referred to between Banquo and his son; but even that hour of
<I>two</I> will not correspond with what the Porter and Macduff say in the present scene.
I suspect Shakespeare in fact meant that the murder should be supposed to be com-
mitted a little before <I>daybreak</I>, which exactly corresponds with the speech of Mac-
duff now before us, though not so well with the other circumstances already men-
tioned, or with Lady Macbeth's desiring her husband to put on his night-gown.
Shakespeare, I believe, was led to fix the time of Duncan's murder near the break
of day by Holinshed's account of the murder of King Duffe: &lquo;&mdash; he was long in
his oratorie, and there continued till it was <I>late in the night.</I>&rquo; Donwald's servants
&lquo;enter the chamber where the king laie, <I>a little before cocks crow</I>, where they
secretlie cut his throat.&rquo;

wrestling, and <I>cast</I> or <I>cast up.</I>&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: I find a similar play upon words in <I>The
Two Angry Women of Abington</I>, 1599: &lquo;&mdash; he reels all that he wrought to-day, and
he were good now to play at dice, for he <I>casts</I> excellent well,&rquo; [Haz. Dods. p. 303].</CC>

<CC><P>44. <B>Enter Macbeth]</B> <SC>Scott</SC> (iii, 35): We can never forget the rueful horror
of [Kemble's] look, which by strong exertion he endeavors to conceal, when on
the morning succeeding the murder he receives Lenox and Macduff in the ante-
chamber of Duncan. His efforts to appear composed, his endeavors to assume the
attitude and appearance of one listening to Lenox's account of the external terrors
of the night, while in fact he is expecting the alarm to arise within the royal apart-
ment, formed a most astonishing piece of playing. Kemble's countenance seemed
altered by the sense of internal horror, and had a cast of that of Count Ugolino in
the dungeon, as painted by Reynolds. When Macbeth felt himself obliged to turn
towards Lenox and reply to what he had been saying, you saw him, like a man
awaking from a fit of absence, endeavor to recollect at least the general tenor of
what had been said, and it was some time ere he could bring out the general reply,
&lquo;'Twas a rough night.&rquo; Those who have had the good fortune to see Kemble and
Mrs Siddons as Macbeth and his lady, may be satisfied they have witnessed the
highest perfection of the dramatic art.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.&mdash;<SC>Knowles</SC> (p. 55): The actor who
betrays to the audience in any portion of this scene the slightest evidence of desper-
ation or forgetfulness on the part of Macbeth, errs most egregiously from true judgment.
The audience require no hint as to what is passing in Macbeth's bosom, nor is there
a moment's opportunity for by-play, as it is called, to render the thing feasible.
He is kept in close conversation from first to last. If he is on his guard with
respect to one of the visitors, be sure he is equally so with respect to both. How
absurd is it, then, for an actor to require that this question shall be repeated, as if,
absorbed in his expectation of what is coming, Macbeth did not hear it in the first
instance. Macbeth's mind being once roused to the necessity of playing his part,
the imminency of his danger keeps it broad awake. He would as soon betray him-
self to Lenox by standing gasping after Macduff, as he would betray himself to
Macduff by being abstracted when the Thane inquires if the King is stirring yet?
When the discovery of the murder came, would not Lenox recollect the statue he
had spoken to, and guess the cause which had turned Macbeth for the time into a
stone? The frame of mind in which we now find Macbeth would rather induce
him to overdo than to fall short. Here is again the mischief of studying partial
effects. Howsoever calm Macbeth may appear without, the storm shall not only be
kept up within, but with aggravated strife.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.

<P>68. <B>New hatch'd]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: A <I>prophecy</I> of an <I>event new hatch'd</I> seems to be a

Johnson on review would scarce approve of the owlet hooting from the moment it

events may be said to be &lquo;the <I>hatch</I> and brood of time.&rquo; See <I>2 Hen. IV:</I> III, i,

it is the <I>thing</I> or <I>event</I>, and not the <I>prophecy</I>, which is the <I>hatch</I> of <I>time;</I> but it must
be acknowledged, the word &lquo;become&rquo; sufficiently marks the future time. If there-

used for <I>hatching</I>, or <I>in the state of being hatch'd.&mdash;&lquo;To</I> the woful time&rquo; means&mdash;

<P>78. <SC>Moulton</SC> (p. 163): The concealment of the murder forms a stage of the
action which falls into two different parts: the single effort which faces the first
shock of discovery, and the very different strain required to meet the slowly gather-
ing evidence of guilt. In the scene of the discovery Macbeth is perfectly at home:
energetic action is needed, and he is dealing with men. His acted innocence
appears to me better than his wife's; Lady Macbeth goes near to suggesting a
personal interest in the crime by her over-anxiety to disclaim it. Yet in this scene,
as everywhere else, the weak points in Macbeth's character betray him: for one
moment he is left to himself, and that moment's suspense ruins the whole episode.
The sense of crisis proves too much for him, and under an ungovernable impulse he
stabs the grooms. He thus wrecks the whole scheme. How perfectly Lady Mac-
beth's plan would have served if it had been left to itself is shown by Lenox's
account of what he had seen.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.</CC>

<CC><P>95. <B>Ring the Bell]</B> <SC>Theobald</SC>: Macduff had said at the beginning of his
Speech, &lquo;Ring the Alarum bell,&rquo; but if the Bell had rung out immediately, not a
Word of What he says could have been distinguish'd. &lquo;Ring the Bell,&rquo; I say, was a
Marginal Direction in the Prompter's Book for him to order the Bell to be rung the
Minute that Macduff ceased speaking. In proof of this, we may observe that the
Hemistich ending Macduff's Speech and that beginning Lady Macbeth's make up a
complete Verse. Now, if &lquo;Ring the bell&rquo; had been part of the Text, can we imag-
ine that Shakespeare would have begun the Lady's speech with a broken Line?&mdash;
<SC>Malone</SC>: It should be remembered that stage-directions were often couched in
imperative terms: &lquo;Draw a knife,&rquo; &lquo;Play musick,&rquo; &lquo;Ring the bell,&rquo; etc. In the
Folio we have here indeed also, &lquo;Bell rings,&rquo; as a marginal direction; but this was
inserted from the players misconceiving what Shakespeare had in truth set down in
his copy as a dramatic direction to the property man, for a part of Macduff's speech;
and to distinguish the direction which they inserted, from the supposed words of the
speaker, they departed from the usual imperative form. Throughout the whole of
the preceding scene we have constantly an imperative direction to the prompter:
&lquo;Knock within.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Knight</SC>: But how natural is it that Macduff, having previously
cried, &lquo;Ring the alarum bell,&rquo; should repeat the order! The temptation to strike
out these words was the silly desire to complete a ten-syllable line.&mdash;<SC>Keightley</SC>:
Macduff, in his anxiety and impatience, reiterates his order.
<P>96. <B>Bell rings]</B> J. <SC>Coleman</SC> (<I>Gentleman's Maga.</I> March, 1889): In [Charles]
Kean's production of Macbeth, the terror-stricken group, at the end of the murder-
scene, created a veritable sensation. When the alarm-bell rang out crowds of half-
dressed men, demented women and children, soldiers with unsheathed weapons, and
retainers with torches, streamed on and filled the stage in the twinkling of an eye.
Wild tumult and commotion were everywhere, while in the centre of the seething
crowd, with pale face and flashing eyes, the murderer held aloft his blood-stained
sword!&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
<P>96. <B>Enter Lady]</B> <SC>Knowles</SC> (p. 57): And now let us inquire how the presence
of Lady Macbeth can be dispensed with at this juncture. Would she take a share
in every other scene of the tragic enterprise, and absent herself from this last and
most critical one? As the mistress of the castle, why should she keep her room
while her stairs and corridors are thronged with the rush of feet in amazeful haste?
Would it not be suspicious that, while the whole castle is afoot, the mistress of it
should remain sitting? There is every reason for Lady Macbeth's co-operation in
this scene, and not one for her absence, except the reason of the actress who per-
sonates Lady Macbeth, that it is not worth while to come on for three or four times for
the mere sake of probability and propriety. Our stage has been injured, and the taste
of our audiences vitiated by the studying of mere effect. Shakespeare perfectly well
knew where Lady Macbeth or any other woman would be found at such a juncture.
Not in her bed-chamber, but in her hall, in the very midst of the hurly-burly. And
there he has placed her, to suffer the rebuke of the actor, to be told most ignorantly
that she has no business there, and to be sent to her chamber again, where if even on</CC>

<P>132. <B>Wherefore did you so]</B> <SC>Knowles</SC> (p. 60): Here occurs the strongest
reason for the presence of Lady Macbeth. Macduff makes no attempt to conceal
that he attaches suspicion to the fact of Macbeth's having slain the grooms. Mac-
beth must extricate himself here thoroughly and at once by vindicating what appears
questionable. Take [Lady Macbeth] away, the situation is deprived of half its im-
pressiveness. And who doubts that he is not only heartened, but inspired by her
presence? He gasps while he replies: &lquo;Who can be wise, amazed, temperate, and
furious, In a moment? No man.&rquo; The danger is warded off for the time. By this
last act of boldness and self-collectedness, he atones for all past remissness and
vacillation. Her spirit is reassured. Her presence is now no longer necessary.
She affects natural exhaustion, and cries to be assisted out.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
<P>133-143. <SC>Vischer</SC> (<I>Vortr&auml;ge</I>, ii, p. 93): It is apparent that he is acting a part.
But how is it with him in reality? His natural self seeks relief from the weight of
its disguising mask. He is ever full to overflowing with fantastic images. In order
to counterfeit it is only needful for him to be his own true self, and he will act the
part well. He has but to express what he should simulate, that is, how utterly
destroyed he feels, and the thing is done.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.</CC>

<CC><P>136. <B>pawser]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 443): -<I>Er</I> is sometimes appended to a <I>noun</I> for the
purpose of signifying an agent. Thus: &lquo;A Roman sworder&rquo;&mdash;<I>2 Hen. VI:</I> IV, i,
135. &lquo;A moraler&rquo;&mdash;<I>Oth.</I> II, iii, 301. &lquo;Justicers&rquo;&mdash;<I>Lear</I>, IV, ii, 79. &lquo;Homager&rquo;&mdash;
<I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.</I> I, i, 31. In the last two instances the -<I>er</I> is of French origin, and
in many cases, as in &lquo;enchant<I>er</I>,&rquo; it may seem to be English, while really it repre-
sents the French -<I>eur.</I> The -<I>er</I> is often added to show a masculine agent where a
noun and a verb are identical: &lquo;Truster&rquo;&mdash;<I>Hamlet</I>, I, ii, 172. &lquo;Causer&rquo;&mdash;<I>Rich.
III:</I> IV, iv, 122. &lquo;my origin and ender&rquo;&mdash;<I>Lov. Comp.</I> 222; and in this [present]

<P>137. <B>lac'd]</B> <SC>Theobald</SC> (Nichols, ii, 523): By &lquo;lac'd,&rquo; I am apt to imagine our Poet

III, v, 8.&mdash;<SC>Warburton</SC>: The whole speech is an unnatural mixture of far-fetched
and commonplace thoughts, that shows him to be acting a part.&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>: No
amendment can be made to this line, of which every word is equally faulty, but by a
general blot. It is not improbable that Shakespeare put these forced and unnatural
metaphors into the mouth of Macbeth, as a mark of artifice and dissimulation, to
show the difference between the studied language of hypocrisy and the natural out-
cries of sudden passion. This whole speech, so considered, is a remarkable instance
of judgement, as it consists entirely of antithesis and metaphor.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: The
allusion is to the decoration of the richest habits worn in the age of Shakespeare,
when it was usual to <I>lace</I> cloth of <I>silver</I> with <I>gold</I>, and cloth of <I>gold</I> with <I>silver.</I>
The second of these fashions is mentioned in <I>Much Ado</I>, III, iv, 19.&mdash;<SC>Harry
Rowe</SC>: The other day, my wooden Macbeth declared in the green-room that this

snow-white skin streaked with his crimson blood.&rquo; This, though not an extraordi-
nary good line, has something like sense to recommend it.&mdash;<SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 529): A
metaphor must not be far-fetched nor dwell upon the details of a disgusting picture,
as in these lines. There is but little, and that far-fetched, similarity between <I>gold
lace</I> and <I>blood</I>, or between <I>bloody daggers</I> and <I>breech'd legs.</I> The slightness of the
similarity, recalling the greatness of the dissimilarity, disgusts us with the attempted
comparison.

<SC>Johnson</SC>: An &lquo;unmannerly&rquo; dagger and a dagger &lquo;breech'd&rquo; are expressions not easily
to be understood. There are undoubtedly two faults here which I have endeavoured
to take away by reading: &lquo;<I>Unmanly drench'd</I> with gore,&rquo;&mdash;<I>I saw</I> drench'd <I>with the
king's blood not only instruments of murder but evidences of cowardice</I>. . . . Warbur-
ton's emendation is perhaps right.&mdash;<SC>Jennens</SC>: Shakespeare's first thought might
have been: &lquo;Their naked daggers were covered with gore.&rquo; <I>Nakedness</I> suggested
the word &lquo;unmannerly,&rquo; and <I>covered</I> the word &lquo;breeches,&rquo; the covering of nakedness.
&mdash;<SC>Farmer</SC>: That is, <I>sheath'd</I> with blood. In the 6th Dialogue of Erondell's
<I>French Garden</I>, 1605 (which I am persuaded Shakespeare read in the English, and
from which he took, as he supposed, this quaint expression), we have: &lquo;Boy, go
fetch your master's silver-hatched daggers, you have not brushed their <I>breeches</I>, bring
the brushes,&rquo; etc. Shakespeare was deceived by the pointing, and evidently sup-
poses <I>breeches</I> to be a new and affected term for <I>scabbards.</I>&mdash;<SC>Heath</SC> (<I>Revisal</I>, etc.
p. 388): Seward in his Notes on Beaumont &amp; Fletcher, i, p. 380, and ii, p. 276,
mentions another interpretation: &lquo;Stained with gore up to the <I>breeches</I>, that is, to
their hilts.&rquo; But, as he justly observes, the lower end of a cannon is called its
<I>breech</I>, yet the <I>breech</I> of a dagger is an expression which could not be used with
propriety. He conjectures the true reading to have been <I>hatch'd</I>, that is, gilt; and
adduces some instances from Fletcher which seem fully to prove the use of the word
in that signification. . . . My own conjecture is: &lquo;<I>In a manner lay drench'd</I> with
gore.&rquo; The qualifying form of expression, <I>In a manner</I>, seems to have a peculiar
propriety. A dagger cannot imbibe blood, nor be saturated with it like a sponge,
which is the idea conveyed by the word <I>drench'd</I>, but it may appear as if it were so.
&mdash;<SC>Douce</SC>: The present expression, though in itself something <I>unmannerly</I>, simply
means <I>covered as with breeches.</I>&mdash;<SC>Nares</SC>: Instead of concluding with Farmer that
Shakespeare had seen that passage from Erondell and mistaken it, we should use it
to confirm the true explanation, viz.: &lquo;Having their very hilt, or breech, covered
with blood.&rquo; Sheaths of daggers are wiped, not brushed, and Shakespeare could not
have supposed them to be here meant; it was evidently the silver hatching that
required the brush. We cannot, however, conceive of Shakespeare looking for
paltry authorities, or even thinking of them when he poured forth his rapid lines.
He doubtless took up the metaphor as it occurred to him without further reflection.
&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Gloss.</I>): Probably Douce is right.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: We doubt not the blade,
and not the <I>handle</I>, is meant. Compare <I>Twelfth Night</I>, III, iv, 274.

Devil,&rquo; believe me that her face was like ashes, as she returned to the chamber to
gild the faces of the grooms with the dead man's blood. That knocking, too,
alarmed the Lady&mdash;believe me&mdash;as much as her husband; and to keep cool and
collected before him, so as to be able to support him at that moment with her advice,
must have tried the utmost strength of her nature. Call her Fiend&mdash;she was a
Woman. Down stairs she comes&mdash;and stands among them all, at first like one
alarmed only&mdash;astounded by what she hears&mdash;and striving to simulate the ignorance
of the innocent&mdash;&lquo;What, in our house?&rquo; &lquo;Too cruel anywhere!&rquo; What she must
have suffered then Shakespeare lets us conceive for ourselves; and what on her
husband's elaborate description of his inconsiderate additional murders. &lquo;The
whole is too much for her&rquo;&mdash;she &lquo;is perplexed in the extreme&rquo;&mdash;and the sinner

<P>170. <B>easie]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 1): In early English many adverbs were formed from
adjectives by adding <I>e</I> (dative) to the positive degree: as <I>bright</I>, adj.; <I>brighte</I>, adv.
In time the <I>e</I> was dropped, but the adverbial use was kept. Hence, from a false
analogy, many adjectives (such as <I>excellent</I>) which could never form adverbs in <I>e</I>
were used as adverbs. We still say colloquially, &lquo;come <I>quick</I>,&rquo; &lquo;the moon shines
<I>bright</I>,&rquo; etc. But Shakespeare could say [as in the present line and in II, i, 26].&mdash;
<SC>Clarendon</SC>: In the next scene &lquo;like&rquo; is used for <I>likely</I>, line 41.
<P>174. <B>there's]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 335): When the subject is as yet future, and, as it were,
unsettled, the third person singular might be regarded as the normal inflection.
Such passages are very common, particularly in the case of &lquo;There is.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Claren-
don</SC>: Like <I>il y a</I> in French. Donalbain suspects all, but most his father's cousin,
Macbeth.

<P>10. <B>trauailing]</B> <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. i.): The words <I>travel</I> and &lquo;travail&rquo; (observes the
Rev. Mr Barry) have now different meanings, though formerly synonymous. <I>Trav-
elling</I>, the ordinary meaning, gives a puerile idea; whereas &lquo;travailing&rquo; seems to
have reference to the struggle between the sun and night.&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Remarks</I>, p.
195): In the speech <I>no mention is made of the sun</I> till it is described as &lquo;the <I>travel-
ling</I> lamp,&rquo;&mdash;the epithet &lquo;travelling&rquo; determining <I>what</I> &lquo;lamp&rquo; was intended: the
instant, therefore, that &lquo;travelling&rquo; is changed to &lquo;travailing,&rquo; the word &lquo;lamp&rquo;
<SC>ceases to signify the sun</SC>. That Shakespeare was not singular in applying the
epithet <I>travelling</I> to the <I>sun</I> might be shown by many passages of our early poets;
so Drayton: &lquo;&mdash; nor regard him [the Sunne] trauelling the signes.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Elegies</I>, p.
185, 1627. . . . I must add that this &lquo;puerile idea&rquo; is to be traced to Scripture&mdash;
<I>Psalm</I>, xix, 5.&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii.): As Shakespeare may have used &lquo;travailing&rquo; in
a double sense, as indicating toil and locomotion, we make no change.&mdash;[R. G.
<SC>White</SC> (ed. ii.): Probably the most extravagant metaphor in literature.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

<P>43. <B>Scone]</B> <SC>Knight</SC>: The ancient royal city of Scone, supposed to have been
the capital of the Pictish kingdom, lay two miles northward from the present town
of Perth. It was the residence of the Scottish monarchs as early as the reign of
Kenneth M'Alpin, and there was a long series of kings crowned on the celebrated
stone enclosed in a chair now used as the seat of our sovereigns at coronations in
Westminster Abbey. This stone was removed to Scone from Dunstaffnage, the yet
earlier residence of the Scottish kings, by Kenneth II, soon after the founding of the
Abbey of Scone by the Culdees in 838, and was transferred by Edward I. to West-
minster Abbey in 1296. This remarkable stone is reported to have found its way
to Dunstaffnage from the plain of Luz, where it was the pillow of the patriarch Jacob
while he dreamed his dream. An aisle of the Abbey of Scone remains. A few
poor habitations alone exist on the site of the ancient royal city.&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC> quotes
an account of Scone from <I>New Statistical Account of Scotland</I>, 1845, x, p. 1047.
<P>46. <B>Colmekill]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: The famous <I>Iona</I>, one of the Western Isles. Hol-
inshed scarcely mentions the death of any of the ancient kings of Scotland with-
out taking notice of their being buried with their predecessors in <I>Colme-kill.</I>&mdash;
<SC>Malone</SC>: It is now called <I>Icolmkill.</I>&mdash;<SC>Knight</SC>: This little island, only three miles
long and one and a half broad, was once the most important spot of the whole
cluster of British Isles. It was inhabited by Druids previous to the year 563,
when Colum M'Felim M'Fergus, afterwards called St. Columba, landed and began
to preach Christianity. A monastery was soon established, and a noble cathedral
built, of which the ruins still remain. The reputation of these establishments ex-
tended over the whole Christian world for some centuries, and devotees of rank
strove for admission into them; the records of royal deeds were preserved there, and
there the bones of kings reposed. All the monarchs of Scotland, from Kenneth III.
to Macbeth, inclusive&mdash;that is, from 973 to 1040&mdash;were buried at Iona. The island
was several times laid waste by Danes and pirates, and the records which were
saved were removed to Ireland, but the monastic establishments survived and
remained in honour till 1561, when the Act of the Convention of Estates doomed all
monasteries to demolition. Such books and records as could be found in Iona were
burnt, the tombs broken open, and the greater number of its hosts of crosses thrown
down or carried away. In the cemetery, among the monuments of the founders and
of many subsequent abbots, are three rows of tombs, said to be those of the Scottish,</CC>

<P>50-52. <B>No Cosin . . . there]</B> <SC>Libby</SC>: That is, Macduff will not follow the for-
tunes of a murderer, but Ross, with an apologetic &lquo;well,&rquo; announces his intention of
going to Scone to be with the successful Macbeth upon whom he has an ancient
claim. Macduff's twice-repeated &lquo;well&rquo; is a sneer: but he will not, or cannot,
quarrel with the smooth-mannered Ross. Unless Ross went to Macbeth to be his
adviser why did Macduff enjoin him to see things well done?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.&mdash;<SC>Manly</SC>:
Macduff's refusal to go to Scone, which, although it seems of no great significance at
the moment, nevertheless causes his later peremptory refusal to attend Macbeth to
come upon us not with the shock of a complete surprise, but as a thing that might have
been expected. Those of us who know the play well are apt to read every event in
the light of the whole play, but obviously the events of a play have at the moment
of their occurrence only the significance which they display upon seeing them first
presented; later a new significance appears as we see their results. This sounds
like a truism; too much closet study of Shakespeare has caused some of us to forget
it.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
<P>53. <B>Least our . . . new]</B> <SC>Deighton</SC>: Let us part, for fear we should find things

apart than together.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.

<P>1. <SC>Vischer</SC> (<I>Vortr&auml;ge</I>, ii, 96): The Third Act usually contains the crisis. May
it not be reasonably supposed that the first murder is fraught with fullest conse-
quences? Hardly; it is only after the second murder that Macbeth verges on
frenzy. Only then does he suffer the impulse of that fearful law of punishment
which leads him headlong downward. This turn is the most powerful in the drama,
and is therefore introduced in the Third Act. Here we reach the parting of the
ways.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
<P>4. <B>the]</B> <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Vers.</I> 75): <I>I' the</I> and <I>o' the</I> are to be pronounced <I>i'th'</I> and
<I>o'th'.</I> (In the Folio they are so printed; frequently <I>i'th, o'th;</I> the latter, by the
way, often <I>a'th'</I> or <I>a'th.</I>) In many places also, where the <I>e</I> in <I>the</I> before a consonant
is at present retained to the injury of the metre, it ought to be elided. In the pres-
ent case read <I>th', metri grati&acirc;.</I> [This reading was adopted in Singer (ed. ii.).]

<CC><P>13. <B>Senit]</B> <SC>Nares</SC>: <I>Sennet, Senet, Synnet, Cynet, Signet</I>, and <I>Signate.</I> A word
chiefly occurring in the stage-directions of old plays, and seeming to indicate a par-
ticular set of notes on the trumpet or cornet, different from a flourish. &lquo;Trumpets
sound a flourish, and then a sennet.&rquo;&mdash;Decker, <I>Satiromastix.</I> &lquo;The cornets sound a
cynet.&rquo;&mdash;Marston, <I>Antonio's Revenge.</I>&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Gloss.</I>): The etymology of the word
is doubtful.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: The word does not occur in the text of Shakespeare.&mdash;
[<SC>Darmesteter</SC>: &lquo;Sennet&rquo; . . . is the old French <I>signet</I>, derived from <I>seing</I>, bell,
which still survives in the word <I>tocsin</I>, literally: that which strikes (toquer) the
bell; <I>seing</I> is the Latin <I>signum:</I> in its early and general sense <I>signal, sign; seing</I>
and <I>signet</I> have survived in <I>blanc-seing</I> and the <I>signet</I> [signature] of printing.&mdash;
<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]
<P>18. <B>all-thing]</B> <SC>Elwin</SC>: So in <I>Henry the Eighth's Primer</I>, the Hymn in the
Compline commences thus: &lquo;O Lorde, the maker of <I>all-thing</I>, We pray the nowe in
this evening.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: It seems to be used as an adverb meaning in <I>every
way:</I> compare &lquo;something,&rquo; &lquo;nothing.&rquo; In <I>Robert of Gloucester</I>, p. 69 (ed. Hearne),
&lquo;alle thing&rquo; appears to be used for <I>altogether:</I> &lquo;As wommon deth hire child alle
thing mest.&rquo; Again, on p. 48, where Hearne prints: &lquo;Ac tho nolde not Cassibel
that heo schulde <I>allyng</I> faile,&rquo; Lord Mostyn's MS has &lquo;althynge,&rquo; meaning <I>altogether.</I>
&mdash;<SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 12): The adjectives <I>all, each, both, every, other</I>, are sometimes inter-
changed and used as pronouns in a manner different from modern usage. In this
instance &lquo;all&rquo; is used for <I>every.</I> We still use &lquo;all&rquo; for &lquo;all men.&rquo; But Ascham (p.
54) wrote: &lquo;<I>Ill</I> commonlie <I>have</I> over much wit,&rquo; and (p. 65): &lquo;Infinite shall be
made cold by your example, that <I>were</I> never hurt by reading of bookes.&rquo; This is
perhaps an attempt to introduce a Latin idiom. Shakespeare, however, writes:
&lquo;<I>What</I> ever <I>have</I> been thought on.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Coriol.</I> I, ii, 4.
<P>19. <B>a solemne Supper]</B> <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 136): That is, <I>a banquet, a high festival.</I>
So in Ariosto, as translated by Harington: &lquo;Nor never did young lady brave and

<P>19. <B>Supper]</B> <SC>Nares</SC>: Dinner being usually at eleven or twelve, supper was very
properly fixed at five o'clock. &lquo;With us the nobilitie, gentrie, and students, doo
ordinarilie go to dinner at eleven before noone, and to supper at five, or betweene
five and sixe at afternoone.&rquo;&mdash;Harrison, <I>Descrip. of England</I>, pref. to Holinshed,
[Bk, ii, p. 166, <I>Sh. Soc.</I> reprint.].
<P>20. <B>Ile]</B> <SC>Harry Rowe</SC>: As Macbeth is here speaking of the present, and not
of the future time, I do not well know why the learned editors should continue to
print &lquo;I'll&rquo; for &lquo;<I>I.</I>&rquo; Browne, in his <I>Vulgar Errors</I>, whimsically says: &lquo;Many
heads that undertake learning were never squared or timbered for it.&rquo; To my com-
pany this observation cannot apply, as there is not a head belonging to them but
what is exactly squared according to the rules of Lavater; so that they have a
decided superiority over those who may be said to &lquo;make their own heads.&rquo;
<P>21. <B>Let]</B> <SC>Malone</SC>: Rowe's change was suggested by D'Avenant's Version.&mdash;M.
<SC>Mason</SC>: I would rather read <I>Set</I> your command, etc.; for unless &lquo;command&rquo; is used
as a noun, there is nothing to which the following words&mdash;&lquo;to the which&rquo;&mdash;can
possibly refer.&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. i.) [after quoting Mason's note, as above, adds]: A
remark which ought not to have come from one familiar with our early writers.&mdash;
<SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii.): We have no difficulty in adopting the correction of the MS Cor-
rector, although <I>Set</I> may appear to come nearer the letters.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: The
phrase, &lquo;command upon me,&rquo; for <I>lay your commands upon me</I>, does not seem un-
natural, though we know of no other instance in which it is employed.
<P>22. <B>vpon]</B> <SC>Keightley</SC>: Insert <I>be</I> before &lquo;upon&rquo;; this removes all difficulty very
simply. <I>Be</I> is omitted constantly. [For modern tendency to restrict meaning of
prepositions, see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 139; also &sect; 191.]
<P>22. <B>the which]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 270): The question may arise why &lquo;the&rquo; is attached
to <I>which</I> and not to <I>who.</I> (The instance, &lquo;Your mistress from <I>the whom</I> I see,&rquo; etc.
&mdash;<I>Wint. Tale</I>, IV, iv, 539&mdash;is, perhaps, unique in Shakespeare.) The answer is
that <I>who</I> is considered definite already, and stands for a noun, while <I>which</I> is con-
sidered as an indefinite adjective; just as in French we have &lquo;<I>le</I>quel,&rquo; but not &lquo;<I>le</I>qui.&rquo;
&lquo;The which&rquo; is generally used either where the antecedent, or some word like the
antecedent, is repeated, or else where such a repetition could be made if desired.&mdash;
<SC>Clarendon</SC>: The antecedent to &lquo;which&rquo; is the idea contained in the preceding
clause.

<P>32. <B>the better]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: The better considering the distance he has to go.
Stowe, <I>Survey of London</I> (ed. 1618, p. 145, misquoted by Malone), says of tilting
at the quintain, &lquo;Hee that hit it full, if he rid not the faster, had a sound blow in

is, &lquo;If he rid not the faster <I>because</I> he had hit it full,&rquo; etc.&mdash;<SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 94): <I>The</I> (in
early Eng. <I>thi, thy</I>) is used as the ablative of the demonstrative and relative, with
comparatives, to signify the measure of excess or defect. This use is still retained.
&lquo;<I>The</I> sooner <I>the</I> better,&rquo; i. e. &lquo;<I>By how much</I> the sooner <I>by so much</I> the better.&rquo;
(Lat. &lquo;<I>quo</I> citius, <I>eo</I> melius.&rquo;) It is sometimes stated that &lquo;the better&rquo; is used by
Shakespeare for &lquo;better,&rquo; etc.: but it will often, perhaps always, be found that <I>the</I>
has a certain force. Thus in &lquo;<I>The</I> rather,&rquo; IV, iii, 184, &lquo;the&rquo; means &lquo;on that</CC>

<P>34. <B>twaine]</B> <SC>Skeat</SC> (<I>Dict.</I>): The difference between <I>two</I> and &lquo;twain&rquo; is one of
<I>gender</I> only, as appears from the Anglo-Saxon forms. &lquo;Twain&rquo; is masculine,
whilst <I>two</I> is feminine and neuter; but this distinction was early disregarded.
Middle English <I>tweien, tweithe, twein</I>, etc.; also <I>twa, two</I>, in which the <I>w</I> was pro-
nounced; the pronunciation of <I>two</I> as <I>too</I> being of rather late date. &lquo;Us <I>tweine</I>&rquo; =
us twain, us two, Chaucer: <I>Canterbury Tales</I>, l. 1135. &lquo;Sustren <I>two</I>&rquo; = sisters two,
<I>Ibid.</I> 1021. Our poets seem to use &lquo;twain&rquo; and <I>two</I> indifferently.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
<P>39. <B>Parricide]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Used in th&egrave; sense of <I>parricidium</I> as well as <I>parri-

48, where it means the latter.

<P>40. <B>But of that to morrow]</B> <SC>Moulton</SC>: The contrast of the two characters
appears here as everywhere. Lady Macbeth can <I>wait</I> for an opportunity of freeing
themselves from Banquo. To Macbeth the one thing impossible is to wait; and
once more his powerlessness to control suspense is his ruin.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.

<P>49-51. <B>Let . . . welcome]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Theobald's punctuation is doubtless

enjoy the society of his friends.&mdash;<SC>Moberly</SC>: So <I>Paradise Lost</I>, ix, 230: &lquo;To short
absence I could yield, For solitude sometimes is best society And short retirement
urges quick return.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

keepeth thee) is afraid of his: and being couragious and high when he is alone,
becommeth fearfull and timorous when he cometh neare vnto the other.&rquo;&mdash;[<SC>Baynes</SC>
(p. 270): Whatever the nature [of the rational soul], it rules, guards, keeps and
controls the man, wielding the lower powers as instruments to its own issues. The
poetical representations of this common view approach at times the more objective
conception of the Greek or Socratic demon and the Roman genius, as the theological
notion of distinct guardian or ruling spirits. In this passage from <I>Macbeth</I> the
term may probably have, with the ordinary meaning, an objective reference of this
kind. In Shakespeare, however, the terms angel and genius are usually employed
to denote the higher nature of man, the rational guiding soul or spirit, which in con-
nexion with the mortal instruments determines his character and fate. In Macbeth
this spirit is that of insatiable and guilty ambition. It is this aspiring lawless genius
that Banquo's innate loyalty of heart and rectitude of purpose silently rebuked. This
was the angel he still had served, whose evil whisperings had prepared him for the
dark suggestions of the weird sisters, and inclined him to trust their fatal incanta-
tions. [See note <I>post</I>, V, viii, 20.] But this may be easily misunderstood without
some definite knowledge of the sense in which the term &lquo;angel&rquo; is used.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]
<P>74. <B>with]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: &lquo;With&rquo; was used formerly of the agent, where now we
should rather say <I>by.</I> Compare <I>Wint. Tale</I>, V, ii, 68. We confine &lquo;with&rquo; to the
instrument, and still say &lquo;with a hand,&rquo; &lquo;with a sword,&rquo; but not &lquo;with a man,&rquo;
&lquo;with a bear.&rquo; See also <I>King John</I>, II, i, 567.

<P>81. <B>Seedes]</B> <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. i.): Macbeth speaks of Banquo's issue throughout

rendered emphatically significant of <I>far-extended descents.</I>&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Rem.</I>): Does
not &lquo;seed&rquo; convey the idea of number as well as <I>seeds?</I>&mdash;<SC>Ibid</SC>. (ed. i.): I do not
venture to retain the reading of the Ff on the strength of a somewhat doubtful
reading in the Second Part of Marlowe's <I>Tamburlaine</I>, &lquo;And live in all your <I>seeds</I>
immortally&rquo; (<I>Works</I>, i, 222, ed. Dyce), since it is a frequent error of the Folio to
put the plural of substantives instead of the singular (see an instance in this play,
III, vi, 27), and since it is unlikely that Shakespeare (who in <I>Tro. &amp; Cres.</I> IV, v,
121, has, &lquo;A cousin-german to great Priam's <I>seed</I>,&rquo; etc.) would so deviate here from
common phraseology as to term a man's issue his <I>seeds.</I>&mdash;<SC>Walker</SC> (i, 240): We
have, indeed, in Chapman and Shirley's <I>Chabot</I>, II, iii, p. 108, Shirley ed. Gifford
and Dyce, &lquo;&mdash; thunder on your head, And after you crush your surviving seeds.&rquo;
But this play is grossly corrupt.&mdash;[<SC>Ibid</SC>. (<I>Crit.</I> i, 234): The interpolation of an <I>s</I> at
the end of a word&mdash;generally, but not always, a noun substantive&mdash;is remarkably
frequent in the Folio. Those who are conversant with the MSS of the Elizabethan
Age may perhaps be able to explain its origin. Were it not for the different degree
of frequency with which it appears in different parts of the Folio, I should think it
originated in some peculiarity in Shakespeare's handwriting.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]</CC>

<CC><P>82. <B>Lyst]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Nowhere else used in the singular by Shakespeare
except in the more general sense of <I>boundary</I>, as <I>Hamlet</I>, IV, v, 99. For the space
marked out for a combat he always uses <I>lists.</I>
<P>83. <B>champion]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Fight with me in single combat. This seems to
be the only known passage in which the verb is used in this sense.
<P>83. <B>vtterance]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: This passage will be best explained by translating it
into the language from whence the only word of difficulty in it is borrowed. &lquo;<I>Que
la destin&eacute;e se rende en lice, et qu' elle me donne un defi</I> a l'outrance.&rquo; A challenge,
or a combat <I>a l'outrance</I>, to extremity, was a fixed term in the law of arms, used
when the combatants engaged with an <I>odium internecinum</I>, an intention to destroy
each other, in opposition to trials of skill at festivals, or on other occasions, where
the contest was only for reputation or a prize. The sense therefore is: Let fate,
that has foredoomed the exaltation of the sons of Banquo, enter the lists against me,
with the utmost animosity, in defence of its own decrees, which I will endeavour to
invalidate, whatever be the danger.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: Cotgrave has: &lquo;<I>Combatre &agrave;
oultrance.</I> To fight at sharpe, to fight it out, or to the vttermost; not to spare one
another in fighting.&rquo; So in Holland's <I>Pliny</I>, ii, 26: &lquo;Germanicus C&aelig;sar exhibited
a shew of sword-fencers at utterance.&rquo;
<P>85. <B>Murtherers]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: These two are not assassins by profession, as is
clear by what follows, but soldiers whose fortunes, according to Macbeth, have been
ruined by Banquo's influence.&mdash;<SC>Coleridge</SC> (p. 249): Compare Macbeth's mode of
working on the murderers with Schiller's mistaken scene between Butler, Devereux,
and Macdonald, in <I>Wallenstein</I> (Part II, Act V, ii.). The comic was wholly out of
season. Shakespeare never introduces it, but when it may react on the tragedy by
harmonious contrast.&mdash;[E. K. <SC>Chambers</SC>: The murderers are former victims of
Macbeth's own, whom he has now induced to believe that they owe their wrongs
to Banquo. Here again Macbeth's histrionic skill, his power of playing upon the
emotions of others, comes out. This passage is sufficient to show that Macbeth was
not perfectly innocent and noble before the witches tempted him.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]</CC>

<P>115. <B>clipt]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: This word was becoming obsolete in Shakespeare's time.

<P>116. <B>valued file]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: That is, the file or list where the value and pecu-

in the same sense as in this, and with a reference to it: Now if you belong to any
class that deserves a place in the valued &lquo;file&rquo; of men, and are not of the lowest
rank, the common herd of mankind, that are not worth distinguishing from each
other. &lquo;File&rquo; and <I>list</I> are synonymous, as in V, ii, 12, of this play. In short, &lquo;the
valued file&rquo; is the catalogue with prices annexed.

<CC><C>[157. <B>perfect Spy</B>]</C>
<P>393): The word &lquo;spy&rquo; is here used for <I>espyal</I> or <I>discovery</I>, and the phrase means
the exact intimation of the precise time, or as Shakespeare immediately interprets
his own words, &lquo;the moment on't.&rquo; Johnson's supposition that the &lquo;spy&rquo; is the
third murderer cannot be correct; for Macbeth promises the two that he will make
them acquainted with this perfect spy, which yet he is so far from doing, that the
third murderer when he joins the others is absolutely unknown to them.&mdash;M.
<SC>Mason</SC>: &lquo;With&rquo; has here the force of <I>by;</I> and the meaning of the passage is: &lquo;I
will let you know, by the person best informed, of the exact moment in which the
business is to be done.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: This passage needs no reformation but that
of a single point. After &lquo;yourselves,&rquo; in line 156, I place a full stop, as no further
instructions could be given by Macbeth, the hour of Banquo's return being quite
uncertain. Macbeth therefore adds: &lquo;Acquaint <I>you</I>,&rquo; etc., <I>i. e.</I> in ancient language,
&lquo;acquaint <I>yourselves</I>&rquo; with the exact time most favourable to your purposes; for such
a moment must be spied out by you, be selected by your own attention and scrupu-
lous observation. Macbeth in the intervening time might have learned, from some
of Banquo's attendants, which way he had ridden out, and therefore could tell the
murderers <I>where</I> to plant themselves so as to cut him off on his return; but who
could ascertain the precise hour of his arrival, except the ruffians who watched for
that purpose?&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: The meaning, I think, is, I will acquaint you with the
time when you may <I>look out</I> for Banquo's coming, with the most <I>perfect</I> assurance
of not being disappointed; and not only with the <I>time</I> in general most proper for
lying in wait for him, but with the very <I>moment</I> when you may expect him.&mdash;<SC>Bos-
well</SC>: I apprehend it means the very moment you are to <I>look for</I> or <I>expect</I>, not
when you may <I>look out</I> for, Banquo. [From this note by Boswell are we to infer
that he took Malone's use of &lquo;look out&rquo; as literally meaning to <I>peep forth</I> from
the ambush wherein the murderers lay hid?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: If the text
be right, it may bear one of two meanings: first, I will acquaint you with the
most accurate observation of the time, <I>i. e.</I> with the result of the most accurate
observation; or secondly, &lquo;the spy of the time&rquo; may mean the man who joins
the murderers in Scene iii, and &lquo;delivers their offices.&rquo; But we have no
examples of the use of the word &lquo;spy&rquo; in the former sense, and according to
the second interpretation we should rather expect &lquo;<I>a</I> perfect spy&rquo; than &lquo;<I>the</I> per-
fect spy.&rquo; . . . &lquo;The perfect spy&rquo; might also be suggested, or possibly &lquo;the per-

<CC><P>169. <B>It is concluded]</B> <SC>Hunter</SC>: In the age of Elizabeth such negotiations were
not very uncommon. An instance had recently occurred in the neighborhood of
Stratford. Lodowick Grevile, who dwelt at Sesoncote, in Gloucestershire, and at
Milcote, in Warwickshire, coveting the estate of one Webb, his tenant, plotted to
murder him and get the estate by a forged will. This was successfully accomplished
by the aid of two servants whom Grevile engaged to do the deed. Fearing detec-
tion, one of the assassins afterwards murdered his comrade. The body was found,
and the investigation led to the arrest and conviction of Grevile and his servant, the
surviving murderer. Grevile stood mute, and was pressed to death on November
14, 1589. The circumstance must have been well known to Shakespeare, as the
Greviles were at this time patrons of the living of Stratford.
<P>169, 170. <B>Banquo . . . Night]</B> <SC>D'Hugues</SC>: These lines contain an ironic and
sneering allusion to the honesty of Banquo, whose honourable and loyal bearing, in
the preceding scenes, has been in such marked contrast to that of Macbeth.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
<P>1. <B>Scena Secunda]</B> E. K. <SC>Chambers</SC>: From the moment of her sin, remorse
begins to lay hold upon Lady Macbeth. She conceals it in Macbeth's presence,
thinking to strengthen him, as of old; but the two lives are insensibly drifting
asunder. As for Macbeth himself, directly there is nothing to be done, he becomes
morbid, brooding over his crimes past and future, and playing about them with
lurid words.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
<P>3. <B>Is . . . Court]</B> <SC>Bell</SC> (p. 308): [Mrs Siddons said this with] great dignity and
solemnity of voice; nothing of the joy of gratified ambition. [May not Lady Mac-

her husband ask concerning Banquo's movements in III, i. ?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]
<P>4. <B>I . . . to Night]</B> <SC>Noel</SC> (p. 52): I seem to read relief in the answer she re-
ceived, which almost suggests that she is afraid of a further crime being committed.
She has read something of Macbeth's significant manner lately, and she is restless
and unhappy, and with that restlessness comes a natural yearning for companionship.

<P>18. <B>scorch'd]</B> <SC>Theobald</SC> (<I>Sh. Restored</I>, p. 185): Shakespeare, I am very well
persuaded, had this notion in his head (how true, in fact, I will not pretend to deter-
mine), that if you cut a serpent, or worm, asunder, there is such an unctious quality
in their blood that the dismembered parts, being placed near enough to touch each
other, will cement and become whole again. Macbeth considers Duncan's sons so
much as members of their Father that though he has cut off the old man, he has not
entirely killed him, but he'll cement and close again in the lives of his sons. Shake-
speare certainly wrote <I>scotch'd.</I> To <I>scotch</I>, however the Generality of our Diction-

Swords, etc., and so our Poet more than once has used it in his works. See

the story of the Hydra.&mdash;<SC>Harry Rowe</SC>: My Prompter, who is a North-Country
man, says that there is no such word as <I>scotch'd.</I> It is <I>scutch'd</I>, a word chiefly
used by the growers and manufacturers of hemp and flax, and implies beating,
bruising, or dividing. The wooden-headed fellow of my company, who plays
the clown, says that snakes are soon killed by lashing them with switches, and
that by smart strokes their bodies may be divided. This has induced some of the
gentlemen of my green-room to adopt &lquo;We have <I>switch'd</I> the snake,&rquo; etc. The
stuffed figure of my company, who plays the Serpent in <I>The History of Adam and
Eve</I>, has suggested a reading that is more conformable to natural history: &lquo;We have
<I>bruised</I> the snake . . . She'll <I>coil</I>,&rquo; etc. My Prompter wishes the original text to be
continued, only substituting <I>coil</I> for &lquo;close,&rquo; and this he calls a good emendation. I
have accordingly adopted it. After all, I do not consider Shakespeare as under any
obligations to his <I>scotching, scutching, bruising</I>, and <I>switching</I> commentators.&mdash;

<CC><P>knyfe <I>scortche</I> not the boorde,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> do not score the table with your knife. The
derivation from <I>score</I> is not wholly satisfactory, as it does not account for the final
<I>ch.</I> I think it is clear that we have here an example of what is really fairly
common in English&mdash;formed as it is by a fusion of Romance with Teutonic&mdash;viz.
the evolution of a new word which has resulted from the confusion of two others.
The ordinary verb <I>scorch</I>, tho' it usually means &lquo;to parch,&rquo; meant originally to
excoriate, or rather, <I>to excorticate;</I> it is derived from the Old French <I>escorcher</I>,
to strip off bark, from a Latin type <I>excorticare.</I> By confusion of this with
the word <I>score</I>, a new verb, <I>scorch</I>, was formed, with the sense of to make
an incision on the surface <I>only</I>, to cut with <I>shallow</I> incisions, to scratch with a
knife. And this it is which Antipholus of Ephesus threatened to do. He did not
want to excoriate or flay his wife's face, but merely to scratch it so as to spoil her
beauty. We can now proceed a step further; for this new verb, <I>to scorch</I>, being
really distinct from the original one, was frequently subjected to a more rapid pronun-
ciation, and is better known under the form <I>to scotch</I>, which has precisely the same
sense. This is well seen by help of the famous passage in <I>Macbeth</I>, III, ii, 13,
&lquo;we have <I>scotched</I> the snake, not killed it,&rquo; which is really a &lquo;correction&rquo; made by
Theobald; for, as a matter of fact, the reading in the Ff is &lquo;scorch'd.&rquo; That is to
say, the Ff are perfectly correct, as is not unfrequently the case, and the editorial
&lquo;correction&rquo; was needless. The sense is, we have <I>scored</I> or <I>scratched</I> the snake, we
have wounded him upon the surface only. The ordinary sense of <I>scorch</I> will not
help us here. The shortening to <I>scotch</I> is proved, however, by two considerations:
(1) the passage in <I>Coriol.</I> IV, v, 198, &lquo;he scotched [him] and notched him like a
carbonado,&rquo; where the riming of the words is evidently intentional, whilst at the same
time these words are nearly equivalent in sense; and (2) by the compound word
<I>hop-scotch</I>, which means a game in which children hop over scotches or slight scores
upon the ground, as it is correctly explained in the <I>New English Dictionary.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]
<P>21-25. <B>But let . . . Nightly]</B> <SC>Coleridge</SC> (i, 249): Ever and ever mistaking the
anguish of conscience for fears of selfishness, and thus as a punishment of that sel-
fishness, plunging still deeper in guilt and ruin.&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC>: But is it not the natural
result of an imagination so redundant and excitable as his, that the agonies of re-
morse should project and embody themselves in imaginary terrors, and so, for security
against these, put him upon new crimes?
<P>21, 22. <B>But . . . suffer]</B> R. G. <SC>White</SC>: These lines are very imperfect. But it
should be observed that other lines in this speech, and several throughout this
scene, are in the same condition.</CC>

<P>47. <B>But . . . eterne]</B> <SC>Fletcher</SC> (p. 134): The natural and unrestrained mean-
ing is, at most, nothing more than this, that Banquo and his son are not immortal. It
is not she, but her husband, that draws a practical inference from this harmless propo-
sition. That &lquo;they are assailable&rquo; may be &lquo;comfort,&rquo; indeed, to him; but it is evi-
dently none to her, and he proceeds to tell her that &lquo;there shall be done A deed of
dreadful note.&rquo; Still provokingly unapprehensive of his meaning, she asks him
anxiously, &lquo;What's to be done?&rquo; But he, after trying the ground so far, finding her
utterly indisposed to concur in his present scheme, <I>does not dare</I> to communicate it to
her in plain terms, lest she should chide the fears that prompt him to this new and
gratuitous enormity, by virtue of the very same spirit that had made her combat those
which had withheld him from the one great crime which she had deemed necessary
to his elevation. It is only through a misapprehension, which unjustly lowers the
generosity of her character and unduly exalts that of her husband, that so many
critics have represented this passage (&lquo;Be innocent of the knowledge,&rquo; etc.) as
spoken by Macbeth out of a magnanimous desire to spare his wife all guilty par-
ticipation in an act which at the same time, they tell us, he believes will give her
satisfaction. It is, in fact, but a new and signal instance of his moral cowardice.

<CC><P>51. <B>shard-borne]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: The beetle borne along by its <I>shards</I> or <I>scaly
wings;</I> as appears from a passage in Gower, <I>Confessio Amantis</I>, [vol. iii, p. 68, ed.
Pauli], &lquo;She sigh, her thought, a dragon tho, Whose scherdes shynen as the sonne.&rquo;
Ben Jonson, in his <I>Sad Shepherd</I>, says: &lquo;The <I>scaly</I> beetles with their <I>habergeons</I>,

See also <I>Cymb.</I> III, iii, 20. Such another description of the beetle occurs in Chap-

beetle&rquo; is the beetle born in dung. Aristotle and Pliny mention beetles that breed in
dung. Poets as well as natural historians have made the same observation. See
Drayton's <I>Ideas</I>, 31: &lquo;I scorn all earthly <I>dung-bred</I> scarabies.&rquo; So, Jonson, [ed.
Gifford, vol. i, p. 61]: &lquo;But men of thy condition feed on sloth, As doth the <I>beetle</I>
on the <I>dung</I> she breeds in.&rquo; That <I>shard</I> signifies <I>dung</I> is well known in the North
of Staffordshire, where <I>cowshard</I> is the word generally used for <I>cow-dung.</I>&mdash;<SC>Patter-
son</SC> (p. 65): The beetle's wings are protected from external injury by two very
hard, horny wing-cases, or elytra. . . . These shards or wing-cases are raised and
expanded when the beetle flies, and by their concavity act like two parachutes in
supporting him in the air. Hence &lquo;the shard-borne beetle,&rquo; a description embod-
ied in a single epithet.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: &lquo;Shard&rquo; is derived from the Anglo-Saxon
<I>sceard</I>, a fragment, generally of pottery. . . . Tollet's reading is unquestionably
wrong, though &lquo;shard&rquo; means &lquo;dung&rquo; in some dialects.

<P>55. <B>dearest Chuck]</B> R. H. <SC>Hiecke</SC> (p. 31): Must all the reiterated terms of en-

passages of this drama, this is the deepest. <I>Unintentionally</I> and <I>unconsciously</I> there
here breathes from Macbeth's soul an echo of that happier time when the mutual
esteem of a heroic pair was accompanied by the delicate attentions of first love.

solely by a fiendish alliance in pursuit of an ambitious end,&mdash;so here this love,
<I>grown cold</I>, was <I>murdered</I> in the murder of the King, and the tenderness in this
scene is naught but a dirge, rising unconsciously from the soul, over the sentiments
of an earlier time, [p. 468, ed. 1873.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.].

<SC>Steevens</SC>: This may mean <I>damp, misty, steaming with exhalations.</I> It is only a
North-Country variation of dialect from <I>reeky.</I> In <I>Coriol.</I> III, iii, 121, we have
&lquo;the reek o' the rotten fens.&rquo; &lquo;Rooky wood,&rquo; indeed, may signify a <I>rookery, the
wood that abounds with rooks;</I> yet merely to say of the <I>crow</I> that he is flying to
a wood inhabited by <I>rooks</I>, is to add little immediately pertinent to the succeeding
observation, v<*>z.: that &lquo;&mdash;things of day begin to droop and drowse.&rquo; I cannot,
therefore, help supposing our author wrote: &lquo;makes wing to <I>rook i' th</I>' wood.&rquo;
That is, to <I>roost</I> in it.&mdash;<SC>Harry Rowe</SC>: A rooky wood is simply a wood where
there are rookeries, and has nothing to do with the &lquo;reek of rotten fens.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Forby</SC>:
That is, <I>foggy.</I> Any East Anglian plough-boy would have instantly removed the
learned commentator's doubt whether it had anything to do with <I>rooks.</I> [The same
meaning is given in <SC>Carr's</SC> <I>Craven Dialect</I>, 1828; <SC>Brockett's</SC> <I>North Country
Words</I>, 1829, and in <SC>Morris's</SC> <I>Glossary of Furness</I>, 1869. The last adds: &lquo;Icel.
<I>rakr.</I> &ldquo;Roky, or mysty, nebulosus.&rdquo;&mdash;<I>Promp. Parv.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Mitford</SC> (<I>Gent.
Maga.</I> Aug. 1844, p. 129): &lquo;Crow&rquo; is the common appellation of the &lquo;rook,&rquo; the
latter word being used only when we would speak with precision, and never by the
country people, as the word &lquo;crow-keeper&rquo; will serve to show, which means the
boy who keeps the <I>rooks</I> (not carrion crows) off the seed-corn. The carrion crow,
which is the <I>crow proper</I>, being almost extinct, the necessity of distinguishing it
from the <I>rook</I> has passed away in common usage. The passage, therefore, simply
means, &lquo;the rook hastens its evening flight to the wood where its fellows are already
assembled,&rquo; and to our mind &lquo;the rooky wood&rquo; is a lively and natural picture: the
<I>generic</I> term &lquo;crow&rquo; is used for the <I>specific</I> &lquo;rook.&rquo;
<P>62. <B>Good things . . . drowse]</B> <SC>Dowden</SC> (p. 244): This line, uttered as the
evening shadows begin to gather on the day of Banquo's murder, we may repeat to
ourselves as a motto of the entire tragedy. It is the tragedy of thick twilight and
the setting-in of thick darkness upon a human soul. We assist at the spectacle
of a terrible sunset in folded clouds of blood. To the last, however, one thin
hand's-breadth of melancholy light remains&mdash;the sadness of the day without its
strength. Macbeth is the prey of a profound world-weariness. And while a huge
<I>ennui</I> pursues crime, the criminal is not yet in utter blackness of night. When the
play opens the sun is already dropping below the verge. And at sunset strange
winds arise, and gather the clouds to westward with mysterious pause and stir, so
the play of <I>Macbeth</I> opens with movement of mysterious, spiritual powers, which
are auxiliary of that awful shadow which first creeps, and then strides, across the
moral horizon.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.

<P>2. <B>Enter three Murtherers]</B> <SC>Allan Park Paton</SC> (<I>Notes and Queries</I> 11 Sept.,
13 Nov. 1869) broached and maintained the theory that the Third Murderer was
Macbeth himself, and adduced in proof eight arguments. <I>First:</I> Although the
banquet was to commence at seven, Macbeth did not go there till near midnight.
<I>Second:</I> His entrance to the room and the appearance of the murderer are almost
simultaneous. <I>Third:</I> So dear to his heart was the success of this plot, that
during the four or five hours before the banquet he must have been taken up with
the intended murder some way or other. He could not have gone to the feast
with the barest chance of the plot miscarrying. <I>Fourth:</I> If there had been a Third
Murderer sent to superintend the other two, he must have been Macbeth's chief
confidant, and as such in all probability would have been the first to announce the
result. <I>Fifth:</I> The &lquo;twenty mortal murthers&rquo; was a needless and devilish kind of
mutilation, not like the work of hirelings. <I>Sixth:</I> The Third Murderer repeated
the precise instructions given to the other two, showed unusual intimacy with the
exact locality, the habits of the visitors, etc., and seems to have struck down the
light, probably to escape recognition. <I>Seventh:</I> There was a levity in Macbeth's
manner with the murderer at the banquet, which is quite explicable if he personally
knew that Banquo was dead. <I>Eighth:</I> When the Ghost rises, Macbeth asks those
about him &lquo;which of them had done it,&rquo; evidently to take suspicion off himself, and
he says, in effect, to the ghost, &lquo;In yon black struggle you could <I>never know me.</I>&rquo;
&mdash;[E. <SC>Hills</SC> (<I>Notes and Queries</I>, 2 Oct. 1869) thus replies to Paton, whose argu-
ments, to save space, will be referred to numerically (<I>First</I>): &lquo;I should not dwell
much on this; for Shakespeare is thoroughly careless about the unities of time
or place, or indeed any unity. Besides, did Macbeth <I>not</I> go there until midnight?
I think Sc. iv. occupies several hours, but obviously it would not be convenient to
break it up into three or four parts. This idea will, of course, explain [Paton's
second and third arguments]. The murder, I admit, comes before Sc. iv.; but that
was necessary for the audience, and is a highly dramatic method. . . . [<I>Fourth</I>]: I</CC>

<CC><C>[2. <B>Enter three Murtherers</B>]</C>
<P>suppose the First and Second Murderers to have been retainers formerly of Banquo,
in which case they would know nothing of the locality of Macbeth's residence.
So the third was a servant (and creature) of Macbeth, who went to inform them
of the time of Banquo's return. That Macbeth had plenty of such confidants is
certain from [III], iv, 162-3. This supposition would also account for the First
Murderer telling the tale, as it would be better for the servant to keep out of the
way, whereas the First and Second Murderers would be unknown to the house-
hold. [<I>Fifth</I>]: Macbeth had told them &ldquo;to leave no botches in the work.&rdquo; Further-
more they were private enemies. [<I>Sixth</I>]: Here Paton seems to have written
from memory. The Third Murderer neither gives nor repeats any orders at all.
He simply replies &ldquo;Macbeth.&rdquo;&rquo; [In a subsequent article Hills admits that he
was &lquo;a little too hasty in saying that the Third Murderer &ldquo;gives no orders.&rdquo; He
certainly &ldquo;repeats no orders,&rdquo; for the orders relate simply to the time and the post
of action.&rquo;] &lquo;I do not think,&rquo; continues Hills, &lquo;that the Third Murderer was the
first to hear the sound of horses: for the First Murderer says: &ldquo;now [<I>sic</I>] near
approaches The object [<I>sic</I>] of our watch.&rdquo; When did the Third Murderer
identify Banquo? Did <I>he</I> strike out the light, who asked why it was done? Obvi-
ously the First Murderer struck it out&mdash;the man who answers &ldquo;Was't not the way?&rdquo;
Now why the First or Second Murderer should strike it out is plain, if the idea
of their being retainers be taken; <I>i. e.</I> if Banquo or Fleance did escape they did
not care to be recognised. And this conduct would appear strange to the Third
Murderer, Macbeth's servant. Lastly, if Macbeth was the Third Murderer, how
was it that neither the First nor Second recognised him? [<I>Seventh</I>]: Even if there
were any great levity in Macbeth's speeches, which I myself cannot see, how far
would that go in an author who has made characters reason the most quietly in the
most awkward predicaments? Besides, would Shakespeare put such lines as &ldquo;Then
comes my fit again&rdquo; [III, iv, 27] or &ldquo;There the grown serpent lies&rdquo; [III, iv, 37]
in the mouth of a man who had been present at the murder, and who therefore knew
the issue of it? [<I>Eighth</I>]: I think the words &ldquo;Thou canst not say <I>I</I> did it&rdquo; just the
sort of words a murderer by deputy would use. To make the man actually engaged
in a murder speak so, would seem to make nonsense of Shakespeare.&rquo; This called forth
a reply from <SC>Paton</SC>, in which he said, &lquo;The entertainment began (the hour specified
<I>must</I> be dwelt on) at seven, and the banquet begins with the fourth scene of the third
act; not far from the time when night is &ldquo;almost at odds with morning.&rdquo; Macbeth
having just joined his guests in another part of the palace, comes with them into the
hall where the banquet is prepared. Giving as his reason that it would make
society the more welcome to him, he had said he would keep himself &ldquo;till supper-
time alone.&rdquo; <I>This</I> is supper-time; he bids the company be seated at the table,
and wishes to all appetite and health.&rquo; To the suggestion by Hills that the Third
Murderer might be a creature of Macbeth, <SC>Paton</SC> objected on the ground that Mac-
beth would not have been likely to entrust a share in the designed murder to such a
one&mdash;a mere gatherer of gossip and political opinion. In <I>Notes and Queries</I>, 30 Oct.
1869, T. S. <SC>Baynes</SC> maintains that he anticipated Paton.&mdash;<SC>Irving</SC> (<I>Nineteenth Cen-
tury</I>, April, 1877): A theory on the subject [of the Third Murderer] has struck
me, which has not, so far as I am aware, been hitherto advanced. What I wish to
contend is, that [the character designated as an] &lquo;Attendant&rquo; is the Third Murderer.
My reasons are as follows: Macbeth utters what little he does say to this attendant
in a tone of marked contempt&mdash;strangely suggestive, to my mind, of his being</CC>

<CC><C>[2. <B>Enter three Murtherers</B>]</C>
<P>some wretched creature entirely in Macbeth's power. The tone of contempt [in
lines 54, 58, 86, Act III, i.] is obvious, and also the fact that this attendant had
been taken into his master's confidence. The next direction is: &lquo;Enter Servant with
two Murderers&rquo;; when Macbeth says to him, in the same tone and manner, &lquo;Now
go to the door and stay there till we call.&rquo; If the attendant left the chamber
by one door and the murderers by another, and if Macbeth used the former egress,
the suggestion would be, that at this moment, while he kept the murderers waiting,
and in expectation of seeing him again (&lquo;I'll call upon you straight&mdash;abide within&rquo;),
he went after the attendant and gave him his instructions. Macbeth thus secures to
himself a check upon the two murderers in the person of this attendant, who is
made an accomplice. A very slight change in the accepted stage business would
make all this stratagem clear to the audience, and it fits in with my theory that the
attendant was a trusty, and not a common, servant. Had he been otherwise, the
most momentous and secret transaction of the play would never have been committed
to him. Coming now to the murder of Banquo (III, iii.), we find that one man is a
stranger to the other two&mdash;at any rate so far as his privity to the enterprise is
concerned. But the manner in which the Second Murderer satisfies the First
strengthens my theory. For either the Second Murderer did not recognise the
stranger at all, owing to the darkness of the night, or else perhaps they did not
recognise him as the attendant whom they had seen before; in which case also they
would have been chary of confiding in him. Indeed, the instant reply of the Second
Murderer would favour the assumption that the stranger was a man they already
knew, and the exact familiarity which the Third Murderer shows with the surround-
ings of the palace and the readiness with which his information is accepted by the
others, suggest that he must have been somebody quite conversant with the palace
usages and approaches. My theory would account for this familiar acquaintance on
the part of the Third Murderer without recourse to any such violent improbability
as that the Third Murderer was Macbeth himself. Think of the effect of the First
Murderer being brought to the banquet room by the attendant, and the latter stand-
ing by during the ghastly recital of the murder. If this expedient were adopted,
there would be no intrinsic absurdity in the appearance of the strange man at the
feast. He might come there with a secrecy the more effectual because of its apparent
openness, for he would be in the company of one of Macbeth's chief retainers. The
conversation so conducted, only just out of earshot of the whole company, might be
no violation of probability, even though the deadliest secret were clothed under the
natural disguise. But the effect upon the audience would be widely different from
that of the present almost unmanageable tradition, which necessitates an improba-
bility so absurd as to render almost ridiculous what might be one of the most thrill-
ing horrors of the tragedy.&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC> (ed. iii.) I am by no means sure but [Paton]
is right. . . . Perhaps the strongest point against this view is, that Macbeth seems
surprised, and goes into a rapture, on being told that &lquo;Fleance is 'scaped&rquo;; but this
may not be very much; he may there be feigning. On the other hand, Macbeth's
actual sharing in the deed of murder would go far to account for his terrible hallu-
cination at the banquet.&mdash;<SC>Moy Thomas</SC> (<I>Athen&aelig;um</I>, 14 Ap. 1877) shows that the
stage-directions whereon Irving lays stress are not to be found in the Folio;
and concludes that: &lquo;If [the Third Murderer and the Attendant] were the same
person they would almost necessarily have been represented by the same actor.
