<CC><P>deficient, and are certainly likely to cause confusion in the prompter's box. To the
argument that the Third Murderer evidently knew &ldquo;all the surroundings of the pal-
ace&rdquo; and, therefore, was likely to be the attendant previously introduced, it is
enough to answer that, whoever he was, he must have been in close connection
with Macbeth.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Libby</SC> (see note on I, ii, 53): If Ross is the Third Murderer, as
we hope to establish, then it is clear that it is because Shakespeare is dealing with
the <I>spy-system</I> that he refuses to give up the name of this villain. It should be
remembered that Shakespeare does not merely neglect to name the Third Mur-
derer, he emphasizes the mystery in every possible way to arouse our curiosity,
once more masking the business for weighty reasons. [<SC>Libby</SC> here quotes <SC>Paton's</SC>
eight arguments in proof that Macbeth is the Third Murderer.] In replying to
these arguments it may be said generally that most of them apply well to Macbeth,
but better to Ross. More particularly they are met as follows: (1) Macbeth went
to the banquet as soon as Ross had returned by a short way and reported. (2) The
murderer (who certainly did not know the short way home) reached Macbeth about
twenty minutes later than Ross. (3) Macbeth had passed a terrible time of inactivity
before Ross returned, and that unhinged his mind: he is more unhinged by that
horrible imagining than he had been by the murder of Duncan. (4) Ross was
Macbeth's chief confidant at this time, and was the first to announce the result.
(5) The twenty mortal murthers was extremely characteristic of that poltroon Ross,
panic-stricken and stabbing in the dark a rival who had recognised him. (6) Ross
knew the place and the guests as only such a spy could know them: he struck down
<I>after</I> the terrible recognition of Banquo's &lquo;O, Slave,&rquo; which applies infinitely better
to this spy than to Macbeth. Ross owed his power to his service of Macbeth. If
Macbeth might have been recognised by Banquo, as <SC>Paton</SC> says, why was he not
recognised by the murderers? (7) Macbeth was amused by the comparison of the
account of the murderer with that of Ross. The fact that he had the news accounts
for his levity. Ross had given Macbeth hopes that the murderers might have
pursued Fleance, and the only point Macbeth really wants information about is the
death or escape of Fleance. (8) When the ghost arises Macbeth asks those about
him &lquo;which of them&rquo; had done it, because he suspects his colleague in crime. On
returning to the room he sees the man whom Ross and the Murderer at the door
had sworn to be dead; he suspects his colleague naturally. Ross endeavors to mis-
lead the other nobles at the banquet and to defend Macbeth. When Paton says
that Macbeth says in effect to the ghost &lquo;In yon black struggle you could never
know me,&rquo; he probably alludes to the speech of Macbeth: &lquo;Thou canst not say I
did it,&rquo; which means that he was not present at the murder.&mdash;<SC>Deighton</SC> refers to
Paton's and Bayne's theory in regard to the Third Murderer being Macbeth, but
thinks that &lquo;the anxiety shown by Macbeth in the next scene seems far too real to
be mere acting.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

<CC><P>7. <B>To]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 187): &lquo;To,&rquo; even without a verb of motion, means <I>motion to
the side of.</I> Hence <I>motion to and consequent rest near.</I> Hence <I>by the side of, in com-
parison with</I>, as in III, iv, 81. Hence <I>up to, in proportion to, according to</I>, as in
the present case. See note on III, i, 63, and I, ii, 16.
<P>9. <B>The West . . . Day]</B> <SC>Corson</SC> (p. 229): The Poet appears to have been so
filled with the spirit of his theme that that spirit radiated upon all the aspects of the
natural world, and was reflected thereform. In the moral world which he is repre-
senting, there are yet some glimmerings of moral light: but these glimmerings are
soon to be swallowed up in moral darkness. And it is to be remarked, too, that the
murder of Banquo and the appearance of his ghost at the banquet, marks the point
where all light goes out for Macbeth and his queen.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
<P>11. <B>timely]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: That is, <I>welcome, opportune.</I> Unless, indeed, we take
it as a poetical metathesis for &lquo;to gain the inn timely, or betimes.&rquo;
<P>11. <B>neere]</B> <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Few Notes</I>, etc.): The First Murderer knew, from the coming
on of night, that Banquo was <I>not far off;</I> but, before hearing the tread of horses and
the voice of Banquo, he could not know that the victim was absolutely <I>near at hand.</I>
<P>14. <B>a Light]</B> <SC>Delius</SC>: Banquo calls for a light from one of his servants, because
he and Fleance are about to strike off into the footway, while the servants make a
circuit to the castle, with the horses.
<P>16. <B>note]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: They who are set down in the list of guests, and expected
to supper.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: For &lquo;note,&rquo; in this sense, see <I>Winter's Tale</I>, IV, iii, 49.
Also in <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.</I> I, ii, 36.&mdash;[<SC>Libby</SC>: This otherwise purposeless remark is quite
dramatic when we consider that Ross is one of the invited guests.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]</CC>

<CC><P>18. <B>Horses]</B> <SC>Horn</SC> (i, 81): Shakespeare, who dared do all that poet ever dared,
nevertheless did not dare to bring upon the stage&mdash;a <I>horse.</I> And very properly; for
there&mdash;where noble poets represent the world's history upon the &lquo;boards that imitate
the world,&rquo; there&mdash;no brutes should be allowed. But in the present scene it is hard
to avoid introducing a horse, and the Poet has to obviate the difficulty in four almost
insignificant lines, in order to account for the absence of the steeds. It is, after all,
undoubtedly better not to shrink from two or three such trivial lines than to have a
horse come clattering on the stage. Would that Schiller had thought of this passage
and so have spared us in his noble <I>Tell</I> that mounted Landvogt!
<P>20, 21. <B>So . . . Walke]</B> <SC>Libby</SC>: The others did not know the short cut to the
castle and would not attempt it in the dark. This tells us that the third murderer
reached home first.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
<P>22. <B>with a Torch]</B> <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. i.): Here again Fleance carries the torch to
light his father; and in the old stage-direction nothing is said about <I>a servant</I>, who
would obviously be in the way, when his master was to be murdered. The <I>servant</I>
is a merely modern interpolation.
<P>30. <B>O Slaue]</B> <SC>Libby</SC>: Banquo recognises Ross.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
<P>30. <SC>Horn</SC> (i, 82): Banquo's death must take place before our eyes in order to
prepare us for his ghost at the banquet. His murder must appear important and
of moment, but it must pass quickly before us; after the preparation that we had for
Duncan's death, the second victim must have less prominence.</CC>

<CC><P>9. <B>State]</B> <SC>Gifford</SC> (<I>The Bondman</I>, Massinger, p. 15, ed. 1805): It is used by
Dryden, but it seems to have been growing obsolete while he was writing; in the
first edition of MacFleckno, the monarch is placed on a &lquo;state&rquo;; in the subsequent
ones he is seated, like his fellow kings, on a throne; it occurs also, and I believe
for the last time, in Swift: &lquo;As she affected not the grandeur of a <I>state</I> with a
canopy, she thought there was no offence in an elbow chair.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Hist. of John
Bull</I>, ch. i.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: The &lquo;state&rquo; was originally the <I>canopy;</I> then the chair
with the canopy over it. Compare Cotgrave: &lquo;<I>Dais</I>, or <I>Daiz.</I> A cloth of Estate,
Canopie, or Heauen, that stands ouer the heads of Princes thrones; also, the whole
State, or seat of Estate.&rquo; See also Bacon's <I>New Atlantis</I> (Works, iii, 148, ed.
Spedding): &lquo;Over the chair is a state, made round or oval, and it is of ivy.&rquo;
<P>10. <B>require]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: That is, ask her to give us welcome. &lquo;Require&rquo; was
formerly used in the simple sense of <I>to ask</I>, not with the meaning now attached to
it of asking as a right. See <I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.</I> III, xii, 12, and also the Prayer-book
Version of <I>Psalm</I> xxxviii, 16.
<P>13. <B>Enter first Murtherer]</B> <SC>Booth</SC>: Enter First Murderer with the Servants,
who bring dishes. &mdash;First Murderer has a few drops of blood upon his cheek.&mdash;He
brings a goblet of wine to Macbeth.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.&mdash;<SC>Sherman</SC>: On the supposition that
Macbeth and the Third Murderer are the same person, it is evident that the First
Murderer cannot now be coming to &lquo;say how much is done&rquo; for the first time. He
must have come much earlier, and failing to find Macbeth, must have been dis-
patched by the Third Murderer, still with him, to search for Fleance. Only now,
after the quest has proved fruitless, and Banquo has been buried (l. 26), does he
appear.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
<P>16. <B>anon]</B> <SC>Delius</SC>: This alludes to the fact that Macbeth has just caught sight of the
Murderer standing in the door, and wishes to dismiss him before pledging the measure.</CC>

<CC><P>19. <SC>Johnson</SC>: &lquo;I am more pleased that the blood of Banquo should be on thy
face than in his body.&rquo; Shakespeare might mean: &lquo;It is better that Banquo's blood
were on thy face than <I>he</I> in this room.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Hunter</SC>: Anything, almost, is to be pre-
ferred to the common explanation that Macbeth addresses this sentence to the Mur-
derer. I would submit as the Poet's intention, that Macbeth goes to the door, and
there sees the Murderer with the evidence of the crime upon him: and with that
infirmity of purpose which belongs to him, that occasional rising of the milk of
human kindness, he is deeply shocked at the sight, especially contrasting it with the
gaiety of the banquet; he retires from the door, meditates, and then, feeling the
importance to him of having got quit of Banquo, he utters the expression aside,
&lquo;'Tis better thee without than he within&rquo;: that, horrible as it is, thus in the midst
of the feast, to behold the assassin of his friend just without the door, it is still better
than that Banquo himself should be alive and within the hall a guest at this enter-
tainment. He thus recovers himself, and then goes to the door again to ask if the
deed had been done effectually, &lquo;Is he dispatch'd?&rquo; In what follows, we cannot
suppose that Macbeth speaks so as to be heard by the Murderer, much less speaks
<I>to</I> him, revealing the secret purpose and thoughts of his mind. They are <I>aside</I>
speeches.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: It is better outside thee than inside him. In spite of the
defective grammar, this must be the meaning, or there would be no point in the
antithesis. For a similar instance of loose construction, see <I>Cymb.</I> II, iii, 153.&mdash;
[<SC>Libby</SC> (see note on I, ii, 53): If this were an aside it might mean, &lquo;'Tis better to
be thee without than Ross within.&rquo; &lquo;Thee&rquo; would pass for a predicate better than
&lquo;he&rquo; for an objective.&mdash;<SC>Chambers</SC> disagrees with Clarendon and follows Hunter's
interpretation, &lquo;It is better that the murderer should be &ldquo;without&rdquo; the banquet than
that Banquo be inside as a guest.&rquo; He adds: &lquo;I conceive that Macbeth speaks with
the murderer at a curtained door, unseen by the banqueters.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]
<P>23. <B>hee's]</B> <SC>Cowden Clarke</SC>: Probably an elision for <I>he is as</I>, not <I>he is.</I>
<P>24. <B>Non-pareill]</B> <SC>Delius</SC>: Shakespeare always uses the definite article with
&lquo;nonpareil,&rquo; except in <I>Temp.</I> III, ii, 108.</CC>

and generally supposed to be a corruption of it, was in Shakespeare's time much
more rarely used than in earlier days, and may now be said to be obsolete, except
in certain words, as <I>a-hunting, asleep</I>, etc. [See <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect;&sect; 24, 140.]
<P>44. <B>feede]</B> <SC>Harry Rowe</SC>: My audience often consisting of cow-keepers, grooms,
ostlers, post-boys, and scullion-wenches, I was apprehensive that they would take
offence at the word &lquo;feed&rquo;; so, by advice of my learned puppet, Doctor Faustus, I
have changed the line into &lquo;Then give the welcome: To <I>eat</I>,&rquo; etc.; the word &lquo;feed&rquo;
belonging, as he says, to the <I>prona atque ventri obedientia.</I> But what kind of men
and women these <I>prona atque ventri obedientia</I> are, I confess I know not.
<P>45. <B>Ceremony]</B> <SC>Staunton</SC> (note on <I>All's Well</I>, II, iii, 185): It has never, that
we are aware, been noticed that Shakespeare usually pronounces <I>cere</I> in <I>ceremony,
ceremonies, ceremonials</I> (but not in <I>ceremonious, ceremoniously</I>), as a monosyllable,

<I>Jul. C&aelig;s.</I> I, i, 70, and <I>Ibid.</I> II, ii, 13.&mdash;<SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> ii, 73): It appears that <I>cere-

least,&mdash;<I>cer'mony</I> and <I>cer'monous.</I> We should therefore perhaps arrange this line:

idea that Lady Macbeth beheld the spectre of Banquo, and that her self-control
and presence of mind enabled her to surmount her consciousness of the ghastly

the text bears out this supposition.&mdash;<SC>Campbell</SC> (<I>Life of Mrs Siddons</I>, ii, 185):
The idea of omitting the ghost of Banquo was suggested to Kemble by some verses
of the poet Edward Lloyd. It was a mere crotchet, and a pernicious departure
from the ancient custom. There was no rationality in depriving the spectator of a
sight of Banquo's ghost merely because the company at Macbeth's table are not
supposed to see it. But we are not Macbeth's guests. We are no more a part of
their company than we are a part of the scenes or the scene-shifters. We are the
Poet's guests, invited to see Macbeth: to see what he sees, and to feel what he feels,
caring comparatively nothing about the guests. I may be told, perhaps, that, accord-
ing to this reasoning, we ought to see the dagger in the air that floats before Mac-
beth. But the visionary appearance of an inanimate object and of a human being
are by no means parallel cases. The stage-spectre of a dagger would be ludicrous;
but not so is the stage-spectre of a man appearing to his murderer. Superstition
sanctions the latter representation; and as to the alleged inconsistency of Banquo's
ghost being visible to us whilst it is unseen by the guests, the argument amounts to
nothing. If we judge by sheer reason, no doubt we must banish ghosts from the
stage altogether, but if we regulate our fancy by the laws of superstition, we shall
find that spectres are privileged to be visible to whom they will; so that the exclu-
sion of Banquo, on this occasion, was a violation of the spiritual peerage of the
drama, an outrage on the rights of ghosts, and a worthier spectre than Ban-
quo's never trod the stage. [Dr Forman's <I>Journal</I>, under date 20th of April,

<P>the mind&rquo; he lay &lquo;in restless ecstacy.&rquo; In the point of view of psychological criti-

the man, when to sleepless nights and days of brooding melancholy is added that
undeniable indication of insanity, a credited hallucination. It was in reality fulfilled
in the case of the woman, although, at the point we have reached, she offers a charac-
ter little likely, on her next appearance, to be the subject of profound and fatal
insanity. Macbeth, however, saved himself from actual insanity by rushing from
the maddening horrors of meditation into a course of decisive, resolute action.
From henceforth he gave himself no time to reflect; he made the firstlings of his
heart the firstlings of his hand; he became a fearful tyrant; but he escaped madness.
This change in him, however, effected a change in his relations to his wife, which
in her had the opposite result. Up to this time her action had been that of sustain-
ing him; but when he waded forward in a sea of blood, when his thoughts were
acted ere they were scanned, then her occupation was gone. Her attention, hereto-
fore directed to her husband and to outward occurrences, was forced inwards upon
that wreck of ill-content which her meditation supplied. The sanitary mental influ-
ence of action is thus impressively shown.&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC> (ed. ii.): I have long been

and <I>1 Hen. IV:</I> I, iii, 183, &lquo;disdained.&rquo; We have &lquo;graced&rquo; in much the same sense
as here in <I>Lear</I>, I, iv, 267, &lquo;A graced palace.&rquo; It is possible, however, that the
word in the present case may mean &lquo;honoured,&rquo; &lquo;favoured,&rquo; as in <I>Two Gent.</I> I,
iii, 58.

<CC><P>66. <B>Thou . . . did it]</B> <SC>Werder</SC> (p. 97): To be appreciated this scene must be
<I>heard</I>&mdash;must be seen; to read it is nothing; it can only be acted. In the tones
of the actor's voice the auditor would hear more than the words, for Macbeth is
struggling under the weight of horror, and this before everything is the point; horror
here is given tongue. The banquet-hall should not be too large, and certainly not
lit in the modern fashion, but with the fitful light of torches.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.

guilty, how are these speeches to be explained? He was full of curiosity, and just
the man to show a prying desire to draw Macbeth out.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
<P>69. <B>Sit worthy Friends]</B> W. <SC>Carleton</SC> (<I>Appendix</I> to Lady Martin's <I>Some of

a wish to conceal her husband's crime, which was indeed natural, together with
the ill-suppressed anguish of a gentle spirit, and a perceptible struggle to subdue
the manifestations of that guilt, whilst attempting to encourage and sustain her hus-

<P>73. <B>shall]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 315): &lquo;Shall,&rquo; meaning <I>to owe</I>, is connected with <I>ought,
must, it is destined.</I> Hence &lquo;shall&rquo; was used by the Elizabethan authors with all
three persons to denote inevitable futurity without reference to <I>will</I> (<I>desire</I>). As in
the present instance: &lquo;You <I>are sure</I> to offend him.&rquo; So probably IV, iii, 56.
<P>73. <B>Passion]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: Prolong his suffering; make his fit longer.&mdash;<SC>Claren-

<P>96. <B>humane]</B> <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> ii, 244): <I>Human</I> is here, I think, <I>civilized.</I>&mdash;
<SC>Clarendon</SC>: The two meanings, <I>human</I> and &lquo;humane&rquo; (like those of &lquo;travel&rquo; and
&lquo;travail&rquo;&mdash;II, iv, 10), were not in Shakespeare's time distinguished by a different
spelling and pronunciation. In both cases the word was pronounced by Shakespeare
with the accent on the first syllable. See, for instance, <I>Coriol.</I> III, i, 327. There
seems to be one exception in <I>Wint. Tale</I>, III, ii, 166. In <I>Oth.</I> II, i, 243, it occurs
in prose. Milton observes the modern distinction in sense and pronunciation be-
tween <I>human</I> and &lquo;humane.&rquo; There are, as might be expected, some passages in
Shakespeare where it is difficult to determine which of the two senses best fits the
word. Indeed both might be blended in the mind of the writer. [See I, v, 17, and
note.]

<P>117. <B>Auant, &amp; quit my sight]</B> <SC>Fitzgerald</SC> (ii, p. 71): Garrick, in his behaviour
to the ghost, was, on the first nights, too subdued and faint when he said [this line]&mdash;
still carrying out his idea of Macbeth being utterly oppressed and overcome by the
sense of his guilt. But an anonymous critic pointed out to him that Macbeth was
not a coward; and with that good sense and modesty which always distinguished him,
he adopted the advice. It is curious to think that even twenty years later, another
anonymous critic wrote to him, to object to this amended view, and said that Macbeth
<I>should</I> show signs of terror. But Garrick recollected his old critic's argument, and
reproduced it in answer to his new one. &lquo;My notion, he says, &lquo;as well as execution,
of the line are, I fear, opposite to your opinion. Should Macbeth sink into pusil-
lanimity, I imagine that it would hurt the character, and be contrary to the opinions
of Shakespeare. The first appearance of the spirit overcomes him more than the
second; but even before it vanishes at first, Macbeth gains strength&mdash;&ldquo;If thou canst
nod, speak too,&rdquo; must be spoke with horror, but with a recovering mind; and
in the next speech with him he cannot pronounce &ldquo;Avaunt and quit my sight!&rdquo;
without a <I>stronger exertion</I> of his powers. I certainly, as you say, recollect a degree
of resolution, <I>but I never advance an inch;</I> for, notwithstanding my agitation, my
feet are immovable.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.</CC>

Macready began in the vehemence of despair, but overcome by terror as he contin-
ued to gaze on the apparition, dropped his voice lower and lower till he became
tremulous and inarticulate, and at last uttering a subdued cry of mortal agony and
horror, he suddenly cast his mantle over his face and sank back almost lifeless on
his seat.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.

[<I>thee</I> for &lquo;then&rquo;] is strongly supported by the punctuation of the old copy.&mdash;<SC>Hen-

neutral sense, to express <I>continuance in a given situation.</I> So also Milton: &lquo;Mean-
while inhabit lax, ye powers of heaven!&rquo; [<I>Paradise Lost</I>, Bk, vii, l. 162].&mdash;<SC>Steev-

me to the desert, I skulk in my house,&rquo; etc.&mdash;<SC>Douce</SC>: Until we are furnished
with examples of the neutral use of &lquo;inhabit&rquo; it may be boldly said, and without
difficulty maintained, that <I>inhibit</I>, in point of meaning, was Shakespeare's word.
Nor is it a paradox to affirm that <I>inhabit</I> is also right, because this may be a

<SC>Capell</SC> (<I>Notes</I>, 19 <I>a</I>): How is this line injured in the solemnity of its movement

<P>153. <B>Stones]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Probably Shakespeare here alludes to some story in
which the stones covering the corpse of a murdered man were said to have moved
of themselves and so revealed the secret.&mdash;<SC>Paton</SC> (<I>N. and Qu.</I> 6 Nov. 1869): Such
a superstition as that referred to in the Clarendon edition would only reveal the mur-
dered man, <I>not</I> the secret murderer. May not the allusion be to the rocking stones,
or &lquo;stones of judgment,&rquo; by which it was thought the Druids tested the guilt or
innocence of accused persons? At a slight touch of the innocent, such a stone
moved, but &lquo;the secret man of blood&rquo; found that his best strength could not stir it.
If Shakespeare visited Macbeth's country to <I>naturalise</I> his materials (as I believe he
did), he could not avoid having his attention drawn to several of these &lquo;clacha
breath.&rquo; One was close to Glamis castle.&mdash;[<SC>B&uuml;ttner</SC> (p. 42) diffidently asks if this
may not refer to the stone image of the Commendatore in <I>Don Giovanni</I>, which on

<P>154. <B>Augures]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: Perhaps we should read <I>auguries</I>, i. e. prognostica-
tions by means of omens.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: In Florio, 1611, &lquo;augure&rquo; is given as the
equivalent both for <I>augurio</I>, soothsaying, and <I>auguro</I>, a soothsayer. In the edition
of 1598 &lquo;augure&rquo; is only given as the translation of <I>augurio</I>, and it is in this sense
that it is used here. The word occurs nowhere else in Shakespeare. For &lquo;augur,&rquo;
in our modern sense, he uses &lquo;augurer.&rquo; We find &lquo;augure&rquo; used in the sense of
&lquo;augur,&rquo; or &lquo;augurer,&rquo; in Holland's <I>Pliny</I>, Bk, viii, c. 28, which was published in
1601.
<P>154. <B>Relations]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: By this word is understood the <I>connection</I> of effects
with causes; to <I>understand relations</I> as <I>an augur</I> is to know how those things <I>relate</I>
to each other which have no visible combination or dependence.&mdash;<SC>Heath</SC>: By
<I>relations</I> it is not improbable that Shakespeare might understand those hidden ties
by which every part of nature is linked and connected with every other part of it, in
virtue whereof the whole of created nature, past, present, and to come, is truly and
properly one. If this be his meaning, as I believe it is, his own natural good under-
standing had opened to him a vein of philosophy which has since done so much
honour to the name of Mr Leibnitz.&mdash;[<SC>Hudson</SC> (ed. iii.): A passage very obscure
to general readers, but probably intelligible enough to those experienced in the
course of criminal trials; where two or three little facts or items of testimony may
be of no significance taken singly or by themselves; yet, when they are put together
and their <I>relations understood</I>, they may be enough to convict or acquit the accused.
&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

Pagan fictions were frequently blended and incorporated. The Lady of the Lake
floated in the suite of Neptune before Queen Elizabeth at Kenilworth; Ariel assumes
the semblance of a sea-nymph, and Hecate, by an easy association, conducts the
rites of the weird sisters in <I>Macbeth.</I>&mdash;<SC>Tollet</SC>: Scot's <I>Discovery of Witchcraft</I>,

Herodias and the Pagan gods,&rquo; and &lquo;that in the night-times they ride abroad
with <I>Diana</I>, the goddess of the Pagans,&rquo; etc.&mdash;Their dame or chief leader seems
always to have been an old Pagan, as &lquo;the Ladie Sibylla, Minerva, or <I>Diana.</I>&rquo;&mdash;

Romans,&rquo; it seems scarcely germane as an illustration of Shakespeare.&mdash;R. G. <SC>White</SC>:
Shakespeare has been censured for mixing Hecate up with vulgar Scotch witches, smell-
ing of snuff and usquebaugh. But he sinned in this regard with many better scholars
than himself; and, had he not such companionship, his shoulders could bear the
blame, as they also could that of pronouncing her name as a disyllable.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>:

they intimated that they desire or expect any. Besides, Hecate has no reason to
find fault with what they have done. <I>She</I> could not have managed the affair better.
How, so far as the Witches are concerned, has Macbeth proved a &ldquo;wayward son,
spiteful and wrathful&rdquo;? . . . I may remind the reader that the managers of Shake-
speare's day were much given to these sensational additions to Shakespeare's plays.
The Hymen of <I>As You Like It</I> and the vision in <I>Cymb.</I> are clear instances of the
kind.&rquo;&mdash;For a further discussion bearing somewhat on these questions, see IV, i, 41.
&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

tion. So also &lquo;manly&rquo; in IV, iii, 275.
<P>7, 8. <B>To Trade . . . death]</B> <SC>Fletcher</SC> (p. 149): The weird sisters are not rep-
resented as the original tempters of Macbeth. Hecate here charges them, not as
having presumed without her concurrence <I>to lead him into temptation</I>, but as having
simply <I>taken part in his wicked intentions.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.

<P>18. <B>Acheron]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: Shakespeare seems to have thought it allowable to
bestow this name on any fountain, lake, or pit, through which there was vulgarly
supposed to be a communication between this and the infernal world. The true

in the valley of <I>Amsanctus</I> in Italy.&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: Shakespeare was led by Scripture
(as Mr Plumtre observed to me) to make his witches assemble at <I>Acheron.</I> See

word is spelt <I>Ekrom.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Few Notes</I>, etc., p. 127): Did these matter-

about it&rquo;? Not he&mdash;no more than Fairfax, who, in his translation of the <I>Gerusa-

when III, v. was inserted, in order to prevent the two witch scenes from coming

pendently, be adopted, how can we reconcile the fact that it is <I>Lenox</I> who, at the
end of IV, i, informs Macbeth of Macduff's flight to England?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.

[<SC>Becket</SC> (note in <I>Lear</I>, i, 152) observes that &lquo;the immediately preceding hemistich,

drawn from which is, that they who should not so pretend or counterfeit, would
be in danger from Macbeth.&rquo; That this note occurs in <I>Lear</I> probably accounts for
its omission by subsequent commentators on <I>Macbeth.</I> It was pointed out by J.
<SC>Crosby</SC> in a private note, and anticipates R. G. <SC>White's</SC> suggestion in his <I>Shake-

som's</SC> marginal MS comment &lquo;Good!&rquo; in a copy of White's volume. White's note
is, nevertheless, here reproduced for the sake of <SC>Dyce's</SC> comment thereon.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

passage, and a recollection of the mistakes that I have made myself and known
others to make, have led me unwillingly to the belief that Malone may have been
right in his opinion that, although the sense requires &lquo;Who <I>can</I> want the thought,&rquo; the
text is as Shakespeare wrote it, and that the disagreement between the words and
the thought is due to a confusion of thought which Shakespeare may have sometimes
shared with inferior intellects.&mdash;<SC>Keightley</SC>: This passage as it stands is evident
nonsense, which Shakespeare never wrote, and if we read <I>We</I> for &lquo;Who,&rquo; we have
the very word he wrote, and most excellent sense.&mdash;<SC>Delius</SC>: As Shakespeare some-
times, in order to express a simple negative, multiplies the negatives <I>not, nor, never</I>,
etc., so, on the other hand, he sometimes adds them, as in this case, to negative verbs
or particles, without altering the sense. Thus in <I>Wint. Tale</I>, III, ii, 55, &lquo;That
any of these bolder vices wanted Less impudence,&rquo; and in <I>Cymb.</I> I, iv, 23, &lquo;a beggar
without less quality,&rquo; the negative &lquo;less&rquo; merely strengthens the negative already
included in &lquo;wanted&rquo; and &lquo;without.&mdash;<SC>Dalgleish</SC>: The affirmative interrogation is
equal to the negative response, &lquo;<I>no one</I> can want,&rquo; etc. See I, v, 30.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>:
This construction arises from a confusion of thought common enough when a nega-
tive is expressed or implied, and is so frequent in Greek as to be almost sanctioned
by usage. Compare <I>e. g.</I> Herodotus, iv, 118: <G><*>kei ga/r o( *pe/rshs ou)de/n ti ma_llon e)p'
h(me/as <*> ou) kai\ e)pi\ u(me/as</G>, and Thucydides, iii, 36, <G>w)mo\n to\ bou/leuma po/lin <*>lhn
diafqei_rai ma_llon <*> ou) tou\s ai)ti/ous</G>. It would be easy to find instances in all Eng-
lish writers of Shakespeare's time. Take the following from his own works, <I>Win-
ter's Tale</I>, I, ii, 260; <I>King Lear</I>, II, iv, 140: &lquo;I have hope You less know how to
value her desert Than she to scant her duty.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Baynes</SC> (p. 275): The passage as it
stands is perfectly good sense, and perfectly good English of Shakespeare's day, as
it still remains perfectly good Northern English or Lowland Scotch of our own day.
In these dialects the verb &lquo;want,&rquo; especially when construed with negative particles,
has precisely the meaning which the critics insist the sense requires. If a farmer in
the North of England, or the Scotch Lowlands, send to borrow a neighbor's horse,
and receives a negative reply, it would probably be conveyed in some such form as,
&lquo;He says he cannot want the horse to-day,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> he cannot do without the horse; he
must have the horse for his own use. In the same way, if an Edinburgh porter say
to his comrade, &lquo;I'll no want a gill of whiskey the morn,&rquo; he would express in a
strong form his determination to have one. This use of the verb was not uncom-
mon amongst English writers in Shakespeare's day. Thus, in <I>The Country Farm</I>,
translated from the French, 1600, we have, &lquo;Ploughing, an art that a householder
cannot <I>want.</I>&rquo; And Markham, speaking of the herb <I>purslane</I>, says, &lquo;&mdash; a ground</CC>

<CC><P>once possessed by them will seldom <I>want</I> them.&rquo; Many words and phrases, now
peculiar to the Scotch Lowlands, were common to both countries in Shakespeare's
day, and every one of the so-called Scotticisms to be found in his dramas is used by
contemporary English writers. As a mere English writer, therefore, Shakespeare

appears to have done so elsewhere. It might, however, then as now, be character-

then positively known that Macduff had fled! . . . The whole dialogue between Lenox
and the Lord is <I>miraculous.</I> It abounds with knowledge of events that had not
happened&mdash;on the showing of Shakespeare himself. . . . You would think, from the

<CC><P>45. <B>I]</B> <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Remarks</I>, etc., p. 199): The semicolon placed after &lquo;Sir, not I&rquo;
[as in Collier's edition] destroys the meaning of the passage. The construction is,
&lquo;and the cloudy messenger turns me his back with an absolute &ldquo;Sir, not I&rdquo; [re-
ceived in answer from Macduff], and hums, as who should say,&rquo; etc.
<P>46. <B>clowdy]</B> <SC>Delius</SC>: That is, <I>foreboding, ominous.</I>
<P>46. <B>me]</B> For other instances of this ethical dative, see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 220, or Shake-
speare <I>passim.</I>
<P>47. <B>as who]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 257): <I>Who</I> is used for <I>any one.</I> Compare <I>Mer. of
Ven.</I> I, ii, 45, and I, i, 93; <I>Rich. II:</I> V, iv, 8. In these passages it is possible to
understand an antecedent to &lquo;who,&rquo; &lquo;as, or like (one) who should say.&rquo; But in [a
passage from North's <I>Plutarch</I> and one from Gower] it is impossible to give this
explanation. Possibly an <I>if</I> is implied after the &lquo;as&rquo; by the use of the subjunctive.
<P>54. <B>suffering]</B> See <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> i, 160) for instances of this peculiar construc-
tion with the adjective. See also <I>Rom. and Jul.</I> III, i, 58.&mdash;<SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 419 <I>a</I>):
When an adjective is not a mere epithet, but expresses something essential, and
implies a relative, it is often placed after a noun. [See V, viii, 11, 12.]
<P>56. <B>Ile . . . him]</B> <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Vers.</I> 273): Single lines of four or five, or six or
seven, syllables, interspersed amidst the ordinary blank verse of ten, are not to be
considered as irregularities; they belong to Shakespeare's system of metre. On the
other hand, lines of eight or nine syllables, as they are at variance with the general
rhythm of his poetry (at least, if my ears do not deceive me, this is the case), so
they scarcely ever occur in his plays,&mdash;it were hardly too much to say, not at all. . . .
With regard to the other, or <I>legitimate</I> short lines, I am inclined to think that some-
times, though very rarely, two lines of this sort occur consecutively in Shakespeare,
for there are passages which cannot be otherwise arranged without destroying the
harmony, as seems to me. So arrange, &lquo;Under a yoke [sic] accurst! [one line].
<I>Lord.</I> I'll send my pray&emacr;rs with him.&rquo; [another line]. A conclusion of a scene
quite in Shakespeare's manner.</CC>

<CC><P>2. <B>Enter the three Witches]</B> <SC>Knowles</SC> (p. 64): Macready suggested the fol-
lowing arrangement of this scene: Let the Witches be placed in different parts of
the cavern. Suppose one at the mouth, intently on the watch; another near the
cauldron, cowering over the livid flame, which, by the way, should be placed under
the charmed pot and not in it; the Third Witch on the side opposite the entrance,
seated perhaps upon a fragment of stone, her arms folded, and rocking to and fro,
upon the rack, as it were, of impatience. Let not a word be spoken, till the audience
have had time to study the picture. 'Tis to the point, and they are sure to feel it,
if you will allow them. The familiars&mdash;the brinded cat, the hedge-pig, and Harper
&mdash;are supposed to be stationed outside the cavern to give notice of the approach of
Hecate. The First Witch hears her familiar: &lquo;Thrice the brinded cat hath mewed.&rquo;
The eyes of the other Witches are instantly turned towards her: a pause ensues
during which they all remain motionless. The Witch near the cauldron hears her
familiar; she starts from her cowering attitude: &lquo;Thrice; and once the hedge-pig
whined.&rquo; Another pause here. Now at length the Third Witch springs upon her
feet: &lquo;Harper cries&rquo;; and then addressing her sisters, and not putting words into
Harper's mouth, which Shakespeare never intended for him: &lquo;'Tis time, 'tis time.&rquo;
[The familiars do <I>not</I>, however, give notice of the approach of Hecate, which occurs
at line 41, but show when the conditions are favourable for the beginning of the
charm.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]&mdash;<SC>Fleay</SC> (<I>Sh. Manual</I>, p. 250): What are the witches of this scene?
are they the &lquo;weird sisters,&rquo; fairies, nymphs, or goddesses? or are they ordinary
witches or wizards, as we should expect from the narrative in Holinshed, and
entirely distinct from the three mysterious beings in I, iii.? I hold the latter view.
In order to support it, it will be necessary to show that they are not weird sisters
in the higher sense: to give a hypothesis as to how they got confused with them:
to try to present some idea of Shakespeare's intentions regarding them. Now lines
3-49 in this scene are admitted by all critics to be greatly superior to the corre-
sponding passage in I, iii, 3-40. <SC>Clark</SC> and <SC>Wright</SC> hold it to be Shakespeare,
except the Hecate bit. [See <I>Appendix, The Witch.</I>] I agree with them; but then
I cannot identify these witches with the Norn&aelig; of I, iii, 53-74. The witches in IV,
i. are just like Middleton's witches, only superior in quality. They are clearly the orig-
inals from whom his imitations were taken. Their charms are of the sort popularly
believed in. . . . Of themselves they have not the prophetic knowledge of the weird sis-
ters, the all-knowers of Past, Present, and Future; they must get their knowledge from
their <I>masters</I>, or call them up to communicate it themselves. Nor do they call themselves
weird sisters, although the three in the early rejected part of I, iii, do so; their knowl-
edge is from the pricking of their thumbs; they are submissive to the <I>great King</I> who
calls them <I>filthy hags, secret, black, and midnight hags;</I> the oracles, their masters, are
ambiguous, delusive: those of the weird sisters were pithy, inevitable; the witches are</CC>

<P>3. <B>brinded]</B> <SC>Murray</SC> (<I>N. E. D.</I>): (Primary form apparently <I>brended</I>, whence

and goddesses to hide themselves in animals, assumed the shape of a <I>cat.</I>&mdash;<SC>John-
son</SC>: A witch, who was tried about half a century before the time of Shakespeare,
had a cat named Rutterkin, as the spirit of one of these witches was Grimalkin.&mdash;

<CC><P>the ancients have supposed that the cat became fat or lean with the increase or wane
of the moon; that it usually brought forth as many young as there are days in a
lunar period; and that the pupils of its eyes dilated or contracted according to the
changes of the planet.&mdash;[<SC>Agnes Repplier</SC> (p. 32): Innumerable legends cluster
around the cat during these picturesque centuries of superstition [the Dark Ages]
when men were poor in letters, but rich in vivid imaginings; when they were
densely ignorant, but never dull. Even after the Dark Ages had grown light, there
was no lifting of the gloom which enveloped the cat's pathway; there was no vis-
ible softening of her lot. The stories told of her impish wickedness have the same
general character throughout Europe. We meet them with modest variations in
France, in Germany, in Sweden, Denmark, England, Scotland, and Wales. . . .
Again and again she figures with direful prominence in the records of demonology.
A black-hearted Scottish witch confessed in the year 1591 that she had impiously
christened a cat; and that she and other witches had carried this animal &lquo;sayling
in their Riddles or Cives into the middest of the sea, and so left it before the towne
of Leith; whereupon there did arise such a tempest at sea, as a greater hath not been
seen. . . .&rquo; Evidence of a most disastrous character was brought against the cat in
countless other trials. We can hardly wonder at the deep suspicion with which
men regarded an animal so mysterious and so closely allied to the supernatural.
Even when her behaviour was harmless or beneficial, they feared a lurking malice
which never lacked the power for evil things.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]
<P>4. <B>once]</B> <SC>Theobald</SC>: I read <I>twice and once;</I> because, as Virgil has remarked,
&lquo;Numero Deus impare gaudet,&rquo; [<I>Ed.</I> VIII, 75]; and <I>three</I> and <I>nine</I> are the num-
bers used in all Inchantments.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: The Second Witch only repeats the
number which the First had mentioned, in order to confirm what she had said;
and then adds, that the <I>hedge-pig</I> had likewise cried, though but once. Or what
seems more easy, the hedge-pig had whined <I>thrice</I>, and after an interval had whined
once again.&mdash;<SC>Elwin</SC>: As <I>even numbers</I> were considered inappropriate to magical
operations, the Second Witch makes the <I>fourth</I> cry of the hedge-pig an <I>odd number</I>,
by her method of counting. She tells three, and then begins a new reckoning.&mdash;
<SC>Clarendon</SC>: The witch's way of saying <I>four times.</I>&mdash;[<SC>Nicholson</SC> (<I>New Sh. Soc.
Trans.</I> 1880-2, part i, p. 106): I hold with those who have it that the second
witch's &lquo;thrice&rquo; is the repetition of the first one's &lquo;Thrice the brinded cat hath
mewed,&rquo; and should therefore be pointed with a comma or semicolon after it, the
&lquo;once&rquo; being the number of times that the hedge-pig has whined.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

sometimes supposed to be assumed by mischievous elves.&mdash;<SC>Krauth</SC> (<I>Notes on The
Tempest</I>, p. 33): The urchin, or hedge-hog, is nocturnal in its habits, weird in its
movements; plants wither where it works, for it cuts off their roots. Fairies of one
class were supposed to assume its form. Urchin came to mean <I>fairy</I> without ref-</CC>

<P>5. <B>Harpier]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: It may be only a misspelling, or a misprint, for <I>harpy.</I>
So in Marlowe's <I>Tamburlaine</I>, etc., 1590: &lquo;And like a <I>harper</I> tyers upon my
life.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii.): In the 8vo ed., which is of the same date, it stands

Probably some animal which the witch thus designates on account of the resem-
blance of its cry to the sound of a harp-string.&mdash;<SC>Jordan</SC>: Hecate's attendant
is only indicated as a little spirit sitting in a thick fog, and each of the other
three witches have attendants in the shape of animals, such as a cat, an urchin,
and a toad. I have conjectured, therefore, with tolerable certainty, that Shake-
speare here wrote: <I>herpler</I>, i. e. waddler (<I>Watschler</I>).&mdash;[<SC>Nicholson</SC> (<I>Notes and
Queries</I>, 7 Feb. 1880): I am led to believe that this is not a name for the
animal whose shape was assumed by the familiar, but the proper name of the
familiar himself, just as other spirits were called Puckle, Hoppo, Tiffen, etc. Not
improbably,&mdash;for Shakespeare was a man who disregarded precedent and history in
unimportant matters,&mdash;it was a fancy name, invented as suggesting by its sound and
association a being ravenous, evil-disposed, and talon-clawed.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]
<P>5. <B>'tis time]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: This Familiar does not cry out that it is time for them to
begin their enchantments; but <I>cries</I>, i. e. gives them the signal, upon which the
Third Witch communicates the notice to her sisters.
<P>7. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: The imagination of the poets contemporary with Shakespeare
ran riot in devising loathsome ingredients for witches' messes. Compare Webster,

craft, to find in it the fat of serpents, spawn of snakes. Jews' spittle,&rquo; etc. Lucan
perhaps excels them all. See <I>Pharsalia</I>, Bk, vi, 667-681.

the printing.&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC> (ed. i.): To our ear the extending of &lquo;cold&rquo; to the time of two
syllables <I>feels</I> right enough.&mdash;<SC>Delius</SC>: In order to weaken the force of the consecu-
tive consonants, an involuntary pause should perhaps occur between &lquo;cold&rquo; and

<SC>White</SC>: The line in the Folio is so detrimentally defective that we gladly, though
perhaps unwarrantably, accept Pope's emendation.&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. ii.): The article,
which is required not only for the metre, but for the sense, has been omitted by mis-
take. Yet the mutilated line has found its defenders and admirers (who, we may be

that mutilated line also).&mdash;<SC>Keightley</SC>: I read &lquo;under<I>neath</I>,&rquo; as in Jonson's line,

stands, the two syllables, &lquo;cold stone,&rquo; when slowly pronounced being equiv-

<P>10. <B>Sweltred]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: This word seems to signify that the animal was moist-

the effect of heat. Webster defines it, &lquo;To exude like sweat.&rquo;
<P>10. <B>Venom]</B> <SC>Hunter</SC>: There is a paper by Dr Davy in the <I>Philosophical Trans-
actions</I> of 1826, in which it is shown that the toad <I>is</I> venomous, and moreover that
&lquo;sweltered venom&rquo; is peculiarly proper, the poison lying diffused over the body
immediately under the skin. This is the second instance in this play of Shake-
speare's minute exactness in his natural history. [&lquo;All manner of Toads, both of
the earth and of the water are venomous, although it be held that the Toads of the
earth are more poysonful then the Toads of the water. . . . But the Toads of the
land, which do descend into the marishes, and so live in both elements, are most
venomous.&rquo;&mdash;Topsell, <I>History of the Serpents</I>, p. 730, ed. 1658.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

<P>24. <SC>Hudson</SC>: Shakespeare so weaves his incantations as to cast a spell upon the
mind, and force its acquiescence in what he represents; explode as we may the
witchcraft he describes, there is no exploding the witchcraft of his description; the
effect springing not so much from what he borrows as from his own ordering thereof.

<CC><P>formerly used in medicine is to be found in a quotation from Hill's <I>Materia Medica</I>
in Johnson's <I>Dict.</I>, s.v. &lquo;The Egyptian mummies,&rquo; says Sir Thomas Browne, &lquo;which

28, ed. 1658.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: Sir Thomas Browne, in his Fragment on Mummies,
tells us that Francis the First always carried mummy with him as a panacea against
all disorders. Some used it for epilepsy, some for gout, some used it as a styptic.
He goes on: &lquo;The common opinion of the virtues of mummy bred great consump-
tion thereof, and princes and great men contended for this strange panacea, wherein
the Jews dealt largely, manufacturing mummies from dead carcasses and giving them

embalmed with myrrh and spice; the other is the liquor running from such <I>mum-
mies</I> when newly prepared, or when affected by great heat; this is sometimes of a
liquid, sometimes of a solid form, as it is preserved in vials or suffered to dry: the
first kind is brought in large pieces, of a friable texture, light and spungy, of a
blackish-brown colour, and often black and clammy on the surface; it is of a strong
but not agreeable smell; the second in its liquid state is a thick, opake, and vis-
cous fluid, of a blackish and a strong, but not disagreeable, smell; in its indurated
state it is a dry, solid substance, of a fine shining black colour and close texture,
easily broken, and of a good smell: this sort is extremely dear, and the first sort so
cheap that we are not to imagine it to be the ancient Egyptian <I>mummy.</I> What our
druggists are supplied with is the flesh of any bodies the Jews can get, who fill them
with the common bitumen so plentiful in that part of the world, and, adding aloes
and some other cheap ingredients, send them to be baked in an oven till the juices
are exhaled and the embalming matter has penetrated. Hill's <I>Materia Medica.</I>&mdash;
<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]
<P>25. <B>Gulfe]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: <I>Gulf</I>, in the sense of arm of the sea, is derived from
the French <I>golfe</I>, Italian <I>golfo</I>, and connected with the Greek <G>ko/lpos</G>; but in the
sense of whirlpool or swallowing eddy, it is connected with the Dutch <I>gulpen</I>, our
gulp, to swallow, and with the old Dutch <I>golpe</I>, a whirlpool. So Wedgwood.
&lquo;Gulf,&rquo; with the latter derivation, is applied also to the stomach of voracious
animals.
<P>26. <B>rauin'd]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: That is, glutted with prey. <I>Ravin</I> is the ancient word

not follow that because <I>ravin</I> may signify <I>prey, ravined</I> should signify <I>glutted
with prey.</I> I believe we ought to read <I>ravin.</I> As in <I>All's Well</I>, III, ii, 120.
<I>Ravined</I> cannot mean <I>glutted with prey</I>, but the reverse.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: In Phineas
Fletcher's <I>Locusts</I>, 1627 [Canto iii, st. 18.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>], <I>raven'd</I> occurs as in the
present text: &lquo;&mdash; But with his raven'd prey his bowells broke.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: To
<I>ravin</I>, according to Minsheu, is to <I>devour</I>, or <I>eat greedily. Ravin'd</I> is used for
<I>ravenous</I>, the passive participle for the adjective.</CC>

<P>30. <B>Ecclipse]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: A most unlucky time for lawful enterprises, and
therefore suitable for evil designs. Compare Milton, <I>Paradise Lost</I>, i, 597: &lquo;As
when the sun . . . from behind the moon In dim eclipse disastrous twilight sheds.&rquo;
And in <I>Lycidas</I>, he says of the unlucky ship that was wrecked, line 101, &lquo;It was
that fatal and perfidious barque Built in the eclipse.&rquo;
<P>32. <B>Finger]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: It is observable that Shakespeare on this great occasion,
which involves the fate of a king, multiplies all the circumstances of horror. The
babe, whose finger is used, must be strangled in its birth; the grease must not only
be human, but must have dropped from a gibbet, the gibbet of a murderer; and even
the sow, whose blood is used, must have offended nature by devouring her own far-
row. These are touches of judgement and genius.
<P>34. <B>slab]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: That is, <I>thick, slimy.</I> The same word is found as a sub-
stantive, meaning <I>mud</I> or <I>slime.</I> There is also <I>slabber</I>, a verb, to soil. Another form
of the adjective is <I>slabby.</I> We find no other example of the adjective slab.&rquo; Etymo-
logically it is doubtless related to <I>slobbery.</I> See <I>Hen. V:</I> III, v, 13.
<P>35. <B>Chawdron]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: That is, <I>entrails</I>, a word formerly in common use
in the books of cookery, in one of which, printed in 1597, I meet with a receipt to
make a pudding of a calf's <I>chaldron.</I> Again, in Decker's <I>Honest Whore</I>, 1635:
&lquo;Sixpence a meal, wench, as well as heart can wish, with calves' chaldrons and
chitterlings,&rquo; [Part i, sc. vii.]. At the coronation feast of Elizabeth of York, queen

<P>39. <B>Baboones]</B> <SC>Murray</SC> (<I>N. E. D.</I>): Adopted from French <I>babuin</I> (13th c.),
modern <I>babouin</I>, or adaptation of medi&aelig;val Latin <I>babewynus</I> (used in England 1295,
see Du Cange), found also in the forms <I>babouinus</I>, baboynus, babuynus (some, if not
all, of which are merely Latinized from French or English); equivalent to Italian
<I>babbuino</I>, Spanish <I>babuino.</I> French has also <I>babion</I>, treated by Littr&eacute; as a distinct
word, but in English identified with <I>baboon</I>, and the source of Low German <I>bavian</I>,
Dutch <I>baviaan</I>, High German <I>pavian</I>, baboon. The earlier history of the word is
unknown.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.&mdash;<SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> ii, 27) calls attention to the accent <I>b&aacute;boon;</I> as
also in <I>Pericles</I>, IV, vi, 189.
<P>41. <B>Enter Hecat]</B> G. <SC>Crosse</SC> (<I>Notes and Queries</I>, 22 Oct. 1898): The intro-
duction of Hecate here is quite objectless. After the entrance of Macbeth she
neither speaks nor takes part in the action. This suggests that her one speech is an
interpolation, probably inserted to harmonise with a former interpolation (Act III,
sc. v.), and to introduce the song &lquo;Black spirits.&rquo; In the same way lines 146-153
may have been inserted to lead up to the witch dance. The idea of the witches
dancing in order to &lquo;cheer up&rquo; Macbeth seems scarcely Shakespearian. [See note
by <SC>Crosse</SC>, III, v, i.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

probably wrote &lquo;the other witches.&rquo; The word &lquo;<I>three</I>&rquo; having been introduced in all

the number of Witches in this scene is six.&mdash;<SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 163): The play opens

witches so far, except the three to whom Hecate enters; and when Macbeth enters,</CC>

<P>47. <B>Song]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: In a former note [ed. 1778] I had observed that the

belong to Middleton more than to Shakespeare; but it was inserted in both dra-

but qy?&mdash;[W. <SC>Scott</SC> (iii, 45): Kemble introduced four bands of children, who
rushed on the stage at the invocation of the witches, to represent the &lquo;Black spirits
and white, Blue spirits and gray.&rquo; There was perhaps little taste in rendering
these a&euml;rial beings visible to the eye, especially when the same manager had made
an attempt to banish even the spirit of Banquo. But he was obliged to discard his
imps for a special reason. Mr Kelly informs us [<I>Reminiscences</I>, ii, 65] that, egged
on, and encouraged by one of their number, a black-eyed urchin, ycleped <I>Edmund
Kean</I>, they made such confusion on the stage that Kemble was fain to dismiss them
to the elements.&mdash;<SC>D'Hugues</SC>: The interpolation of the four lines from Middleton's
<I>Witch</I> does not seem sufficiently justified. In III, v. we have a similar stage-direc-
tion: &lquo;Song within: Come away, come away,&rquo; etc. Shakespeare has likewise here
written, &lquo;Music and a Song: Black spirits,&rquo; etc. If this song of the Fourth Act should
be inserted, why not that of the third? It is likely that Hecate disappeared after
the song by the witches, and that she took no part in the subsequent conversation
with Macbeth.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

<P>55. <B>coniure]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: &lquo;Conjure&rquo; seems to be used by Shakespeare always

<P>60. <B>bladed]</B> <SC>Collier</SC> (<I>Notes</I>, etc., p. 425, ed. ii.): We are to recollect that
&lquo;bladed&rquo; corn is never &lquo;lodged&rquo; or layed; but corn which is heavy in the ear is
often borne down by wind and rain. Shakespeare must have been aware that green
corn, or corn in the blade, is not liable to be affected by violent weather. Hence we
may infer that he wrote [according to the (MS)] &lquo;<I>bleaded</I> corn,&rquo; which means, in
some of the provinces, and perhaps in Warwickshire, ripe corn, corn ready for the
sickle. <I>Blead</I> is a general name for fruit; and the <I>bleading</I> of corn means the yield-
ing of it, the quantity of grain obtained.&mdash;<SC>Singer</SC> (<I>Sh. Vind.</I>, etc., p. 256): Hear</CC>

<P>64. <B>Germaine]</B> <SC>Theobald</SC> (note on <I>Lear</I>, III, ii, 8: &lquo;Crack nature's mould,
all germins spill at once&rquo;): Mr Pope has explained Germains to mean <I>relations</I>, or
<I>kindred</I> Elements. Then it must have been <I>germanes</I> (from the Latin, <I>germanus</I>).
But the Poet here means &lquo;spill all the <I>Seeds of Matter</I>, that are,&rquo; etc. To retrieve
which Sense we must write <I>Germins;</I> and so we must again in <I>Macbeth.</I> And to
put this Emendation beyond all Doubt, I'll produce one more Passage, where our
Author not only uses the same Thought again, but the Word that ascertains my Ex-
plication. In <I>Wint. Tale</I>, IV, iv, 490: &lquo;Let Nature crush the sides o' th' Earth
together, And marr the <I>Seeds</I> within.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Elwin</SC>: Nature's <I>german</I> are <I>nature's kin-
dred</I>&mdash;that is, <I>mankind in general. The treasure of nature's german</I> is, therefore,
<I>the best of the human race.</I>&mdash;<SC>Delius</SC>: It is unnecessary to read &lquo;germen<I>s</I>, since
&lquo;germen&rquo; is in itself a collective noun.&mdash;R. G. <SC>White</SC>: Germins are sprouting seeds.
The word is here used in the largest figurative sense.</CC>

of Kenneth II. of Scotland: &lquo;If a <I>sowe eate hir pigges</I>, let hyr be stoned to death
and buried.&rquo;&mdash;Holinshed's <I>History of Scotland</I>, edit. 1577, p. 181.
<P>74. <B>Farrow]</B> <SC>Skeat</SC> (<I>Dict.</I>): To produce a litter of pigs. &lquo;That thair sow ferryit
was thar&rquo; =that their sow had farrowed.&mdash;Barbour's <I>Bruce</I>, xvii, 701. Cf. Danish
<I>fare</I>, to farrow. Formed, as a verb, from Middle English <I>farh</I>, which means (not
a litter, but) a single pig. The word is scarce, but the plural, <I>faren</I>, occurs in <I>King
Alisaunder</I>, 2441.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
<P>74. <B>sweaten]</B> For instances of irregular participial formation, see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 344.
<P>75. <B>Gibbet]</B> <SC>Douce</SC>: Apuleius, in describing the process used by the witch,
Milo's wife, for transforming herself into a bird, says that &lquo;she cut the lumps of
flesh of such as were hanged.&rquo; See Adlington's translation, 1596, p. 49, a book
certainly used by Shakespeare on other occasions.
<P>78. <B>deaftly]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: That is, <I>aptly, fitly.</I> It is connected with Anglo-
Saxon ged&oelig;ften, p. p. ged&oelig;ft, to be fit, ready, prepared.

<CC><P>warning to those managers who put too much faith in such mechanical aids. It
occurred when the armed head ought to have arisen, but when, though the trap-
door gaped, no apparition arose. The galleries began to hiss; whereupon the
scene-shifters in the cellarage, redoubling their exertions, and overcoming, perforce,
the obstinacy of the screw which was to raise the trap, fairly, out of too great and
urgent zeal, overdid their business, and produced before the audience, at full length,
the apparition of a stout man, his head and shoulders arrayed in antique helmet and
plate, while the rest of his person was humbly attired after the manner of a fifth-rate
performer of these degenerate days&mdash;that is to say, in a dimity waistcoat, nankeen
breeches, and a very dirty pair of cotton stockings. To complete the absurdity, the
poor man had been so hastily promoted that he could not keep his feet, but pros-
trated himself on his nose before the audience, to whom he was so unexpectedly
introduced. The effect of this accident was not recovered during the whole even-
ing, though the play was performed with transcendant ability.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

<P>99. <B>double]</B> <SC>Rushton</SC> (<I>Sh. a Lawyer</I>, p. 20): Referring not to a single, but to
a conditional, bond, under or by virtue of which, when forfeited, double the prin-
cipal sum was recoverable.&mdash;<SC>Lord Campbell</SC> (p. 111): Macbeth did not consider
what should be the penalty of the bond, or how he was to enforce the remedy, if the
condition should be broken. He goes on, in the same legal jargon, to say that he
&lquo;shall live <I>the lease</I> of nature.&rquo; But unluckily for Macbeth, the lease contained no
covenants <I>for title</I> or <I>quiet enjoyment:</I>&mdash;there were likewise <I>forfeitures</I> to be incurred
by the tenant,&mdash;with a <I>clause of re-entry</I>,&mdash;and consequently he was speedily <I>ousted.</I>
&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: By slaying Macduff he will bind fate to perform the promise.&mdash;
[<SC>Manly</SC> (p. 152): Contrary to Holinshed, Shakespeare makes Macbeth change his
intention in regard to Macduff at once; this obviates the necessity of introducing a
motive for the change, which would impede the rapid movement of the play.&mdash;
<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

<CC><P>the ornament that rises above it.&mdash;R. G. <SC>White</SC>: Shakespeare makes Macbeth call the
crown &lquo;the round of sovereignty&rquo; here and elsewhere&mdash;first, obviously, in allusion
to the form of the ornament. That is prose; but immediately his poetic eye sees
that a crown is the external sign of the complete possession of the throne. It is the
visible evidence that the royalty of its wearer lacks nothing, but is &lquo;<I>totus, teres, atque
rotundus</I>&rquo;&mdash;that it is finished, just as &lquo;our little life is <I>rounded</I> with a sleep.&rquo; But
the crown not only completes (especially in the eye of Macbeth, the usurper) and
rounds, as with the perfection of a circle, the claim to sovereignty, but it is figura-
tively the top, the summit, of ambitious hopes. Shakespeare often uses &lquo;top&rquo; in this
sense&mdash;<I>e. g.</I> &lquo;the top of admiration,&rquo; &lquo;the top of judgement,&rquo; &lquo;the top of honor,&rquo;
&lquo;the top of happy hours.&rquo; All this flashed upon Shakespeare through his mind's
eye, as he saw the circlet upon the top of the child's head.

such it occurs throughout the play in every instance but one; the exception is the

home, approve of this etymon as very apt. Yet is it Dun-seangain in the Irish,

which Macbeth should be suppos'd to say here. We must restore: &lquo;Rebellious

<I>rebellious head</I>, or <I>rebellion's head</I>, do not agree with the context; for Macbeth,
relying on the statements of the apparition, was firmly impressed with the belief
that none of woman born could prevent his living &lquo;the lease of nature.&rquo; Confid-
ing in the literal truth of this prophecy, his fears were concentrated on the prob-
able reappearance of the dead, alluding more especially to the ghost of Banquo;
and these fears were then conquered by the apparent impossibility of the movement
of Birnam wood to Dunsinane. The first prophecy relieves him from the fear of
mortals; the second, from the fear of the dead.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: The expression is
evidently suggested to Macbeth by the apparition of the armed head.&mdash;[<SC>Darmes-
teter</SC>: Referring to Banquo, who had already risen from the tomb to oust Macbeth
from his chair.&mdash;<SC>Sprague</SC>: There is no need of changing &lquo;dead&rquo; to <I>head;</I> but if
we do so change it, let us believe that the head is that of the murdered but still
living Banquo.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

<CC><P>126. <B>noise]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC> (note on <I>2 Hen. IV:</I> II, iv, 13): A <I>noise of musicians</I>
anciently signified a concert or company of them. In <I>Westward Hoe</I>, by Dekker
and Webster, 1607: &lquo;All the noise that went with him, poor fellows, have had their
fiddle-cases pulled over their ears,&rquo; [V, i, <I>ad fin.</I>].&mdash;<SC>Gifford</SC> (<I>The Silent Woman.</I>
Jonson's <I>Works</I>, vol. iii, p. 402): This term, which occurs perpetually in our old
dramatists, means a <I>company</I> or <I>concert. . . .</I> When this term went out of use I
cannot tell; but it was familiar in Dryden's time, who has it in his <I>Wild Gallant</I>
[&lquo;Hark, what noise is that! Is this music of your providing, Setstone?&rquo; V, iii.&mdash;
<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.] and elsewhere: &lquo;I hear him coming, and a whole noise of fiddlers at his
heels.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Maiden Queen</I>, [III, i.].&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Gloss.</I>): I may also mention that Wycher-
ley uses the word in the sense of &lquo;a company,&rquo; without any reference to music: &lquo;a
whole <I>noise</I> of flatterers.&rquo;&mdash;<I>The Plain Dealer</I>, I, i.&mdash;<SC>Anonymous</SC> (qu. <SC>Litchfield</SC>?):

<CC><P>which a celebrated magician made unto Catharine de Medicis, the French Queen,
whose impious cruelty led her to desire of him a magical exhibition of all the kings
that had hitherto reigned in France, and were yet to reign. The shapes of all the
kings, even unto the husband of the Queen, successively showed themselves in the
enchanted circle in which the conjuror made his invocations; and they took as many
turns as there had been years in their government. The kings that were to come
did thus in like manner successively come upon the stage, namely, Francis II,
Charles IX, Henry III, Henry IV; which being done, then two Cardinals, Riche-
lieu and Mazarine, in red hats, became visible in the spectacle. But after these
cardinals there entered wolves, bears, tigers, and lions to consummate the entertain-
ment.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Magnalia Christi Americana</I>, by Cotton Mather, 1702, Bk, ii, p. 29.
Shakespeare has shown his art in not suffering more than eight kings to appear in
the procession, the rest being shown only on the mirror.&mdash;<SC>Delius</SC>: A &lquo;show,&rquo; in
theatrical language, is a procession, or pantomine in which the actors remained
silent, hence usually called a &lquo;dumb show.&rquo;&mdash;[<SC>Chambers</SC> (p. 130): The &lquo;eight
Kings&rquo; are Robert II. (1371), Robert III, and the six Jameses. Those in the
glass are the successors of James.&mdash;<SC>Tolman</SC> (p. 13): Why is Mary Stuart omitted,
who, between the reigns of James V. and James VI, was the nominal sovereign for
a full quarter of a century? To be sure the literal promise to Banquo was, &lquo;Thou
shalt get <I>kings</I>&rquo;; but Mary was a sovereign, if not a king; and what a fine fitness
would there have been in bringing into this drama, though but for a moment, her
bewitching form. Though Shakespeare had paid compliments to Elizabeth, the
antagonist of the Stuart queen, he was now the loyal subject of James I. He
naturally felt, we may suppose, that it would be impolitic to remind his sovereign
and his audiences of the character and fate of the king's mother.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]
<P>134. <B>Thou . . . Banquo]</B> <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii. 196): This is finely imagined. Macbeth
does not compare what he saw to Banquo, but to the fearful image of Banquo
which he lately beheld.&mdash;[<SC>B&uuml;ttner</SC> (p. 46) tells us that the &lquo;ghost of Robert II.
bears an unmistakable family likeness to Banquo himself.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

<P>149. <B>sprights]</B> <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> i, 193, 205): It may safely be laid down as a
canon, that the word <I>spirit</I> in our old poets, wherever the metre does not compel us
to pronounce it disyllabically, is a monosyllable. And this is almost always the case.
The truth of the above rule is evident from several considerations. In the first place,
we never meet with other disyllables&mdash;such, I mean, as are incapable of contraction
&mdash;placed in a similar situation; the apparent exceptions not being really exceptions
(see S. V. <I>passim</I>). Another argument is founded on the unpleasant ripple which
the common pronunciation occasions in the flow of numberless lines, interfering with
the general run of the verse; a harshness which, in some passages, must be evident
to the dullest ear. Add to this the frequent substitution of <I>spright</I> or <I>sprite</I> for spirit
(in all the different senses of the word, I mean, and not merely in that of <I>ghost</I>, in
which <I>sprite</I> is still used); also <I>spreet</I>, though rarely (only in the ante-Elizabethan
age, I think, as far as I have observed); and sometimes <I>sp'rit</I> and <I>sprit.</I> (For the
double spelling, <I>spright</I> and <I>sprite</I>, one may compare <I>despight</I> and <I>despite;</I> which in
like manner subsequently assumed different meanings, <I>despight</I> being used for <I>con-
tempt, despectus.</I>) Perhaps it would be desirable, wherever the word occurs as a
monosyllable, to write it <I>spright</I>, in order to ensure the proper pronunciation of the</CC>

<P>152. <B>Antique round]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: These ideas, as well as that in I, iii, might
have been adopted from a poem, entitled <I>Churchyard's Dreame</I>, 1593: &lquo;All <I>hand</I>
in <I>hand</I> they traced on A tricksie <I>ancient round;</I> And soone <I>as shadowes were they
gone</I>, And might no more be found.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: &lquo;Antic,&rquo; in its modern sense of
<I>grotesque</I>, is probably derived from the remains of ancient sculpture rudely imitated
and caricatured by medi&aelig;val artists, and from the figures in Masques and Antimasques,
dressed in ancient costume, particularly satyrs and the like. But it acquired a much
wider application. In <I>Twelfth Night</I>, II, iv, 3, the word means old-fashioned, quaint.
Sometimes it means simply <I>ancient</I>, as <I>Hamlet</I>, II, ii, 491. Whatever be its signifi-
cation, and however it be spelt, it is always accented by Shakespeare on the first
syllable.

<P>1. <B>Scena Secunda]</B> <SC>Fletcher</SC> (p. 166): It mars the whole spirit and moral of the
play, to take anything from that depth and liveliness of interest which the dramatist
has attached to the characters and fortunes of Macduff and his Lady. They are the
chief representatives in the piece, of the interests of loyalty and domestic affection,
as opposed to those of the foulest treachery and the most selfish and remorseless
ambition. . . . It is not enough that we should hear the story in the brief words in
which it is related to Macduff by his fugitive cousin, Ross. The presence of the
affectionate family before our eyes,&mdash;the timid lady's eloquent complaining to her
cousin, of her husband's deserting them in danger,&mdash;the graceful prattle with her boy,
in which she seeks relief from her melancholy forebodings,&mdash;and then the sudden
entrance of Macbeth's murderous ruffians,&mdash;are all requisite to give that crowning
horror, that consummately and violently revolting character to Macbeth's career,
which Shakespeare has so evidently studied to impress upon it. Nothing has more
contributed to favor the false notion of a certain sympathy which the dramatist has
been supposed to have excited for the character and fate of this most gratuitously
criminal of his heroes, than the theatrical narrowing of the space, and consequent
weakening of the interest, which his unerring judgement has assigned in the piece
to those representatives of virtue and humanity, for whom he has really sought to
move the sympathies of his audience. It is no fault of his if Macbeth's heartless
whinings have ever extracted one emotion of pity from reader or auditor, in lieu of
that intensely aggravated abhorrence which they ought to inspire.&mdash;<SC>Coleridge</SC> (i.</CC>

<CC><P>250): This scene, dreadful as it is, is still a relief, because a variety, because
domestic, and therefore soothing, as associated with the only real pleasures of life.
The conversation between Lady Macduff and her child heightens the pathos, and is
preparatory for the deep tragedy of their assassination. . . . To the objection that
Shakespeare wounds the moral sense by the unsubdued, undisguised description
of the most hateful atrocity,&mdash;that he tears the feelings without mercy, and even
outrages the eye itself with scenes of insupportable horror,&mdash;I, omitting <I>Titus
Andronicus</I> as not genuine, and excepting the scene of Gloster's blinding in <I>King
Lear</I>, answer boldly in the name of Shakespeare, not guilty!&mdash;<SC>Bodenstedt</SC>: To
omit this scene, as is usually the case on the stage, is to present Macbeth's character
in a far more favorable light than Shakespeare intended, and to weaken the force
of Macduff's cry of agony, and Lady Macbeth's heart-piercing question in the sleep-
walking scene. We must be made to see how far Macbeth's unavailing bloodthirsti-
ness reaches, which spares not even innocent women and children. Moreover, in
this tragedy of hypocritical treachery and faithless ambition, Macduff and his wife
are the exponents of honest loyalty and domestic virtue.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: The scene
of the murder of Lady Macduff and her children is traditionally placed at Dunne-
marle Castle, Culross, Perthshire.&mdash;[<SC>Leighton</SC> (<I>Robinson's Epitome</I>, Nov. 1878):
The purpose of this scene seems simply to illustrate, by presenting absolutely before
our eyes a massacre of innocents, the devilish wickedness of Macbeth. If it were
necessary to do this, we would expect of the genius of Shakespeare in this play,
where that genius is so powerfully illustrated, that the scene should be made to serve
at the same time some purpose of contrast or characterization, and the lack of any
such secondary purpose lends its weight to heighten suspicion against genuineness
of authorship. Its repulsive character has no excuse of necessity; hence, &aelig;sthetic-
ally, it has no right to be. The tragedy is more perfect and symmetrical without
it. It points no lesson, develops no character, explains no necessary action; but
retards the movement, and shocks us with its accumulation of murders, of which we
already have had a surfeit. In the misfortune of the presumably innocent mother
and child, it makes more striking another instance of inexplicable ethical injus-
tice.&mdash;<SC>Libby</SC> (see note on I, ii, 53): Ross came as Macbeth's spy to lead a gang
of assassins: during his interview with the lady the murderers await him outside,
and within <I>three minutes</I> of his exit they enter, within <I>four minutes</I> the poor little
fellow is dead, and within <I>five minutes</I> the lady is butchered. Where is the sword
of Ross, who has just said, &lquo;Shall not be long but I'll be here again&rquo;? . . . Unless
Ross can be cleared of the charge of allowing the Macduffs to be murdered before
he had left the castle (there is much to show that he directed the assassins) his
character is worse than his master's.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

<CC><P>1878): It has always appeared to me that the character of Macduff suffers seriously
by the accusation of his wife, and that such effect mars the play, inasmuch as he,
being principally opposed to Macbeth, should be presented generous, chivalrous,
and good; in contrast with the usurper of Duncan's throne, who is selfish, treach-
erous, and wicked. To enlist our sympathies to the fullest extent, and to make
the moral of the play most effective, the spirit of ill, represented by Macbeth, should
be opposed by a spotless champion of good and right, and not by one suffering in
reputation under such accusations as his wife makes against the fugitive Thane.&mdash;
<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
<P>13. <B>touch]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: Natural sensibility. He is not touched with natural affec-
tion. [For other uses of this word, see <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I>).&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]
<P>13. <B>Wren]</B> <SC>Harting</SC> (p. 143): There are three statements here which are likely
to be criticised by the ornithologist. First, that the wren is the smallest of birds,
which is evidently an oversight. Secondly, that the wren has sufficient courage to
fight against a bird of prey in defence of its young, which is doubtful. Thirdly,
that the owl will take young birds from the nest.
<P>22. <B>fits]</B> <SC>Heath</SC>: What befits the season.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: The <I>violent disorders</I> of
the season, its convulsions; as in <I>Coriol.</I> III, ii, 33.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: The critical con-
junctures of the time. The figure is taken from the fits of an intermittent fever.
<P>22. <B>I dare not]</B> <SC>Mull</SC> (p. cii.): It seems strange that no communication was
made to Lady Macduff that her husband had gone to the English Court on an im-
perative mission, an intimation which would have rendered her some comfort prob-
ably.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.</CC>

<CC><P>24. <B>know our selues]</B> <SC>Upton</SC> (p. 322): That is, to be traitors.
<P>24. <B>hold Rumor]</B> <SC>Heath</SC>: To interpret rumour.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: To believe, as
we say, &lquo;I <I>hold</I> such a thing to be true&rquo;; <I>i. e.</I> I take it, I believe it to be so. The
sense then is, When we are led by our fears to believe every rumour of danger we
hear, yet are not conscious to ourselves of any crime for which we should be dis-
turbed with those fears. Thus in <I>King John</I>, IV, ii, 145.&mdash;<SC>Delius</SC>: To &lquo;hold
rumour&rquo; is contrasted with to &lquo;know&rquo; in the next line.&mdash;<SC>Dalgleish</SC>: When we
accept or circulate rumours, because we <I>fear</I> them to be true.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: It is
uncertain whether this very difficult expression means &lquo;when we interpret rumour in
accordance with our fear,&rquo; or &lquo;when our reputation is derived from actions which
our fear dictates,&rquo; as Lady Macduff has said in lines 6, 7, &lquo;When our actions do
not, Our fears do make us traitors.&rquo; See the use of &lquo;From&rquo; in III, vi, 24.&mdash;<SC>Hud-
son</SC> (ed. ii.): Fear makes us credit rumour, yet we know not what to fear, because
ignorant when we offend. A condition wherein men believe the more because they
fear, and fear the more because they cannot foresee the danger.

<P>81. <B>To fright]</B> For other instances where &lquo;to&rquo; is equivalent to <I>in</I> or <I>for</I> with the

<P>82. <B>worse]</B> <SC>Warburton</SC>: We should read &lquo;To do <I>worship</I> to you,&rquo; etc. That
is, but at this juncture to waste my time in the gradual observances due to your
rank, would be the exposing your life to immediate destruction.&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>: To do
<I>worse</I> is to let her and her children be destroyed without warning.&mdash;<SC>Edwards</SC>
(p. 74): That is, to fright you more, by relating all the circumstances of your
danger; which would detain you so long, that you could not avoid it.
<P>82. <B>fell]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Florio gives &lquo;<I>Fello</I>, fell, cruel, moodie, inexorable, fello-
nious, murderous.&rquo; Hence &lquo;fellone,&rquo; a felon.
<P>85. <B>Whether]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 493): A proper Alexandrine with six accents is seldom
found in Shakespeare. (&sect; 494): In V, iv, 12, &lquo;The n&uacute;m &verbar; bers &oacute;f &verbar; our h&oacute;st &verbar; and
m&aacute;ke &verbar; <I>disc&oacute;very</I>&rquo; (discov'ry), we have an Alexandrine only in appearance. The last
foot contains, instead of one extra syllable, two extra syllables, one of which is slurred.
[A term phonetically unintelligible to me.&mdash;<SC>Ellis</SC>, <I>Early Eng. Pronunciation</I>, Part
iii, p. 944.] (&sect; 496): In other cases the appearance of an Alexandrine arises from
the non-observance of contractions: &lquo;I d&aacute;re &verbar; ab&iacute;de &verbar; no l&oacute;nger &verbar; <I>Wh&iacute;ther</I> should &verbar; I
fly?&rquo; So in V, iii, 7: &lquo;All m&oacute;rt &verbar; al <I>c&oacute;nse</I> &verbar; <I>quence</I>(<I>s</I>) h&aacute;ve &verbar; pron&oacute;unced &verbar; me thus.&rquo;
&mdash;<SC>Ellis</SC>: These &lquo;contractions&rquo; would have a remarkably harsh effect in the in-
stances cited, even if they were possible. No person accustomed to write verses
could well endure lines thus divided [as above. In the present instance] the line
belongs to two speeches and &lquo;should&rquo; may be emphatic. . . . I should be sorry to buy
immunity from Alexandrines at the dreadful price of such Procrustean &lquo;scansion.&rquo;
<P>88. <B>sometime]</B> See I, vi, 17.</CC>
