<CC><P>1. <B>Sc&oelig;na Tertia]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: The Poet no doubt felt that this scene was
needed to supplement the meagre parts assigned to Malcolm and Macduff.&mdash;
<SC>French</SC> (p. 293): The present Earl of Fife, James Duff, 1868, who is also Vis-
count Macduff, is lineally descended from the Macduff of the play.&mdash;[<SC>Verity</SC>:
Dramatically this scene seems, at first sight, more open to criticism than any other
in the play. . . . The real design is, I think, to mark the pause before the storm.
No dramatic theme remains except the great avengement. . . . But to bring this
about suddenly would violate probability. The <I>d&eacute;nouement</I> must be lead up to
gradually; there must be an antecedent period in which the storm clouds gather:
and this long scene, as it were, fills the period.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]
<P>7. <B>Birthdome]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: Our birthdom, or birthright, says he, lies on the
ground; let us, like men who are to fight for what is dearest to them, not abandon
it, but stand over it and defend it. This is a strong picture of obstinate resolution.
So, Falstaff says to Hal: &lquo;If thou see me down in the battle, and <I>bestride me</I>, so.&rquo;
&mdash;<I>1 Hen. IV:</I> V, i, 121. <I>Birthdom</I> for <I>birthright</I> is formed by the same analogy
with <I>masterdom</I> in this play, signifying the <I>privileges</I> or <I>rights</I> of a <I>master.</I> Per-
haps it might be <I>birthdame</I> for <I>mother;</I> let us stand over our <I>mother</I> that lies bleed-
ing on the ground.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: &lquo;Birthdom&rquo; is formed on the analogy of &lquo;king-
dom,&rquo; &lquo;earldom,&rquo; &lquo;masterdom,&rquo; I, v, 68, with this difference, that &lquo;king,&rquo; &lquo;earl,&rquo;
&lquo;master,&rquo; designate persons, and &lquo;birth&rquo; a condition; the termination &lquo;-dom&rquo; is
connected with &lquo;doom,&rquo; and &lquo;kingdom&rquo; signifies the extent of a king's jurisdiction.
It loses its original force when joined to adjectives, as in &lquo;freedom,&rquo; &lquo;wisdom,&rquo; etc.,
and is then equivalent to the German -<I>heit</I>, in <I>Weisheit, Freiheit</I>, our &lquo;-hood.&rquo;
&lquo;Birthdom&rquo; here does not, as we think, signify &lquo;birthright,&rquo; but &lquo;the land of our
birth,&rquo; now struck down and prostrate beneath the usurper's feet.

<P>32. <B>doubts]</B> <SC>Delius</SC>: That is, in this meeting at the English Court, so sur-

<CC><P>42. <B>affear'd]</B> <SC>Pope</SC>: A law term for <I>confirmed.</I>&mdash;<SC>Heath</SC> (p. 403): A law term
which signifies estimated, proportioned, adjusted; not confirmed. It is used here
in its common acceptation for affrightened. [See <SC>Elwin</SC>.] Malcolm's title to the
crown is affrightened from asserting itself; or, in plainer English, He is affrightened
from asserting his title to the crown.&mdash;<SC>Ritson</SC>: To <I>affeer</I> is to assess, or reduce to
certainty. All amerciaments are by Magna Charta to be <I>affeered</I> by lawful men,
sworn to be impartial. This is the ordinary practice of a Court Leet, with which
Shakespeare seems to have been intimately acquainted, and where he might have
occasionally acted as an <I>affeerer.</I>&mdash;<SC>Elwin</SC>: There is a play upon the word &lquo;af-
feer'd.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> i, 275): Perhaps we should read <I>assur'd</I> or <I>affirm'd.</I>
Affear'd may have originated in <I>feare</I>, five lines below.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: Confirmed.
In Cowel's <I>Law Dict.</I> s. v.: &lquo;<I>Affeerers</I> may probably be derived from the French
<I>affier</I>, that is, <I>affirmare, confirmare</I>, and signifies in the common law such as are
appointed in Court-Leets, upon oath, to set the fines on such as have committed
faults arbitrarily punishable, and have no express penalty appointed by statute.&rquo; [To
same effect, <SC>Murray</SC> (<I>N. E. D.</I>)&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]
<P>56. <B>Shall]</B> See III, iv, 73.

<CC><P>59. <B>should]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 324): &lquo;Should&rquo; is sometimes used as though it were the
past tense of a verb <I>shall</I>, meaning <I>is to</I>, not quite <I>ought.</I> Compare the German
&lquo;sollen.&rquo; <SC>Ibid</SC>. (&sect; 325): &lquo;Should&rquo; was hence used in direct questions about the past
where <I>shall</I> was used about the future. . . . It seems to increase the emphasis of the
interrogation, since a doubt about the past (time having been given for investiga-
tion) implies more perplexity than a doubt about the future.
<P>60-65. E. K. <SC>Chambers</SC>: I think there is a touch of deeper psychological insight
in this [than a trial of Macduff's patriotism]. Is it not true that in the critical moments
of life one is often suddenly oppressed with a sense of one's own weaknesses, and
dormant, if not actual, tendencies to evil, which seem to cry aloud for expression,
confession? For a similar instance, compare <I>Hamlet</I>, III, i, 124.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
<P>62. <B>open'd]</B> <SC>Collier</SC> (<I>Notes</I>, etc., p. 414): The sense afforded by &lquo;open'd&rquo; is so
inferior to that given by the MS Corrector that we need not hesitate in concluding
that Shakespeare, carrying on the figure suggested by &lquo;grafted&rquo; as applied to fruit,
must have written &lquo;ripen'd.&rquo;
<P>68. <B>euils]</B> <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> ii, 197): &lquo;<I>In</I> evils,&rquo; apparently, in the same sense as
<I>Oth.</I> I, i, 21: &lquo;A fellow almost damned in a fair life.&rquo; Tomkins, <I>Albumazar</I>, v, 11,
Dodsley, ed. 1825, vol. vii, p. 193: &lquo;&mdash; O wonderful! Admir'd Albumazar in two
transformations!&rquo; <I>admired on account of two transformations which he has wrought.</I>
Perhaps also, <I>1 Hen. IV:</I> V, iv, 121, is in point: &lquo;The better part of valour is
discretion; in the which better part I have saved my life&rquo;; <I>through which, by reason
of which.</I> [See also the same article for instances of the pronunciation of &lquo;evil&rquo; as
a monosyllable; as also Abbott (&sect; 466).]

<CC><P>ing to <I>luxure</I>, not <I>luxe.</I> This sense of the word is now obsolete. In the modern
sense we find it as early as Beaumont and Fletcher, and in Milton it has always
either the modern sense, or that of <I>luxuriant.</I> [See <I>Much Ado</I>, IV, i, 194, this
edition.]

<I>Lear</I>, III, ii, 58, the word is found as a substantive. And in <I>Mid. N. D.</I> II, i, 92,
we have the same figure which is used in the present passage.
<P>77, 78. <B>Better . . . reigne]</B> <SC>Coleridge</SC> (i, 251): The moral is&mdash;the dreadful

<P>80. <B>In Nature]</B> <SC>Delius</SC>: This belongs to &lquo;tyranny&rquo;; such organic intemperance
is compared with the political tyranny of Macbeth.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: If the words are
to be construed according to Delius, we should interpret them thus: &lquo;intemperance
is of the nature of a tyranny,&rquo; remembering <I>Jul. C&aelig;s.</I> II, i, 69, &lquo;The state of man,
Like to a little kingdom, suffers then The nature of an insurrection.&rquo; Or we may
join &lquo;intemperance in nature,&rquo; and interpret <I>want of control over the natural appe-
tites.</I> The former seems preferable. In any case &lquo;tyranny&rquo; here means <I>usurpation</I>,
in consequence of which the rightful king loses his throne. See note on III, vi, 25.

<P>87. <B>That]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 277): &lquo;That&rquo; is still used provincially for <I>such</I> and <I>so:</I>
e. g. &lquo;He is <I>that</I> foolish <I>that</I> he understands nothing.&rquo; So <I>Hamlet</I>, I, v, 48. &lquo;That&rquo;
is more precise than <I>of that kind</I> or <I>such.</I> &lquo;That,&rquo; meaning <I>such</I>, is used before the
infinitive where we use the less emphatic <I>the</I>, as in the present instance.

<P>100. <B>stickes]</B> <SC>Theobald</SC> (Nichols's <I>Lit. Ill.</I> ii, 530): I should think <I>strikes

<P>101. <B>Summer-seeming]</B> <SC>Theobald</SC>: <I>Summer-teeming</I>, i. e. the Passion, which
lasts no longer than the <I>Heat</I> of Life, and which goes off in the <I>Winter</I> of Age.
Summer is the season in which Weeds get Strength, grow rank, and dilate them-
selves.&mdash;<SC>Heath</SC> (p. 404): &lquo;Summer-seeming&rquo; gives a very apt and proper sense;
that is, Which hath no other inconvenience than that of an extraordinary heat for
the time, such as we commonly experience in summer, and which is of no long dura-
tion. However, as the integrity of the metaphor, which is taken from the growth
of a plant, and particularly the root of it, is not well preserved, I am inclined to
believe Shakespeare wrote, &lquo;summer-<I>seeding</I>,&rquo; i. e. Than lust, which, like a summer
plant, runs up to seed during that season, and quickly afterwards dies away.&mdash;
[<SC>Steevens</SC> in 1785 quoted Blackstone as the author of this conjecture, <I>summer-seed-
ing</I>, although Heath anticipated the latter by twenty years. Attention was called to
Heath's claims in the Anonymous Variorum edition of 1807; but with this excep-
tion, and that of the Cambridge Editors, every editor who has noticed the conjecture
has accorded it to Blackstone. I have been unable to find where <SC>Steevens</SC> obtained
this note of the eminent Justice: it is not in the list published by the <I>Shakespeare
Society</I> in vol. xii. of their Papers.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>: When I was younger and
bolder I corrected it thus: &lquo;Than <I>fume, or seething</I> lust,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> angry passion of
boiling lust.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: Lust that <I>seems</I> as hot as <I>summer.</I>&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: In Donne's
poems [<I>Love's Alchemy.</I>&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>] we meet with &lquo;winter-<I>seeming.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC>:
The passion that burns awhile like summer, and like summer passes away; whereas
the other passion, <I>avarice</I>, has no such date, but grows stronger and stronger to the
end of life.&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC>: We are unwilling to disturb the old text, though we have
a strong persuasion that Shakespeare wrote &lquo;summer-<I>seaming</I> lust,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> lust <I>fat-
tened</I> by summer heat.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: Befitting, or looking like, summer. Avarice
is compared to a plant which strikes its roots deep and lasts through every season;
lust to an annual which flourishes in summer and then dies.&mdash;<SC>Allen</SC> (MS): We
should (I think) write thus: This avarice Sticks deeper&mdash;grows with more pernicious
root&mdash;Than summer-'<I>seeming</I> lust. Shakespeare conceives of <I>avarice</I> (&lquo;the good old-
gentlemanly vice&rquo; of Byron) as a plant of <I>Autumn</I> and <I>Winter</I>, deeper rooted, more
lasting; of <I>Lust</I>, as a plant of <I>Summer</I>, earlier and more rapid in its growth, but
less enduring. Lust is, therefore, a vice that naturally goes with (and in so far
<I>beseems</I>) <I>Youth</I>, the <I>Summer</I> of life. &lquo;Seeming,&rquo; then, is but <I>beseeming</I>, with its</CC>

<CC><P>The late Mr W. W. Williams (<I>The Parthenon</I>, 1 Nov. 1862, p. 849) has shown
that Walker is wrong by the following quotation from <I>Jul. C&oelig;s.</I> III, i, 257, &lquo;That

<P>135. <B>traines]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: That is, <I>artifices, devices, lures.</I> Cotgrave gives
&lquo;Traine: . . . a plot, practise, conspiracie, deuise&rquo;; and &lquo;Trainer: to weaue; also,
to plot, contrive, practise, conspire, deuise.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Baynes</SC> (p. 312): A technical term
both in hawking and hunting: in hawking, for the lure, thrown out to reclaim a
falcon given to ramble, or &lquo;rake out,&rquo; as it is called, and thus in danger of escaping
from the fowler; and in hunting, for the bait trailed along the ground, and left
exposed to tempt the animal from his lair or covert, and bring him fairly within
the power of the lurking huntsman. Thus Turbervile, &lquo;When a huntsman would
hunt a wolfe, he must <I>trayne</I> them by these means . . . there let them lay down their
<I>traynes.</I> And when the wolves go out in the night to prey and to feede, they will
crosse upon the <I>trayne</I> and follow it,&rquo; etc. Again, &lquo;&mdash; if they fayle to come into the
<I>trayne</I>, then let him send out varlettes to <I>trayne</I> from about all the coverts,&rquo; etc.
<P>140. <B>Vnspeake]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 442): <I>Un</I>- seems to have been preferred by Shake-
speare before <I>p</I> and <I>r</I>, which do not allow <I>in</I>- to precede except in the form of <I>im-.
In</I>- also seems to have been in many cases retained from the Latin. As a general
rule, we now use <I>in</I>- where we desire to make the negative a part of the word, and
<I>un</I>- where the separation is maintained,&mdash;&lquo;<I>un</I>true,&rquo; &lquo;<I>in</I>firm.&rquo; Hence <I>un</I>- is always
used with participles. Perhaps also <I>un</I>- is stronger than <I>in</I>-. &lquo;<I>Un</I>holy&rquo; means
more than &lquo;not holy,&rquo; almost &lquo;the reverse of holy.&rquo;
<P>142. <B>For]</B> This passage is cited by <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 148) as an example of the first
meaning of &lquo;for&rquo; as connected with <I>as being.</I> See III, i, 145. For the second
meaning, see IV, ii, 46.</CC>

<P>151. <B>Old Seyward]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: <I>Old Siward</I>, son of Beorn, Earl of Northum-

of Earl Godwin and his sons, 1053. According to Holinshed, p. 244, col. 1, who
follows Hector Boece, fol. 249, b. ed. 1574, Duncan married a daughter of Siward.
Fordun calls her &lquo;consanguinea.&rquo; It is remarkable that Shakespeare, who seems to
have had no other guide than Holinshed, on this point deserts him, for in V, ii, 5,
he calls Siward Malcolm's uncle. It is true that &lquo;nephew&rquo; was often used like
&lquo;nepos,&rquo; in the sense of grandson, but we know of no instance in which &lquo;uncle&rquo; is
used for &lquo;grandfather.&rquo;

So also in Bunyan's Life, quoted by Mr. Wilton Rix, <I>East Anglian Nonconformity,

<CC><P>153. <B>chance</B>, etc.] <SC>Warburton</SC>: May the lot Providence has decreed for us be
answerable to the justice of our quarrel.&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC> (<I>Obs.</I>): If there be not some
more important error in the passage, it should at least be pointed thus: &lquo;&mdash; and the
chance, of goodness, be,&rquo; etc. That is, may the event be, of the goodness of heaven
(<I>pro justitia divina</I>), answerable to the cause.&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>: I am inclined to believe
that Shakespeare wrote &lquo;and the chance, O goodness, Be,&rquo; etc. This some of his
transcribers wrote with a small <I>o</I>, which another imagined to mean <I>of.</I> The sense
will then be, &lquo;and O thou sovereign Goodness, to whom we now appeal, may our
fortune answer to our cause.&rquo;&mdash;H. C. K. (<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> 15 Oct. 1853): The radical
meaning of the word <I>belike</I> is to lie or be near, to attend; from which it came to ex-
press the <I>simple condition</I> or <I>state of a thing.</I> Now it is not easy to see why Mal-
colm should wish that &lquo;chance&rquo; should &lquo;be <I>like</I>&rquo;&mdash;i. e. similar to, their &lquo;warranted
quarrel&rquo;; inasmuch as that quarrel was most unfortunate and disastrous. Surely it
is far more probable that Shakespeare wrote <I>belike</I> (<I>belicgan, geliggen</I>) as one word,
and that the passage means simply: &lquo;May good fortune attend our enterprise.&rquo;&mdash;
<SC>Staunton</SC>: This passage has been inexplicable heretofore from &lquo;Belike&rquo; being
always printed as two words, <I>Be like.</I> The meaning is, And the fortune of good-
ness <I>approve</I> or <I>favour</I> our justifiable quarrel.&mdash;<SC>Delius</SC>: &lquo;Chance of goodness&rquo; is
equivalent to <I>successful issue</I>, and &lquo;like&rquo; is also to be understood in connection with
it:&mdash;may the issue correspond in goodness to our good, righteous cause. &lquo;Chance
of goodness&rquo; forms one idea like &lquo;time of scorn,&rquo; <I>Oth.</I> IV, ii, 54.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>:
&lquo;May the chance of success be as certain as the justice of our quarrel.&rquo; The sense
of the word &lquo;goodness&rquo; is limited by the preceding &lquo;chance.&rquo; Without this, &lquo;good-
ness&rquo; by itself could not have this meaning. It is somewhat similarily limited and
defined by the word &lquo;night&rquo; in <I>Oth.</I> I, ii, 35: &lquo;The goodness of the night upon you,
friends!&rquo; And by &lquo;bliss,&rquo; <I>Meas. for Meas.</I> III, ii, 227: &lquo;Bliss and goodness on
you, father.&rquo; As in <I>Lear</I>, I, iv, 306, &lquo;brow of youth&rquo; means &lquo;youthful brow,&rquo; and
in <I>Mer. of Ven.</I> II, viii, 42, &lquo;mind of love&rquo; means &lquo;loving mind.&rquo;

vnto his successors the Kyngs of this Realme.&rquo; Edward's miraculous powers were
believed in by his contemporaries, or at least soon after his death, and expressly
recognised by Pope Alexander III. who canonized him. The power of healing was
claimed for his successors early in the twelfth century, for it is controverted by
William of Malmesbury, and asserted later in the same century by Peter of Blois,
who held a high office in the Royal Household (see Freeman's <I>Norman Conquest</I>,

<CC><P>was supposed to be conferred by the unction of the &lquo;Sainte Ampoule&rquo; on their

before. James the First's practice of touching for the evil is mentioned several
times in Nichols's <I>Progresses</I>, e. g. vol. iii, pp. 264, 273. Charles I. when at York,
touched seventy persons in one day. Charles II. also touched, when an exile at
Bruges, omitting, perhaps for sufficient reason, the gift of the coin. He practised
with signal success after his restoration. One of Dr Johnson's earliest recolle&ccedil;tions
was the being taken to be touched by Queen Anne in 1712 (Boswell, vol. i, p. 38).
Even Swift seems to have believed in the efficacy of the cure (<I>Works</I>, ed. Scott, ii,
252). The Whigs did not claim the power for the Hanoverian sovereigns, though
they highly resented Carte's claiming it for the Pretender in his <I>History of England.</I>
[For information on this subject, see Chambers's <I>Book of Days</I>, vol. i, p. 82, and
W. B. <SC>Rye</SC>, <I>England as Seen by Foreigners</I>, pp. 151, 275.]
<P>170. <B>solicites]</B> <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> iii, 274): <I>Solicit</I>, like many other words derived
from the Latin,&mdash;as <I>religion</I> for <I>worship</I> or <I>service</I>, etc.,&mdash;had not yet lost its strict
Latin meaning.&mdash;<SC>Lettsom</SC> (<I>foot-note</I>): The original signification of the Latin word
seems to have been <I>to move</I>, and the various meanings attached to it by lexicogra-
phers are but modifications of this primary one. In the language of Shakespeare,
Edward <I>solicited</I>, or <I>moved</I>, heaven by means known to himself; Suffolk (<I>1 Hen. VI:</I>
V, iii, 190) proposed to <I>solicit</I>, or move, Henry by speaking of the wonderful en-
dowments of Margaret; and Hamlet (V, ii, 369), though his speech was cut short
by death, seems to have been thinking of the events that had <I>solicited</I>, or <I>moved</I>,
him to recommend Fortinbras as successor to the throne. [See <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I>)
for examples of &lquo;solicit&rquo; in sense of <I>to prevail by entreaty.</I>]
<P>173. <B>meere]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 15): As in Latin; equivalent to <I>unmixed with anything
else;</I> hence, by inference, <I>intact, complete.</I> In this case <I>the utter despair.</I> In accord-
ance with its original meaning, &lquo;not <I>merely</I>,&rquo; in Bacon, is used for <I>not entirely.</I> [For
instances of this use of &lquo;mere,&rquo; see <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I>) and Shakespeare <I>passim.</I>]</CC>

<CC><P>174. <B>stampe]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: The coin called an <I>angel.</I> See <I>Mer. of Ven.</I> II, vii,
56. Its value was ten shillings.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: There is no warrant in Holinshed
for the statement that the Confessor hung a golden coin or stamp about the necks
of the patients. This was, however, a custom which prevailed in later days. Pre-
viously to Charles II.'s time some current coin, as an angel, was used for the pur-
pose, but in Charles's reign a special medal was struck and called a &lquo;touch-piece.&rquo;
The identical touch-piece which Queen Anne hung round the neck of Dr Johnson
is preserved in the British Museum.

<P>195. <B>extasie]</B> <SC>Murray</SC> (<I>N. E. D.</I>): The classical senses of <G>e)/kstasis</G> are &lquo;in-
sanity&rquo; and &lquo;bewilderment&rquo;; but in late Greek the etymological meaning received
another application, viz., &lquo;withdrawal of the soul from the body, mystic or prophetic
trance&rquo;; hence in later medical writers the word is used for trance, etc., generally.
Both the classical and post-classical senses came into the modern languages, and
in the present figurative use they seem to be blended.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.

What! Flowers in the Highlands! Yes, my dear departed friend, Heath-flowers
in abundance. And it is to these flowers that Shakespeare alludes, it being custom-
ary with the Highlanders, when on a march, to stick sprigs of heath in their bonnets.
We cannot say that a vegetable &lquo;expires,&rquo; but, in common with animal life, it may
be said to &lquo;die.&rquo; The alteration gives sense to the passage.

<P>241. <B>Quarry]</B> <SC>Wedgwood</SC>: Among falconers any game flown at and killed.&mdash;

is called the querry.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> 9 May, 1857. Considered with reference to the
dogs, the <I>cur&egrave;e</I> or <I>querre</I> was the practical object of the chase, and thus came to be
applied to the game killed.

<P>254. <B>Children]</B> <SC>Ritson</SC> (p. 76): That is, Malcolm, not Macbeth.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>:

<CC><P>274. <B>Heauen]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Probably the original MS had &lquo;May God&rquo; or &lquo;Then

<P>274. <B>too]</B> <SC>Hudson</SC> (ed. ii.): The little word &lquo;too&rquo; is so used here as to intensify,
in a remarkable manner, the sense of what precedes. Put him once within the
reach of my sword, and if I don't kill him, then I am worse than he, and I not only
forgive him myself, but pray God to forgive him also: or perhaps it is, then I am as
bad as he, and may God forgive us both.
<P>275. <B>time]</B> <SC>Gifford</SC> (<I>Massinger's Works</I>, vol. ii, p. 356): The Commentators
might have spared their pains [in changing &lquo;time&rquo; to <I>tune</I>], since it appears from
numberless examples that the two words were once synonymous. &lquo;Time,&rquo; however,
was the more ancient and common term; nor was it till long after the age of Mas-
singer that the use of it, in the sense of harmony, was entirely superseded by that
of <I>tune.</I>&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC>: &lquo;Time&rquo; could here scarcely be right, even were we to take Gif-
ford's statement for granted. No misprint could be more easy than &lquo;time&rquo; for <I>tune</I>,
and <I>vice vers&acirc;;</I> and perhaps none was more frequently committed.&mdash;<SC>Elwin</SC>: Shake-
speare has, in several instances, used <I>tune</I> in this figurative sense, but in no case
has he so applied the word &lquo;time,&rquo; nor anywhere employed it as synonymous with
<I>tune.</I>&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC>: Who, except Knight, will suppose that Gifford would have defended
the reading &lquo;time&rquo; in such a passage as this?&mdash;R. G. <SC>White</SC> (<I>As You Like It</I>, V, iii,
37): In the MS of any period it is very difficult to tell &lquo;time&rquo; from <I>tune</I>, except by
the dot of the <I>i</I>, so frequently omitted. I can speak from experience that in ninety-
nine cases out of a hundred in which &lquo;time&rquo; is written, it will be at first put in type
as <I>tune.</I> (<I>King John</I>, III, iii, 26, &lquo;I had a thing to say, But I will fit it to some
better <I>time</I>,&rquo; where the original has <I>tune.</I>) &lquo;Time&rquo; and <I>tune</I> were never used as
synonymous.
<P>275. <B>manly]</B> See III, v, 4.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: In adjectives which end in &lquo;-ly,&rquo; the
familiar termination of the abverb, we find the adjective form frequently used for the
latter, as in <I>Hamlet</I>, I, ii, 202: &lquo;Goes slow and stately by them.&rquo; So also in the
Liturgy, &lquo;godly and quietly governed.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Coleridge</SC> (i, 251): How admirably
Macduff's grief is in harmony with the whole play! It rends, not dissolves, the
heart. &lquo;The tune of it goes manly.&rquo; Thus is Shakespeare always master of himself
and of his subject,&mdash;a genuine Proteus;&mdash;we see all things in him, as images in a
calm lake, most distinct, most accurate,&mdash;only more splendid, more glorified. This
is correctness in the only philosophical sense. But he requires your sympathy and
your submission; you must have that recipiency of moral impression without which
the purposes and ends of the drama would be frustrated, and the absence of which
demonstrates an utter want of all imagination, a deadness to that necessary pleasure
of being innocently,&mdash;shall I say deluded?&mdash;or rather, drawn away from ourselves
to the music of noblest thought in harmonious sounds. Happy he, who not only in
the public theatre, but in the labours of a profession, and round the light of his own
hearth, still carries a heart so pleasure-fraught.</CC>

<P>1. <B>Scena Prima]</B> <SC>Maginn</SC> (p. 170, foot-note) says that this scene is in blank
verse &lquo;and so palpably&rquo; that he &lquo;wonders it could ever pass for prose.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ritter</SC>:
After the stormy close of the preceding Act, the placid calm of this chamber, the
subdued whispering of the Gentlewoman and the Doctor, and of Lady Macbeth
herself, impart a feeling of horror.&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC> (ed. ii.): I suspect that the matter of
this scene is too sublime, too austerely grand, to admit of anything so artificial as
the measured language of verse; and that the Poet, as from an instinct of genius,
felt that any attempt to heighten the effect by any arts of delivery would impair it.
The very diction of the closing speech, nobly poetical as it is, must be felt by every
competent reader as a letting down to a lower intellectual plane. Is prose then,
after all, a higher style of speech than verse? There are parts of the New Testa-
ment which no possible arts of versification could fail to enfeeble.&mdash;[A. H. <SC>Tolman</SC>
(<I>Atlantic Monthly</I>, Feb. 1892): In this scene . . . it is the invisible world of moral
reality which is made strangely manifest before our eyes. Lady Macbeth would not
reveal those guilty secrets for all the wealth of all the world, but in the awful war that
is raging in her breast her will is helpless. Her feet, her hands, her lips conspire
against her. In the presence of the awful, unseen Power that controls her poor,
divided self, we hush the breath and bow the head.&mdash;E. K. <SC>Chambers</SC>: It is not
quite easy to see why prose is used in this scene. Perhaps it appeared proper to the
broken utterances of sleep-walking; and of course the Doctor and Gentlewoman,
whose emotions are on a lower plane throughout, could not be allowed to use blank
verse if Lady Macbeth did not.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

<P>6. <B>walk'd]</B> <SC>Bucknill</SC> (p. 38): Whether the deep melancholy of remorse tends to
exhibit itself in somnambulism is a fact which, on scientific grounds, may be doubted.
<P>7. <B>Field]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: This is one of Shakespeare's oversights. He forgot that
he had shut up Macbeth in Dunsinane, and surrounded him with besiegers. That
he could <I>not go into the field</I> is observed by himself with splenetic impatience, V, v,
4-8. It is clear also, from other passages, that Macbeth's motions had long been
circumscribed by the walls of his fortress. The truth may be that Shakespeare
thought the spirit of Lady Macbeth could not be so effectually subdued, and her
peace of mind so speedily unsettled by reflection on her guilt, as during the absence
of her husband. For the present change in her disposition, therefore, our Poet
(though in the haste of finishing his play he forgot his plan) might mean to have
provided, by allotting her such an interval of solitude as would subject her mind to
perturbation, and dispose her thoughts to repentance. It does not appear, from any
circumstance within the compass of this drama, that she had once been separated
from her husband after his return from the victory over Macdonwald and the king of
Norway.&mdash;<SC>Anonymous</SC> (qu. <SC>Litchfield</SC>?): Did Shakespeare mean more, here, by
Macbeth's going <I>into the field</I>, than his leaving his Castle for some time to superintend
the fortifications of Dunsinane, and to inspect his troops, which are not to be sup-
posed to have been confined <I>within</I> the fortress until Macbeth heard of the approach
of Malcolm and his formidable army? The nobility were leaving him, and Ross has
said that he &lquo;saw the tyrant's power afoot.&rquo; His Majesty's presence &lquo;in the field&rquo;
was therefore necessary in order to make serious preparation for the attack which, he
well knew, was in contemplation. He was not <I>yet</I> &lquo;surrounded with besiegers,&rquo; as
Steevens states: he did not even know that the English force was advancing.&mdash;
&mdash;<SC>Knight</SC>: In the next scene the Scotchmen say, &lquo;the English power is <I>near.</I>&rquo;
When an enemy is advancing from another country is it not likely that the com-
mander about to be attacked would first go &lquo;into the field&rquo; before he finally resolved
to trust to his &lquo;castle's strength&rquo;?&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: We must suppose that Macbeth
had taken the field to suppress the native rebels who were &lquo;out,&rquo; see IV, iii, 212,
and that the arrival of their English auxiliaries had compelled him to retire to his
castle at Dunsinane.

<P>18. <SC>Delius</SC>: The speeches of the Doctor in this scene have a certain cadence
verging on blank verse, without quite gliding into it. This kind of rhythmical prose
Shakespeare frequently uses when changing from verse to prose, in order to soften
the change from the one to the other.
<P>20. <B>Enter Lady, with a Taper]</B> <SC>Bell</SC> (p. 312): I should like her to enter less
suddenly [than does Mrs Siddons]. A slower and more interrupted step, more
natural. She advances rapidly to the table, sets down the light, and rubs her
hand, making the action of lifting up water in one hand at intervals.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.&mdash;
<SC>Anon</SC>. (<I>Blackwood's Maga.</I> June, 1843, p. 711): Mrs Siddons' sleep-walking scene
had one fault&mdash;it was too awful. She more resembled a majestic shade rising from
the tomb than a living woman, however disturbed by wild fear and lofty passion.
. . . She wanted the agitation, the drooping, the timidity. She spoke with the solemn
tone of the voice from a shrine. She stood more the sepulchral avenger of regicide
than the sufferer from its convictions. Her grand voice, her fixed and marble coun-
tenance, and her silent step, gave the impression of a supernatural being, the genius
of an ancient oracle&mdash;a tremendous Nemesis.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.&mdash;<SC>Wilson</SC> (p. 643): <I>North.</I>
I am always inclined to conceive Lady Macbeth's night-walking as the summit, or
topmost peak of all tragic conception and execution&mdash;in Prose, too, the crowning
of Poetry! But it must be, because these are the <I>ipsissima verba</I>&mdash;yea, the escaping
sighs and moans of the bared soul. There must be nothing, not even the thin and
translucent veil of the verse, betwixt her soul showing itself, and yours beholding.
Words which your &lquo;hearing latches&rquo; from the threefold abyss of Night, Sleep, and
Conscience! What place for the enchantment of any music is here? Besides, she

<CC><P>breathings&mdash;gaspings. And observe that Lady Macbeth carries&mdash;a candle&mdash;besides
washing her hands&mdash;and besides speaking prose&mdash;three departures from the severe
and elect method, to bring out that supreme revelation. I have been told that the
great Mrs Pritchard used to touch the palm with the tips of her fingers, for the
washing, keeping candle in hand;&mdash;that the Siddons first set down her candle, that
she might come forwards and wash her hands in earnest, one over the other, as if
she were at her wash-hand stand, with plenty of water in her basin&mdash;that when
Sheridan got intelligence of her design so to do, he ran shrieking to her, and, with
tears in his eyes, besought that she would not, at one stroke, overthrow Drury Lane
&mdash;that she persisted, and turned the thousands of bosoms to marble.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.&mdash;
<SC>Corson</SC> (p. 249): The artistic purpose of this night-walking scene appears to be,
to reflect the real womanly nature of Lady Macbeth to which she did such violence
in the part she took upon herself to play, that it suffered, for a time, a total eclipse.
&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.&mdash;W. <SC>Carleton</SC> (in <I>Appendix</I> to <I>Some of Sh.'s Female Characters</I>, p. 403):
There is in [Helen Faucit's sleep-walking scene] such a frightful reality of horror&mdash;
such terrible revelations of remorse&mdash;such struggles to wash away, not the blood
from the hand, but the blood from the soul, as made me shudder. . . . How the
deadly agonies of crime were portrayed by the parched mouth, that told of the burn-
ing tortures within! And when you looked on those eyes, or those corpse-like
hands, now telling their unconscious tale of crime, and thought of their previous
energy in urging &oacute;n its perpetration, you could not help looking fearfully for a
moment into your own heart, and thanking God you were free from the remorse of
murder.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.&mdash;<SC>Pfeil</SC> (<I>Deutsche Revue</I>, Feb. 1894, p. 239): As regards the
symptoms of somnambulism. The affection is a convulsive condition in which the
muscular power is greatly increased. The sufferer sees, as it were, with the out-
stretched finger-tips&mdash;for the most part this is the rule&mdash;while the open, sightless
eyes stare continually into vacancy. The movements are erratic and much more
energetic than in the waking state; never slow, gliding or languid, as though
drunk with sleep. It would be most correct and, for the audience, most realistic
should Lady Macbeth rush hastily across the stage with an impetuous run&mdash;neither
gliding nor tottering&mdash;as was done by one of our celebrated actresses (Krelinger).
In her right hand she carries a candle, rather than a candelabrum. The candle
should be carried straight, not crooked; since, as is well known, a somnambulist
walks in security along the edge of a roof, and would assuredly carry a light straight.
The left arm should be stretched out with fingers outspread as though feeling the
way.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.

<CC><P>51. <B>smell]</B> <SC>Verplanck</SC>: It was, I believe, Madame de Sta&euml;l who said, somewhat
extravagantly, that the smell is the most poetical of the senses. It is true that the
more agreeable associations of this sense are fertile in pleasing suggestions of placid,
rural beauty, and gentle pleasures. Shakespeare, Spenser, Ariosto, and Tasso abound
in such allusions. Milton, especially, who luxuriates in every variety of &lquo;odorous
sweets&rquo; and &lquo;grateful smells,&rquo; delighted sometimes to dwell on the &lquo;sweets of groves
and fields,&rquo; the native perfumes of his own England&mdash;&lquo;The smell of grain, or tedded
grass, or kine, Or dairy;&mdash;&rquo; and sometimes pleasing his imagination with the &lquo;gentle
gales&rquo; laden with &lquo;balmy spoils&rquo; of the East; and breathing&mdash;&lquo;Sabean odours from
the spicy shores Of Araby the blest.&rquo; But the smell has never been successfully
used as a means of impressing the imagination with terror, pity, or any of the deeper
emotions, except in this dreadful sleep-walking scene of the guilty Queen, and in
one parallel scene of the Greek drama, as wildly terrible as this. It is that passage
of the <I>Agamemnon</I> of &AElig;schylus, where the captive prophetess, Cassandra, wrapt in
visionary inspiration, scents first the smell of blood, and then the vapours of the
tomb breathing from the palace of Atrides, as ominous of his approaching murder.
These two stand alone in poetry; and Fuseli, in his Lectures, informs us that when,
in the kindred art of painting, it has been attempted to produce tragic effect through
the medium of ideas drawn from this &lquo;squeamish sense,&rquo; even Raphael and Poussin
have failed, and excited disgust instead of terror or compassion. He justly remarks
that &lquo;taste and smell, as sources of tragic emotion, seem scarcely admissible in art
or in the theatre, because their extremes are nearer allied to disgust, or loathsome or
risible ideas than to terror.&rquo;

<P>61. <B>beds]</B> <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 197): Shakespeare was afraid lest the audience should go
away from so impressive a scene as this, with the persuasion that sleep-walking was
<I>always</I> to be taken as a sign of a burthened conscience. This gentle and kind-
hearted man therefore adds this expression as a protection of the persons subject to it.
<P>63. <B>Banquo's]</B> <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 197): Query if it ought not to be <I>Duncan?</I> The

<P>67, 68. <B>What's . . . vndone]</B> <SC>Tweedie</SC>: Not a single sentiment of repentance

Nothing like remorse can be discovered from her expressions. In truth, the only
feeling of <I>human</I> nature which she, at any time, exhibits, and that alone which
redeems her from being an incarnate fiend, is the tender remembrance of her father,
which prevented her plunging the poniard into the body of her sleeping sovereign,
as she quitted her chamber purposely to do.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.</CC>

<P>79. <B>mated]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: That is, <I>astonished, confounded.</I>&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: The orignal
word was <I>amate</I>, which Bullokar, 1616, defines &lquo;to dismay, to make afraid.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Hal-
liwell</SC>: &lquo;He hath utterly <I>mated</I> me.&rquo;&mdash;Palsgrave, 1530.&mdash;<SC>Corson</SC> (note on &lquo;wyn-
ter, that him naked made and mate.&rquo;&mdash;Chaucer, <I>Legende of Good Women</I>, line 126):
Subdued, dejected, struck dead; Fr. <I>mat&eacute;.</I> &lquo;Whan he seyh hem so piteous and so
<I>maat.&rquo;&mdash;Cant. Tales</I>, 957. &lquo;O Golias, . . . How mighte David make thee so <I>mate?&rquo;
&mdash;Ibid.</I> 5355. The word still lives in <I>check-mate.</I>&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: Cotgrave has:
&lquo;<I>Mater.</I> To mate, or giue a mate vnto; to dead, amate, quell, subdue, ouercome.&rquo;
The word, originally used at chess, from the Arabic <I>sh&aacute;h m&aacute;t</I>, &lquo;the king is dead,&rquo;
whence our &lquo;check-mate,&rquo; became common in one form or other in almost all Euro-
pean languages. See <SC>Bacon</SC>, <I>Essay</I> xv.: &lquo;Besides, in great oppressions, the same
things, that provoke the patience, doe withall mate the courage.&rquo; &lquo;Mate,&rquo; to match,
is of Teutonic origin. Both senses of the word are played upon, <I>Com. of Err.</I> III,
ii, 54. We have the form &lquo;amated&rquo; in Fairfax's <I>Tasso</I>, Bk, xi, st. 12: &lquo;Upon the
walls the Pagans old and young Stood hush'd and still, amated and amazed.&rquo;
<P>5. <B>Vnkle]</B> &lquo;King Duncane hauing two sonnes by his wife which was the daughter
of Siward earle of Northumberland, he made the elder of them, called Malcolme,
prince of Cumberland,&rquo; etc.&mdash;Holinshed. See <I>Appendix.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.&mdash;<SC>French</SC> (p. 296)

<P>7. <B>the . . . the]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 92): &lquo;The&rquo; is used to denote notoriety. Thus we
frequently speak of &lquo;<I>the</I> air.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Bacon</SC>, <I>Essay</I> 231, however wrote, &lquo;<I>The</I> matter (the
substance called matter) is in a perpetual flux.&rquo;
<P>7. <B>bleeding]</B> <SC>Capell</SC> (ii, 28): A substantive, meaning blood, or actions of blood.
&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: Compare &lquo;bleeding war,&rquo; <I>Rich. II:</I> III, iii, 94. But it is more
startling to find it joined with &lquo;alarm,&rquo; which is only the prelude to battle.&mdash;[<SC>Deigh-

verbal noun. . . . The idea of a &lquo;bleeding alarm,&rquo; which is extraordinary even if
&lquo;bleeding&rquo; be an equivalent to bloody, is hereby got rid of.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]
<P>8. <B>mortified]</B> <SC>Theobald</SC>: That is, the man who had abandoned himself to
Despair, who had no Spirit or Resolution left.&mdash;<SC>Warburton</SC>: That is, a <I>Religious</I>
man; one who has subdued his passions, is <I>dead</I> to the world, has abandoned it,
and all the affairs of it; an <I>Ascetic.</I>&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: So, in <I>Monsieur D'Olive</I> [Chap-
man], 1606: &lquo;He like a <I>mortified</I> hermit clad sits.&rquo; [Act I, Sc. i.] And in
Greene's <I>Never too Late</I>, 1616: &lquo;I perceived in his words the perfit idea of a
mortified man,&rquo; [p. 29, ed. Grosart. The narrator is talking with a Hermit.&mdash;
<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.] Again in <I>Love's Lab.</I> I, i, 28.&mdash;<SC>Knight</SC>: One indifferent to the con-
cerns of the world, but who would be excited to fight by such &lquo;causes&rquo; of revenge
as Macduff comes with.&mdash;<SC>Elwin</SC>: The expression is derived from St. Paul, <I>Rom.</I>
viii, 13; <I>Col.</I> iii, 5.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: Johnson (<I>Dict.</I> s. v.) quotes this passage to illus-
trate the sense he gives to &lquo;mortify,&rquo; viz. &lquo;to macerate or harass, in order to reduce
the body to compliance with the mind.&rquo; We have the word in this sense, <I>Love's
Lab.</I> I, i, 28 [cited by Steevens]; also <I>Lear</I>, II, iii, 15, where &lquo;mortified&rquo; means
<I>deadened with cold and hunger.</I> But in the present passage such a sense seems
scarcely forcible enough. May it not mean &lquo;the dead man&rquo;?&mdash;&lquo;mortified&rquo; in the
literal sense. So Erasmus, on the Creed, Eng. tr. fol. 81<I>a</I>: &lquo;Christ was mortified
and killed in dede as touchynge to his fleshe: but was quickened in spirite.&rquo; In
<I>Hen. V:</I> I, i, 26, &lquo;mortified,&rquo; though figuratively applied, does not mean &lquo;sub-
dued by a course of asceticism.&rquo; Both senses are combined in <I>Jul. C&oelig;s.</I> II, i, 324.
If &lquo;the mortified man&rquo; really means &lquo;the dead,&rquo; the word &lquo;bleeding&rquo; in the former
line may have been suggested by the well-known superstition that the corpse of a
murdered man bled afresh in the presence of the murderer. It is true that this inter-
pretation gives an extravagant sense, but we have to choose between extravagance
and feebleness. The passage, indeed, as it stands in the text, does not read like
Shakespeare's.</CC>

<P>17. <B>Great Dunsinane]</B> <SC>Chalmers</SC> (<I>Caledonia</I>, i, 414, and foot-note): Tradi-
tion relates that Macbeth resided ten years, after his usurpation, at Carnbeddie, in
the neighboring parish of St. Martin's, the vestiges of his castle are still to be seen,
which the country people call Carn-beth, and Macbeth's Castle. Carnbeddie is
about three and a half statute miles from Dunsinan hill. <I>Stobie's Map.</I> As Mac-
beth had a castle, which was his usual residence, it is not likely that he would build
another on Dunsinan hill so near; he probably kept up the British fortress, on this
hill, as a place of retreat on any emergency, from which it has got the name of Mac-
beth's Castle. No <I>well</I> appears to have been discovered upon Dunsinan hill, which
would be an indispensable requisite to any castle for a constant residence.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.

sense? The words <I>course</I> and &lquo;cause&rquo; are often confounded by printers.&mdash;<SC>Dalgleish</SC>:
His cause is not one that can be carried on by the usual expedients, his excitement
is either madness or rage.&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC>: Surely change [to <I>course</I>] may be dis-

ii, 30. The &lquo;distemper'd cause&rquo; is the disorganized party, the disordered body over
which he rules. Instead of being like a &lquo;well-girt man,&rquo; <G>eu)/zwnos a)nh/r</G>, full of vigour,
his state is like one in dropsy. We have the same metaphor more elaborated in
<I>2 Hen. IV:</I> III, i, 38, sqq.&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC> (ed. ii.): &lquo;Cause&rquo; is evidently wrong.</CC>

<CC><P>10. <B>Epicures]</B> <SC>Theobald</SC>: Hardicanute, a Contemporary of Macbeth, and who
reigned <I>here</I> just before the Usurpation of the latter in <I>Scotland</I>, was such a Lover
of good Cheer that he would have his Table cover'd four times a day, and largely
furnish'd. Now as Edward, his successor, sent a Force against Scotland, Macbeth
malevolently is made to charge this temperate Prince (in his subjects) with the Riots
of his Predecessor.&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>: The reproach of epicurism is nothing more than a
natural invective uttered by an inhabitant of a barren country against those who
have more opportunities of luxury.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: Shakespeare took the thought from
Holinshed, pp. 179, 180: &lquo;&mdash; the Scotish people before had no knowledge nor
understanding of fine fare or riotous surfet; yet after they had once tasted the sweet
poisoned bait thereof,&rquo; etc. &lquo;&mdash; those superfluities which came into the realme of
Scotland with the <I>Englishmen</I>,&rquo; etc. Again: &lquo;For manie of the people abhorring
the riotous maners and superfluous gormandizing brought in among them by the
<I>Englyshemen</I>, were willing inough to receiue this Donald for their king, trusting
(bicause he had beene brought up in the Isles, with old customes and maners of
their ancient nation, without tast of the <I>English likerous delicats</I>) they should by his
seuere order in gouernement recouer againe the former temperance of their old pro-
genitors.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 198): It may be doubted whether Shakespeare had any
thought of comparing the fare of the Scottish nation with that of the English,
the sumptuous feasting of the latter being a common topic of reproach. So, Ariosto,
<I>Canto</I> viii, st. 24.
<P>11. <B>sway]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: The mind by which my movements are directed, as in
<I>Twelfth Night</I>, II, iv, 32. The other interpretation, &lquo;The mind by which I bear
rule,&rquo; is not impossible.
<P>12. <B>sagge]</B> <SC>Tollet</SC>: To <I>sag</I>, or <I>swag</I>, is to sink down by its own weight,
or by an overload. It is common in Staffordshire to say &lquo;a beam <I>sags.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Nares</SC>:
To <I>swag</I> is now used, and is perhaps more proper. To <I>sagg on</I>, to walk heavily:
So Nash's <I>Pierce Pennilesse</I>, vii, 15: &lquo;When sir Rowland Russet-coat, their dad,
goes <I>sagging</I> every day in his round gascoynes of white cotton.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Forby</SC> (<I>Vocab.
of East Anglia</I>): To fail, or give way, from weakness in itself, or over-loaded.
With us it is perfectly distinct from <I>swag.</I> [To the same purport, <SC>Carr</SC>, <I>Craven
Dialect.</I>]&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: Mr Atkinson, in his <I>Glossary</I>, mentions &lquo;sag&rquo; as being still
in use in Cleveland, Yorkshire. We have heard a railway porter apply it to the
leathern top of a carriage weighed down with luggage. [A word of every-day use
in America among mechanics and engineers.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<CC><P>14. <B>Loone]</B> <SC>Coleridge</SC> (i, 175): A passion there is that carries off its own

pendently of associations and habits from any particular rank of life or mode of
employment; and in this consists Shakespeare's vulgarisms [as in this line]. This is
(to equivocate on Dante's words) in truth <I>nobile volgare eloquenza.</I>&mdash;W. <SC>Chambers</SC>:

<P>20. <B>Patch]</B> <SC>Douce</SC> (i, 257): It has been supposed that this term originated from
the name of a fool belonging to Cardinal Wolsey, and that his parti-coloured dress
was given to him in allusion to his name. The objection to this is, that the motley
habit worn by fools is much older than the time of Wolsey. Again, it appears that
&lquo;Patch&rquo; was an appellation given not to one fool only that belonged to Wolsey. There
is an epigram by Heywood, entitled <I>A saying of Patch my lord Cardinal's foole;</I>
but in the epigram itself he is twice called <I>Sexten</I>, which was his real name. In a
MS <I>Life of Wolsey</I>, by his gentleman usher Cavendish [now well known from the
printed copy&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC>], there is a story of another fool belonging to the Cardinal, and
presented by him to the King. A marginal note states that &lquo;this foole was callid
Master Williames, owtherwise called <I>Patch.</I>&rquo; In Heylin's <I>History of the Reforma-
tion</I> mention is made of another fool called <I>Patch</I> belonging to Elizabeth. But the
name is even older than Wolsey's time; for in some household accounts of Henry
VII. there are payments to a fool who is named <I>Pechie</I> and <I>Packye.</I> It seems there-
fore more probable on the whole that fools were nick-named &lquo;Patch&rquo; from their dress;
unless there happen to be a nearer affinity to the Italian <I>pazzo</I>, a word that has all
the appearance of a descent from <I>fatuus.</I> This was the opinion of Tyrwhitt in a
note on <I>Mid. N. D.</I> III, ii, 9. But although in [<I>Mer. of Ven.</I> II, v, 46], as well as</CC>

<CC><P>in a multitude of other places, a &lquo;patch&rquo; denotes a fool or simpleton, and, by corrup-

jester seems to be supported by <I>Mid. N. D.</I> IV, i, 237, where Bottom says: &lquo;Man
is but a patched fool.&rquo;

<P>26-35. <SC>Fletcher</SC> (p. 152): This passage is exactly of a piece with that in which

a character, are but an additional title to our detestation; the man who sets at
naught all human ties, should at least be prepared to abide in quiet the inevitable
consequences. But the moral cowardice of Macbeth is consummate.

<CC><C>[26. <B>cheere . . . dis-eate</B>]</C>
<P>both by Percy and by Collier's MS. <I>Chair</I>, in the sense of throne, was very common.
See <I>Rich. III:</I> V, iii, 251. So too in Peele's <I>David and Bethsabe:</I> &lquo;&mdash; as king&mdash;be de-
pos'd from his detested <I>chair.&rquo;&mdash;Works</I>, p. 478, ed. Dyce, 1861.&mdash;R. G. <SC>White</SC>: [<I>Cheer</I>
for &lquo;chair&rquo; is] a mere phonographic irregularity of spelling. <I>Chair</I> is pronounced
&lquo;cheer&rquo; even now by some old-fashioned folk, Mother Goose among them: &lquo;She went
to the Ale house To fetch him some beer, And when she got back The dog sat on a
chair.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Cowden-Clarke</SC>: Note, in corroboration [of &lquo;cheer&rquo;], that &lquo;cheer&rquo; and
&lquo;sick&rquo; are used with similar antithesis in <I>Hamlet</I>, III, ii, 173: &lquo;You are so sick of
late, So far from cheer,&rquo; etc.&mdash;<SC>Bailey</SC> (ii, 41): I submit the following reading for
consideration without feeling much confidence in it: &lquo;Will <I>charter</I> me ever or <I>dis-
seize</I> me now.&rquo; Where <I>charter</I> is, of course, to be compressed into a monosyllable,
and <I>disseize</I> is a law term for dispossess. &lquo;Will <I>clear</I> me ever,&rquo; etc., would be more
Shakespearian than &lquo;cheer me ever,&rquo; and would form no bad reading.&mdash;<SC>Ellis</SC> (<I>Athe-
n&oelig;um</I>, 25 January, 1868): At present <I>chair</I> and &lquo;cheer&rquo; generally rhyme with
<I>there</I> and <I>here</I>, but they are not unfrequently pronounced by the peasantry as rhymes
to <I>here</I> only, and many old gentlemen may, perhaps, still be met with who pro-
nounce <I>break, great, steak</I>, and <I>chair</I> with the same vowel <I>e</I> in <I>here.</I> Compared to
our present pronunciation, this is old; compared to Shakespeare's, it is very young.
It was not generally prevalent till about the middle of the eighteenth century, and
never seems to have really succeeded, although it was largely adopted. The word
<I>chair</I> is spelt <I>chayere</I> in the <I>Promptorium</I>, 1440, <I>chayre</I> in Palsgrave, 1530, and
Levins, 1570, and in F<SUB>1</SUB> it is <I>chaire.</I> Now the sound of the digraph <I>ai</I> was that we
generally give to <I>Isaiah, aye</I>, or the Etonia Greek <G>kai</G>, during the whole of the six-
teenth century, and did not assume its present sound as <I>e</I> in <I>there</I> till well on in the
seventeenth century. For myself, I feel no doubt that Shakespeare's <I>chaire</I> rhymed
to the Etonian <G>xair</G>, and to the German <I>Feier</I>, which is a so-called <I>broad</I> sound of
the modern English <I>fire.</I> Now as to &lquo;cheer.&rquo; The word is &lquo;<I>cheere</I>, vultus,&rquo; and
&lquo;<I>cheryn</I>, or make good <I>chere</I>, hillaro, exhillaro, letifico,&rquo; in the <I>Promptorium; &lquo;chere</I>,
acveil,&rquo; in Palsgrave; &lquo;<I>cheare</I>, exhilarare, <I>cheareful</I>, hilaris,&rquo; in Levins; <I>cheare</I> in
<I>Rom. &amp; Jul.</I> Q<SUB>1</SUB>; generally <I>cheere</I> in F<SUB>1</SUB>; but usually throughout the seventeenth
century, and into the eighteenth, it is <I>chear.</I> These orthographies are significant.
Down to the beginning of the fifteenth century long <I>e</I> or double <I>ee</I>, both of which
were common, and <I>ea</I> (which was rarely, if ever, used, except occasionally in <I>ease,
please</I>, and their derivatives) had the sound of <I>e</I> in <I>there</I> only. The fifteenth cen-
tury, with its civil wars, greatly altered our pronunciation, and in particular many
<I>e</I>'s fell into the sound of <I>e</I> in <I>here</I>. . . . After the middle of the sixteenth century <I>ee</I>
was appropriated to <I>e</I> in <I>here</I>, and <I>ea</I> to <I>e</I> in <I>there</I>. . . . &lquo;Cheer,&rquo; however, was one of
the exceptional words in the seventeenth century which rhymed to <I>here.</I> The spell-
ing &lquo;cheere,&rquo; generally used in F<SUB>1</SUB>, shows that the <I>printer's reader of that book</I> (no
one else with certainty) also rhymed it thus. . . . There seems some reason to sup-
pose that <I>disease</I>, in this line from <I>Macbeth</I>, is the correct reading, and that the
hyphen was inserted to prevent the word being pronounced quite as <I>disease</I>,
although the lines immediately following may have been suggested by the near
coincidence of sounds between <I>dis-ease</I>, render un-easy, quasi <I>dis-cheer</I>, compare
<I>dis-able</I>, and the ordinary <I>disease.</I> Observe, also, in this scene the description of a
&lquo;minde diseas'd,&rquo; and the play on the word in <I>2 Hen. IV:</I> IV, i, 54. <I>Chair</I> and
<I>disseat</I> introduce two verbs not found in Shakespeare, and have no connexion with
any other ideas in the scene.&mdash;<SC>Viles</SC> (<I>Athen&oelig;um</I>, 8 February, 1868): I find <I>chair</I></CC>

<P>27. <B>way of life]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC> (<I>Obs.</I>): As there is no relation between the &lquo;way of life&rquo;
and &lquo;fallen into the sear,&rquo; I am inclined to think that the <I>W</I> is only an <I>M</I> inverted,
and that it was <I>my May of life;</I> I am now passed from the spring to the autumn of
my days; but I am without those comforts that should succeed the sprightliness of
bloom, and support me in this melancholy season. Shakespeare has <I>May</I> in the
same sense elsewhere.&mdash;<SC>Warburton</SC>: Macbeth is not here speaking of his <I>rule</I> or
government, or of any sudden change; but of the gradual decline of life, as appears
from line 29. And &lquo;way&rquo; is used for <I>course, progress.</I>&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC> (1773, 1778,
1785) quotes passages from Shakespeare's contemporaries to prove the correctness

in II, i, 69.&mdash;<SC>Mason</SC> (1785): The old reading should not have been discarded, as
the following passages prove that it was an expression in use at that time, as &lquo;<I>course</I>
of life&rquo; is now. In Massinger's <I>Very Woman:</I> &lquo;In way of life [youth] I did enjoy
one friend,&rquo; [vol. iv, p. 305, ed. 1805. See note by Gifford, <I>infra.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.] Again
[in <I>The Roman Actor</I>, vol. ii, p. 334, Massinger's <I>Works</I>, ed. Gifford], &lquo;If that when
I was mistress of myself, And in my <I>way of youth</I>,&rquo; etc.&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC> (1790): <I>May</I> (the
month), both in manuscript and print, always is exhibited with a capital letter, and
it is exceedingly improbable that a compositor at the press should use a small <I>w</I>
instead of a capital <I>M.</I>&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC> (1793): In <I>Pericles</I>, I, i, 54: &lquo;&mdash; ready for the
<I>way of life</I> or death.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Gifford</SC> (Massinger, <I>A Very Woman</I>, vol. iv. p. 305. ed.
1805): The phrase is neither more nor less than a simple periphrasis for &lquo;life&rquo;; as
&lquo;way of youth&rquo; in the text is for &lquo;youth.&rquo; A few examples will make this clear:
&lquo;&mdash; So much nobler Shall be your way of justice.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Thierry and Theodoret.</I> [II,
iii. Examples are quoted from <I>The Queen of Corinth</I> and <I>Valentinian.</I>] In <I>Mac-

the more trite it is proved to be, the less likely is it that Shakespeare should have
used it here; the contrast of &lquo;the yellow leaf&rquo; with the green luxuriance of May so
completely supports our text that we have no misgiving in adopting it.&mdash;R. G.

<P>30. <B>As]</B> <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> i, 127): <I>As</I>, in the sense of <I>to wit.</I> [On <I>Hen. VIII:</I>
IV, i, 88]: &lquo;As&rquo; is here used not in the sense of <I>for instance</I>, but in that of <I>namely,
to wit:</I> it expresses an enumeration of particulars, not a selection from them by way
of example. This is a frequent,&mdash;perhaps, indeed, the one exclusive,&mdash;signification
of <I>as</I>, when employed in this construction; e. g. <I>3 Hen. VI:</I> V, vii, 4, sqq. (a
striking instance). This is the true construction of &lquo;as&rquo; in a number of passages,
where it has been, or is likely to be, mistaken for the modern usage.

<P>45, 61, 68. <B>your . . . thou . . . your]</B> <SC>Skeat</SC> (<I>William of Palerne</I>, p. xlii, E. E.
Text. Soc. 1867): <I>Thou</I> is the language of a lord to a servant, of an equal to an
equal, and expresses also companionship, love, permission, defiance, scorn, threat-
ening; whilst <I>ye</I> is the language of a servant to a lord, and of compliment, and
further expresses honour, submission, entreaty.&mdash;<SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 231): &lquo;Thou&rquo; in Shake-
speare's time was very much like <I>d<*></I> now among the Germans, the pronoun of (1)
affection towards friends, (2) good-humoured superiority to servants, and (3) con-
tempt or anger to strangers. It had, however, already fallen somewhat into disuse,
and, being regarded as archaic, was naturally adopted (4) in the higher poetic style
and in the language of solemn prayer.&mdash;<SC>Ibid</SC>. (&sect; 235): In almost all cases where <I>thou</I>
and <I>you</I> appear indiscriminately used, further considerations show some change of
thought or some influence of euphony sufficient to account for the change of pronoun.
<P>45. <B>Patient]</B> <SC>Bodenstedt</SC>: There is not a trace of genuine sympathy in anything
that Macbeth, after this question, says of Lady Macbeth. The strength of his selfish
nature crops out everywhere.
<P>50, 51. <B>Can'st thou . . . Sorrow]</B> <SC>Oxon</SC> (p. 10): He is asking for himself more
than his wife. The allusion here to &lquo;a mind diseased&rquo; and to &lquo;these terrible dreams
which shake us nightly&rquo; (III, ii, 24), and Lady Macbeth's words, &lquo;You lack the
season of all natures, sleep&rquo; (III, iv, 172), make us inclined to think that, after the
murder of Duncan, Macbeth was in a state of delirium produced by insomnia.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
<P>50. <B>not Minister]</B> <SC>Badham</SC> (p. 281): I suspect that the negative was introduced
by the players, who misplaced the accent upon &lquo;minister.&rquo; That the change in the
pronunciation was taking place in Shakespeare's time, is proved by his indifferently
using both modes. The words &lquo;canst thou do this?&rquo; sufficiently indicate the spirit
of the question. &lquo;Canst thou not&rquo; dallies with the false supposition, and is far too
playful an irony to consist with the terrible moralizings of remorse with which Mac-
beth closes his career. Read: &lquo;Canst thou minister to a,&rquo; etc.</CC>

<CC><P>from the corrupted word. What then if we change the treatment, and read: &lquo;What

English language I am at a loss for anything better than cataclysm in the sense of
deluge. But Herodotus (Bk, ii, ch, 87) uses <G>klu/sma</G> in the sense of <G>klusth\r</G>. It
would be worth while to look in <I>The famous Hystorye of Herodotus in Englyshe</I>, to
see how this is rendered. <SC>Wellesley</SC>: In Malone's copy of F<SUB>2</SUB> <I>C&aelig;ny</I> is corrected
in old pen and ink to <I>C&oelig;ne.</I> [No mention that I can find is made of this in the
eds. of 1773, 1785, Malone's 1790, Steevens's 1793, Reed's 1803, 1813, Boswell's
1821, nor in Malone's 1st or 2d Supplement.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] This contemporary MS cor-
rection hits the pronunciation, though it misses the orthography, of the right word
<I>Sene</I>, a monosyllable, the proper English word for <I>Senna.</I> In the <I>Great Herbal</I>
printed by Peter Treveris, in the <I>Herbal</I> printed by Thomas Petyt in 1541, in the
reprint of the same by William Copland, in Lyte's <I>New Herbal</I>, 1578 and 1619, in
Gerarde's <I>Herbal</I>, 1597, there are whole chapters <I>Of Sene.</I> And it is <I>Sene</I> in Cot-
grave and Howell's dictionaries, and Parkinson in his <I>Herbal</I>, 1640, mentions two
sorts of <I>Sene</I> tree&mdash;1. <I>Sene</I> of Alexandria; 2. the <I>Sene</I> of Italy. Burton's <I>Anatomy</I>,
even so late as the ed. 1660, p. 378, mentions &lquo;Colutea, which Fuchsius, cap. 168,
and others take for <I>Sene</I>, but most distinguish.&rquo; The printers of that period used <I>&oelig;</I>
for <I>ee</I> or a long <I>e.</I> We have <I>Scena</I> and <I>Sc&aelig;na</I> indifferently in F<SUB>1</SUB>. We find a Sien-
nese set down as &lquo;<I>Scen&aelig;se</I>&rquo; in &lquo;<I>Supposes&rquo; Englished</I> by Gascoigne, 1566; and the
volume is &lquo;Imprinted by Abel Jeffes dwelling in the Fore Str&aelig;te without Cr&aelig;ple-
gate, n&aelig;re unto Grub-str&aelig;te.&rquo; If therefore it should appear that <I>Senna</I> never occurs
as an English word till long after Shakespeare, ought we not to read &lquo;What Rhu-
barb, Sene or,&rquo; etc.&mdash;[<SC>Nicholson</SC> (<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> 21 Feb. 1880): I suggest the following:
F<SUB>2</SUB> and F<SUB>3</SUB> read <I>C&aelig;ny</I>, and F<SUB>4</SUB> <I>Senna</I>, a word generally adopted, but apparently a mere
guess, derived from the supposed pronunciation of <I>C&oelig;ny.</I> Other alterations in F<SUB>2</SUB> de-

that the editor of F<SUB>2</SUB> thought &lquo;Cyme&rquo; an error. The <I>y</I> being used to express the want-
ing syllable, I think he was right in believing that the <I>m</I> of &lquo;Cyme&rquo; was a misprint
or misreading for <I>ne</I>, and that Shakespeare's word was <I>Cynea</I>, or an Anglicised form
of it, <I>Cynee</I>, the <I>Canina Brassica</I>, the mercury, French and dog mercuries, etc., of our
older authors. What is wanted is a &lquo;purgative drug,&rquo; similar to rhubarb. John Parkin-
son, writing in 1640, says, p. 298: &lquo;The decoction of the leaves of Mercury, or the
juice thereof taken in broth or drink . . . purgeth chollerick and waterish humours.

<CC><C>[10-13. <B>Let euery Souldier . . . Erre in report of vs</B>]</C>
<P>by Percy Society, vol. iii.), they conceal their numbers by the boughs of trees.&mdash;
<SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Remarks</I>, p. 202): This incident was versified by Deloney from a passage
in that very Holinshed who supplied Shakespeare with the materials for <I>Macbeth.</I>
[The lines in Deloney's ballad are as follows: &lquo;Thus did the Kentish Commons
crie unto their leaders still, And so marcht forth in warlike sort and stand on Swans-
combe hill. . . . And for the Conquerors coming there they privily laid waight, And
thereby sodainely appald his lofty high conceipt. For when they spied his approch, in
place as they did stand, Then marched they to hem him in, each one a bough in hand.
So that unto the Conquerors sight amazed as he stood, they seemed to be a walking
grove, or els a mooving wood.&rquo;&mdash;J. W. <SC>Redhouse</SC> (<I>Academy</I>, 24 July, 1886) states
that the Arabian writer, Mes'&umacr;diyy (<SC>a. d.</SC> 943), relates in <I>Meadows of Gold and
Mines of Gems</I>, ch. xlvii, an incident &lquo;wherein boughs were used to conceal an
army, which ruse caused the total destruction of the ancient Arabian tribe of the
Jedis, not very long after the confusion of tongues at Babel. . . . &ldquo;Certain troops
were commanded to pluck up by the roots, every man, a young tree from a forest they
had to pass through, and carry this before him, so as to hide the advancing host.
The army advanced and, having surprised the town, slaughtered the inhabitants and
thus exterminated the tribe.&rdquo;&rquo; &lquo;If the Birnam Wood incident really occurred,&rquo; adds
Redhouse, &lquo;here is a surprising coincidence; and if it was a monkish embellishment
it might be interesting to trace the story from the East, if possible.&rquo;&mdash;M. <SC>Jastrow,
Jr.</SC> (<I>Poet-Lore</I>, 1890, vol. ii, p. 247) also gives the Arabic Legend quoted by Red-
house, and states that the story may be found &lquo;in a commentary to an old Arabic
poem known among scholars as the &ldquo;Himyaritic Kas&icirc;d&ecirc;,&rdquo; by Neshwan, el-Himyari
(<I>i. e.</I> the Himyarite), who flourished in the twelfth century of this era. The sources
from which it is drawn go back to the generation immediately following upon
Mohammed, so that this Arabic version is, in all probability, the oldest recorded.&rquo;
In conclusion Jastrow remarks: &lquo;While I am inclined to regard the Arabic version as
approaching close to the primitive form,&mdash;certainly far more primitive in its features
than any of the others,&mdash;I do not think that scholars will hit upon Arabia as the final
source. Woods and forests are not the characteristic features of Arabia, and, while
parts of Arabia, more particularly along the southern coast, are wooded, the district
of Jemama, where the seat of the Gadisites is placed [Redhouse has &lquo;Jedis&rquo;], is not
so. Here nature presents a sterile and rugged aspect. We have the desert and the
rocks, but not the shady woods. It is likely that we will eventually be led to India,
the home of so many tales that have wandered all over the world.&rquo;&mdash;G. <SC>Neilson</SC>
(<I>Scottish Antiquary</I>, Oct. 1897, p. 53): The moving wood itself, divested of its pro-
phetic associations, is not peculiar to Macbeth's mythical history, but, though much
less luxuriant in form, occurs in one or two other places. Saxo Grammaticus (bk, vii.)
describes the like stratagem on shore made use of by Hakon, son of Hamund, advancing
to attack Sigar. Hakon's order was that boughs should be cut and carried by his
men; so that, when they advanced into the open, a woody shade might not be want-
ing. Sigar's sentinel rushes to his bedside to announce that he saw leaves and
shrubs marching in the manner of men. Sigar asks in reply, How far distant is the
coming wood? And when he knows that it is at hand he pronounces it a portent
of his own death&mdash;from which some commentators have concluded that Saxo's words
imply a previous oracle like Macbeth's (see <I>Saxo</I>, ed. Stephanius, 1644, pp. 84,
132-3, and Elton's translation of the first nine books. Nutt, 1894, pp, 185, 286). . . .
There was, however, in Scottish history one example of a moving wood which there is</CC>

<CC><P>no need to brand as mythical. In 1332, after the battle of Dupplin, in which he had
defeated the national party, Edward Baliol took possession of Perth. Patrick, Earl
of March, in an assault upon that city, went to the wood of Lamberkine, &lquo;And thare
ilk man a fagote made [Swa] towart Perth held strawcht the way. Wyth thai fagottis
thai thowcht that thai Suld dyt the dykis suddanly, And till thare fays pas on
playnly. Qwhen thai off the town can thame se That semyd ane hare wode for to be
Thay ware abaysyt grettumly&rquo; (Wyntoun, viii, 3582-89). . . . It does not seem impos-
sible to conceive that this scheme of Earl Patrick's, for filling up with fascines from the
wood of Lamberkine the antemural fosses of Perth, may, in the ninety years between
Dupplin battle and the writing of Wyntoun's <I>Cronykil</I>, have contributed largely to
the Perthshire legend of Birnam and Dunsinane. . . . The story of Macbeth and the
moving grove seems by no means a common one, and the occurrence of two versions
in one county of Scotland must arouse questions regarding the relation of the one to
the other. Time, circumstances, and assigned cause unite to favour the record of
Earl Patrick's exploit at Perth as true. It stands every test, including that of geog-
raphy, for Lamberkine is only some two miles west of Perth. Macbeth's story, on
the other hand, is not only admittedly unhistorical; geography is fatal even to its
vraisemblance. Dunsinane lies, as the crow flies, fully fifteen miles south-east of
Birnam, and the Tay flows between. One finds it hard to think of Malcolm and
Siward's troops bearing their boughs all that distance. The Birnam tale is radically
legendary; the Lamberkine incident is almost beyond question historical; but there
is in each the rare phenomenon of the moving wood, and the scene is in each case
within a few miles of Perth. The query, therefore, grows pertinent&mdash;Have we at
bottom one tale or two? We have, on the one hand, a simple historical fact, and
on the other a variant with added marvel and <I>diablerie</I>. . . . There is more helpful-
ness than hazard in the suggestion that the true incident at Lamberkine in 1332
may have furnished a nucleus for the embellished legend of Birnam, which is not
known to have been reduced to writing earlier than 1420. So there would be one
historical original and its legendary outgrowth; a simple fact and what it became
when magnified and touched with miracle by popular imagination.&mdash;See also <I>Appen-
dix: Source of the Plot</I>&mdash;<SC>Simrock</SC>.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

<CC><P>or '<I>vantage</I>, in the time of Shakespeare, signified <I>opportunity.</I> He shut up himself
and his soldiers (says Malcolm) in the castle, because when there is an opportunity
to be gone, they all desert him.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: Read, if alteration be necessary, &lquo;&mdash; ad-
vantage to be <I>got.</I>&rquo; But the words of the text will bear Dr Johnson's explanation,
which is most certainly right: &lquo;For wherever an opportunity of flight is <I>given</I> them,&rquo;
etc.&mdash;<SC>Henley</SC>: Where advantageous offers are made to allure the adherents of Mac-
beth to forsake him.&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC> (<I>Notes</I>, p. 416): Advantage was hardly so much to
be &lquo;given&rquo; as to be procured by revolt; and as it also seems unlikely that the same
verb should have been used in the very next line, we may feel confident that when
the MS Corrector puts it <I>gotten</I>, he was warranted in making the change.&mdash;<SC>Clar-
endon</SC>: This passage, as it stands, is not capable of any satisfactory explanation. . . .
We should have expected <I>was</I> rather than &lquo;is,&rquo; unless, indeed, &lquo;where&rquo; be taken in
in the sense of <I>wherever.</I> The meaning is, &lquo;where they had a favourable oppor-
tunity for deserting.&rquo; . . . We rather incline to think that the word &lquo;given&rquo; would not
have been used in the second line, if it had not been already used in the first, a play
upon words very much in Shakespeare's manner. Perhaps it should stand thus:
&lquo;&mdash; advantage given to flee,&rquo; or, &lquo;&mdash; advantage to 'em given.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Allen</SC> (MS): Read
&lquo;For <I>there</I>, there is advantage to be given.&rquo; To give advantage is equivalent to
giving odds (as in Chess). He who is in a fortress can give odds of ten to one to
the attacking party. Shakespeare is familiar with the idea of giving odds, e. g.
<I>Rich. II:</I> I, i, 62, &lquo;Which to maintain I would allow him odds,&rquo; and <I>1 Hen. IV:</I>
IV, iii, 2, &lquo;You might give him the advantage.&rquo;&mdash;[<SC>Sprague</SC>: If we regard the an-
tithesis as being between &lquo;advantage&rquo; and &lquo;revolt,&rquo; perhaps the Folio text will afford
a sufficient meaning. Thus: wherever there is an advantageous position, or other
favour, that might be given to Macbeth by loyal subjects, there his subjects have
abandoned the post to the enemy, have withheld all benefit from Macbeth, and have
given him not &lquo;advantage,&rquo; but &lquo;revolt!&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]
<P>20. <B>more and lesse]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: The same with <I>greater and less.</I> In the interpo-

Less.</I>&mdash;<SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; <B>17</B>): <I>More</I> and <I>most</I> are frequently used as the comparative and
superlative of the adjective &lquo;great.&rquo; Thus, in the present instance, and also in <B><I>1 Hen.</I></B>
<I>IV:</I> IV, iii, 68; <I>2 Hen. IV:</I> I, i, 209. That &lquo;less&rquo; here refers to rank, and not to
number, is illustrated by &lquo;What <I>great</I> ones do, the <I>less</I> will prattle of.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Twelfth
Night</I>, I, ii, 33. [Compare: &lquo;Mirth is to be vsed both of more and lesse.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Ralph
Roister Doister; Prologue.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

<CC><P>The meaning of this obscurely worded sentence must be: In order that our opinions
may be just, let them await the event that will test their truth. Rowe's reading
gives indeed a sense, but scarcely that which is required.
<P>28. <B>haue . . . owe]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: When we are governed by legal kings, we shall
know the limits of their claim, <I>i. e.</I> shall know what we have of our own, and what
they have a right to take from us. To &lquo;owe&rquo; is here to <I>possess.</I>&mdash;<SC>Delius</SC>: Although
Shakespeare frequently uses to &lquo;owe&rquo; in the sense of to <I>possess</I>, yet in this instance
that meaning would be tautological, connected as the word is with &lquo;have&rquo;; it must
therefore be taken in its present meaning <I>to be indebted.</I> The decision of the battle
will show us what we have and at the same time what it is our duty yet to do.&mdash;
<SC>Clarendon</SC>: &lquo;Owe&rquo; is here used in its ordinary modern sense. Siward says that
the issue will enable them to balance their accounts, as it were.
<P>29. <B>speculatiue]</B> For the scansion of this line, see <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; <B>468</B>), or II, iv, 13.
<P>30. <B>arbitrate]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Elsewhere in Shakespeare it is followed by an
accusative indicating not the &lquo;issue,&rquo; but the quarrel, as <I>Rich. II:</I> I, i, 50, 200;
<I>King John</I>, I, i, 38.&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC> (ed. ii.): Referring, apparently, to Malcolm's last
speech, which proceeds somewhat upon conjecture and seeming likelihood.
<P>31. <B>warre]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: It has been understood that local rhymes were introduced
in plays to afford an actor the advantage of a more pointed exit, or to close a scene
with additional force. Yet, whatever might be Shakespeare's motive for continuing
such a practice, it may be observed that he often seems immediately to repent of it;
and, in the tragedy before us, has repeatedly counteracted it by hemistichs which
destroy the effect, and consequently defeat the supposed purpose of the antecedent
couplets. See I, v, 83; III, ii, 66; III, iv, <B>175</B>; IV, i, 183; V, ii, 40.

<P>8. <B>forc'd]</B> <SC>Collier</SC> (<I>Notes</I>, p. <B>417</B>): <I>Farc'd</I> is misrepresented &lquo;forced&rquo; in the

letter <I>a</I> by the MS Corrector, the meaning is that the ranks of the besiegers were
<I>stuffed</I> or <I>filled out</I> by soldiers who had revolted from Macbeth.&mdash;<SC>Singer</SC> (<I>Sh. Vind.</I>

ened; had they not received an accession of force.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: In <I>Tro. &amp; Cress.</I>
V, i, 64, the word is used, as <I>farced</I> elsewhere, in a culinary sense.

<P>12. <SC>Dyce</SC>: At line 20, Collier observes: &lquo;We must suppose that Seyton has
gone to what we now call &ldquo;the wing&rdquo; of the stage to inquire.&rquo; But &lquo;going to the
wing&rquo; and standing there to glean information was surely as unusual on the old
stage as it is on the modern; and I have no doubt that formerly Seyton went out
and re-entered, just as he does when this play is performed now-a-days.&mdash;<SC>Claren-
don</SC>: Perhaps Seyton should not leave the stage, but an attendant should come and
whisper the news of the Queen's death to him.
<P>14. <B>cool'd]</B> <SC>Malone</SC>: The blood is sometimes said to be <I>chilled;</I> but I do not

So in V, ii, 30.&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC> (<I>Notes</I>, p. <B>417</B>): The MS Corrector here has <I>quailed</I> for
&lquo;cool'd,&rquo; a much more forcible word; but this is one of the places where it is
possible that the person recommending the change may have exercised his taste,
rather than stated his knowledge. It seems scarcely likely that one word should
have been mistaken for the other, but this observation will, of course, apply to
many of the extraordinary errors that have been from time to time pointed out.&mdash;</CC>

<P>15. <B>Night-shrieke]</B> <SC>Delius</SC>: He is thinking perhaps of the night of Duncan's

<P>18, 19. <B>Direnesse . . . start me]</B> <SC>Snider</SC> (i, 200): The main fact now to be
noticed in Macbeth's character is that he is no longer swayed by his imagination.
This change was indicated at the end of his interview with the Weird Sisters; he is
now able to dismiss such sights altogether. His outward activity must help to
absorb his mind, for his foes are marching against him; the reality before him is
quite as terrible as any image can be. But Macbeth himself states clearly the main
ground of this remarkable change. Previously he had declared that his dire phan-
tasms were merely the result of his inexperience in crime. [III, iv, 173-175.]
Familiarity with crime has hardened his thoughts; repetition of guilt has seared his
conscience. Hence no retributive ghosts appear after the murder of Macduff's
family. But his whole mind is seared, too&mdash;it is a desolation . . . Since the cessa-
tion of his imagination his spirit is dead, because his imagination was the centre of
his spiritual activity.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.

alone, resumes much of that connexion with humanity which he had so long aban-</CC>

<P>22. <B>word]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: It is not apparent for what &lquo;word&rquo; there would have been a
