I read therefore: &lquo;&mdash; a time for&mdash;such a <I>world!</I>&mdash;&rquo; It is a broken speech, in which
only part of the thought is expressed, and may be paraphrased thus: The queen
is dead. <I>Macbeth.</I> Her death should have been deferred to some more peaceful
hour; had she lived longer, <I>there would at length have been a time for</I> the honours
due to her as a queen, and that respect which I owe her for her fidelity and love.
Such is the <I>world</I>&mdash;such is the condition of human life that we always think <I>to-mor-
row</I> will be happier than to-day, but to-morrow and to-morrow steals over us un-
enjoyed and unregarded, and we still linger in the same expectation to the moment
appointed for our end. All these days, which have thus passed away, have sent
multitudes of fools to the grave, who were engrossed by the same dream of future
felicity, and, when life was departing from them, were, like me, reckoning on
to-morrow. Such was once my conjecture, but I am now less confident. Macbeth
might mean that there would have been a more convenient <I>time</I> for such a <I>word</I>, for

tidings must have been brought,&mdash;such a tale told. The <I>word</I> was, of course, the
word brought by Seyton of the queen's decease: &lquo;The queen, my lord, is dead.&rquo; Dr
Johnson's blunder grew out of obliviousness or inadvertence that &lquo;should&rquo; is used
indifferently to denote either what <I>will be</I> or what <I>ought to be;</I> that the tyrant dis-

<P>23. <B>To morrow]</B> <SC>Halliwell</SC>: It is not impossible that Shakespeare may here
have recollected a remarkable engraving in Barclay's <I>Ship of Fooles</I>, 1570, copied from
that in the older Latin version of 1498: &lquo;They folowe the crowes crye to their great
sorrowe, <I>Cras, cras, cras</I>, to-morowe we shall amende, And if we mend not then, then
shall we the next morowe, Or els shortly after we shall no more offende; Amende,
mad foole, when God this grace doth sende.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Allen</SC> (MS): That is, each day, that
has successively become <I>yesterday</I>, has been a <I>to-morrow</I>, and (as such) has been an
<I>ignis fatuus</I>, lighting <I>fools</I> the way to death. That Shakespeare had this meteoric
phenomenon in his mind appears certain from the fact that his words give a correct
translation of its Latin name and define its office. <I>Ignis fatuus</I> (by the idiomatic
substitution of grammatical for logical concord) is <I>Fools' light</I>&mdash;a light which, creep-
ing along in advance, deceives and makes <I>fools</I> of men, and so <I>lights</I> them the <I>way</I>,
through the darkness, <I>to death.</I> As Shakespeare called Ophelia's drowning in the
shallow brook a <I>muddy</I> death, so it may have occurred to him here to call the death
of the wayfarer, in the night, a <I>dusky</I> death. [See <I>Text. Notes</I>, l. 27.&mdash;<SC>Moberly</SC>:
It is remarkable how often, and with what wonderful variety of thought, Shake-
speare's mind, in the last years of his life, appears to have dwelt upon death. &lquo;We
in our folly,&rquo; says Macbeth, &lquo;reckon upon a hereafter in which day follows day; but
trace the days backward, and which of them has not had a death on the day pre-
ceding it. So may our to-morrow be if we die to-day.&rquo; In a somewhat different
spirit, the cowardly Claudio, in <I>Meas. for Meas.</I> (III, i, 118-132), employs all the
frightful, material images of the <I>Inferno</I>,&mdash;the imprisonment in ice; the being blown
about by the viewless winds; the contrast between life and motion, and the &lquo;kneaded
clod&rquo; that man must become. Lastly, the courageous but reflective Hamlet is re-
pelled from suicide by the dread uncertainty as to what will be found in that &lquo;undis-
covered country&rquo; whence no traveller returns.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]
<P>24. <B>Creepes]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Capell proposed to read <I>Creep;</I> but in this particular
case the singular seems more suitable to the sense, &lquo;each to-morrow creeps,&rquo; etc.
<P>25. <B>time]</B> M. <SC>Mason</SC>: Shakespeare means not only the time that <I>has been</I>, but

<I>recording</I> or <I>recordable</I>, one participle for another.&mdash;<SC>Dalgleish</SC>: Time, of which a
record shall be kept, as opposed to eternity.&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC> (ed. ii.): It means simply
the last syllable of the <I>record</I> of time. See I, vi, 7; III, iv, 96, for other instances

<CC><P>26. <B>Fooles]</B> <SC>Hunter</SC>: Having found in a contemporary writer the word <I>foules</I> used
for <I>crowds</I>, it occurred to me that for &lquo;fools&rquo; we might read <I>foules</I> in this sense of <I>crowds</I>,
and this led to what may have been the real intention of the Poet. Macbeth, when
he hears of the death of his lady, thinks first of the unseasonableness of the time;
some time &lquo;hereafter&rquo; would have been the time for such a piece of intelligence as
this; this introduces the idea of the disposition there is in man to <I>procrastinate</I> in
everything; we are forever saying &lquo;tomorrow,&rquo; and this though we see men dying
around us, every &lquo;yesterday&rquo; having conducted crowds of human beings to the grave.
This introduces more general ideas of the vanity of man, who &lquo;walketh in a vain
show, and is disquieted in vain,&rquo; a passage of Scripture which seems to have been in
the Poet's mind when he wrote what follows; as is also . . . &lquo;we spend our years as
a tale that is told.&rquo; Shakespeare's intimate acquaintance with the Scriptures, observ-
able in all his plays, is shewn sometimes in a broad and palpable allusion or adapta-
tion, and sometimes, as here, in passages of which the germ only is in that book.
At the same time there is something in this passage partaking of the desperation of
the thane's position, and perhaps intended to shew what thoughts possess a mind
like his, burthened with heavy guilt, and having some reason to think retribution
near at hand. The word <I>foule</I> for <I>crowd</I> occurs in Archibold's <I>Evangelical Fruit
of the Seraphical Franciscan Order</I>, 1628, MS Harl. 3888, &lquo;The <I>foule</I> of people
past over him in time of sermon,&rquo; f. 81.
<P>27. <B>dusty]</B> <SC>Theobald</SC>: Perhaps Shakespeare might have wrote <I>dusky</I>, i. e.

sion in <I>Psalm</I> xxii. &lquo;<I>Dusty</I> death&rquo; alludes to the expression of &lquo;dust to dust&rquo; in
the burial service.&mdash;<SC>Douce</SC>: Perhaps no quotation can be better calculated to show
the propriety of this epithet than the following grand lines in <I>The Vision of Piers
Plowman</I>, a work which Shakespeare might have seen: &lquo;Deth came dryuende after,
and al to doust passhed Kynges &amp; knyghtes, kayseres and popes.&rquo;&mdash;[B. Passus xx,
ll. 99, 100; ed. Skeat.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC>: Shakespeare was not the first to apply
the epithet &lquo;dusty&rquo; to death. Anthony Copley, in his <I>Fig for Fortune</I>, 1596, has

<P>27. <B>Out . . . Candle]</B> <SC>Coleridge</SC> (i, <B>252</B>): Alas for Macbeth! now all is inward

<CC><P>28. <B>Shadow, a poore Player]</B> <SC>Hunter</SC> (i, 298, note on <I>Mid. N. D.</I> V, i, 430,
&lquo;If we shadows have offended&rquo;): &lquo;Shadows&rquo; is a beautiful term by which to ex-
press actors, those whose life is a perpetual personation, a semblance but of some-
thing real, a shadow only of actual existences. The idea of this resemblance was
deeply inwrought in the mind of the Poet and Actor. When, at a later period, he
looked upon man again as but &lquo;a walking shadow,&rquo; his mind immediately passed to
the long-cherished thought, and he proceeds: &lquo;A poor player, That struts and frets
his hour upon the stage, And then is heard no more.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
<P>28. <B>Player]</B> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: For references to the stage, see I, iii, 144; II, iv, 8,
9; also <I>Tro. and Cress.</I> I, iii, 153.&mdash;<SC>Birch</SC> (p. 449): The light of revelation, faith,
and hope, according to Shakespeare, have shown us fools the way to dusty death.
This life, that Christians humbly imagine gives evidence of the attributes of eternity,
signifies nothing, is a tale told by an idiot; and by whom is the tale said to be told
but by its maker? How often have we been told by Shakespeare that we are fools,
death's fools, and here we have it repeated with one of the material epithets usually
assigned to the end of man&mdash;dusty. We have again Jaques's &lquo;all the world's a
stage, and all the men are players,&rquo; with parts as brief as at the Blackfriars, or in
the Globe on Bankside. There we had the last scene of his sad, eventful history,
&lquo;sans everything&rquo;; but here, of his hopes we have the stern echo of Shakespeare's
materialism, which, like an owl amidst ruins, cries, &lquo;No more!&rquo; There are three
lines of Catullus, which have always been supposed to express his disbelief in a
future state, if not his atheism. In this speech of Macbeth's we have a similarity
of idea in the opening line, an exact translation of two words in the second, and the
last contains, word for word, the constant expressions, elsewhere, of Shakespeare
on Death: &lquo;Soles occidere et redire possunt, Nobis, cum semel occidit brevis lux.
Nox est perpetuo una dormienda.&rquo; [<I>Carmina</I>, v, 4.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.] The conclusion of
Macbeth's speech is similar to a line in the <I>Troades</I> of Seneca: &lquo;Post mortem nihil
est, ipsaque mors nihil.&rquo; [Act II, l. 398.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.] Campbell might have written
of Shakespeare those celebrated lines on Atheism, where he speaks of the brief
candle as &lquo;momentary fire,&rquo; which &lquo;lights to the grave his chance-erected form.&rquo;
[Let not the reader forget the avowed aim of the book from which this extract,
merely as a &lquo;specimen brick,&rquo; is taken.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>58. <B>Ring . . . Bell]</B> <SC>Theobald</SC> (<I>Sh. Restored</I>, p. 157): Is it ever customary in a

was not this Business always done by Beat of Drum? In short I believe these
Words were a Stage-direction crept from the Margin into the Text thro' the last
Line but One being deficient without them, occasioned probably by a Cut that had
been made in the Speech by the Actors. They were a Memorandum to the Promptor
to ring the <I>Alarum-bell</I>, i. e. the Bell, perhaps at that Time used, to warn the
<I>Tragedy-Drum</I> and <I>Trumpets</I> to be ready to sound an Alarm. And what confirms
me in this Suspicion, is, that for the four Pages immediately following, it is all along
quoted in the Margin, <I>Alarum</I>, etc.

<CC><P>children who came into the world in this extraordinary manner were consecrated to
Apollo; and therefore invulnerable. &lquo;Ripp'd from the womb, the infant 'scap'd
the steel.&rquo; [The passage in Virgil to which Tweedie refers is, possibly, in the <I>&AElig;neid</I>,
Bk, x, ll. 315-317: &lquo;Inde Lichan ferit, exsectum jam matre perempt&acirc;, Et tibi,
Ph&oelig;be, sacrum, casus evadere ferri Quod licuit parvo.&rquo; It does not appear who
is responsible for Tweedie's translation, which fails to convey the idea contained
in this passage from Virgil.&mdash;<SC>Henry</SC> (<I>Note on &AElig;neid</I>, ad loc. cit.): We have
another, and very interesting, instance of this custom, viz. of the dedication of a
child which had narrowly, and, as it seemed miraculously, escaped death, to the
services of a particular divinity, in Camilla, dedicated by her father to Diana. Nor
has the custom even yet entirely disappeared. We still dedicate&mdash;not, indeed, to
Ph&oelig;bus or Diana, but to the Virgin&mdash;children who have escaped miraculously, as
it is thought, some very imminent danger of death. In strictly Roman Catholic
countries such children&mdash;easily distinguishable among their playmates by their pecu-
liar, generally entirely white, costume&mdash;are very frequently to be met with.&mdash;R. P.
<SC>Harris</SC>, M. D. (<I>Tolerance in Pregnant Women</I>, Philadelphia, 1892), has collected
upwards of seventeen instances wherein premature birth was due, not to the C&aelig;sa-
rean section, but to lacerations by horns of cattle; and suggests that &lquo;such a cas-
ualty may have happened to the mother of Macduff, in view of the fact that several
other women have suffered the same form of injury, whose sons, thus liberated, have
lived to mature age.&rquo; See also <I>Appendix</I>, p. 399.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

See <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 423.
<P>26. <B>palter]</B> <SC>Craik</SC> (<I>Jul. C&aelig;s.</I> II, i, 126): To shuffle, to equivocate, to act or
speak unsteadily or dubiously with the intention to deceive.&mdash;<SC>Clarendon</SC>: The deri-
vation of the word is uncertain: &lquo;paltry&rquo; comes from it.
<P>28. <B>Ile . . . with thee]</B> <SC>Fletcher</SC> (p. 154): There is no want of physical cour-
age implied in Macbeth's declining the combat with Macduff. He may well believe
that now, more than ever, it is time to &lquo;beware Macduff.&rquo; He is at length con-
vinced that &lquo;fate and metaphysical aid&rquo; are against him; and, consistent to the last
in his hardened and whining selfishness, no thought of the intense blackness of his
own perfidy interferes to prevent him from complaining of falsehood in those evil
beings from whose very nature he should have expected nothing else. There is no
cowardice, we say, in his declining the combat under such a conviction. Neither is
there any courage in his renewing it; for there is no room for courage in opposing
evident fate. But the last word and action of Macbeth are an expression of the
<I>moral</I> cowardice which we trace so conspicuously throughout his career; he surren-
ders his life that he may not be &lquo;baited with the rabble's curse.&rquo;</CC>

<CC><P>to this stage-direction, &lquo;on a pole.&rquo; This explains &lquo;stands&rquo; in Macduff's speech.&mdash;

<P>74. <B>Pearle]</B> <SC>Malone</SC>: This means <I>thy kingdom's wealth</I>, or rather, <I>ornament.</I>
So, Sylvester, <I>England's Parnassus</I>, 1600: &lquo;Honor of cities, pearle of kingdomes
all,&rquo; [p. 268, ed. Collier, <I>Sonnet on the Peace</I>, iii.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]. Florio, in a Sonnet
prefixed to his [<I>Worlde of Wordes</I>], 1598, calls Lord Southampton &lquo;bright Pearle
of Peeres.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Nares</SC>: Anything very valuable, the choice or best part; from the
high estimation of the real pearl. In the present case it means the chief nobility.&mdash;
<SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 201): This is an expression for which it is not easy to account. There
is as strange a use of the same word in Sylvester's <I>Du Bartas</I>, p. 554: &lquo;These para-
sites are even the <I>pearls</I> and rings (Pearls, said I, perils) in the ears of kings.&rquo; It is
possible that Shakespeare might allude to this passage of Sylvester.&mdash;<SC>White</SC>: Rowe's
change was a very proper one, I think. A man may be called a pearl, and many men
pearls, <I>par excellence;</I> but to call a crowd of noblemen <I>the pearl</I> of a kingdom is an
anomalous and ungraceful use of language.&mdash;<SC>Keightley</SC>: &lquo;Pearl&rquo; is here a collect-
ive term,&mdash;a singular with a plural sense. The word was often so used.&mdash;<SC>Claren-
don</SC>: Perhaps in the present passage &lquo;pearl&rquo; is suggested by the row of pearls which
usually encircled a crown.

<P>&lquo;<SC>The Tragedie of Macbeth</SC>&rquo; was first printed in the Folio of 1623, where it
occupies twenty-one pages: from p. 131 to p. 151 inclusive, in the division of
<I>Tragedies</I>, between <I>Julius C&aelig;sar</I> and <I>Hamlet.</I> The Acts and Scenes are all there
indicated.
<P><SC>Collier</SC>: We may presume, as in other similar cases, that it had not come from
the press at an earlier date, because in the books of the Stationers' Company it is
registered by Blount and Jaggard, on the 8th of November, 1623, as one of the plays
&lquo;not formerly entered to other men.&rquo;
<P><SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 152): The numerous corrections (decidedly and unquestionably so)
made by the editors of F<SUB>2</SUB>, and the numerous other deviations of the text of F<SUB>1</SUB>, show
that the original editors performed their duty in a very imperfect manner, and that
therefore there is just room for a bolder conjectural criticism on this play than per-
haps on any other; neither can the variations of F<SUB>2</SUB> from F<SUB>1</SUB> be always accepted as
improvements or authoritative determinations of the true text.
<P><SC>Cambridge Editors</SC>: Except that it is divided into Scenes, as well as Acts, it is
one of the worst printed of all the plays, especially as regards the metre, and not a
few passages are hopelessly corrupt.
<P><SC>Clarendon</SC>: Probably it was printed from a transcript of the author's MS, which
was in great part not copied from the original, but written to dictation. This is con-
firmed by the fact that several of the most palpable blunders are blunders of the ear
and not of the eye.

<C>DATE OF THE PLAY</C>
<P><SC>Capell</SC> (<I>Notes</I>, ii, 26): The matter treated on [in IV, iii, 158-180] leads to a
discovery of what all must wish to have settl'd&mdash;the chronology of the play. That
it's general fable was made choice of on the score of King James, is acknowledg'd
on all hands; and this engrafted particular, of the <I>virtue</I> of kingly <I>touches</I>, serv'd
the purpose of incense to him, as well as its witchery and the fortunes of his an-
cestor Banquo: <I>Touching</I> for the &lquo;<I>evil</I>&rquo; was reviv'd by this king in his reign's
beginning, and practis'd with great ceremony, a ritual being establish'd for it: the
mention of it's source, when a novelty, had some grace on the stage, and in the ear
of it's reviver; and to that period, the king's third or fourth year, [James ascended
the throne in March, 1602-3.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] reason bids us assign the speech in question.
This conjecture about it's date, it will be said, stands in need of some strength'ning:
call we in then to it's aid another conjecture, built upon what is found in [Farmer's
Essay, quoted on p. 396.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]. A Latin play on this subject was parcel of the
king's entertainment at Oxford in 1605; that it preceded the play before us, is nearly
certain; For what writer would, on such an occasion, think of dressing up one upon
<PB N=354>
<HE>354 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>a fable that was then in exhibition elsewhere? and that it preceded not long, highly
probable; weighing the rapid pen of this Author, and the advantage to be expected
from a quick bringing it on upon his own newly-establish'd stage in the Black-friars.
<P><SC>Malone</SC> (vol. ii, p. 407, ed. 1821): I have observed some notes of time in this
tragedy that appear to me strongly to confirm the date I have assigned to it [viz.
1606]. They occur in II, iii, 7, 8: &lquo;Here's a <I>farmer</I> that hang'd himself on th'
<I>expectation of plenty.</I>&rquo; The price of corn was then, as now, the great criterion of
plenty or scarcity. That in the summer and autumn of 1606 there was a prospect
of plenty of corn appears from the audit-book of the College of Eton; for the price
of wheat in that year was lower than it was for thirteen years afterwards, being thirty-
three shillings the quarter. In the preceding year (1605) it was two shillings a
quarter dearer, and in the subsequent year (1607) three shillings a quarter dearer.
In 1608 wheat was sold at Windsor market for fifty-six shillings and eight pence a
quarter; and in 1609 for fifty shillings. In 1606 barley and malt were considerably
cheaper than in the two years subsequent.
<P>In the following words in the same scene there is still stronger confirmation of
the date of this tragedy: &lquo;here's an <I>equivocator</I>, that <I>could swear in both scales
against either scale;</I> who <I>committed treason enough for God's sake;</I> yet could not
<I>equivocate</I> to heaven.&rquo;
<P>Warburton long since observed that there was here an allusion to the Jesuits as
&lquo;the inventors of the execrable doctrine of equivocation.&rquo; If the allusion were only
thus general, this passage would avail us little in settling the time when <I>Macbeth</I>
was written; but it was unquestionably much more particular and personal, and had
direct reference to the doctrine of <I>equivocation</I> avowed by Henry Garnet, Superior
of the order of Jesuits in England, on his trial for the Gunpowder Treason, on the
28th of March, 1606, and to his detestable <I>perjury</I> on that occasion, or, as Shake-
speare expresses it, &lquo;to his swearing in both scales against either scale,&rquo; that is, flatly
and directly contradicting himself on oath.
<P>This trial, at which King James himself was present incognito, doubtless attracted
very general notice; and the allusion to his gross equivocation and perjury thus
recent, and probably the common topic of discourse, must have been instantly under-
stood, and loudly applauded.
<P>In a letter from Mr John Chamberlain to Mr Winwood, April 5, 1606, concerning
the trial, it is stated, &lquo;. . . that by the cunning of his keeper, Garnet, being brought
into a fool's paradise, had diverse conferences with Hall, his fellow priest, in the
Tower, which were overheard by spials set on purpose. With which being charged,
he stiffly denied it; but being still urged, and some light given him that they had
notice of it, he persisted still, <I>with protestation upon his soul and salvation, that there
had passed no such interlocution:</I> till at last, being confronted with Hall, he was
driven to confess. And being asked in this audience how he could solve this lewd
perjurie, he answered, &ldquo;that, so long as he thought they had no proof, he was not
bound to accuse himself; but when he saw they had proof, he stood not long in
it.&rdquo; And then fell into a large discourse <I>defending equivocation</I>, with many weak
and frivolous distinctions. The other example was of Francis Tresham, who . . .
protested that he had not seen him [Garnet] these sixteen years last past. Whereas
it was manifestly proved both by Garnet himself, Mrs Vaux, and others, that he had
been with him in three several places this last year, and once not many days before
the blow should have been given. And [Garnet] being now asked what he knew
of this man, he smilingly answered that he thought he meant to <I>equivocate.</I>&rquo;
<PB N=355>
<HE><I>DATE OF THE PLAY</I> 355</HE>
<P>A few extracts from Garnet's Trial, printed by authority, will still more clearly
show that the perjury and equivocation of the Jesuit were here particularly alluded
to by Shakespeare.
<P>In stating the case, Sir Edward Coke, the Attorney General, observed that,
&lquo;. . . Mr Lockerson, who being deposed before Garnet, delivered upon his oath
that they heard Garnet say to Hall, &ldquo;They will charge me with my prayer for the
good success of the great action, in the beginning of Parliament.&rdquo; . . . &ldquo;It is true,
indeed (said Garnet), that I prayed for the good success of the great action; but
I will tell them that I meant it in respect of some sharper laws, which I feared
they would make against Catholics; and that answer will serve well enough.&rdquo;&rquo;
Again: &lquo;Garnet having protested that &ldquo;When Father Greenwell made him ac-
quainted with the whole plot, . . . he was very much distempered, and could never
sleep quietly afterwards, but sometimes <I>prayed to God that it should not take effect&rdquo;;</I>
the Earl of Salisbury replied, that &ldquo;he should do well to speak clearly of his devo-
tion in that point, for otherwise he must put him to remember that <I>he had confessed</I>
to the Lords that he had offered sacrifice to God for stay of that plot, <I>unless it were
for the good of the Catholick cause.</I>&rdquo;&rquo; Further: Lord Salisbury reminded Garnet,
&lquo;after the interlocution between him and Hall, when he was called before all the
lords, and was asked, not what he said, but whether Hall and he had conference
together (desiring him <I>not to equivocate</I>), how stiffly he denied it upon his soul,
retracting it with so many detestable execrations, as the Earl said, it wounded their
hearts to hear him; and yet as soon as Hall had confessed it, he grew ashamed,
cried the lords mercy, and said he had offended, <I>if equivocation did</I> not help him.&rquo;
<P>Here certainly we have abundant proofs of &lquo;an <I>equivocator</I> that could <I>swear in
both scales against either scale</I>, who committed <I>treason</I> enough <I>for God's sake</I>, and
yet could not <I>equivocate</I> to heaven.&rquo; [<SC>Taunton</SC> (<I>History of the Jesuits in England</I>,
p. 325, foot-note) says that one of the aliases of Garnet was &lquo;Farmer&rquo;; and that
this was well known. A discussion on this point may be found in <I>Literature</I>, vol.
viii, 1901.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]
<P>If it should be maintained that in strict reasoning these observations only prove
that <I>Macbeth</I> was written subsequently to the trial of Garnet, it may be remarked
that allusions of this kind are generally made while the facts are yet recent in the
minds of the writer and of the audience, and before their impression has been weak-
ened by subsequent events.
<P>The third circumstance mentioned by the Porter is that of &lquo;an English tailor
stealing out of a French hose,&rquo; the humor of which, as Warburton has rightly
remarked, consists in this, that the French hose being then very short and strait, a
tailor must be master of his trade who could steal anything from them. From a
passage in <I>Henry V</I>, and from other proofs, we know that about the year 1597 the
French hose were very large and lusty; but doubtless between that year and 1600
they had adopted the fashion here alluded to; and we know that French fashions
were very quickly adopted in England. The following passage occurs in <I>The Black
Year</I>, by Anthony Nixon, 1606: &lquo;Gentlemen this year shall be much wronged by
their taylors, for their consciences are now much larger than ever they were, for
where [whereas] they were wont to steale but half a yeard of brood cloth in making
up a payre of breeches, now they do largely nicke their customers in the lace too,
and take <I>more than enough</I> for the <I>new fashions</I> sake, besides their old ones.&rquo; The
words in italics may relate only to the lace, but I rather think that the meaning is,
that whereas formerly tailors used to steal half a yard of cloth in making a pair of
<PB N=356>
<HE>356 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>breeches, they now cheat in the lace also; and steal more than enough of the cloth
for the sake of making the breeches close and tight, agreeably to the new fashion.
<P>In July, 1606, the King of Denmark came to England on a visit to his sister,
Queen Anne, and on the third of August was installed a Knight of the Garter.
&lquo;There is nothing to be heard at court,&rquo; says Drummond of Hawthornden in a letter
dated on that day, &lquo;but sounding of trumpets, hautboys, musick, revellings and
comedies.&rquo; Perhaps during this visit <I>Macbeth</I> was first exhibited.
<P>[The date of <I>Macbeth</I> thus assigned to 1606 by Malone was accepted by <SC>Steevens,
Chalmers</SC> (the latter placed it the twenty-eighth in the order of composition), and
other commentators, until the appearance in 1836 of <SC>Collier's</SC> <I>New Particulars
regarding the Works of Shakespeare.</I> In this volume mention is made of the dis-
covery among the Ashmolean MSS of notes on the performance of some of Shake-
speare's plays written by one who saw them acted during the lifetime of the Poet.
These notes] &lquo;bear the following title: &ldquo;<I>The Booke of Plaies and Notes thereof, <*>
Formans, for common Pollicie</I>,&rdquo; and they were written by Dr Simon Forman, the
celebrated Physician and Astrologer, who lived at Lambeth, the same parish in
which Elias Ashmole afterwards resided. Forman was implicated in the murder of
Sir Thomas Overbury, but died in 1611, before the trial. . . . The last date in his
<I>Book of Plays</I> is the 15th of May, 1611, so that he was a frequenter of the theatres
until a short period before his sudden decease in a boat on the Thames. He was
notorious long before his connection with Lady Essex, and excited a vast deal of
jealousy on the part of the regular medical practitioners of London, by giving un-
licensed advice to the sick, as well as by casting nativities; but he was at length able
to procure a degree from Cambridge. . . . The words &ldquo;for common policy&rdquo; in the
title of Forman's <I>Notes</I> mean that he made these remarks upon plays he saw repre-
sented because they afforded a useful lesson of prudence or &ldquo;policy&rdquo; for the &ldquo;com-
mon&rdquo; affairs of life. . . . On the 20th of April, 1610, which happened on a Saturday,
the astrological Doctor was present at the performance of <I>Macbeth</I>, the production
of which on the stage Malone fixed in 1606. This may be the right conjecture, and
Forman may have seen the tragedy for the first time four years after it was originally
brought out; but it is by no means impossible that 1610 was its earliest season, and
it is likely that in April that season had only just commenced at the Globe, which
was open to the weather; the King's Players acted at the covered theatre of the
Blackfriars during the winter. Malone's reasoning to establish that <I>Macbeth</I> was
written and acted in 1606, is very inconclusive, and much of it would apply just as
well to 1610. . . . [Forman's] description of the plot of <I>Macbeth</I> is more particular
and remarkable than perhaps any of the others which he has given; he writes&rquo; [The
following extract from <I>Dr Forman's Book of Plays</I> is a copy of the reprint by F.
J. <SC>Furnivall</SC>.&mdash;<I>Sh. Soc. Trans.</I> 1875-76, p. 417.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]:

howe Mackbeth and Bancko, 2 noble me<I>n</I> of Scotland, Ridinge thorowe a wod,
the[r] stode before them 3 women feiries or Nimphes, And saluted Mackbeth,
sayinge, 3 tyms vnto him, haille mackbeth, King of Codon; for thou shalt be

And nothing to me. Yes, said the nimphes, haille to thee Banko, thou shalt beget

<P>prouid for him, for he wold Sup w<I>i</I>th him the next dai at night, &amp; did soe. And
mackebeth contriued to kull Dunkin, &amp; thorowe the p<I>er</I>suasion of his wife did that

<P>&lquo;Then Mack Dove fled to England to the king<I>es</I> sonn, And soe they Raised an

<P>&lquo;Obserue Also howe mackbet<I>es</I> quen did Rise in the night, in the night in her
slepe, &amp; walke and talked and confessed all &amp; the doctor noted her wordes.&rquo;
<P>&lquo;Besides mis-spelling some of the names, as Mackbet, Mackdove, Dunston Anyse,
&amp;c., Forman's memory seems to have failed him upon particular points: thus he
makes the &ldquo;Fairies or Nymphs&rdquo; (<I>vice</I> Witches), hail Macbeth as &ldquo;<I>King</I> of Codor,&rdquo;
instead of <I>Thane</I> of Cawdor, and old Duncan subsequently creates him &ldquo;Prince of
Northumberland.&rdquo; After the murder, Forman states that neither Macbeth nor his
wife could wash the blood from their hands, by reason of which they were both
&ldquo;amazed and affronted.&rdquo; If this were a mob-accordant incident in the play in 1610,
it was among the omissions made by the player-editors when it was published in
1623.&rquo;
<P><SC>Collier</SC> subsequently somewhat modified his conjecture that in 1610 <I>Macbeth</I>
was in &lquo;its earliest season.&rquo; In his edition (<I>Introd.</I> vol, vii, p. 96, 1843) Collier
says: &lquo;Our principal reason for thinking that <I>Macbeth</I> had been originally repre-
sented at least four years before 1610, is the striking allusion in IV, i, to the union
of the three kingdoms . . . in the hands of James I. That monarch ascended the
throne in March, 1602-3, and the reference to &ldquo;two-fold balls&rdquo; and &ldquo;treble scep-
tres&rdquo; would have had little point, if we suppose it to have been delivered after the
king who bore the balls and sceptres had been more than seven years on the throne.
James was proclaimed king of Great Britain and Ireland the 24th of October, 1604,
and we may perhaps conclude that Shakespeare wrote <I>Macbeth</I> in the year 1605,
and that it was first acted at the Globe, when it was opened for the summer season
in the Spring of 1606. . . . We are generally disposed to place little confidence in
such passages [as those quoted by Malone in reference to the cheapness of corn, and
the doctrine of equivocation], not only because they are frequently obscure in their
application, but because they may have been introduced at any subsequent period,
<PB N=358>
<HE>358 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>either by the author or actor, with the purpose of exciting the applause of the audi-
ence by reference to some circumstance then attracting public attention.&rquo;
<P><SC>Hunter</SC> (<I>New Illus.</I> ii, 153): To the probabilities [of Malone and Chalmers] I
add another, which arises out of a new, but I believe a just, view of the import of
the passage in I, iii, 120. This passage has hitherto been taken as merely meta-
phorical; but it seems to me that Shakespeare really intended that the robes per-
taining to the dignity of Thane of Cawdor, to which Macbeth was just elevated,
should be produced on the Stage by Ross and Angus; that in fact the ceremony
of investiture should take place on the stage. It is at least more in accordance
with the turn of the expression, than to suppose that Macbeth spoke thus in mere
metaphor.
<P>Now, it happened that this ancient ceremony of investiture had been lately gone
through by Sir David Murray on his being created Lord Scone. We are told that
he &lquo;was with the greatest solemnity invested in that honour on the 7th of April,
1605, by a special commission, directed to the Earl of Dumfermling, the Lord Chan-
cellor, to that effect. The ceremony was in presence of the earls Angus, Suther-
land, Marischal, Linlithgow; the lords Fleming, Drummond, and Thirlestane.&rquo;
This particular investiture in a Scottish dignity probably suggested to Shakespeare
the idea of introducing the investiture of Macbeth as Thane of Cawdor. The Earl
of Angus, we see, appears both in the play and in the actual performance of the
ceremony; and Sir David Murray, it may also be observed, received the dignity
under circumstances not very unlike those under which Macbeth acquired the
Thanedom of Cawdor. He had a large share in saving the life of the King at the
time of the Gowrie conspiracy, and the King gave him for his reward, first, the
barony of Ruthven, which had belonged to the Earl of Gowrie, and next the lands
of Scone, of which the Earl of Gowrie had been commendator, and had lost them
by treason. &lquo;What he hath lost noble Macbeth hath won.&rquo;
<P><SC>Knight</SC>: We can have no doubt that this play belonged to the last ten years of
Shakespeare's life, and was probably not far separated from the Roman plays.
<P><SC>Grant White</SC> says: &lquo;I have little hesitation in referring the production of
<I>Macbeth</I> to the period between October, 1604, and August, 1605. I am the more
inclined to this opinion from the indications which the play itself affords that it was
produced upon an emergency. It exhibits throughout the hasty execution of a
grand and clearly-conceived design. But the haste is that of a master of his art,
who, with conscious command of its resources, and in the frenzy of a grand inspira-
tion, works out his conception to its minutest detail of essential form, leaving the
work of surface-finish for the occupation of cooler leisure. What the Sistine Ma-
donna was to Raffael, it seems that <I>Macbeth</I> was to Shakespeare&mdash;a magnificent
impromptu; that kind of impromptu which results from the application of well-
disciplined powers and rich stores of thought to a subject suggested by occasion. I
am inclined to regard <I>Macbeth</I> as, for the most part, a specimen of Shakespeare's
unelaborated, if not unfinished, writing, in the maturity and highest vitality of his
genius. It abounds in instances of extremest compression, and most daring ellipsis,
while it exhibits in every Scene a union of supreme dramatic and poetic power, and
in almost every line an imperially irresponsible control of language. Hence, I think,
its lack of formal completeness of versification in certain passages, and also some
of the imperfection in its text, the thought in which the compositors were not always
able to follow and apprehend.
<P><SC>Halliwell</SC>, in his Folio edition, that rare treasury of all that can arch&aelig;ologic-

<P>ally illustrate Shakespeare, agrees with Dr Farmer in the tolerably certain conject-
ure &lquo;that this tragedy was written and acted before the year 1607, if, as seems prob-
able, there is an allusion to Banquo's ghost in the <I>Puritan</I>, 4to, 1607: &ldquo;we'll ha'
the ghost i' th' white sheet sit at upper end o' th' table.&rdquo;&rquo;
<P>The Editors of the <SC>Clarendon</SC> edition &lquo;do not agree with some critics in think-
ing that this allusion [to &ldquo;the two-fold balls and treble sceptres&rdquo;] necessarily implies
that the play was produced immediately after James's accession, because an event of
such great moment and such permanent consequences would long continue to be
present to the minds of men.&rquo; And the Porter's reference to the &lquo;farmer who
hanged himself&rquo; would be quite &lquo;as apposite if we supposed it to be made to the
abundant harvest of any other year, and the Jesuit doctrine of equivocation was at
all times so favorite a theme of invective with Protestant preachers, that it could not
but be familiar to the public, who in those days frequented the pulpit as assiduously
as the stage.&rquo;
<P>After quoting the extract from Forman's diary the Editors add that when the as-
trologer saw <I>Macbeth</I>, in &lquo;all probability it was then a new play, otherwise he would
scarcely have been at the pains to make an elaborate summary of its plot. And in
those days the demand for and the supply of new plays were so great, that even the
most popular play had not such a &ldquo;run&rdquo; nor was so frequently &ldquo;revived&rdquo; as at
present. Besides, as we have shown, there is nothing to justify the inference, still
less to prove, that <I>Macbeth</I> was produced at an earlier date. In Beaumont and
Fletcher's <I>Knight of the Burning Pestle</I>, a burlesque produced in 1611, we find an
obvious allusion to the ghost of Banquo. Jasper, one of the characters, enters &ldquo;with
his face mealed,&rdquo; as his own ghost. He says to Venturewell, V, i (vol. ii, p. 216,
ed. Dyce),&mdash;
<BQ>&ldquo;When thou art at thy table with thy friends,<LB>
Merry in heart and fill'd with swelling wine,<LB>
I'll come in midst of all thy pride and mirth,<LB>
Invisible to all men but thyself.&rdquo;<LB></BQ>
<P>This supports the inference that <I>Macbeth</I> was in 1611 a new play, and fresh in the
recollection of the audience.&rquo;
<P>In <I>Kempes nine daies wonder</I> (p. 21, <I>Cam. Soc.</I> ed. by Dyce, 1840) the merry
morrice dancer says: &lquo;I met a proper vpright youth, onely for a little stooping in
the shoulders, all hart to the heele, a penny Poet, whose first making was the miser-
able stolne story of Macdoel, or Macdobeth, or Macsomewhat, for I am sure a Mac
it was, though I never had the maw to see it.&rquo; On this the learned Editor remarks
that &lquo;this mention of a piece anterior to Shakespeare's tragedy on the same subject
has escaped the commentators.&rquo; Collier, in his first edition, thought that this infer-
ence of an older piece than <I>Macbeth</I> was &lquo;doubtful, as it is obvious that Kemp did
not mean to be very intelligible; his other allusions to ballad-makers of his time are
purposely obscure.&rquo; But before the appearance of his second edition in 1858, Col-
lier's indefatigable industry had discovered another reference to the &lquo;miserable stolne
story.&rquo; &lquo;It may admit of doubt,&rquo; he says, &lquo;whether there was not a considerably
older drama on the story of <I>Macbeth</I>, for we meet with the following entry in the
Registers of the Stationers&rquo; Company; the notice of it is, we believe, quite new,
and we quote the very words of the register:
<P>&lquo;&ldquo;27 die Augusti 1596. Tho. Millington&mdash;Thomas Millington is likewyse fyned

<P>&lquo;This shows the existence of a so-called &ldquo;ballad&rdquo; on the subject; and if &ldquo;The

been publicly represented, and that it was not merely a printed &ldquo;ballad.&rdquo; Kemp, as

he may mean to refer to a pre-existing production of which the author of the play

<P><SC>Malone</SC> (vol. ii, pp. 419 and 440) mentions one or two other slight indications

<P>Furthermore, Malone says that it is probable that Shakespeare &lquo;about the time of

found an account of the &ldquo;insane root that takes the reason prisoner,&rdquo; which he has

<P>[<SC>Fleay</SC> (<I>Sh. Manual</I>, p. 257) gives the following theory as to the composition
of <I>Macbeth:</I> &lquo;It was written during Shakespeare's third period: I think after
<I>Hamlet</I> and <I>Lear</I> (see Malone); so that its date was probably 1606. Metrical
evidence is of no use in determining the date: as we cannot tell how Middleton
altered the play, or <I>how much he omitted</I>, except that the weak-ending test is not
opposed to Malone's date. At some time after this, Middleton revised and abridged
it: I agree with the Cambridge Editors in saying not later than 1613. There is a
decisive argument that he did so after he wrote the <I>Witch</I>,&mdash;namely, that he borrows
the songs from the latter play, and repeats himself a good deal. It is to me very
likely that he should repeat himself in <I>Macbeth</I>, and somewhat improve on his orig-
inal conception, as he has done in the corresponding passages: and yet be unable to
<PB N=361>
<HE><I>DATE OF THE PLAY</I> 361</HE>
<P>do a couple of new songs, or to avoid the monotony of introducing Hecate in both
plays (Hecate being a witch in both, remember). I can quite understand a third-
rate man, who in all his work shows reminiscences of others, and repetitions of
Shakespeare, being unable to vary such conceptions as he had formed on the subject.
I believe that Middleton, having found the groundlings more taken with the witches,
and the cauldron, and the visions in IV, i, than with the grander art displayed in
the Fate goddesses of I, iii, determined to amalgamate these, and to give us plenty
of them. Hence, the witches call themselves weird sisters in the lyric part of I,
iii.; hence the speech of Macbeth: &ldquo;I will tomorrow . . . to the weird sisters.&rdquo; I
believe also the extra fighting in the last scenes was inserted for the same reason.
But finding that the magic and the singing and the fighting made the play too long,
. . . he cut out large portions of the psychological Shakespeare work, in which, as
far as quantity is concerned, this play is very deficient compared with the three other
masterpieces of world-poetry, and left us the torso we now have.&rquo;
<P><SC>Ibid</SC>. (<I>Life of Sh.</I> p. 155): When James I. was at Oxford in August, 1605, he had
been addressed in Latin by the three Witches in this story at an entertainment given
by the University. No doubt James would be pleased by their prophecies, and desir-
ous that they should be promulgated in the vulgar tongue. No more likely date can
be found for the holograph letter which he is said to have addressed to Shakespeare.
It may possibly be that that letter was a command to write <I>Macbeth.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]

<C>&lquo;THE WITCH&rquo;</C>
<P><SC>Towards</SC> the close of the last century a MS copy of a play by Thomas Middle-
ton was discovered, called <I>The Witch.</I> <SC>Dyce</SC>, in his edition of Middleton (<I>Works</I>,
1840, vol. iii, p. 247, and in vol. i, p. l.), says that copies from this MS were printed
in 1778 by Isaac Reed for distribution among his friends. <SC>Malone</SC> (<I>Variorum</I> of
1821, vol. ii. p. 420) says that this piece, <I>The Witch</I>, had long remained &lquo;unnoticed
in MS 'till it was discovered in 1779 by the late Mr Steevens in the collection of the
late Thomas Pearson, esq.&rquo; The question, however, is now of little importance by
whom this drama of Middleton was first discovered, or when it was discovered;
the similarity of the scenes of sorcery in <I>The Witch</I> to those in <I>Macbeth</I> was mani-
fest, and to Steevens the fame of the discovery is generally accorded, and the ela-
tion consequent thereon goes far now-a-days in condoning the zeal with which he
endeavored to prove that the greater poet copied from the less.
<P><SC>Steevens</SC> (ed. Malone, vol. i, p. 359, 1790) inferred from an expression in the
Dedication of <I>The Witch</I>, that it was written &lquo;<I>long</I> before 1603,&rquo; and that therefore
Shakespeare must have been the copyist if <I>Macbeth</I> were not written until 1606, and
sustains the inference of plagiarism by adducing the following examples of similarity
in the two dramas: &lquo;The Hecate of Shakespeare says, [III, v, 23]: &ldquo;I am for the
air,&rdquo; etc. The Hecate of Middleton (who like the former is summoned away by
a&emacr;rial spirits) has the same declaration in almost the same words: &ldquo;I am for aloft,&rdquo;
etc.&mdash;[<SC>Ed.</SC>] Again, the Hecate of Shakespeare says to her sisters, [IV. i, 151]:
<BQ>&ldquo;I'll charm the <I>air</I> to give a sound,<LB>
While you perform your antique round,&rdquo; etc.<LB>
&ldquo;[<I>Musick. The Witches dance and vanish.</I>&rdquo;<LB REND=RIGHT></BQ>
<P>[Did Steevens forget that it is D'Avenant's Hecate, not Shakespeare's, who says
this?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.] The Hecate of Middleton says on a similar occasion:

Whilst we shew reverence to yond peeping moone.&rdquo;<LB>
&ldquo;[<I>Here they dance, and exeunt.</I>&rdquo;<LB REND=RIGHT></BQ>
<P>&lquo;In this play, the motives which incline the Witches to mischief, their manners,
the contents of their cauldron, etc., seem to have more than accidental resemblance
to the same particulars in <I>Macbeth.</I> The hags of Middleton, like the weird sisters
of Shakespeare, destroy cattle because they have been refused provisions at farm-
houses. The owl and the cat (Gray Malkin) give them notice when it is time to
proceed on their several expeditions. Thus Shakespeare's Witch: &ldquo;Harper cries;&mdash;
'tis time, 'tis time.&rdquo; Thus too the Hecate of Middleton:
<BQ>&ldquo;<S>Hec.</S> Heard you the owle yet?<LB>
&ldquo;<S>Stad.</S> Briefely in the copps.<LB>
&ldquo;<S>Hec.</S> 'Tis high time for us then.&rdquo;<LB></BQ>
<P>&lquo;The Hecate of Shakespeare, addressing her sisters, observes, that Macbeth is but
&ldquo;a wayward son, who loves for his own ends, not for them.&rdquo; The Hecate of Mid-
dleton has the same observation, when the youth who has been consulting her retires:
&ldquo;I know he loves me not, nor there's no hope on't.&rdquo; Instead of the &ldquo;grease that's
sweaten from the murderer's gibbet&rdquo; and the &ldquo;finger of birth-strangled babe,&rdquo; the
Witches of Middleton employ &ldquo;the gristle of a man that <I>hangs after sunset</I>&rdquo; (i. e. of
a murderer, for all other criminals were anciently cut down before evening) and the
&ldquo;fat of an unbaptized child.&rdquo; They likewise boast of the power to raise tempests
that shall blow down trees, overthrow buildings, and occasion shipwreck; and, more
particularly, that they can &ldquo;make miles of wood walk.&rdquo; Here too the Grecian
Hecate is degraded into a presiding witch, and exercised in superstitions peculiar to
our own country. So much for the scenes of enchantment; but even other parts of
Middleton's play coincide more than once with that of Shakespeare. Lady Macbeth
says [II, ii, 8]: &ldquo;the surfeited grooms Do mock their charge with <I>snores.</I> I have
<I>drugg'd</I> their <I>possets.</I>&rdquo; So, too, Francisca, in the piece of Middleton:
<BQ>&ldquo;&mdash; they're now all at rest,<LB>
&ldquo;And Gaspar there and all:&mdash;List!&mdash;fast asleepe;<LB>
&ldquo;He <I>cryes</I> it hither.&mdash;I must disease<SUP>*</SUP> you strait, sir:<LB>
&ldquo;For the maide-servants, and the girles o' the house,<LB>
&ldquo;I <I>spic'd</I> them lately with a <I>drowsie posset</I>,&rdquo; etc.<LB></BQ>
<P>&lquo;And Francisca, like Lady Macbeth, is watching late at night to encourage the
perpetration of a murder.
<P>&lquo;The expression which Shakespeare has put into the mouth of Macbeth [II, i,
60], &ldquo;There's no such thing,&rdquo;&mdash;is likewise appropriated to Francisca when she
undeceives her brother, whose imagination has been equally abused.&rquo;
<P><SC>Malone</SC> was at first overborne by these arguments of Steevens's; but afterwards,
in the <I>Variorum</I> of 1821 (vol. ii, pp. 425-438), took the opposite ground, and in a
long dissertation endeavored to prove, from internal evidence, that <I>The Witch</I> &lquo;must
have been produced after 1613,&rquo; &lquo;and if so, it can have no claim to contest pre-
cedence with <I>Macbeth</I>, which unquestionably was acted in 1606.&rquo;

<P><SC>Dyce</SC>, in his account of Middleton (<I>Works</I>, vol. i, p. lii, 1840), says: &lquo;Though
his [Malone's] reasoning appears to me very far from convincing, I am by no
means disposed to assert that the conclusion at which he so laboriously arrived is
not the right one [viz. that the performance of <I>Macbeth</I> in 1606 was anterior to <I>The
Witch</I>]. Gifford, indeed, has unhesitatingly pronounced that Shakespeare was the
copyist;<SUP>*</SUP> but, notwithstanding the respect which I entertain for that critic, his inci-
dental remarks on the present question have little weight with me; he has assigned
no grounds for his decision; he had not, I apprehend, considered the subject with
much attention, and on two occasions, at least, he appears to have alluded to it
chiefly for the sake of giving additional force to the blows which he happened to be
aiming at the luckless &ldquo;commentators.&rdquo; As Shakespeare undoubtedly possessed
the creative power in its utmost perfection, and as no satisfactory evidence has been
adduced to show that <I>The Witch</I> was acted at an earlier period than <I>Macbeth</I>, he
must not be hastily accused of imitation. Yet since he is known to have frequently
remodelled the works of other writers, it may be urged that when he had to intro-
duce witches into his tragedy, he would hardly scruple to borrow from [Middleton's]
play as much as suited his immediate purpose. But, after all, there is an essential
difference between the hags of Shakespeare and of Middleton; and whichever of the
two may have been the copyist, he owes so little to his brother-poet that the debt
will not materially affect his claim to originality. Concerning the tragi-comedy, <I>The
Witch</I>, I have only to add that its merit consists entirely in the highly imaginative
pictures of preternatural agents, in their incantations and their moonlight revelry:
the rest of it rises little above mediocrity.&rquo;
<P>Like Gifford, <SC>Lamb</SC> too had not seen Malone's proof that <I>The Witch</I> was subse-
quent in date to <I>Macbeth</I>, when in 1808 he published his <I>Specimens of English Dra-
matic Poets</I>, yet his poetic insight clearly discerned the &lquo;essential differences&rquo; be-
tween the Weird Sisters and The Witch. &lquo;Though some resemblance may be traced
between the Charms in <I>Macbeth</I> and the Incantations in this Play [Middleton's
<I>Witch</I>, in <I>Dramatic Poets</I>, p. 152, Bohn's ed. 1854], which is supposed to have
preceded it, this coincidence will not detract much from the originality of Shake-
speare. His witches are distinguished from the witches of Middleton by essential
differences. These are creatures to whom man or woman plotting some dire mis-
chief might resort for occasional consultation. Those originate deeds of blood, and
begin bad impulses to men. From the moment that their eyes first meet with Mac-
beth's, he is spell-bound. That meeting sways his destiny. He can never break
the fascination. These witches can hurt the body; those have power over the soul.
Hecate, in Middleton, has a son, a low buffoon: the hags of Shakespeare have
neither child of their own, nor seem descended from any parent. They are foul
Anomalies, of whom we know not whence they are sprung, nor whether they have
beginning or ending. As they are without human passions, so they seem to be
without human relations. They come with thunder and lightning, and vanish to
airy music. This is all we know of them. Except Hecate, they have no names;
which heightens their mysteriousness. Their names, and some of the properties,
which Middleton has given to his hags, excite smiles. The Weird Sisters are serious

<P>things. Their presence cannot co-exist with mirth. But in a lesser degree, the

<P><SC>Collier</SC> (ed. i, 1843) says in reference to Malone's conviction that <I>The Witch</I>
was a play written subsequently to the production of <I>Macbeth:</I> &lquo;Those who read
the two will, perhaps, wonder how a doubt could have been entertained; . . .
what must surprise everybody is that a poet of Middleton's rank could so degrade
the awful beings of Shakespeare's invention; for although, as Lamb observes, &ldquo;the
power of Middleton's witches is in some measure over the mind,&rdquo; they are of a
degenerate race, as if, Shakespeare having created them, no other mind was suffi-
ciently gifted to continue their existence.&rquo;
<P><SC>Hudson</SC> (1856) says: Malone has perhaps done all the case admits of to show
that <I>The Witch</I> was not written before 1613; but in truth, there is hardly enough to
ground an opinion upon one way or the other. And the question may be safely
dismissed as altogether vain; for the two plays have nothing in common but what
may well enough have been derived from Scot's <I>Discovery of Witchcraft</I>, or from
the floating witchcraft lore of the time, some relics of which have drifted down in
the popular belief to a period within our remembrance.&rquo;
<P>R. G. <SC>White</SC> (1861): Shakespeare would not have hesitated a moment about
imitating Middleton, or any other writer, had it suited his purpose to do so; but I
believe the Scenes in <I>The Witch</I> to be the imitations, not only because they have the
air, at once timid, constrained, and exaggerated, which indicates in every art a copy
by a very much inferior hand, but because witchcraft was an essential motive power
in the very story which Shakespeare had chosen to dramatise. And witchcraft being
thus inherent in his plot, and the superstitions of his day furnishing him ample ma-
terial with which to fulfil his indication,&mdash;exactly the material too which he used,&mdash;
I cannot believe that, with his wealth of creative power, he would ever have thought
of going to the work of a younger dramatist for the mere supernatural costume with
which to dress out such mysterious and unique creatures of his imagination as the
three weird sisters of this tragedy.
<P>To the instances of similarity between <I>The Witch</I> and <I>Macbeth</I>, given by Steevens,
Messrs. <SC>Clark</SC> and <SC>Wright</SC> (<I>Clarendon Press Series</I>, p. viii, 1869) add the follow-
ing: &lquo;the innocence of sleep&rquo; (p. 316, Dyce's ed.) and &lquo;I'll rip thee down from
neck to navel&rquo; (p. 319, ibid.), which recall <I>Macbeth</I>, II, ii, 47, and I, ii, 28. . . .
<P>&lquo;We have no means of ascertaining the date of Middleton's play. We know
that he survived Shakespeare eleven years, but that he had acquired a reputation
as early as 1600, because in <I>England's Parnassus</I>, published in that year, a poem
is by mistake attributed to him. (See Dyce's account of Middleton, <I>Works</I>, vol. i,
p. xiv.)
<P>&lquo;If we were certain that the whole of <I>Macbeth</I>, as we now read it, came from
Shakespeare's hand, we should be justified in concluding from the data before us
that Middleton, who was probably junior and certainly inferior to Shakespeare, con-
sciously or unconsciously imitated the great master. But we are persuaded that there
are parts of <I>Macbeth</I> which Shakespeare did not write, and the style of these seems
to us to resemble that of Middleton. It would be very uncritical to pick out of
Shakespeare's works all that seems inferior to the rest, and to assign it to somebody
else. At his worst, he is still Shakespeare; and though the least &ldquo;mannered&rdquo; of
all poets, he has always a manner which cannot well be mistaken. In the parts of
<I>Macbeth</I> of which we speak we find no trace of this manner. But to come to par-
<PB N=365>
<HE><I>DATE OF THE PLAY</I> 365</HE>
<P>ticulars. We believe that the second scene of the first act was not written by Shake-
speare. Making all allowance for corruption of text, the slovenly metre is not like
Shakespeare's work, even when he is most careless. The bombastic phraseology
of the sergeant is not like Shakespeare's language even when he is most bombastic.
What is said of the thane of Cawdor, lines 64, 65, is inconsistent with what follows
in scene iii, lines 77, 78, and 125 sqq. We may add that Shakespeare's good sense
would hardly have tolerated the absurdity of sending a severely wounded soldier to
carry the news of a victory.
<P>&lquo;In the first thirty-seven lines of the next scene, powerful as some of them are,
especially 21-26, we do not recognise Shakespeare's hand; and surely he never
penned the feeble &ldquo;tag,&rdquo; II, i, 73.
<P>&lquo;Of the commencement of the third scene of the second act, Coleridge said long
ago that he believed &ldquo;the low soliloquy of the Porter, in II, iii, to have been
written for the mob by some other hand.&rdquo;
<P>&lquo;If the fifth scene of act III. had occurred in a drama not attributed to Shake-
speare, no one would have discovered in it any trace of Shakespeare's manner.
<P>&lquo;The rich vocabulary, prodigal fancy, and terse diction displayed in IV, i, 3-40,
show the hand of a master, and make us hesitate in ascribing the passage to any one
but the master himself. There is, however, a conspicuous falling-off in lines 41-49,
after the entrance of Hecate.
<P>&lquo;In III, v, 16, it is said that Macbeth &ldquo;loves for his own ends, not for you&rdquo;;
but in the play there is no hint of his pretending love to the witches. On the con-
trary, he does not disguise his hatred. &ldquo;You secret, black, and midnight hags!&rdquo;
he calls them. Similarly, IV, i, 147-154, cannot be Shakespeare's.
<P>&lquo;In IV, iii, lines 160-180, which relate to the touching for the evil, were prob-
ably interpolated previous to a representation at Court.
<P>&lquo;We have doubts about the second scene of act V.
<P>&lquo;In V, v, lines 54-57 are singularly weak, and read like an unskilful imitation of
other passages, where Macbeth's desperation is interrupted by fits of despondency.
How much better the sense is without them!
<P>&lquo;In V, vii, 80, 81, the words, &ldquo;Before my body I throw my warlike shield,&rdquo; are
also, we think, interpolated.
<P>&lquo;Finally, the last forty lines of the play show evident traces of another hand than
Shakespeare's. The double stage-direction, &ldquo;<I>Exeunt, fighting</I>&rdquo;&mdash;&ldquo;<I>Enter fighting,
and Macbeth slaine</I>,&rdquo; proves that some alteration had been made in the conclusion
of the piece. Shakespeare, who has inspired his audience with pity for Lady Mac-
beth, and made them feel that her guilt has been almost absolved by the terrible
retribution which followed, would not have disturbed this feeling by calling her a
&ldquo;fiend-like queen&rdquo;; nor would he have drawn away the veil which with his fine
tact he had dropt over her fate, by telling us that she had taken off her life &ldquo;by
self and violent hands.&rdquo;
<P>&lquo;We know that it is not easy to convince readers that such and such passages are
not in Shakespare's manner, because their notion of Shakespeare's manner is partly
based on the assumption that these very passages are by Shakespeare. Assuming,
however, that we have proved our case so far, how are we to account for the intru-
sion of this second and inferior hand? The first hypothesis which presents itself is
that Shakespeare wrote the play in conjunction with Middleton or another as &ldquo;col-
laborateur.&rdquo; We know that this was a very common practice with the dramatists
of his time. It is generally admitted that he assisted Fletcher in the composition
<PB N=366>
<HE>366 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>of <I>The Two Noble Kinsmen;</I> and Mr Spedding has shown conclusively, as we think,
that Fletcher assisted him in the composition of <I>Henry VIII.</I>
<P>&lquo;We might suppose, therefore, that after drawing out the scheme of <I>Macbeth</I>,
Shakespeare reserved to himself all the scenes in which Macbeth or Lady Macbeth
appeared, and left the rest to his assistant. We must further suppose that he largely
retouched, and even re-wrote in places, this assistant's work, and that in his own
work his good nature occasionally tolerated insertions by the other. But, then,
how did it happen that he left the inconsistencies and extravagances of the second
scene of the first act uncorrected?
<P>&lquo;On the whole, we incline to think that the play was interpolated after Shake-
speare's death, or at least after he had withdrawn from all connection with the
theatre. The interpolator was, not improbably, Thomas Middleton; who, to please
the &ldquo;groundlings,&rdquo; expanded the parts originally assigned by Shakespeare to the
weird sisters, and also introduced a new character, Hecate. The signal inferiority
of her speeches is thus accounted for.&rquo;

cool,&rdquo; is wretched. See how the passage reads without it:
<BQ>&ldquo;give to the edge of the sword<LB REND=RIGHT>
His wife, his babes, and all unfortunate souls<LB>
That trace him in his line. But no more sights!<LB>
Where are these gentlemen?&rdquo;<LB></BQ>

<HE><I>DATE OF THE PLAY</I> 367</HE>
<P>&lquo;In V, i, end [78-80]:
<BQ>&ldquo;<I>Doctor.</I> So, good-night,<LB REND=RIGHT>
My mind she has mated and amazed my sight.<LB>
I think, but dare not speak.&rdquo;<LB></BQ>
<P>Omit second line of couplet.
<P>&lquo;In V, ii, [39], the invitation &ldquo;to pour in our country's purge as many drops of
us as are needed to dew the sovereign flower and kill the weeds&rdquo; is unlike Shake-
speare.
<P>&lquo;V, iii, [71, 72], after Macbeth's emphatic declaration:
<BQ>&ldquo;I will not be afraid of death and bane<LB>
Till Birnam forest come to Dunsinane,&rdquo;<LB></BQ>
<P>the Doctor's washy sentiment,
<BQ>&ldquo;Were I from Dunsinane away and clear<LB>
Profit again would hardly draw me here,&rdquo;<LB></BQ>
<P>is surely out of place. Why should our sympathy with Macbeth be interrupted by
the Doctor's private sentiments?
<P>&lquo;V, iv, [26-30]:
<BQ>&ldquo;The time approaches,<LB>
That will with due decision make us know<LB>
What we shall say we have, and what we owe:<LB>
Thoughts speculative, their unsure hopes relate;<LB>
But certain issue, strokes must arbitrate,&rdquo;<LB></BQ>
<P>cannot surely be Shakespeare's.
<P>&lquo;V, vi, [15, 16]:
<BQ>&ldquo;<I>Make</I> all our trumpets <I>speak; give</I> them all breath<LB>
Those <I>clamorous</I> harbingers of blood and death.&rdquo;<LB></BQ>
<P>This tautology cannot be Shakespeare's; besides, the whole sentiment is too weak
for the situation. In a few of these I may have missed some inner &aelig;sthetic mean-
ing which is too deep for my comprehension; but the number of them is far too
great for me to be wrong in all. I conclude, therefore, that Middleton altered the
endings of many scenes by inserting rhyming tags: whether he cut anything out
remains to be seen. The next point I notice is, that the account of young Siward's
death and the unnatural patriotism of his father, which is derived from Holinshed's
<I>History of England</I>, and not of Scotland, like the rest of the play, is a bit of padding
put in by Shakespeare after finishing the whole tragedy; this shows great haste in
its composition: to my mind it would be decidedly better if the first whom Macbeth
combated turned out to be the fated warrior not born of woman. . . . The severely
wounded captain in I, ii, who mangles his metre so painfully, I surrender at once
to the Cambridge Editors as Middleton's. In all probability, however, this scene
replaces one of Shakespeare's; one of whose lines at least, &ldquo;The multiplying vil-
lanies of nature,&rdquo; seems to be left in it as it now stands. In this scene Ross comes
in afterwards, and is sent to Macbeth to greet him with his new title; he says, &ldquo;<I>I</I>'ll
see it done.&rdquo; Lennox also is present, not Angus. Ross and Angus take the message
<PB N=368>
<HE>368 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>to Macbeth in I, iii, where Angus speaks ten lines, and then disappears till V, ii.;
he there has seven lines to repeat; so that in all he has seventeen. He is not the
slightest use in the play. Lennox could have done his work better in I, iii. On
account of his after connection with Macbeth, V, ii. is not wanted at all. I think,
therefore, that Middleton has cut down Angus's part in the original play by omitting
scenes in which he appeared. This shows that the play has been greatly abridged
for acting purposes. The metre of:
<BQ>&ldquo;And betimes I will to the weird sisters&rdquo;;<LB></BQ>
<P>the poverty of thought in
<BQ>&ldquo;For mine own good,<LB REND=RIGHT>
All causes shall give way; I am in blood<LB>
Stept in so far, that, should I wade no more,<LB>
Returning were as tedious as go o'er.<LB>
Strange things I have in head, that will to hand,<LB>
Which must be acted ere they may be scann'd&rdquo;;<LB></BQ>
<P>the putting of this long tag in Macbeth's mouth when he is so bewildered that he
answers Lady Macbeth's&mdash;
<C>&ldquo;You lack the season of all natures, sleep&rdquo;&mdash;</C>
<P>by
<C>&ldquo;Come, we'll to sleep,&rdquo;</C>
<P>are all marks of inferior work, and make me sure that this part has been worked
over by Middleton. IV, i, [113-119], has been worked over in a similar way:
<BQ>&ldquo;That will never be:<LB REND=RIGHT>
Who can impress the forest; bid the tree<LB>
Unfix his earth-bound root? sweet bodements! good!<LB>
Rebellious dead, rise never, till the wood<LB>
Of Birnam rise; and our high-plac'd Macbeth<LB>
Shall leave the lease of nature, pay his breath<LB>
To time and mortal custom.&rdquo;<LB></BQ>
<P>&lquo;&ldquo;Our high-plac'd Macbeth&rdquo; cannot be said by Macbeth himself: it must be
part of a speech of a witch. &ldquo;Sweet bodements!&rdquo; looks also like Middleton, and the
whole bit is, in my opinion, a fragment of <I>Hecate's</I> inserted by him. &ldquo;Rebellious
dead&rdquo; seems to me an allusion to Banquo's ghost, misplaced by Middleton. If we
read &ldquo;Rebellion's head&rdquo; it seems a mistaken interpretation of the armed head appa-
rition: in any case it is not Shakespeare. But more detail would be wearisome.
Enough is given for my purpose to make it likely that Middleton was a recaster of
the play, not a joint author.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]
