<C>MUSIC</C>
<P>W. <SC>Chappell</SC> (<SC>Grove's</SC> <I>Dict. of Music</I>): Three musicians [Locke, Eccles, and
Leveridge] have composed music for Sir William D'Avenant's additions to Shake-
speare's tragedy of <I>Macbeth</I>. . . . Downes (<I>Roscius Anglicanus</I>) says: &lquo;The tragedy
of <I>Macbeth</I>, altered by Sir William D'Avenant, . . . with all the singing and dancing
in it, the first composed by Mr Lock. . . .&rquo;
<P>Downes is the only contemporary authority who refers to the authorship, but the
Hon. Roger North remarks, &lquo;in music Matthew Lock had a robust vein,&rquo; a criticism
peculiarly applicable to the music in <I>Macbeth.</I>
<P>The only reason that can be assigned why modern musicians should have doubted
Matthew Lock's authorship is that a manuscript of it exists in the handwriting of
Henry Purcell. His autograph seems to have been tolerably well ascertained.
<P>[Chappell, continuing, shows by &lquo;the inexorable logic of dates&rquo; that Purcell
could not have been the composer of a work which appeared when he was in his
fourteenth year. For a fuller statement of Lock's claim to the authorship, see arti-
cle in Grove's <I>Dictionary</I>, above quoted; and for an exposition of Purcell's claim,
see article by W. H. <SC>Cummings</SC>: <I>Who Wrote the Macbeth Music?</I>&mdash;Concordia, 27
Nov. 1875.&mdash;<SC>Ed</SC>. ii.]
<PB N=544>
<HE><I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P><SC>Elson</SC> (p. 336): The Germans took up the tragedy [of <I>Macbeth</I>] very early,
and in 1787 J. F. Reichardt set incidental music to B&uuml;rger's translation. The
famous Spohr wrote music to the tragedy, all of which is lost with the exception of
the overture, and even that is rarely heard at present. Weyse published some excel-
lent incidental music to the play some seventy-five years ago. Some extremely
modern music to <I>Macbeth</I> was composed by the American Edgar S. Kelley, but it
has been seldom heard save at the performances of the play in San Francisco in
1885. Very much orchestral music has been written about <I>Macbeth</I>, a half-dozen
overtures, among them one by Raff and one by Br&uuml;ll, and a symphonic poem by
Richard Strauss, which is probably the greatest musical outcome of the play. As
regards operatic settings, one finds only three, not one of them of importance.
Auguste Hix wrote a French version to a libretto by Rouget de l'Isle (composer
of the &lquo;Marseillaise&rquo;), which was afterward translated into German. The music
was by Hippolyte Ch&eacute;lard. . . . It was produced for the first time at the Paris Op&eacute;ra,
June 29, 1827. . . . The trio of Witches and several choruses were remarked, but the
opera failed, and was only performed five times. . . . The libretto departs widely
from Shakespeare's tragedy. Another setting was made by Taubert and performed
in Germany, which also departed from the Shakespearian path.
<P>But the strangest alterations that Shakespeare was obliged to submit to, on his
journey to the operatic stage, took place in the version composed by Verdi, in
1847, before he decided to follow Wagner into the domain of earnest librettos.
<I>Macbeth</I>, with a ballet introduced, with Lady Macbeth singing a drinking-song,
with a chorus of murderers, with Macduff singing a liberty song, must have been
comical enough for any Shakespearian, but the Italians accepted it cordially, and
the &lquo;liberty-song&rquo; was received with frenzy, as a protest against Austrian tyranny.&mdash;
<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.
<P><SC>Grove</SC> (<I>Dictionary of Music</I>) gives, in addition to the operatic settings men-
tioned by Elson, &lquo;The first act of an Opera, <I>Macbeth</I>, by von Collin, published in
1809; and sketches by Beethoven for the overture and first chorus therein, given by
Nottebohm in <I>Mus. Wochenblatt</I>, 1879, No. 10.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed</SC>. ii.
<P>[The passages from Shakespeare's <I>Macbeth</I> for which music has been written,
and the composers thereof, will be found in the New Shakspere Society Publica-
tions, Series viii, No. 3. <SC>Roffe</SC>, <I>Handbook of Shakespeare Music</I>, may also be
consulted for a detailed account of the same. The musical notation is, however,
not given in either of the above-mentioned works.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC> ii.]
<P><SC>Fletcher</SC> (p. 173): Lock's musical accompaniments are not only the master-
piece of their author, but one of the most vigorous productions of native English
musical genius. Let them be performed and enjoyed anywhere and everywhere but
in the representation of the greatest tragedy of the world's great dramatist,&mdash;<I>for
which representation</I>, let every auditor well observe, their author, Lock, <I>did not com-
pose them.</I> For D'Avenant's abominable travesty were they written, and with that
they ought to have been repudiated from the stage.

<C>PLAN OF THE WORK, <SC>Etc.</SC></C>
<P>In this Edition the attempt is made to give, in the shape of <SC>Textual Notes</SC>,
on the same page with the Text, all the <SC>Various Readings</SC> of <I>Macbeth</I>, from the
Second Folio down to the latest critical Edition of the play; then, as <SC>Commentary</SC>,
follow the Notes which the Editor has thought worthy of insertion, not only for the
purpose of elucidating the text, but at times as illustrations of the History of Shake-
spearian criticism. In the <SC>Appendix</SC> will be found criticisms and discussions which,
on the score of length, could not be conveniently included in the <I>Commentary.</I>

<SHL>
<P>These last sixteen editions I have not collated beyond referring to them in dis-
puted passages, and recording, here and there in the <I>Commentary</I>, the views of
their editors.
<P>Within the last twenty-five years,&mdash;indeed, since the appearance, in 1864, of
the <I>Globe Edition</I>,&mdash;the text of <SC>Shakespeare</SC> is become so settled that to collate,
word for word, the text of editions which have appeared within this term, would
be a fruitless task. When, however, within recent years an Editor revises his text
in a Second or a Third Edition, the case is different; it then becomes interesting to
mark the effect of maturer judgement.
<P>The present <SC>Text</SC> is that of the <SC>First Folio</SC> of 1623. Every word, I might
say almost every letter, has been collated with the original.
<P>In the <SC>Textual Notes</SC> the symbol Ff indicates the agreement of the <I>Second,
Third</I>, and <I>Fourth Folios.</I>
<P>I have not called attention to every little misprint in the Folio. The <I>Textual
Notes</I> will show, if need be, that they are misprints by the agreement of all the
Editors in their corrections.
<FHL>
<NOTE>* Additions to Revised Edition.</NOTE>
<PB N=547>
<HE><I>LIST OF BOOKS</I> 547</HE>
<P>Nor is notice taken of the first Editor who adopted the modern spelling, or who
substituted commas for parentheses, or changed? to!.
<P>The sign + indicates the agreement of <SC>Rowe, Pope, Theobald, Hanmer,
Warburton</SC>, and <SC>Johnson</SC>; hereafter this symbol will include the <I>Variorum of
1773.</I>
<P>When in the <I>Textual Notes</I> <SC>Warburton</SC> precedes <SC>Hanmer</SC>, it indicates that
<SC>Hanmer</SC> has followed a suggestion of <SC>Warburton</SC>.
<P><SC>Furness</SC> indicates that a reading other than that in the <I>First Cambridge</I> has
been followed in the former edition.
<P>The words <I>et cet.</I> after any reading indicate that it is the reading of <I>all other</I>
editions.
<P>The words <I>et seq.</I> indicate the agreement of all subsequent editions.
<P>The abbreviation (<I>subs.</I>) indicates that the reading is <I>substantially</I> given, and
that immaterial variations in spelling, punctuation, or stage-directions are disre-
garded.
<P>When <I>Var.</I> precedes <I>Steev.</I> or <I>Mal.</I> it includes the <I>Variorums</I> of 1773, 1778, and
1785; when it follows <I>Steev.</I> or <I>Mal.</I> it includes the <I>Variorums</I> of 1803, 1813, and
1821.
<P>An Emendation or Correction given in the <I>Commentary</I> is not repeated in the
<I>Textual Notes</I> unless it has been adopted by an Editor in his Text; nor is <I>conj.</I>
added in the <I>Textual Notes</I> to the name of the proposer of the conjecture unless the
conjecture happens to be that of an Editor, in which case its omission would lead to
the inference that such was the reading of his text.
<P><SC>Coll</SC>. MS refers to <SC>Collier's</SC> copy of the Second Folio bearing in its margin
manuscript annotations.
<P>In citing plays or quoting from them, the Acts, Scenes, and Lines of the <I>Globe
Edition</I> are followed, unless otherwise noted. Of course, all references to <I>Macbeth</I>
refer to the present text.
